docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: TandemEngine is an inference engine, and we measure its speed on raw /v1/completions (measurement.md, the rows in CHANGELOG.md). These pages are the whole documentation; each covers one part of the engine and names the files that implement it. Start with overview.md, then install.md.

docs.title: Adding a model
docs.text: TandemLLM serves models of the Qwen3.8 family: the 27B, a hybrid of Gated DeltaNet and attention layers, and Flash-Next, a mixture of experts on the same hybrid, from turboderp's EXL3 packs. LiquidAI's LFM2.5-24B-A2B (short convolutions, attention and a mixture of 64 experts, lfm2.5-24b-a2b.md), ships in 0.9.0 and is the first from another family. Flash-Next was the first model added through the adapter path below, and the path is written from what it took. This page lists the seams where a new model plugs in, what each one expects, and the tests a new model must pass before its numbers mean anything. Some of the engine is still specific to this family, and the last section says which parts.

docs.title: The adapter path in ten steps
docs.text:
A new architecture is a package under engine/models/<name>/ with its own registry entry, and data files. Nothing under server/, engine/cache.py, engine/disk_cache.py, engine/spill.py, engine/methods/ or engine/settings.py changes for it, and tests/test_adapter_guards.py holds every package to that: work on one model never moves another model's fingerprint. architecture.md shows the layers; Flash-Next's package (engine/models/flashnext/) is the worked example.

  1. Config. A reader that turns the checkpoint's config.json into the model's config object and stops on a field it does not know, naming it. Flash-Next's (config.py) keeps three lists: fields it reads, fields that only matter for training (IGNORED), and fields whose other values would change the arithmetic (FIXED).
  2. Weights. A reader for the checkpoint's files and a Linear object for every weight the model multiplies by (Weight formats). A new format needs a new class and a row-invariant kernel (kernels.md). Flash-Next's reader (pack.py) audits the pack before anything loads: a missing tensor, a truncated shard or a wrong sha256 stops it with the name.
  3. A reference forward in torch, checked against the published implementation layer by layer. Flash-Next's (ref.py) equals transformers' qwen4_exp in fp32 within 5e-6 on a tiny random model, and its engine equals the official decoder layer on the served pack within BF16 noise.
  4. The engine with the hot verbs: forward, forward_tree, forward_block, commit_tree, rollback_to, picks, hidden_post_norm, kv.length, state (the live state the cold verbs copy) and reset. Every verified row must equal the decode step's row bit for bit, or speculation is not lossless on it.
  5. The cold verbs: caps, cost(), cache_state() with its sections and views, resume_at(n), settle(), discard_pending(), trim_pending(n), manifest(), memory_parts(), resident_files() and precapture(); with joint verify also tree_batchable(parents) (which blocks share a joint pass), forward_tree_multi(items) (the joint pass itself: every lane's block over the weights once, each row its lone verify's bits) and, optionally, joint_policy() (the pass's row cap, cut and rows by lane count for the weights the family serves: what its kernels keep row-invariant; without it 32 rows and the share cut) and joint_graphs_report() (the joint pass's captured graphs for /health, when the family captures them), and joint_attn(layer, payloads) (the graphed lanes' attention of a layer: the shared default runs a launch a lane; a family may run every lane in one). The round runner also asks a family's engine for five optional hooks, each absent by default: prefetch_rows(items) (a static method: the round's drafted trees as (engine, tokens, parents), handed over before the cuts so host reads such as Flash-Next's PLE rows can start), host_blocks (a class attribute: True when the joint pass reads a block on the host, so QSE_RUNNER_HOST_BLOCKS hands it host tensors), joint_capture_ok (an attribute the runner sets before each joint pass: True when a joint graph may be captured in it, on the runner's thread with no request waiting; the family reads it and sets it back to False) joint_stats() (the joint pass's measured shape, for /health parallel.joint_stats and the runner's line; None when nothing is counted) and host_timers(timed) (with QSE_RUNNER_COUNTERS: the family wraps its own host calls with the runner's timer, timed(obj, attr, name)). A family whose joint pass leaves the host idle while the GPU runs calls engine.methods.busy.busy() between the pass's issue and its wait: the runner's held work (QSE_RUNNER_BUSY_WORK, QSE_RUNNER_GC) runs there; a family that never calls it keeps the runner's work where it was. The server's prefill burst runs a family's own joint prefill when its engine has prefill_joint_ok(rows, start) and a static prefill_joint(items) (each prompt's logits, streams, KV and state its own prefill's bits; optional prefill_joint_prepare(rows, start) runs a member's own steps on its thread first, so a failure there fails that member alone). They are not part of ServeSpec yet. Flash-Next keeps them in serving.py (FlashNextServing); the 27B's are installed on its class by engine/models/qwen3_5/adapter.py.
  6. A draft head, if the checkpoint ships one. The shared MTP drafter (engine/methods/mtp_drafter.py) asks the head for depth, reset(), prime(), capture_all(), launch(), read() (the top-2 tokens and their probabilities a depth), views() and resume(n); the engine offers it through draft_heads(). Flash-Next's head is mtp.py.
  7. A server builder, serve(a, ctx) -> dict: load the weights, build the engine, the tokenizer and the drafter, and return them with the record /health shows.
  8. The registry entry, in the package's own arch.py (What a family declares): register(Arch(name, architectures, model_types, config, engine, package, serve, manifest, ...)). engine/models/__init__.py finds it; nothing else is edited.
  9. Data files: a StairCut price file for each profile and device (ops/prices/<model>/<profile>.<device>.json; without one the cut learns its prices online), the weight profiles (ops/profiles/<name>.env) and the Setup Guide's entry (models/<id>/model.yaml, below).
  10. Pass the tests under The tests a new model must pass.
flowchart TD
    m["methods, written once<br/>StairCut and its prices, the MTP drafter, the walk, every cache tier, the server, the governor"]
    a["model adapters, one per architecture<br/>qwen3_5: the 27B · qwen4_exp: Flash-Next · hot and cold verbs, ModelState"]
    f["weight formats<br/>the Linear protocol today; plugins with read and bind planned"]
    h["hardware, planned<br/>KernelImpl keyed by op, format and device; device profiles"]
    t["topology, planned<br/>Mesh at world 1: no collective on the code path"]
    m --> a --> f --> h --> t
    classDef planned stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    class h,t planned

The engine's layers. A layer reads only the layers under it, and per-model numbers are data the adapter returns or files under models/ and ops/. Filled: built; outlined: planned.

docs.title: The seams
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    CFG[config.json] --> TC[TextConfig, engine/config.py]
    CK[checkpoint files] --> LAY[Layout, engine/loader.py]
    LAY --> W[Weights]
    W --> LIN[Linear interface, engine/linear.py]
    TC --> MODEL[target model, engine/model.py]
    LIN --> MODEL
    MODEL --> DR[drafters declare what they read]
    ENV[environment] --> SET[EngineSettings, engine/settings.py]
    SET --> MODEL

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
engine/config.py::load_config reads config.json into a TextConfig with every size the engine needs, from the layer count to the rotary settings. It also answers which layers are recurrent (is_linear, linear_layers, attention_layers). It accepts a vision-language config (the text model under text_config) and a text-only config (the keys at the top level).

A new family either fits TextConfig or extends it. The rest of the engine asks TextConfig, never the raw JSON.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
engine/loader.py::Layout says how a checkpoint names its tensors, in one place. The engine addresses every tensor by a canonical name (embed_tokens.weight, lm_head.weight, norm.weight, layers.N.<module>.<proj>), which is the language model's own naming with the checkpoint's wrapper prefix taken off.

attribute what it says prefixes wrapper prefixes to strip, first match wins (model.language_model., then model.) skip_inside, skip_start tensors the language model never reads, such as a vision tower (engine/vision.py reads that one itself) mtp_file where the checkpoint keeps its prediction head embed, head, final_norm canonical names of the three model-level tensors projections the projection names a checkpoint may store as FP8 pairs or as plain matrices

A checkpoint without lm_head.weight reads the embedding as its head only when the config says the two are tied. tests/test_layout.py builds tiny checkpoints of both kinds on the CPU and checks that they read to the same canonical names. It also pins the served checkpoint's key set: 1,250 language-model keys read, 333 vision keys skipped.

docs.title: Weight formats: the Linear interface
docs.text:
Every weight the engine multiplies by implements one small interface (engine/linear.py):

class Linear(Protocol):
    shape: (N, K)
    nbytes: int                 # bytes read per use
    def matmul(x[..., K]) -> [..., N]
class format file FP8Block e4m3 codes with one BF16 scale per 128 by 128 block, as the checkpoint stores them tools/fp8_linear.py NVFP4Block e2m1 codes, an e4m3 scale per 16 weights, one fp32 scale tools/nvfp4_linear.py FP8Head e4m3 with one fp32 scale per row, fp32 logits tools/head_gemv.py BF16Block a plain BF16 matrix engine/linear.py

The model calls w.matmul(x) and never asks which format it holds. A new format is a new class with those three members, plus a kernel that keeps the row-invariance rule (kernels.md). A BF16 checkpoint loads through the same path: its projections become BF16Blocks. tests/test_bf16_load.py checks that a tiny BF16 checkpoint on disk gives the same forward, bit for bit, as plain tensors.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: engine/settings.py is the registry of every QWEN38_* switch the engine reads: its default and the module that reads it. SETTINGS.get(name) is the only way engine code reads one, and tests/test_settings.py fails on any other read. EngineSettings(env, prefix) gives the same reads over another mapping or another prefix, which is how a profile file can be described or a second configuration built in a test.

docs.title: What a drafter reads
docs.text:
A drafter reads parts of the target: hidden states at some layers, the embedding, the head. Each drafter declares these through Drafter.requires():

key meaning hidden_size the width of the hidden states its taps read tap_layers the target layers it reads tensors target tensors it reads by name, such as the head vocab_size the id space of its proposals

At load, engine.drafters.check_target compares these with the target and refuses a mismatch by name. A DFlash2 drafter trained for another model fails there instead of drafting garbage. The lookup drafter's stores record the tokenizer's sha256 (engine/tokfp.py). Under another tokenizer a read skips the store with one log line, and a write refuses it.

A new model needs its own block drafter. DFlash2 drafters are trained against one target's hidden states, and a drafter from another model accepts nothing. The lookup drafter works for any model once its corpus is rebuilt with the new tokenizer (tools/build_corpus.py).

docs.title: The tokenizer and the chat template
docs.text: The server renders prompts with the model's own chat template and reads the model's own tool-call and reasoning formats. For Qwen3.8 that means the <think> block, which the template opens in the prompt, and tool calls in the model's XML form (server/api/toolcall.py). A model with another format needs its own parser behind the same OpenAI output. tests/fixtures/qwen38_chat_template.jinja is the fixture the server tests render with.

docs.title: What a family declares
docs.text:
A family's arch.py registers its entry; engine/models/__init__.py imports every package's arch.py and keeps the entries in their rank order. Besides the import paths, an entry carries what the shared code needs to know, as data:

field what it says read by spec ServeSpec(tool_format, reasoning): the form the model writes tool calls in (a name in server/api/toolformats/) and ReasoningSpec(opens_itself), a model that writes its own <think> the request loop, the conductor's checks, the forced-call constraint shares, uses the package's files other families build on, and the other packages' files this family builds on the guards: a manifest or an import across packages must be declared, and a change to a shared file moves exactly its dependents' fingerprints hooks EngineHooks(pdl, side_stream): launch options the family turns on in the shared kernels, which take them as plain arguments the family's engine default the family a server without a checkpoint directory serves (one family is) the loader

A family's own knobs go in its package's knobs.py (a KNOBS table of the same shape as engine/settings.py's), which joins the shared table at import and belongs in the family's manifest. A family's own C++ or CUDA kernel is a source file in its package: a module engine/models/<family>/<name>.py that compiles it keeps the sources in engine/models/<family>/csrc/<name>/ and builds through engine/native_build.py (kernels.md); the folder counts in the fingerprint with the module. A tool-call form the server does not know yet is a module in server/api/toolformats/ behind the ToolFormat interface (rewrite to the JSON tier, a stream reader, the diagnosis of a broken block, the reminder's example line, the forced-call constraint); tests/test_toolformats.py runs the same contract on every form. TandemApp's conductor reads calls with its own copy (tandemapp/toolformats/), so a new form lands there too, with its cases in contracts/engine-api-v1/toolcalls/, which both copies must pass. A model that is the base of community packs says so in its model.yaml (community_base), and its package writes their weight profiles and checks their files (community.py, named by community_base.hook).

docs.title: The model layer: architecture registry and per-model state
docs.text:
engine/models/__init__.py says which architecture a checkpoint is. Each entry names the checkpoint's architectures strings and model_types, a config reader and an engine class by import path, so registering a model imports nothing. architecture(raw_config) returns the entry, or fails with a message that names the checkpoint's architecture and every registered one.

name selected by config engine server builder qwen3_5 Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration, qwen3_5_text engine.config.load_config engine.models.qwen3_5.adapter.Qwen38Engine (engine/model.py's class with the adapter's cold verbs) engine.models.qwen3_5.serving.serve (the default family) qwen4_exp Qwen4ExpForConditionalGeneration, qwen4_exp_text engine.models.flashnext.config.load_flashnext_config engine.models.flashnext.engine.FlashNextEngine engine.models.flashnext.serving.serve lfm2_moe Lfm2MoeForCausalLM, lfm2_moe engine.models.lfm2_moe.config.load_lfm2_moe_config engine.models.lfm2_moe.engine.Lfm2MoeEngine engine.models.lfm2_moe.serving.serve nemotron_h NemotronHForCausalLM, NemotronHPuzzleForCausalLM, the Omni architectures, nemotron_h, nemotron_h_puzzle engine.models.nemotron_h.config.load_nemotron_h_config engine.models.nemotron_h.engine.NemotronHEngine engine.models.nemotron_h.serving.serve

The server has one loader (server/app.py _load, SRV-341). An entry's serve names the function that builds the model for it, serve(a, ctx) -> dict: the engine in the server loop's interface, the tokenizer, the drafter, the snapshot path, the device, the tree mode and accept rule, and its own record for /health (weights_info); ctx.keys(path, weights) sets the tokenizer's and the weights' fingerprints, ctx.mark(stage) writes the load ledger, ctx.log(line) the log. The engine says what the server may ask of it beyond the loop's verbs in caps (engine/models/adapter.py Capabilities: the caches and the KV pool, side slots, the cache grid, the shadow reader, joint verify); the loader turns off, with a log line, what a model cannot hold yet. Its cold verbs are cost(), manifest(), precapture(drafter), settle(), discard_pending(), trim_pending(n); the walk of a verified block is engine/methods/walk.py for every model. A model registered this way starts and answers without an edit under server/ (tests/test_load_shared.py registers a third one on CPU).

engine/models/state.py is the cache state interface (ModelState), and every cache tier reads a sequence through it (eng.cache_state(), ENG-157). Its sections are the recurrent state by name, copied whole; its views are the position-indexed buffers with their token axis, sliced by length. It has nbytes, clone, restore and a signature that refuses a restore across shapes. The 27B's state is Qwen38State: sections gdn.S and gdn.conv (the same tensors, so a restore lands in the buffers its graphs captured), views K and V. Flash-Next's is FlashNextCacheState (serving.py): 36 GDN states and conv tails, the n-gram convolution and its token context, and mtp.h_last as sections (110.3 MiB); K, V and the indexer keys of its 12 attention layers as views, with the MTP layer's own rows from its drafter (29,952 bytes a token). A model without recurrent state has no sections. tests/test_cache_any_model.py runs a made-up state through every tier with no edit in the cache code.

A model's own code lives in its package under engine/models/. The disk tier's fingerprint v2 (engine/disk_cache.py) leaves engine/models/ and engine/methods/ out, together with knobs owned under engine/models/ and tools/fn_, so adding a model sweeps none of the 27B's saved sessions (tests/test_fn_fingerprint.py). Fingerprint v3 (engine/methods/manifest.py) hashes what the adapter's manifest() lists: the model's files that compute stored rows, the knob registry, its own tile tables; the tools/ kernels they import, every listed module's C++ and CUDA source files (csrc/) and the tables their knobs name follow. A new model writes its manifest() (Flash-Next: engine/models/flashnext/serving.py), and its fingerprint then moves with its kernels and tables and with nothing else (tests/test_fp_v3.py).

docs.title: The tests a new model must pass
docs.text:
In this order, each on the new model:

  1. tools/refcheck.py: argmax agreement with the published reference implementation on teacher-forced positions. The reference runs in its own process, because only one model fits on the board at a time. On Qwen3.8 the engine agrees on 99.25 % of 400 positions and on all 242 confident ones.
  2. tools/quality_gate.py for every quantised weight set (quantisation.md).
  3. tools/verify_spec.py, the agreement gate with its near-tie rule, with every drafter (exactness.md).
  4. The CPU suite, including tests/test_refactor_gate.py. That test records the exact bytes of a tiny model's run (every logit and every byte of state after a prefill, a decode, a block verify, a rollback, a tree verify and a commit) and fails if any byte moves. A change that is supposed to change arithmetic re-records the fixture and says why.
  5. ops/gate.sh and the client smoke set before the numbers are published (measurement.md).

Flash-Next took the same gates in its own form, and a new model should take them too:

  • tests/test_load_shared.py: the model starts through the one loader, and no model name, hasattr(eng or isinstance(eng appears under server/.
  • tests/test_cache_any_model.py and the model's own cache test: a restore from every tier equals a cold prefill.
  • tests/test_fp_v3.py: the model's fingerprint v3 moves with its kernels and tables and with nothing else, and the 27B's does not move.
  • The load-time self-check: a recorded decode replayed as chains and trees of every verify width, every row bit for bit (3,936 rows on Flash-Next 3.05). A difference turns speculation off for the process and names the layer and the row.
  • tools/fn_spec_check.py and tools/fn_server_check.py --compare: speculative greedy equals plain greedy, in the engine and through the server, and seeded sampled answers equal their plain twins (--sampled).

docs.title: What is still specific to Qwen3.8
docs.text:
• engine/model.py implements this family's forward: the Gated DeltaNet layer with its gated norm, attention with a gated output and partial rotary, and the dense MLP. A new family needs its own layer code behind the same verify, commit and cache interfaces. A model with a mixture of experts also needs expert routing inside the verify.
  • The second family, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (engine/models/flashnext/, turboderp's EXL3 packs), is served through the same server and request loop with its MTP drafter, the same caches, the KV pool and side slots (server.md, caches.md); it reads images through its own tower, which its builder hands to the server's image path (ctx.vision, VIS-97).
  • The recurrent-layer kernels assume Gated DeltaNet's state shape (heads of 128 by 128).
  • Tile tables and router prices are measured for each model's shapes on the GB10. A new model or a new board needs its own sweep (tools/fp8_probe.py --sweep, tools/nvfp4_skinny.py, Flash-Next's tools/fn_tiles.py) and its own price file. A kernel registry keyed by op, weight format and device (ENG-251) and device profiles (ENG-255) are planned, not built.
  • Some modules read their switches into globals at import. Two engines with different settings cannot share one process yet.
  • Runtime names still carry the old project name, from the QWEN38_ and QSE_ variable prefixes to the Qwen38Engine class. A later release renames them.

docs.title: Register the model for the setup guide
docs.text:
The dashboard's setup guide (#/setup, setup.md) lists one tile per models/<id>/model.yaml. The folder is named after the model's id, and the file follows schema 1: the weight profiles (one per ops/profiles/<name>.env), the measured table, the tools that run beside the model with their memory and serve.env keys, the parallelism limits, the methods and the device presets. models/README.md lists the fields; models/qwen3.8-27b/model.yaml is the worked example, with the source of every number next to it.

models/<id>/model.yaml                  the registry entry
models/<id>/measurements/<build>-*.json the raw data the measured table came from (optional)
models/schema/model.schema.json         the schema, for an editor (python -m server.setup.registry --schema)

Check a new file with python -m server.setup.registry --check. It refuses a file whose numbers do not add up (two recommended profiles, a tool that needs one that is off, a docs link that is not there), and tests/test_setup_registry.py fails when the file names a serve.env key nothing reads or when a profile in ops/profiles/ has no entry. Memory is in GiB and comes from the engine's own [memory] load stages line and the dashboard's memory split, never from a guess.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
A decode step of Qwen3.8-27B reads about 27 GB of weights in the vendor's FP8 format. The DGX Spark reads memory at 273 GB/s on paper and about 240 GB/s in practice. Those two numbers put a floor of about 100 ms under every step, or 10 tok/s, before any code runs. TandemLLM exists to get under that floor while writing the model's own greedy text, with one documented exception at near ties (exactness.md).

It does two things. It cuts the bytes a step reads, from 27 GB to 15 GB. And it makes one step produce about 4.6 tokens: cheap drafters guess, and one pass of the big model checks all the guesses.

The engine serves a second model the same way, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a mixture of experts of the same family that reads about 4.23 GB a plain token from turboderp's 3.05 EXL3 pack. The box runs one of the two at a time. Most of this page describes the 27B. The second model says what differs, and Methods written once shows how one server, one set of caches and one speculation method serve both.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
engine/config.py reads config.json and nothing else. Its text model has 64 decoder layers, hidden size 5120, a dense SiLU MLP of width 17,408 in every layer, and a vocabulary of 248,320 tokens. The model has no mixture of experts. A 0.92 GB vision tower sits in the same checkpoint. The language-model loader skips it by name and engine/vision.py loads it on its own for image input (server.md).

Every fourth layer (3, 7, 11 and so on up to 63) is full attention, 16 layers in all. Gated DeltaNet fills the other 48. It is a recurrent layer that keeps a fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache.

layer kind count state per sequence Gated DeltaNet 48 an fp32 state of 48 heads, each 128 by 128 (3.15 MB) and a 4-wide convolution tail (80 KB), per layer full attention 16 BF16 keys and values, 4 KV heads of 256, so 4 KB a token per layer

That split shapes most of the code. Published work on speculation and caching assumes attention, where undoing a token means moving a pointer back by one row. A recurrent state has absorbed every token and has no inverse, and the engine needs exact ways to undo, branch and restore it. speculative-decoding.md shows the undo and the branch, and caches.md shows the restore.

[GDN] [GDN] [GDN] [attention]   x 16   = 64 layers: 48 Gated DeltaNet, 16 full attention

The layer pattern of Qwen3.8-27B: three Gated DeltaNet layers, then one full-attention layer, sixteen times.

docs.title: The byte budget
docs.text:
A decode step reads every weight once. This table sums the bytes from the checkpoint's safetensors headers.

group bytes a step 48 Gated DeltaNet layers 18.43 GB 16 attention layers 5.96 GB the output head, BF16, 248,320 rows by 5,120 2.54 GB total, FP8 as shipped 26.93 GB

The three MLP projections are 63.6 % of that. Quantising them first, then the rest, moved the budget down in steps, and each step had to pass the quality gate (quantisation.md):

weight set bytes a step floor at 273 GB/s FP8 as shipped 26.93 GB 98.6 ms NVFP4 MLPs 19.44 GB 71.2 ms plus the FP8 (e4m3) head 18.17 GB 66.5 ms plus NVFP4 GDN and attention projections 15.01 GB 55.0 ms

State is small beside the weights. The 48 recurrent states are 151 MB together. KV costs 64 KB a token across the 16 attention layers, so 2.1 GB at 32k tokens and about 17 GB at the full 262,144-token context.

weight set GB read per decode step floor at 273 GB/s FP8 as shipped 26.93 98.6 ms NVFP4 MLPs 19.44 71.2 ms + FP8 head 18.17 66.5 ms + NVFP4 GDN, attention (served) 15.01 55.0 ms

Bytes a step for each weight set, and the floor each sets under one step at 273 GB/s (arithmetic). The served set is the last bar. The board reads about 240 GB/s in practice, so the real floors are about 14 % higher.

docs.title: The decode loop
docs.text:
Speed is one fraction:

tok/s = tokens committed a round / (draft ms + verify ms + commit ms)

A round starts from the last committed token. Next, the drafters propose a tree of guesses after it. One forward pass then runs over the whole tree through all 64 layers. The engine reads the model's own choice at every node and keeps the longest path where the model agrees with the guesses. It always keeps one more token, the model's own choice after the last accepted guess, so a round yields at least one token. Then it commits the state of that path and starts again.

On the served profile (the published NVFP4 set, StairCut on) a round on the benchmark row takes 93.4 ms and commits 4.58 tokens, and the row's rate is 49.89 tok/s. The rate is the mean of the 50 requests' own rates (measurement.md), not the quotient of the two means (4.58 tokens in 93.4 ms is 49.0 tok/s). Without speculation, the same box writes 13.69 tok/s at 72.8 ms a token (measured on 28 September on an earlier build, whose path with speculation off is unchanged).

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    participant D as Drafters and router
    participant M as Target model
    C->>S: POST /v1/chat/completions
    S->>M: prefill the prompt (or restore it from a cache)
    loop every round, about 93 ms
        S->>D: last committed token and context
        D->>S: a draft tree (up to 32 nodes)
        S->>M: verify the whole tree in one pass
        M->>S: the model's own token at every node
        S->>M: commit the accepted path (KV rows and recurrent state)
        S->>C: stream the committed tokens
    end

docs.title: The second model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
docs.text:
Flash-Next keeps the 27B's hybrid, Gated DeltaNet layers with an attention layer every fourth, and changes most of what sits around it. engine/models/flashnext/config.py reads its config and refuses any field it does not know by name.

part Flash-Next the 27B layers 48: 36 Gated DeltaNet, 12 attention 64: 48 Gated DeltaNet, 16 attention MLP 512 experts a layer, 10 routed and 1 shared run a token dense, width 17,408 residual stream 4 streams of 2,560 joined by hyper-connection mixers one stream of 5,120 attention sparse past 2,051 tokens: an indexer scores blocks and each row reads the 512 best full extra input a hashed n-gram embedding (16 table rows a token) in front of layer 1 none draft layer one multi-token-prediction (MTP) layer in the checkpoint none; DFlash2 drafters beside it state a sequence 110.3 MiB of sections plus 29,952 bytes a token about 147 MiB plus 64 KB a token weights served turboderp's EXL3 packs, 2.05 to 6.05 bits a weight NVFP4 with an e4m3 head, or EXL3

A plain decode token on the 3.05 pack reads about 4.23 GB (arithmetic from the pack's headers, with the mixers as int8). The engine decodes 45.8 tok/s at 1k of context without speculation, about 21.8 ms a token (measured 2026-10-11, one run a class). Its verify rows equal its decode rows bit for bit, so greedy speculation on Flash-Next writes the plain greedy text token for token, with no near-tie exception (exactness.md). The one known difference is where a think budget closes: at the first block boundary past the cap (ENG-235). Through the server on 2026-10-12, one greedy request of up to 512 tokens a class with the MTP drafter and the lookup: prose 51, chat 64, code 83, an edit 132 and a copy 133 tok/s, against 41.5 to 45.7 plain. quantisation.md covers the packs and speculative-decoding.md the drafter.

docs.title: Methods written once, models plugged in
docs.text:
A second model could have meant a second server, a second set of caches and a second StairCut. The engine avoids that with five layers that depend only downward. A method (speculation, a cache tier, the memory governor, the server) reads a model through its adapter and through data files. It never branches on a model's name, never asks hasattr of an engine and never touches a private field. tests/test_load_shared.py registers a third, made-up architecture on the CPU and gets an answer on /v1/chat/completions with no edit under server/.

flowchart TB
    subgraph M[methods, written once]
        SPEC[StairCut, PriceModel, the MTP drafter, the walk]
        CACHE[every cache tier, the KV pool]
        SRV[server, memory governor, extension host, setup guide]
    end
    subgraph A[model adapters, one per architecture]
        Q35[qwen3_5: the 27B]
        FN[qwen4_exp: Flash-Next]
    end
    subgraph F[weight formats]
        FMT[EXL3, NVFP4, FP8, int8 rows, BF16]
    end
    subgraph H[hardware]
        KREG[kernel registry by op, format and device]
        DEV[device profile]
    end
    subgraph T[topology]
        MESH[Mesh, world 1]
    end
    M --> A --> F --> H --> T
    A --> H

Half of it is built. Since 2026-10-12 the adapters, the state, the shared methods and the server's one loader serve every model. Four parts are still design, each with its ticket: format plugins, a kernel registry, device profiles and the mesh.

layer what where today methods StairCut with its price model and calibration, the MTP tree drafter, the walk of a verified block, fingerprint v3 engine/methods/ built (ENG-245, ENG-243); the 27B still cuts with its own StairCut in engine/lenrouter.py until ENG-257 methods every cache tier over the model's state engine/cache.py, disk_cache.py, spill.py, kvpool.py built (ENG-157, ENG-241) methods one loader driven by the registry server/app.py _load built (SRV-341) model adapters the registry, Capabilities, CostModel, ModelState engine/models/ built for qwen3_5 and qwen4_exp weight formats the Linear protocol engine/linear.py, tools/*_linear.py, engine/models/flashnext/pack.py built; a format plugin with read and bind and one checkpoint reader are planned (ENG-253) hardware KernelImpl keyed by (op, fmt, device), resolved once at load none yet: each weight object holds its kernel, and tile tables sit under ops/ per model planned (ENG-251) hardware device profiles engine/methods/device.py names the device for price files; the Setup Guide's device preset sits in each model.yaml devices/<id>.yaml and a probe at start planned (ENG-255) topology Mesh, Collectives, ShardSpec at world 1 none: one process, one GPU planned (ENG-259), then two boxes (ENG-233)

docs.title: Model adapters
docs.text:
engine/models/__init__.py keeps a registry of architectures, each registered by its own package's arch.py. An entry names the architectures strings and model_types that select it, its config reader, its engine class, its server builder and its manifest, all by import path, and what the shared code needs to know about the model as data (its tool-call form and reasoning, the files it shares with other families, the kernel options it turns on; adding-a-model.md). architecture(config) returns the entry, or fails naming every registered one.

name model engine server builder qwen3_5 Qwen3.8-27B engine.models.qwen3_5.adapter.Qwen38Engine the server's own, _build_qwen3_5 qwen4_exp Qwen3.8-Flash-Next engine.models.flashnext.engine.FlashNextEngine engine.models.flashnext.serving.serve

An adapter is the engine object with a fixed set of verbs. The hot verbs run every round, so they are the engine's own bound methods and never a wrapper: a decode and a verify call the same kernels through the same Python frames as before the layering, and CUDA graphs capture the same launches.

hot verb what it does forward(ids, start) a prompt chunk, a forced phrase or one decode token at the state's length forward_tree(block, parents, start) a draft block in depth-first order; logits of every row forward_block(block, start) a chain whose commit waits for rollback_to or the next call commit_tree(path), rollback_to(keep) keep a verified path; cut a chain back picks, hidden_post_norm the verify's own greedy tokens; the rows a drafter syncs from kv.length, reset() where the sequence stands; start a new one in place (the KV rows stay)

The cold verbs run between requests or around a cache copy. The 27B's are installed on its class by engine/models/qwen3_5/adapter.py, so engine/model.py keeps its bytes and its disk-tier fingerprint.

cold verb what it gives caps Capabilities: caches on or off, side slots, the cache grid (anchor_grid: 1,024 for the 27B, 4,096 for Flash-Next), the shadow reader, joint verify cost() CostModel: section bytes, view bytes a token, and the prefill workspace (floor, bytes a token, cap) cache_state() the sequence's state as ModelState (below) resume_at(n), settle(), discard_pending(), trim_pending(n) continue at n after a restore; land a pending commit; forget an uncommitted verify; cut a pending chain manifest() the files and tables its stored rows depend on (fingerprint v3, caches.md) memory_parts(), resident_files() the dashboard's memory split; files it keeps in the page cache on purpose precapture(drafter) the verify graphs it captures at load

A model may offer more, and the server checks for each before it uses it: draft_heads() (Flash-Next's MTP layer), side_slot() (a slot over the same weights), forward_tree_multi() (several slots' blocks in one pass), idle_captures() (graphs to capture while the server is idle). Without them the server takes the 27B's path or leaves the feature off.

docs.title: ModelState: sections and views
docs.text:
The caches copy a sequence through eng.cache_state() (engine/models/state.py), and they know no model. A state has two parts:

part what the 27B Flash-Next sections fixed-size tensors by name, copied whole gdn.S, gdn.conv 36 GDN states and conv tails, the n-gram convolution and its token context, mtp.h_last: 115,662,864 bytes views position-indexed buffers with their token axis, sliced by length K and V (and their e4m3 scales when on) K, V and the indexer keys of 12 layers, the MTP layer's own: 29,952 bytes a token

Every tier keeps sections in the state's order and views by length. A signature over names, shapes and dtypes refuses a restore across models. Derived buffers are not stored: Flash-Next's pooled indexer keys are rebuilt from the keys in resume_at. tests/test_cache_any_model.py runs a made-up state, whose sections and views have dtypes and shapes neither model uses, through four tiers with no edit in the cache code.

docs.title: Weight formats
docs.text:
Every weight the engine multiplies by implements Linear (engine/linear.py): a shape, the bytes a use reads, and matmul. The model calls w.matmul(x) and never asks the format. Today's classes: FP8Block, NVFP4Block, FP8Head, BF16Block, EXL3Block (tools/exl3_linear.py), and Flash-Next's Int8Rows for its mixers. Flash-Next's routed experts are not Linear objects: a layer's experts and its shared expert sit in one MoEBank (tools/fn_kernels.py), which the MoE kernels read directly. Each object holds its kernel, so a call costs nothing extra.

The planned format plugin adds two verbs to that: read (one reader for every checkpoint: headers, byte ranges, row and column slices, expert ranges) and bind (set the object's kernel once from the registry below). Until then the 27B reads through engine/loader.py and Flash-Next through engine/models/flashnext/pack.py.

docs.title: Kernels and devices, then the mesh
docs.text:
The planned registry will describe each kernel as a KernelImpl: the op (gemv, moe_experts, attention_rows and so on), the weight format, the row regime, the device features it needs, whether it is row-invariant, and its entry point with its tile table and torch reference. A format will resolve its op once at load, keyed by (op, fmt, device). A device without a kernel will get the reference, and an exact model there will serve plain decode until a row-invariant twin exists, because the load-time self-check gates speculation (kernels.md).

A device profile will hold what the memory governor and the Setup Guide read about a board (memory, reserve, floor, whether page cache counts as available) and what the kernel build reads (bandwidth, compute capability, features). Today the DGX Spark's numbers sit in each model.yaml and in the profiles, and engine/methods/device.py turns the GPU's name into the id price files are keyed by (dgx-spark for the GB10).

The mesh marks where two boxes will split a model. At world 1, the only size built, it is absent from the code path: no collective runs and the graphs hold the same kernels. Its seams are ENG-259's and come before any work across boxes: weights read by slice, a shard tag on each state view, and the mesh in cache keys and price file names.

docs.title: Stages: one model in two processes
docs.text:
A model can be cut between two layers and run as two processes (ENG-307). The front stage holds the embedding and layers [0, k). The tail stage holds layers [k, layers), the head and the sampler, and it is the engine a client talks to. Each round the tail sends a step header: the block's tokens and parents, the length it starts at, and the commit path of the block before it. The front answers with the carry, the block's rows as they leave layer k - 1. Logits never cross. Each side keeps the KV rows and the recurrent sections of its own layers, under the names they have in one process.

part where the link: typed frames over one TCP connection, a cap on a frame's size, a deadline on every receive, a 1 s heartbeat, an HMAC challenge handshake that compares both engines' identity blocks engine/methods/link.py the protocol: step header, carry, commit path, epochs, the desync answer, and the StageAdapter interface a family implements engine/methods/stages.py a family's stage code, and its tail stage in the server's engine interface engine/models/<family>/stages.py, tail.py what a stage keeps of its own half of a state under a key: sections, row segments, a folder engine/methods/stage_store.py the server's part: the flags, the key file, the front's process, the tail's link and its refusals server/stage.py

Both families run their torch reference as stages on the CPU, and tests/test_stages.py holds two real processes to the single process at every cut of both tiny test models: logits, sections and KV rows are compared with torch.equal.

lfm2_moe also runs its engine as stages (--stage, server.md). A stage's engine is the engine itself, built over a config whose layer lists hold the stage's own layers, so it loads, keeps and commits only those. Its two passes are the engine's row pass and prompt-chunk pass with the layer loop over [lo, hi); tests/test_lfm2_moe_stage.py compares the loop bodies with the engine's as syntax trees and the rows with the engine's at every cut. The carry is what the engine holds at a layer boundary, the stream and the next layer's norm of it: [rows, 2, hidden] in bf16. Each block runs on the kernels the one process runs it on (a prompt chunk, a decode step, a verify block), eager. The tail checks the cut at load: decode steps against a verify block of the same tokens, bit for bit. A replay after a desync would run decode steps as prompt chunks, on other kernels, so the tail ends that request and drops the sequence instead.

flashnext runs its engine as stages too. The stage's engine is a subclass of the engine built over the same kind of config view. It cuts three passes to [lo, hi): the trunk's layer loop, the row pass and the prompt-chunk pass. tests/test_fn_stage.py compares their statements with the engine's as syntax trees. The staging, verify, commit, the folded commit and the graph classes are the engine's own code, so a stage captures its decode, verify and commit graphs as the one process does. A graph's body ends at the cut: the carry enters it through static buffers and leaves it in the graph's own tensors, and the copy to and from the host runs outside the graph. The carry is the 4 streams and the next site's norm, [rows, 2, 4 x hidden] in bf16, and the streams alone in front of the PLE layer. The tail keeps the draft layer, which reads the streams of the last layer.

Flash-Next's kernels are CUDA, so no kernel of it runs on the CPU. The CPU tests run the real loader, engine, graph classes and serving adapter on a small EXL3 pack in the served layout, with host stand-ins for the launches. There every cut gives the one engine's logits, streams and state bit for bit, eager and with graphs.

On the CPU LFM2 MoE's kernels run under Triton's interpreter.

Both families have run split on one GPU box, the two stages as two processes joined through tools/linkrelay.py. LFM2.5 2.5 bpw cut at layer 20 and Flash-Next 2.05 bpw cut at layers 12 and 24 wrote the single process's tokens on 20 greedy prompts; Flash-Next also on a prompt of 31,991 tokens. A stalled link ended the request with an error after 5 s, and a new link served the same tokens. No two-box speed is measured: on one box both stages share the GPU.

A missed deadline (5 s for a block, 60 s for a prompt chunk) takes the link down, and the request ends with stage_down. A new connection gets a new epoch, and both sides start it from an empty state. A front whose length is not the tail's answers desync; the tail then replays the sequence's tokens. A front whose own pass fails answers stage with the reason and ends the link, so the request ends with that reason and not with a timeout. The link refuses a peer with another key, code, weights, family or layer range, and it has no second transport to fall back to. The handshake proves both ends hold the key; it does not encrypt frames, so the link belongs on a private network segment.

State beyond the running sequence (ENG-423, Flash-Next with --stage-caches on). Each stage names a state by a key: a digest of the blocks that wrote it, in order, with each block's kind, shape and kept path. Both stages compute it from what they ran, and the tail sends it with every header, so a front that holds other rows is found by content. The tail's caches keep the tail's sections and rows with the key as one more section. Reading the sections asks the front to keep its half under that key; putting a state back sends the key to the front. The front keeps a state's sections as a copy and its rows as segments that stay in place until a pass would write over them. A front that does not hold a key is rebuilt from the tail's log of blocks, each sent again as the kind it was, with no carry coming back. A state that neither stage has a log of is refused before any length moves, and the cache that offered it falls back. Slots have a sequence each on both stages, each on a stage engine of its own over the one copy of the weights; a joint round is one request and one carry. tests/test_stage_state.py holds the protocol on a toy family and tests/test_fn_split_state.py holds Flash-Next with the caches as they are: the resident prefix, the end of a generation, a guest, the state store, the disk tier on both sides, a front that starts again, and joint rounds against the one engine's.

docs.title: One request, one engine
docs.text: With --parallel 1 the engine holds one sequence at a time; the shipped ops/serve.env runs 8 lanes since 0.15.0 (SRV-707, QSE_PARALLEL=8). Requests wait for the engine lock in a bounded queue (8 by default), and a request that waits longer than the queue timeout gets a 503. The numbers on this page describe that single-request loop. With --parallel N the engine holds N sequences over one copy of the weights and verifies them in one joint pass (parallel-requests.md), as ops/serve.env and the profiles of every family with side slots do, except Ornith's and Flint's, which keep one sequence.

docs.title: The benchmark report
docs.text:
TandemLLM bare engine: raw /v1/completions, no conductor or chat layer.

tools/release_report measures a running TandemLLM server on your own GPU and writes one HTML page: decode speed by prompt length, prefill, requests at once, chats that share a long system prompt, latency under load, a conversation that comes back, the repository's card tool, and whether speculation changes the text. It works for any model the server serves. The plan is sized from what your server reports, so a 24 GB card gets shorter prompts and fewer requests at once than a DGX Spark.

Every request goes to /v1/completions with X-Tandem: raw. The prompt is the model's chat template with thinking off, rendered on the client and checked id for id against the server's /v1/tokenize, as tools/parallel_card.py does. A response that does not come back with X-Tandem: raw makes its row invalid, and an invalid row shows its reason, never a number.

The page is a view of tools/measure's records: python -m tools.measure plan says which rows a release still needs, run measures only those, and render report writes the page, with every row's source (a gate run, an earlier report, a measuring run). The commands below still measure a whole report in one go.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Start your server as you normally do, wait until it is idle, then run the tool with the engine's Python (it needs the model's tokenizer, which transformers loads from the weights folder):

python -m tools.release_report plan                       # what it will run, and how long
python -m tools.release_report run --out ~/tandem-report --quick
python -m tools.release_report render ~/tandem-report/data.json

--url defaults to the local server, http://127.0.0.1:8000. The page is ~/tandem-report/report.html. Drop --quick for the full report.

Before it sends a measured request, the tool:

  • refuses a server that is busy (requests running, waiting or decoding). --wait-idle 300 waits up to 300 s first.
  • refuses a server with the response cache on, since it could answer a repeated greedy request without the engine. Start the server with RESPONSE_CACHE=off.
  • sends one probe request of about 2,000 tokens and refuses the server if the answer is not served raw.
  • prints the plan, the lengths it skips and why, and a time estimate from the probe's speed.

A loaded conductor is fine: its router hands raw requests to /v1/completions back unchanged, and the tool records it. The tool never changes a server setting and calls no admin route. It writes only under --out. run and render make no network call except to your server.

docs.title: How long it takes
docs.text:
The estimate comes from your box. On one DGX Spark with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, --quick takes 20 to 25 minutes and the full run about 2.5 hours (measured on v0.15.1: the sections took 136 minutes, plus a server start per part), most of it in long prompts: a 240k-token prompt prefills for about 7 minutes. Run the full report in parts with --only; every run adds its sections to the same data.json:

python -m tools.release_report run --out ~/tandem-report --only a h
python -m tools.release_report run --out ~/tandem-report --only c e i
python -m tools.release_report run --out ~/tandem-report --only i d f g    # after a restart

The order matters for section i. After the rest of the suite it measures the longest prompts on a warm engine; as the first requests of a freshly started server it measures them fresh. The page compares the two.

docs.title: What each section measures
docs.text:
Section What it sends What the page shows a, b One request at a time at 1k, 4k, 16k, 32k, 55k, 64k, 96k, 128k, 192k and 240k tokens, up to what fits your server's window. Real prose with a fresh nonce line first, greedy, thinking off, 512 tokens out. 3 runs up to 16k, 2 above Decode tok/s (completion tokens after the first, over the time from the first to the last token), whether the engine drafted and its tokens per pass (from the response's timings), prefill tok/s and the time to the first token c N requests released together, N from 1 to the server's slot limit, each with its own ~2k-token prompt and 512 tokens out; then N prompts of ~32k tokens Aggregate tok/s over the wall time, prefill included, and the slowest first token. /health is read every 0.2 s: a round counts only if N requests were decoding at once, and a level without such a round is invalid d 5 chats and as many as the server has slots, all at once on one new ~28k-token system prompt The first and the last chat's first token, and the tokens each found in the cache e A ~64k prompt arriving while two chats decode; then a ~97k conversation: turn 1, turn 2, three other ~60k prompts, turn 3 The long prompt's first token and the decoders' combined speed before and during its prefill; each turn's first token f One ~56k prompt, up to 1,024 tokens, three tasks: a summary, code, and a copy of text in the prompt Mean decode and the best one-second window g tools/parallel_card.py against the same server, its default arguments and --fixed-prompts The card tool's own rows h Eight fixed prompts, greedy, 512 tokens; needles in ~32k and ~128k of prose The texts, and, after a second run on a server with speculation off, whether they are identical i The 128k and 192k prompts after the rest of the suite, and as the first requests of a fresh server Warm against fresh (or against section a's rows when there is no fresh run) j A multiple-choice set (--hle --hle-data FILE, a local JSON-lines file), off by default The score with its 95 % interval k Nothing Every limit the server runs with, the GPU (name, memory, compute capability, driver, CUDA, torch) and the box during each run: GPU clock and power under load, the highest temperature, the lowest free memory

A section that does not fit your server is listed with the reason: a prompt over the largest slot window, a concurrency test on a server with one slot, a needle longer than the window. Fidelity against plain decoding needs a second run of the same build with speculation off:

python -m tools.release_report run --out ~/tandem-report --variant plain    # server started with --drafter none

A server that runs no drafter skips that comparison, since all its texts are plain ones.

The prompt text is bench/heldout_prose.txt by default, repeated to the length. A long prompt then repeats the same 1,224 words, and the page says so. --prose wikitext2 reads WikiText-2 from your local Hugging Face cache instead (about 2.3 M tokens that do not repeat), and --prose FILE reads any text file. Nothing is downloaded.

docs.title: Launch mode
docs.text:
--ref vX.Y.Z --pack ID starts a fresh server of that tag on your box, from a git archive of the tag, with its own config copy, on a free port from 8100, with the conductor, the response cache and the chat service off (tools/gate starts its servers the same way). It measures through the same path as --url, stops the server, and for section h starts a second one with speculation off:

python -m tools.release_report run --ref v0.15.1 --pack flashnext-3.05 --out ~/tandem-report

docs.title: Several packs of one model
docs.text:
Run each pack into its own folder, then put them on one page: an overview of the packs side by side (their headline figures, one request's decode by prompt length, the card tool's levels), then each pack's own sections.

python -m tools.release_report combine q4/data.json q6/data.json --label "EXL3 4.0" --label "EXL3 6.0" --model Qwen3.8-27B --out 27b/data.json
python -m tools.release_report render 27b/data.json

combine refuses packs of different releases.

docs.title: Share the page
docs.text:
The page is one HTML file of about 50 KB with its charts inline, and it loads nothing from the network. Paths, host names, user names and addresses are taken out of every string that comes from the run, and render refuses to write a page that still names your box. It is safe to attach to an issue or a pull request. The raw files under --out/raw are not scrubbed; keep them local.

For every release the maintainers run the full report on the reference DGX Spark and attach the page to the GitHub release as tandemllm-<version>-report-<model>.html, one page a model (operations.md). publish is that upload step. It measures nothing, and you do not need it to make or share your own page.

docs.title: Benchmarks with tool-eval-bench
docs.text: tool-eval-bench scores tool calling over an OpenAI-compatible API: tool selection, arguments, multi-step chains, restraint, error recovery, injection resistance and structured output. It detects TandemLLM by its model owner or Server header. This page says how to run it against TandemLLM and which settings a run must name, so that another box gets the same score (OPS-189).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv tool install git+https://github.com/SeraphimSerapis/tool-eval-bench.git

The numbers below are from bench 2.8.1.

docs.title: Two paths
docs.text:
A benchmark of the model runs the plain engine. The X-Tandem: raw header serves it: no turn class, no notes, no effort change, the session monitor off (server.md). A request with the header reads the persistent suffix store and never writes into it (SPD-151, caches.md), so repeating the bench does not teach the engine its answers. Run the default path, without the header, only when the conductor itself is under test. The two runs then differ in the conductor alone, and the decision journal shows what it added to each turn.

Without a header the bench, a client kind no profile maps that offers tools, gets the tools profile (SRV-621): the raw path's prompt ids, with the loop guards and the tool-call checks acting (D1, D1b, D2, E1, C3, C4). An answer that differs from the raw run's comes from a journaled monitor act or the secret echo mask (SRV-625: a key from a tool result repeated in the answer, extra.secret_mask). --header X-Tandem-Profile=tools names the profile; --header X-Tandem-Profile=general runs the profile the default path served before.

# the model alone
tool-eval-bench run --short --base-url http://<host>:8000/v1 --model TandemLLM \
  --header X-Tandem=raw --seed 42 --timeout 600
# the conductor in front of it
tool-eval-bench run --short --base-url http://<host>:8000/v1 --model TandemLLM \
  --seed 42 --timeout 600

--short runs the 15 core scenarios. Leave it out for the full suite, 69 scenarios. --hardmode adds category P on top; a score with it is not comparable to one without. The bench's default temperature is 0, so the engine decodes greedily. Keep --parallel at 1, or at most the server's --parallel slots (/health, parallel.max_running): a scenario that queues behind another counts the wait as its latency. The bench's default request timeout, 120 s, cuts long reasoning and scores it as a failure, so give --timeout 600 with thinking on.

/v1/models lists the relay backends beside TandemLLM, so pass --model TandemLLM. /metrics needs a bearer token and has none of the counters the bench's speculative-decoding report reads.

docs.title: Settings that change the score
docs.text:
setting where what it changes weight pack /health weights.name, the setup guide's model profile, ops/use-profile.sh the logits: answers on a near tie can differ between packs thinking the bench's --no-think on by default; off was faster and scored lower in the runs below default effort --reasoning-effort (REASONING_EFFORT in ops/serve.env, medium; the setup guide's thinking effort) the raw path's effort sentence and how long the model thinks; a client's own word wins, --backend-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort": "high"}' profile X-Tandem-Profile, else the profile mapped to the client kind, else tools_profile for an unmapped client that offers tools (the bench: tools), else default_profile the conductor run only: classes, packages, effort, memory; tools adds none of them to the prompt memory the profile's memory block the conductor run only: a keyless client on a single-user box gets the owner's notes; general and tools have memory off reasoning format reasoning_format in the request, --reasoning-format where the thinking goes; see below response cache --response-cache a rerun of an identical request within the hour replays its greedy answer: timings change, answers do not

Name the pack, the thinking setting, the effort, the profile and the path with every score. /health gives the version and the pack in version, for example 0.11.4+exl3-6.0, and the bench records it.

A plain API client gets the thinking in reasoning_content and the answer alone in content (SRV-245). Up to 0.11.4 the raw path left it inline as <think>...</think> in content. Scenarios that check the exact answer then failed: valid JSON only (TC-22), a terse answer (TC-24). Since SRV-617 the raw path follows the same rule for an SDK, curl or an unnamed client, as the bench is. Against an older server, send the format yourself:

--backend-kwargs '{"reasoning_format": "reasoning_content"}'

docs.title: A batch
docs.text:
tools/teb_batch.sh runs rows one at a time against one server and keeps what each ran under; tools/teb_summary.py prints the table (OPS-209).

bash tools/teb_batch.sh --base-url http://<host>:8000/v1 --out results/teb-1020 \
  --health "ssh <host> curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/health" \
  --restart "ssh <host> tandem restart" standard
python3 tools/teb_summary.py results/teb-1020 --md --misses
  • Every row: --seed 42 --temperature 0 --timeout 600 --no-live --parallel 1. The batch stops when /health reports no slot.
  • standard is four rows: raw at xhigh (--header X-Tandem=raw --backend-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort":"xhigh"}'), the conductor with no header, and both again with --hardmode-only. pack adds --variant-seed 7 on both paths and, with --pack DIR, a held-out scenario pack on both. A row of your own is label:flags.
  • The conductor rows pin no profile. The server resolves each request by what it offers: tools when it offers tools, the default profile when it offers none, as any client meets it. A hard-mode scenario without tools then runs under the default profile. Pinned to tools on 2026-10-20, hard mode scored 82 twice and failed TC-88 both times; unpinned it scored 86 and passed TC-88 (n = 1 each; one scenario, the cause not tested). Pin a profile in a row of your own with --header X-Tandem-Profile=<name>.
  • batch.knobs holds the bench's version, the server's version and pack, its slots, max_len, the default max_tokens, sampling, the prefix and response cache settings, and the output of --knobs CMD (the effort default and the slots from serve.env, for example).
  • Each row keeps its result JSON, log, flags, start and end times and /health before and after. A row during which the response cache's hits grew replayed answers of an earlier request; the summary marks it, and its times are not the engine's. --restart before the batch empties the cache.

docs.title: Results on a DGX Spark
docs.text:
tool-eval-bench.md has the latest results: every thinking setting on the raw path, four conductor profiles and hard mode.

Qwen3.8-27B in the EXL3 6.0 pack, TandemLLM 0.11.4, default effort xhigh, seed 42, temperature 0, timeout 600 s, one scenario at a time. The bench ran on another machine on the LAN. Each row is one run (n = 1).

Core 15:

path score deployability responsiveness time not passed raw, thinking on 100 89 63 102 s none raw, thinking on, effort medium 97 82 48 117 s TC-14 partial raw, thinking off 90 81 60 88 s TC-03, TC-14 partial conductor, chat profile with memory 93 80 49 187 s TC-03 conductor, general profile 93 79 47 161 s TC-03

Full suite, 69 scenarios:

The first core row ran on main after SRV-617. The other rows ran on 0.11.4: the full raw row with thinking on sent reasoning_format: reasoning_content itself, and the medium row got the thinking inline in content.

TC-03 asks the model to tell Sarah the meeting moved. The conductor classes the turn as message writing, adds the write-message package, and the model drafts the email instead of looking up the contact and sending it (SRV-615). On the raw path TC-03 sits near a tie: one run of the core 15 missed it, the next passed. On every path the structured-output scenarios TC-65 to TC-69 end partial or failed, and TC-68, schema violation resistance, fails.

The first request of each scenario pays the prefill of the tool prompt, about 4,400 tokens; on the Spark the first token arrives after about 7 s, which the responsiveness score counts. Later turns reuse the prefix.

docs.title: 2026-10-19: structured outputs with tools, the tools profile, C5 and the secret mask
docs.text:
The settings above hold. The conductor rows ran with no header, so the bench, an unnamed client that offers tools, got the tools profile (SRV-621). Both arms ran on the same build, and no answer in the full-suite rows was a response-cache replay.

Full suite, 69 scenarios:

path score deployability responsiveness time not passed raw, thinking on 95 83 54 13.3 min TC-23, TC-49, TC-58, TC-62, TC-67 partial; TC-68 conductor, tools profile 96 83 53 12.2 min TC-23, TC-49, TC-62, TC-67 partial; TC-68

With --variant-seed 7 and a held-out pack of 12 scenarios of our own, kept outside the repository, raw scored 96 and the conductor 97. The pack passed 12 of 12 on both paths. Those two runs replayed the answers of unchanged requests from the cache, so their times are not given.

  • TC-65, TC-66 and TC-69 pass on both paths: the schema now reaches the engine alongside the tools, and the model's first answer token picks a call or the document (SRV-619).
  • TC-58 passes on the conductor only: the server masks the key the file held in the answer (SRV-625).
  • TC-51 passed on both paths in this run; C5 (SRV-623) journaled no act in it.
  • The graders of TC-23 and TC-49 read "doesn't provide historical data" and "no email will be sent" as failures (OPS-193). TC-67 adds one calculator call the grader counts as unrelated. TC-68 asks for a value the model declines to invent.

docs.title: Caches
docs.text:
A long prose prompt sent twice took 44.4, 93.7 and 208.3 s to its first token at 32k, 64k and 128k tokens from cold, and 0.3, 0.6 and 1.1 s the second time, resumed from the resident prefix (the paper, one request each, published NVFP4 set). A prefill is the most expensive thing the engine does, and the caches exist so that it runs once per token of a conversation instead of once per turn.

Every cache here restores exact state, and none of them is meant to change the output. exactness.md says precisely what "exact" means for each, and what has been measured.

docs.title: What a state is
docs.text:
To continue a sequence at token L, the engine needs:

  • the KV rows of the 16 attention layers for tokens 0 to L (64 KB a token);
  • the 48 recurrent states and their convolution tails (about 147 MiB, whatever L is);
  • the drafters' own position-indexed KV (about 40 KB a token for both drafters).

The recurrent part is the hard one. A KV row depends only on the tokens up to it, so rows written for an earlier request stay valid. The recurrent state has absorbed every token and cannot be rewound, so a cache must have taken a copy at L.

The caches know no model (ENG-157). Every tier reads a sequence through the engine's adapter: eng.cache_state() gives its recurrent sections by name and its position-indexed views with their token axes (engine/models/state.py; for the 27B the sections gdn.S and gdn.conv, the views K and V and, with an e4m3 cache, their scales), eng.settle() lands a pending commit before a copy, eng.resume_at(n) puts the engine at length n after a copy was written back, and eng.cost() gives the bytes the budgets count. A snapshot, an anchor, the end anchor, a pinned or parked anchor and a disk or spill anchor are the sections' tensors in the state's order; rows are the views' rows. A disk anchor file of format 2 names each section as the state does; the 27B's files of format 1 ("S", "conv") are read as gdn.S and gdn.conv. tests/test_cache_any_model.py runs a made-up third architecture (two sections, and three views whose shapes and token axes differ from both models') through the snapshot, the resident prefix, the disk tier after a restart and the session spill with no edit in the cache code. Side slots go through the same interface since ENG-241: a model that builds its own (side_slot, Flash-Next) gives each slot its own state. The side lane's borrowed engine (Borrow) has not been checked on Flash-Next.

Flash-Next (ENG-157): its sections are the 36 GDN states and conv tails, the PLE conv state and its token context, and mtp.h_last, the last committed row's streams, which the MTP layer reads next with the token that follows: 115,662,864 bytes (110.3 MiB) in all; its views are K, V and the indexer keys of its 12 attention layers, and the MTP drafter adds its own layer's (kv_views): 29,952 bytes a token, 122.7 MB a 4,096-token chunk file. The pooled indexer keys are rebuilt from the keys after every restore (resume_at); the MTP drafter picks up at the row before the line and waits there for its next token, as it did when the rows were written (state_resume). The grid is 4,096 tokens, Flash-Next's prefill chunk, so a resumed prefill runs the chunks a cold one runs and the resident prefix, the state store, the disk tier and the spill restore the same bits a cold prefill writes. The end anchor and a session snapshot hold the state a generation wrote, through the decode and verify kernels, and are held to the same gate as the 27B's: on 2026-10-12, of seven requests resumed from caches, the five from grid anchors, the state store and the disk tier after a restart answered bit for bit as a cold server (logprobs equal), and the two from end anchors answered the same first token, one the same text (logprobs within 0.044) and one a longer list at a near tie (its token 13: p 0.53 for "," against the cold run's end of answer). A file header now takes as many 4 KiB lines as its metadata needs (Flash-Next's anchor lists 75 sections); every file written before it has one line and reads as it did.

docs.text:

Time to first token for a long prose prompt, cold and sent a second time (log scale). Measured: the StairCut paper, published NVFP4 weights, one request each.

what happens which cache answers read cold turn 1, a new session disk tier (the 24k head) the user's first message turn 2, the answer and a tool result end anchor of turn 1's answer the tool result opencode's title call (a guest) guest stash (rows copied aside) its own 2k prompt turn 3, after a 33k thinking end anchor of the thinking the tool result, not the 33k a 10k request of another session parked session (the 53k rows) the other session's 10k a deploy restarts the engine session spill (written at the drain) the next message the same session, the next morning disk tier (the head again) everything past the head

One agent conversation through the cache tiers. Top: what the client does. Middle: the cache the prefill resumes from. Bottom: what it still reads cold. A turn after a long thinking resumes at the end anchor and reads only the tool result; a title call is a guest whose rows are stashed and put back; another session's request parks the conversation; a restart brings it back from the session spill; the next morning only the common head is still on the NVMe. The token counts are the measured cases of The resident prefix to Live conversations on the NVMe.

docs.title: Resident prefix
docs.text:
An agent client such as opencode sends one conversation that only grows: each turn's prompt is the previous prompt, plus the previous answer, plus a tool result. At 190k tokens a whole snapshot would be about 20 GB, so the state store cannot keep one.

engine/cache.py::ResidentPrefix uses the observation that the previous prompt's KV is still in the engine's own buffer, row for row. It leaves the KV in place and clones only the recurrent state and convolution tails (146.8 MiB) at every 1,024-token boundary of the prefill. These copies are called anchors. A new request that shares the first c tokens of the resident prompt resumes at the largest anchor at or below c. The engine copies the recurrent state back, sets the KV length, tells the drafters their caches are valid up to there, and prefills the rest.

first turn: cold prefill next turn: resumed from the anchors

The first turn of a ~42k-token opencode session prefills everything; the next turn resumes from the anchors and its prefill bar starts near the end. Recorded against the served engine (published NVFP4 weights, StairCut on); sped-up parts are marked in the clip.

Resuming this way computes the same state as a cold prefill on the same grid. Anchors come only from prefill chunks, never from rows a verify round wrote, and the resumed request forwards the rest of its prompt on the same 1,024-token grid a cold prefill uses. tests/test_resident.py checks, on a small random model, that the resumed logits, recurrent state, convolution tails and KV rows equal a cold prefill's bit for bit. In the paper's long-context check on the real model, the cold and the resumed request wrote the same 256 tokens at 32k and 128k and different ones at 64k; that difference is not explained.

A short unrelated request between two turns, such as a title request, would overwrite rows the conversation needs. Such a guest request (at most --resident-guest-max tokens, 8,192, and under a quarter of the resident prompt: both must hold) gets the rows it can reach copied aside first, into a 1 GiB stash (--resident-stash-gb, the guest's rows and a 512-row margin), and they are copied back before the next request. The stash holds the rows the guest can write: its prompt, its max_tokens, 2,048 rows for the monitor's hidden tokens when the monitor runs, and two margins of 512 rows (0.3.47-test, SRV-207; before, every row the 1 GiB held, so a 410-token question asked the memory policy for 1 GiB and a refusal cut the resident rows at the guest's start). With --parallel N a guest takes an idle side slot first and needs no stash (parallel-requests.md). A request whose session comes back, an agent's worker (X-Tandem-Worker: 1 or X-Tandem-Parent-Session), is never a guest, whatever its length (ENG-371). The 2.5 GiB anchor budget (--resident-gb) holds 17 anchors, and the newest 4 are never evicted, because the next turn resumes near the end.

Grid anchors make every turn re-read the previous prompt from its last 1,024-token line (on one night of opencode traffic, 507 tokens a turn at the median for 197 new ones). Resuming at a finer line was built and measured: a forward that starts at a 64-row line inside a grid chunk does not reproduce the rows of the cold forward over that chunk on the served kernels (logits, state and KV rows of 4 resumed turns at 49k to 202k tokens all differed from a cold prefill's), so it is not in the engine.

A request too long to be a guest replaces the resident prompt. opencode's compaction request is one: no tools, no system text, the history as one user message, sharing nothing with the conversation, and the turn after it starts with the same tool block and system text as every turn before. Before such a request cuts the rows, the head of the old prompt is pinned: its KV rows and up to 8 anchors spread over it (the anchors every 4,096 tokens up to 32,768, which eviction keeps for this) are copied aside, as long a head as --resident-pin-gb holds (4 GiB with its anchors, about 33,000 tokens; its own budget, no longer taken out of the state store's). A later request that shares more with the pinned head than with the rows in place gets them copied back and resumes at the largest pinned anchor it shares. tests/test_resident_pin.py checks that restore against a cold prefill bit for bit.

Two sessions used in turn (A, then B, then A) share their head and nothing after it, and each switch re-read the other session past the head. When a request of another session (the body's conversation id, else opencode's x-session-id; without either, a prompt that parts from the rows in place) replaces the resident prompt, the rows it is about to overwrite, from where the two part up to the replaced prompt's newest anchor that fits, are parked with its newest 4 anchors (--resident-park-gb, 4 GiB, about 35,000 tokens past the head). A later request that shares more with the parked prompt than with the rows in place gets them back: the parked rows and the rows in place are swapped a block at a time, so B is parked while A comes back. The shared head has to be in place. A parked prompt is not pinned as well, and a compaction drops its session's parked rows instead of parking them. In a hold on 2026-10-01, A came back after B with 41,984 of 53,209 tokens reused and 11,225 re-read in 16.4 s, where it would have re-read about 45,000. tests/test_resident_park.py checks every swap against a cold prefill bit for bit. This swap stays in the engine's memory; the swap of long chats to the SSD is the session spill (Live conversations on the NVMe).

The park keeps the end anchor too. Open WebUI never sends an answer's reasoning back, so a chat's copy parts from the rows inside its first answer, and a park of rows and grid anchors could offer nothing above the first reasoning, which the disk tier's head already gave: on 0.4.7 (2026-10-08) parks 4, park_hits 0, and chat B, parked with 36,841 tokens, came back with 12,288 from the disk and 16,370 re-read in 23.7 s. When the rows up to the end of the last generation fit the park, they are parked whole and the end anchor moves with them (its two state buffers take one of the four anchor places), with its hidden spans and the end alignment's regions. A copy that continues the parked conversation to its end (every token, the hidden spans put back, or aligned by the end alignment, the tests an NVMe entry's offer makes) is offered the end; the server's hook before its replay brings the park back first, so the replay and the resumed turn work on its rows, and the swap parks the other conversation's end the same way. A parked end that a third session gives up goes to the NVMe with its regions. An end the park cannot hold is dropped with its rows as before, and the rows up to the newest anchor that fits are parked.

docs.title: After a long generation
docs.text:
The rows a generation writes are never anchored on the prefill's grid, and until 0.3.14-test the resident prefix held the turn's prompt, not its answer: the next turn shared at most that prompt with it and resumed at its last anchor, so it re-read the whole previous output. A session snapshot would hold the state after the generation, but it costs about 151 MB plus 104 KB a token, and a long session's is over the served entry cap (STORE_ENTRY_GB=1, about 7,000 tokens) and the whole store (CACHE_GB=2). Measured on 2026-10-02 (rrr2, opencode): turn 1 prefilled 34,038 tokens and thought 32,773, closed by the D2 backstop with the hidden phrase; turn 2's 66,964-token prompt resumed at 33,792 = 33 × 1,024 and re-read 33,172 tokens in about 44 s. Every one of that session's 15 turns, and the 18:08 session's, resumed at the previous prompt's last 1,024 line, whether the monitor had hidden a phrase or not (tests/test_reread_after_think.py).

The end anchor (0.3.14-test, --end-anchor, END_ANCHOR in serve.env, on). At the end of every generation ResidentPrefix.keep_end keeps one more anchor: the recurrent states and convolution tails at the last position the engine forwarded (147 MiB, the same two buffers turn after turn), with the rows in place marked valid up to there. A generation that stopped part way through an accepted block (the end token, a stop, the budget) has the engine a few rows ahead of the committed tokens; its pending commit is cut back to them first (trim_pending, as --session-trim cuts the session snapshot), and when the state has already absorbed them, no end anchor is kept. Rows past the end token or the budget are not committed at all since 0.11.3 (SRV-530, _end_cut): the walk accepted them whenever the draft had them (the lookup copies </tool_call>, <|im_end|>, from the same tool call earlier in the prompt), a NemotronH state walked them, and 31 of 54 Super VL turns on 2026-10-16, every one a tool call, kept no end anchor (ahead). The commit now stops at the last kept token's row, the length Qwen's cut back stopped at; end_cut in the resident prefix's report counts the blocks, and the log says [spec] the accepted path ran N row(s) past the end: not committed. The next request that starts with every one of those tokens (the prompt and the answer as the client sends them back) resumes there and forwards only what is new: the turn after a 33k thinking forwards its tool result and the template's glue instead of 33,172 tokens. It is taken when it starts later than the anchors in place, the pinned head and the parked session; a state store entry or the disk only when they start later still. cached_tokens in the journal is then the previous prompt plus its generation, and the source is end.
