Page cache the engine keeps on purpose (Flash-Next's n-gram table under the warm policy, resident_files()) is free to the kernel, so MemAvailable counts it as available; every floor check (the residency planner, the roles' governor, the side slots' admission, the KV pool's floor) takes it off first (server/memsplit.py counted_available), /health's cache.resident_files and the split's pinned_cache report it. The table's other policy, cold (QWEN38_FN_TABLE=cold), reads its rows with O_DIRECT through a hot-row cache of QWEN38_FN_TABLE_CACHE_GB (2) and leaves nothing in the page cache: on 3.05 on 2026-10-12, 0 bytes resident after a 1k prefill and 256 decoded tokens, the same greedy text as warm at 1k and 8k, and one decode rate of 40.9 tok/s against 42.0 warm. 2.05 keeps its table warm. 3.05 reads it cold: warm, with the whole table resident, MemAvailable less the table fell to 8.4 GiB during a 146,400-token request at a 147,456-token window, under the 15 GiB floor. 4.05 and up read it cold because their weights and a warm table do not fit together.

The workspace by forwarded rows (0.15.1, measured 2026-11-02 on Flash-Next 3.05, SRV-773). The line above prices a prompt by its whole context, but a prefill runs in chunks of FN_PREFILL_CHUNK rows (4,096) and only the prompt's streams grow with its rows past one chunk: a resumed turn of 21 rows took 0.10 GiB at every context from 8k to 146k tokens, where the line charged 2.75 to 10.39 GiB. Flash-Next's adapter therefore states cost().workspace_rows(n, rows), the gate's charge for rows forwarded onto n served rows at the last row's context class: a chunk of T rows takes 0.25 GiB + 176,000 B x T + 32 B x T x class (fitted on 26 continuation rows: 0.180 GiB, 170,274 B, 29.9 B; max |resid| 0.68 GiB), every forwarded row 20,480 B of streams (hc_count 4 x hidden 2,560, bf16, from the config). A resumed prefill of one chunk or less is charged 1.15 x (its chunk + its streams) + 0.5 GiB, at least 0.75 GiB; more than a chunk, and every cold prompt, 1.15 x (a whole chunk + its streams) + 1 GiB, never under the line at the gate (the parallel admission counts a cold prompt by its rows alone, without the line's floor); both at most 10.75 GiB. Against the measured rows the charge covers 28 of 28 continuations (+0.38 GiB the least) and 7 of 7 cold or seeded prefills; a 21-row follow-up at 62,886 tokens now costs 0.80 GiB (the line: 4.47), a 2k cold prompt 2.75 as before, a 262k one 10.75. Not measured: a cold forward under 4,151 rows, and how long the streams live past the first draft round. Other families keep the line (workspace_rows None), and the policy still learns the line upward from a cold prefill of 64k rows or more, never from a continuation (Budget.mark(rows=...)).

docs.title: Routes and knobs
docs.text: GET /v1/cache/stats reports every cache's counters. GET /v1/cache/memory is the engine's memory by owner, ?pools=1 with the allocator's pools (SPD-257); /health's memory.owners is its summary, rebuilt at most every 10 s (age_s). POST /v1/cache/clear empties them; with an admin password set it needs that token as a bearer header.

docs.title: Peek and prewarm
docs.text:
POST /v1/cache/peek takes a chat body (messages, tools, the effort fields) and the conversation's session (the x-session-id its requests send) and answers where its rows are without running the model: {"tier", "cached_tokens", "reread_tokens", "reread_eta_ms", "tokens", "restore_ms", "session"} (SRV-349, server/cache_peek.py). The body is rendered as a request would be, the session's notes of every kind are replayed where its next turn carries them (the router's, and the memory, library, outcome, identity and client notes the conductor puts in), and the tiers are asked what engine/cache.py's prefill asks them. A note the router chooses for the turn itself, as on a session's first turn, is not counted: it goes in at the end of the last message, after every cached row. tier is resident (an anchor or the end anchor of the rows in place, or a side slot's conversation the next request carries over), ram_park (the parked session or the pinned head), ram_snapshot (the state store), nvme_spill, disk_tier or none; cached_tokens is the line in the served prompt's positions, as the usage frame's cache_n. reread_eta_ms is the re-read at the median prefill rate of this process's last long prefills (before the first one, the caches' prior), plus the NVMe or disk read. The peek counts nothing on the dashboard. While a request waits for the engine it answers 409 at once; otherwise it waits up to 3 s for the engine lock (the end of a turn and the engine's idle work after it, the graph captures, about a second) before it answers 409. A model a --backends backend serves gets a 404.

POST /v1/cache/prewarm takes the same body. When the peek says nvme_spill, no request runs or waits and the engine lock is free (after the same wait), it reads the conversation back as its next request would (the resident conversation goes to the NVMe first when it is worth keeping), so the send resumes at the end anchor: {"prewarmed": true, "restore": {...}}. Otherwise {"prewarmed": false, "why"}: not_on_nvme (RAM needs nothing; the disk tier reads its rows during the prefill, where that is cheaper), resident_in_use (another conversation used the rows in the last 120 s), too_long (the read would take over 3 s), or a 409 while busy. A request that arrives during a prewarm waits at most one block (about 4,096 rows): the save of the conversation in place and the restore both stop between blocks when a request waits, the entry stays on the NVMe and the conversation in place stays in RAM (why: yielded).

The usage frame carries the split beside the OpenAI fields: usage.tandem = {"parts": {"system", "tools", "history", "injected", "images"}, "harness": {"class", "effort", "packages": [{"name", "tokens"}]}, "cache": {"tier", "source", "cached", "reread"}}. System, tools, history and images add up to the client prompt count (prompt_tokens in the default client usage mode); injected is hidden_tokens (the router's notes and the end anchor's replay), so the five are the prompt the engine read, cached plus reread. The split keeps this accounting basis with --usage-context engine; that option changes the API's prompt and cached totals for clients that compact from usage (server.md). harness is null for a request no router plan served. The Chat tab's chatd reads both (docs/chat.md).

knob what --cache-budget-gb (CACHE_GB) the state store's budget --no-session-cache, --no-prefix-cache turn off one use of the state store --prefix-chunk the prefill chunk size and snapshot grid, default 1,024 --resident-gb, --resident-stash-gb, --resident-guest-max, --resident-tail the resident prefix's anchors, guest stash, longest guest and protected tail --resident-pin-gb, --resident-park-gb the pinned head, the parked session --end-anchor (END_ANCHOR) the end of the last generation as a restore point, on; off is 0.3.13-test's resident prefix --store-entry-gb one state store snapshot at most --mem-ceiling-gib, --mem-peak-gib, --reserve-slack-gib the engine between requests, during a prefill, and the allocator's reserve --store-boundaries, --session-trim the state store's boundaries per prefill, the session snapshot's trim --prompt-token-cache millions of tokens of tokenised chat messages kept between requests --suffix-store, --suffix-store-mb, --suffix-store-scope, --suffix-store-readonly the persistent suffix store --response-cache, --response-cache-mb, --response-cache-ttl the response cache --disk-cache (QSE_DISK_CACHE), --disk-cache-min-tokens, --disk-cache-head-anchors the disk tier's directory (or off), the shortest prefix it writes, a session head's anchors; its budget, TTL, admission and on/off are settings.memory.disk_cache --session-spill (SESSION_SPILL), --session-spill-gb (SESSION_SPILL_GB), --session-spill-min-tokens live conversations on the NVMe (on, needs the disk tier; off writes and reads nothing, the idle backfill with it), their budget (64 GB), the shortest resident conversation an eviction writes (16,384); settings.memory.session_spill overrides the budget live --session-spill-codec (SESSION_SPILL_CODEC) zstd (0.4.3-test): new blocks as byte planes compressed with zstd, lossless; off: as they are. Blocks on the disk are read either way --session-spill-idle (SESSION_SPILL_IDLE), --session-spill-idle-s (SESSION_SPILL_IDLE_S), --session-spill-idle-every-s the idle backfill (on): a conversation of 4,096+ tokens idle 20 s is written while its rows stay, changed blocks only, never while its slot is busy, at most every 60 s (no serve.env line for the last); skipped past the day's write budget --session-spill-resave-s, --session-spill-resave-min-tokens SRV-887: an eviction, switch or idle save of a conversation whose entry was written less than this long ago (300 s; 0: always write) and that grew by fewer than this many tokens since (8,192) is skipped; the entry stays and the next restore prefills the rest. A drain always writes QSE_RECLAIM_GRAPHS on (the default): idle slots' graph sets are dropped, the least recently used first: by the KV pool's ladder after the caches and the small models and before any conversation's rows, and by an idle window over QSE_GRAPH_POOL_GIB (a family whose engine keeps a graph set only: Flash-Next and Ornith); off (0, false): never QSE_GRAPH_POOL_GIB the growth of the graphs' pools over what they held after the load past which an idle window drops idle slots' graph sets, the least recently used first, down to 3/4 of it, and below which alone it captures graphs ahead (8 GiB; 0: no cap). Without the memory policy's pools probe (the policy off, or no expandable segments) there is no cap. Each drop logs [graphs] dropped slotN: G graphs, X GiB back (why=cap\|reclaim); /health memory.graphs counts them QSE_GRAPH_SET_MIN_IDLE_S the cap never drops the graph set of a slot that served in the last this many seconds (300); the KV pool's ladder may --disk-write-budget-gb (DISK_WRITE_BUDGET_GB) the engine's NVMe writes a local day past which optional writes stop (200 GB; 0: none); settings.memory.disk_writes.budget_gb overrides it live QWEN38_SPILL_PARK on: the parked conversation a new park gives up goes to the spill first (0.4.1); off: given up

POST /v1/cache/clear?tier=disk empties the disk tier, ?tier=all the disk and the caches in RAM.

docs.title: Community weights
docs.text:
A community pack is a set of weights someone else published on Hugging Face that TandemLLM can load: a smaller quantisation, or a fine-tune of a model we serve. The setup guide lists each one under its model, after our own profiles, with the author's GitHub avatar, the Hugging Face repository as owner/name, the format, the size and the speed a maintainer measured.

Some community quants are the packs one of the model's own profiles serves: turboderp's EXL3 packs of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next are the flashnext-<bpw> profiles. Their entries (models/qwen3.8-flash-next/community/turboderp-flashnext-<bpw>.json) name that profile in profile, so the card says who made the pack and its Use button selects the profile. They ship with the release in models/community-builtin.json, beside the profiles they describe; a box never fetches them.

Listing a pack takes one JSON file. You send a pull request that adds models/<model>/community/<id>.json, and nothing else.

docs.title: What happens to your file
docs.text:
1. You open a pull request with the file. The community check on the pull request runs python -m server.setup.registry --check and python -m server.setup.community --index --check.
  2. A maintainer reads it, then downloads the pack at your commit and runs it on a DGX Spark. If it loads and answers, the maintainer fills verified and sets status to verified. If it does not, the entry stays submitted, or becomes broken with a note.
  3. After the merge, every TandemLLM box sees the pack the next time someone opens the weights step of the setup guide. The box asks GitHub for models/community-index.json on the main branch. When GitHub does not answer, the box uses its last copy, then the copy that came with its release.

To have a maintainer write the file for you, open an issue with the "Add a community weight pack" form (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/community-quant.yml). The setup guide's "Add yours" button opens that form with the model already filled in.

docs.title: The file, field by field
docs.text:
The file name is the id: models/qwen3.8-27b/community/thinkingcap-27b-kearuga-exl3-4.00.json holds the entry with "id": "thinkingcap-27b-kearuga-exl3-4.00". That file is the first entry and a good one to copy. The JSON Schema is models/schema/community.schema.json.

Field Required What it holds schema yes 1 id yes The file name without .json. Lowercase letters and digits, with single dots or dashes between them, at most 80 characters. name yes The name the card shows and the model calls itself when asked, at most 120 characters. base_model yes The TandemLLM model it runs on, which is the folder it sits in: qwen3.8-27b or nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b (Bases), or any model when profile names one of its own profiles. finetune_of no The Hugging Face id of the fine-tune, or null for a quantisation of the stock model. author.github yes Your GitHub user name. The card shows https://github.com/<you>.png and links to your profile. author.name no The name you go by. author.social no Any of x, huggingface and bluesky as handles (0xWhiteMage, name.bsky.social), and mastodon and website as https URLs. No other keys. hf.repo yes owner/repo on Hugging Face. It must be public: a box downloads it without a token. hf.revision yes The full 40-character commit. A branch name is refused, because a branch can change after the review. format yes exl3. The schema also knows nvfp4, fp8 and gguf, and the check refuses them until TandemLLM can load them. bpw yes Bits per weight, between 1 and 16. size_gb yes The download in GB (10^9 bytes): the sum of the repository's file sizes at that commit. load yes standalone when the pack is the whole model, or overlay when it holds EXL3 projections that go over the base checkpoint. modalities yes text, image, audio and video, each true or false: what works in TandemLLM today. modalities_in_pack no What the pack contains, even when TandemLLM cannot serve it yet. The card shows those in grey. drafters yes tandem-exl3 for our EXL3 draft models (K3 drafters and K4 draft head), dflash2 for our BF16 draft models, in-pack for a draft layer inside the pack (only with profile), or none. On Nemotron 3.5 Super VL only none: the pack brings no drafter of its own and drafts with the model's own (Bases). license yes The license as its SPDX names, e.g. Apache-2.0. license_url no An https link to the license file, best at your commit. description no One or two plain sentences, at most 500 characters. The card shows it as text: no HTML, no Markdown. tags no Up to 12 lowercase words, such as fine-tune or reasoning. added yes The date of the pull request, YYYY-MM-DD. status yes submitted. A maintainer changes it. verified no Filled by the maintainer who ran it: build, device, date, tok/s per kind of text (prose, code, chat, plain), tokens per round, and a note. links no https links, such as pr for a pull request that made the pack load. profile no The model's own profile that serves this pack, for a pack TandemLLM already runs as one of its profiles. The entry must have that profile's repository, format and bits a weight. Set by a maintainer.

The check refuses a modality the load path cannot serve. A standalone pack is text only for now (ENG-271), even when it carries a vision tower: write "image": false and list image in modalities_in_pack. An overlay keeps the base checkpoint's vision tower, so "image": true is allowed there. A text-only entry's profile also writes QSE_PACK_VISION=off, which ops/serve.env applies after the Setup Guide's run/setup.env, so a box whose setup turned vision on still starts the pack text only and ops/start.sh says so (SPD-167; before, the start failed on the pack's tower). A 27B pack's profile also carries its base's Setup Guide defaults for parallel requests (SPD-165: 4 slots, the KV pool, side windows of 262,144 tokens, the admission floor and the fixed keys from models/qwen3.8-27b/model.yaml), so ops/use-profile.sh community/<id> serves four chats at once without the guide; one request alone measured the same as with one slot (prose 38.4 against 37.4 tok/s, 8K prefill 867 against 855). The switch's smoke turn (ops/use-profile.sh) gets two tries within SMOKE_TIMEOUT_S (300 s, as the single try had) and logs the whole answer before it rolls back; an answer in the reasoning field counts. No path serves audio or video yet.

docs.title: Bases
docs.text:
Base Loader Load paths Serves Drafters qwen3.8-27b the 27B family's (engine/loader.py) standalone, overlay text; images on overlay tandem-exl3, dflash2 or none nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b NemotronH (engine/models/nemotron_h, nemotron-h.md) standalone text none: LiLiCorr and the lookup, from the model's own profile

A Nemotron 3.5 Super VL pack (ENG-377) is served with the model's own EXL3 profile nearest in size (nemotron-super-vl-exl3-4.0 for a 3.5 bpw pack): its memory limits, its sampler, NVIDIA's LiLiCorr drafter and the lookup, with the pack in place of that profile's weights. Its files must be a NemotronH checkpoint: config.json flat (NemotronHForCausalLM) or the Omni wrapper's llm_config, 88 layers, an EXL3 quantization_config, every shard the index names. A pack that lists image in modalities_in_pack holds the RADIO tower too: vision_model.radio_model.* and vision_projector.* (or mlp1.*) tensors, preprocessor_config.json and the config's vision_config. python -m server.setup.community check-pack community/<id> [--dir <folder>] checks the files and names what differs; the loader's audit checks every tensor's shape and rate at load.

docs.title: What is not accepted
docs.text:
• A pack that is private or gated, or that needs a token to download.
  • A branch or tag in hf.revision instead of a commit.
  • A format other than EXL3, until a loader for it is in TandemLLM.
  • A base model outside Bases, unless the entry names one of that model's own profiles in profile.
  • A claim in modalities that the load path does not serve.
  • Links that are not https, and HTML or Markdown in any text field.
  • A license that does not let others download and run the weights.
  • A pull request that changes anything besides the one JSON file. A maintainer regenerates the index models/community-index.json (and models/community-builtin.json for the entries with profile), or you run python -m server.setup.community --index.

docs.title: Running a pack
docs.text:
On the box, ops/use-profile.sh community/<id> writes the pack's profile from its entry, downloads the pack at the pinned commit into ~/.tandemllm/community/<id>, checks every weight file against the sha256 Hugging Face publishes, and fetches our draft models if they are missing. Then it stops the engine, starts it on the pack and sends one test chat. It refuses a download that would leave less than 60 GB of disk free, and it rolls back to the previous profile when the start or the test chat fails. --dry-run prints every URL and size without downloading. The setup guide's "Use" button runs the same steps after its review page.

The engine estimates a pack's memory from our own profile of the same format and the nearest size (exl3-4.0 for a 4.0 bpw EXL3 pack). The number is only an estimate until a maintainer has loaded the pack.

docs.title: The packs in the setup guide
docs.text:
The weights step of the setup guide (#/setup) shows a Community weights section below our profiles, one card per pack. A card shows the maker's GitHub avatar and @login, the networks the entry lists, the fine-tune it comes from, the format, the bits a weight and the download size. It also lists the modalities the pack holds, in grey with the reason when TandemLLM cannot serve one yet, and which of our drafters it runs with. Once a maintainer has run the pack, its card shows the measured speed too. A badge gives the license, another the status, and a link leads to the Hugging Face repository.

You can search over names, authors, handles, tags and the fine-tune's source, and sort by five keys, newest first by default. “Use” selects a pack the way a radio card selects one of our profiles, as community/<id>. Every later step takes that name, Wren included. A pack that cannot run images turns the Vision tool off, as the server would. “Add yours” opens the issue form of Submitting a pack with the model filled in.

docs.title: Where the list comes from
docs.text:
The list is models/community-index.json, one entry per file under models/<model>/community/. A box asks GitHub for that file on the public repository's main branch at two moments only: when the weights step opens and when you press Refresh (POST /v1/setup/community/sync). Nothing fetches it on a timer. The box sends the ETag of its last copy, so an unchanged list costs one 304 answer.

When the fetch fails, the page shows the box's last copy (~/.tandemllm/community/index.json). A box that never fetched one shows the list that came with its release. Look at the section's head to see which source the list came from and which entries it dropped. A 404 from GitHub is not an error: the repository has published no list yet, and the page shows a quiet note, “no published list yet”, beside the bundled list. A real failure is one short line without the URL, such as “GitHub could not be reached”; the server's log has the URL and the detail. QSE_COMMUNITY_URL points the box at another index, and QSE_COMMUNITY_URL=off never fetches.

A fetched index is untrusted. One with the wrong shape never replaces the cached copy, and an entry reaches the page only after it passes the registry's checks, those of How verification works.

docs.title: Packs on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
docs.text:
A pack on Super VL loads on NemotronH (Nemotron 3.5 Bolt and Super VL) and is served with our EXL3 profile nearest in size: nemotron-super-vl-exl3-4.0 for a 3.5 bpw pack. It takes that profile's memory limits, its sampler, NVIDIA's LiLiCorr drafter and the lookup, with the pack in place of the weights; the entry's drafters is none. The pack must be standalone, a NemotronH checkpoint with 88 layers, in EXL3. python -m server.setup.community check-pack community/<id> checks a downloaded pack's files and names what differs: the config, the layer count, the quantisation, every shard the index names, and the image tower when the entry lists images.

field value id nemotron-super-vl-exl3-3.5bpw author styles01 (pull request #63) pack aitamedia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-EXL3-3.5bpw, EXL3: routed experts at 3.5 bits, every other projection at 5, an fp16 head; 57.8 GB, standalone modalities text; the pack holds no image tower drafters LiLiCorr and the lookup, from nemotron-super-vl-exl3-4.0 speed 33.2 tok/s prose, 53.9 code, 37.4 chat, 99.0 edit, 112.3 copy; 25.9 without speculation; every drafted text the plain run's agreement top token equal to the converter's own forward (1.6.0) on the pack at 510 of 512 positions, both others near ties; KL 0.0019 memory 53.58 GiB of weights at load; the served profile (262,144 tokens, 3 slots) starts and answers in 110 s license OpenMDW-1.1

The first pack on Super VL. Speed: one run per kind of text on a DGX Spark with 0.12.1, 512 greedy tokens, thinking off, as the entry's verified block records it (measured); models/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b/measurements/0.12.1-summary.json has the runs.

Plain decoding runs at 25.9 tok/s on this pack and at 31.1 on our 4.0 pack (0.11.0). From the headers, a decode token reads 7.95 GB of this pack and 6.74 GB of ours.

docs.title: An example: the first community pack
docs.text:
bash ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/use-profile.sh community/thinkingcap-27b-kearuga-exl3-4.00 --dry-run
bash ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/use-profile.sh community/thinkingcap-27b-kearuga-exl3-4.00

The script writes the pack's profile from its entry to run/community/<id>.env, which serve.env reads; --dry-run writes it into a folder of its own.

field value id thinkingcap-27b-kearuga-exl3-4.00 author 0xWhiteMage fine-tune of bottlecapai/ThinkingCap-Qwen3.8-27B pack 0xWhiteMage/ThinkingCap-Qwen3.8-27B-Kearuga-EXL3-4.00bpw, EXL3 at 4.0 bits a weight, 16.38 GB, standalone modalities text; the pack also holds a 6-bit vision tower, which the standalone path does not serve yet drafters ours, the EXL3 K3 drafters and K4 draft head speed 42.3 tok/s prose, 84.0 code, 41.4 chat license PolyForm-Small-Business-1.0.0, with Apache-2.0 for Qwen's part

The first community pack. Speed: the entry's verified block (measured on 0.14.2, 2026-10-26: one greedy request a kind of up to 512 tokens, thinking off, through the conductor, 8 lanes; models/qwen3.8-27b/measurements/verified-2026-10-26-thinkingcap-27b-kearuga-exl3-4.00.json).

docs.title: Design: Simple mode for the Setup Guide
docs.text: The Setup Guide speaks to two audiences with one machine: the person who wants a working chat in three pages, and the person who wants every knob. It is one guide with one state machine, not a second installer: plan, estimate, physics guard, apply job, progress and review are reused exactly as the advanced flow runs them. No server route, registry field or engine concept is added.

docs.title: The switch
docs.text: Simple|Advanced sits above the wizard's own steps. The choice is a browser memory (localStorage, key tandem.setup.simple) — a fresh browser opens in simple mode; a browser once switched remembers. Entering a mode re-derives the current step from the mode being entered: a step the fold holds collapses onto the folded page, the tiles' twin (the standard intro) opens on the quant cards, and the tiles and the running install are pages of both modes.

docs.title: The simple flow
docs.text:
Three pages, one list: the model tiles, the quant cards, the folded settings page.

  1. The tiles. The models this box can serve, one card each, recommended first.
  2. The quant cards. The model's profiles, the recommended one preselected; the card says what the choice costs (download, memory) in the same words the advanced page uses.
  3. The settings page. One fold per topic — components, the chats and their window, methods, the review — the step's whole body behind its title bar, every fold holding what the advanced step shows. The review fold opens by default, so a Finish that waits always says so in the open.

A fourth page lives outside the walk: the install job, reached by Finish and returning to the folded page when it ends.

A first-opened model with nothing running yet gets the simple answers — the model's full window, as many chats at it as the card measured it can carry (never past the card's own measurement, slots.max), and the response cache where the model offers it. Laya stays off: it needs the chat (beta), which is off by default. The pool is turned on only when it buys chats the plain reservation cannot carry. A box that already serves the model keeps its own settings: opening the guide in a new browser must never change what is running.

A disabled Finish is never silent: the blockers ride beside the button, the plan's own errors included, and a plan check that has not answered says it is still checking — or that it did not answer and asks for a Retry.

The Advanced escape hatch shows inside a model — on the quant cards and on the settings page, not on the tiles page; it is the same switch, so there is one way back and no orphaned state.

docs.title: What advanced keeps
docs.text: Everything: the rail, all steps, every field and help, Wren, the folded pages. The e2e files that drive the advanced flow ask for it by name, since a fresh browser now lands in simple mode; everything else keeps the guide's default.

docs.title: Why not a separate simple installer
docs.text: A second flow means two state machines to keep in step, two places where a stale response can write, and a wall between the two audiences the same person crosses in one evening. Here the mode is one input to the reducer — activeSteps and normalizeStep decide which pages exist and where a step belongs — and the install job belongs to the model that started it: opening another model leaves the job on its own model's progress page.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: The Setup Guide's pages are TandemApp's since 0.16.0, and so are their tests, in TandemLLM/TandemApp: dashboard/tests/setup-state.test.ts covers the mode switch, the active page list, the route normalization, resume in the right mode, the job's model scope and the simple defaults (the card's cap, the pool only when it pays). dashboard/e2e/setup-simple.spec.ts walks the three pages on the mock and finishes on the review fold.

docs.title: Exactness
docs.text: Under greedy decoding, TandemLLM writes the text that its target model writes one token at a time, with one exception: at a near tie between the two best tokens, a batched verify can round the other way. Drafters, the lookup store and the caches change how fast the text arrives, not what it says; the shape of the verified tree can move a near tie. This page states the promise precisely, names the exception, and lists the checks that hold the engine to it.

docs.title: The promise
docs.text:
Our reference is plain greedy decoding on the same weights: one forward pass per token, take the highest-scoring token, repeat. For every greedy request, the engine's output tokens equal the reference's tokens up to the first near tie where the two paths choose differently.

"The same weights" matters. A profile chooses the weights. The NVFP4 profile is held to NVFP4 plain decoding, not to the BF16 release or the FP8 checkpoint. The difference between weight sets is a quality question, and quantisation.md measures it with a separate gate. Speculation never adds to that difference.

The promise, with the near-tie exception, covers:

  • any drafter, including a drafter that is wrong on purpose on every token;
  • chains and trees of any shape the router builds, and both block widths;
  • a request resumed from the prefix cache or the resident prefix;
  • request options that change the scores (penalties, logit_bias, structured-output masks), because the engine applies them to every verified row exactly as plain decoding applies them to its one row.

docs.title: The one exception: near ties
docs.text:
Two tokens can score the same up to one rounding step of the arithmetic. Then which one wins an argmax depends on the order of a floating-point sum. A batched verify and a one-token step do not always sum in the same order, so at such a position the two can pick different tokens. After that position the texts differ, and both are correct greedy continuations of their own prefixes.

TandemLLM keeps this rare by design. The head returns fp32 logits, and every matrix-product kernel fixes its reduction order by the weight's shape and never by the row count (kernels.md). Two differences remain between a batched verify and a one-token step: the output head uses one kernel for a single row and another for several rows, and the verify path of the recurrent and attention layers does the one-token arithmetic in a different order. A small fp32 difference that falls on a BF16 rounding boundary changes one value, and the recurrent state and the KV cache carry it forward, so over a long output the verify's logits drift from the one-token decode's. Where the two best tokens are closer than that drift, the two paths can choose differently.

The agreement gate, tools/verify_spec.py, prints the gap between the top two logits in BF16 units (ulps) whenever outputs differ. A difference passes only when the gap at that position is within one ulp. Anything larger is a bug. The gate decodes a fixed number of tokens and does not stop at the model's end-of-turn token. A difference after that token is not part of any answer served with the default stop tokens, so it is judged separately: in the StairCut release's checks, the two differences above one ulp (1.46 and 1.73) both fall after the end of the answer.

The paper measures how often this happens with StairCut in its served configuration on the published NVFP4 set. Of 30 prompts (held-out prose, code and chat, 256 new tokens), 17 outputs are identical to plain greedy decoding up to the end of the answer: 13 over all 256 tokens, and 4 more that differ only past the end of the answer (largest gap 1.46 ulp). The other 13 follow plain decoding up to a near tie inside the answer, with a gap of 0.04 to 0.76 ulp, take the other token and continue from there; in one of them the token taken is the end-of-answer token, so that answer ends early. No output differs inside the answer at a larger gap. The one-ulp rule names the condition under which the two decoders can differ; it does not show that the difference is harmless.

The table below has a measurement on the 0.4.0 code (lookup store off, 2026-10-05): one raw greedy turn with a prompt of about 5,000 tokens at temperature 0, sent alone twice and once with 10 side-lane guests. Each parting is a near tie. Where the runs alone parted, the gap between the two best tokens was 0.022 and 0.029 nats at token 12, and 0.052 and 0.021 nats at token 504. Each text after the parting is a correct greedy continuation of its own prefix. --no-learn-cost takes out what earlier requests taught the router, not the timings inside the request.

runs compared --no-learn-cost learned costs alone, twice token 12 token 504 alone, and with 10 side-lane guests token 61 token 573

Where two runs of one 5,000-token raw greedy turn first wrote a different token. (measured), the 0.4.0 code, lookup store off.

against plain greedy, 30 prompts outputs identical over all 256 tokens 13 differ only after the answer ended 4 take the other token at a near tie in the answer 13

StairCut in its served configuration against plain greedy decoding on 30 prompts of held-out prose, code or chat (256 new tokens). 17 outputs are identical to the end of the answer. The 13 that diverge inside the answer do so at a gap of 0.04 to 0.76 ulp; no output differs inside the answer at a larger gap. Measured: the StairCut paper, published NVFP4 weights.

docs.title: Parallel requests
docs.text:
With --parallel N (server.md) two or more decoding requests verify their trees in one pass. The promise is the same: each request writes its own greedy text up to a near tie. Two things can move a near tie that a request alone would not meet. A joint round verifies the request's tree cut to its share (16 nodes at two requests, 8 at four), another tree shape than the one it verifies alone. And the joint pass runs eagerly, or on the 27B from its own CUDA graphs once its shape has come QWEN38_JOINT_GRAPHS_AFTER (4) times, where a lone request's verify runs from the lone verify graphs; a graphed joint pass gives every lane's logits, state and KV bit for bit what the eager joint pass gives (tools/joint_graph_check.py). The batch itself is not one of them: every projection kernel keeps a row's result independent of the other rows up to the joint pass's row cap, which each model family sets for the weights it serves (joint_policy; 32 by default, 64 for the 27B on EXL3 weights, where the skinny kernel takes 33-64 rows as adjacent 32-row chunks and an 8 x 8-row joint pass measured each engine's rows bit for bit its own eager verify, SPD-159). The rows between the projections that are one program a row (the add-norms, the GDN gated norm) run once for all engines and keep their bits too (SPD-163); the GDN gate inputs stay per engine, because the library's bf16 GEMM does not keep a row's bits across row counts. On the box, tools/parallel_verify_check.py gives each slot's logits from the joint pass bit for bit what its own verify gives (with the lone verify eager too, as the joint one is), and on the CPU tests/test_parallel_verify.py holds two and three requests in lockstep to the tokens each writes alone.

What a request writes beside others is measured against what it writes alone (tools/parallel_bench.py, agreement): where a text differs, the tool prints the first differing token and the gap between the two best tokens there in the alone run. On 30 prompts (10 held-out prose continuations, 10 held-out code continuations, 10 chat questions; 256 tokens, greedy, store off; 2026-10-05, single runs), 17 of 30 texts were identical to their alone text with two requests at once and 15 of 30 with four; every first difference sat at a top-2 logprob gap between 0.0019 and 0.118 nats, under one BF16 step of a logit of magnitude 16 to 32 (0.125; the logits' magnitude there was not recorded). The packed draft proposes bit for bit what each slot's own draft proposes (tools/packed_draft_check.py, two slots on either drafter arm, four on the narrow one). One request at a time takes the path it takes without --parallel.

docs.title: Stronger than the promise: release identity
docs.text:
Every release candidate is also held to the release before it. Before a change ships, 13 plain requests (the five benchmark workloads, streamed and not, one with thinking, one with tools, one under penalties, one seeded sampled request) must come back byte-identical to the current release (tools/api_text_check.py). The served configuration must also produce bit-identical logits with the new flags off (tools/flagoff_identity.py). A speed change that alters one token of text does not ship. StairCut (2026-09-29) is the one documented exception. Its verify shapes differ from rc10's, so at near ties its text can differ from rc10's. It is held to plain greedy decoding instead, under the near-tie rule above.

0.15.0 moves the summation order in two places on purpose, each held by a gate against a reference instead of to 0.14.2's bits:

  • The 27B's prompt reading (SPD-191, SPD-245). The GDN prep kernel (QWEN38_GDN_PREP: a chunk's convolution, SiLU and the l2 norm of q and k in one kernel) is held to an fp64 reference of the recurrence, teacher-forced over every prompt position: KL 3.9e-4 against 3.8e-4 for the path before it on code at 8K, 0.0086 against 0.0096 on repeated prose at 2K. Its scan at 16 x 4 and the chunk-64 GDN prefill walk value-block fastest (QWEN38_GDN_CHUNKED) keep the recurrent state's bits and round a few chunk outputs one bf16 ulp the other way; tools/gdn_tile_gate.py holds each against the path before it on prose, code and repeated text at 2K, 8K and 32K tokens, 64 teacher-forced steps: top-1 64 or 65 of 65 on every row, the KL of the GDN prep move's size. QWEN38_GDN_CHUNKED=0, QWEN38_GDN_PREP_BV=32 QWEN38_GDN_PREP_WARPS=8 and QWEN38_GDN_PREP=0 give the earlier orders.
  • Flash-Next's mixer GEMV and mix_up on the tensor cores (SPD-241, QWEN38_FN_MIXER_MMA=1): every row independent of its call, top-1 agreement 99.6, 99.6 and 98.8 % against the CUDA-core kernels and KL 5e-4 to 1.7e-3 (tools/fn_mma_agree.py), the class of the accepted split-GEMV order change (97.7, 99.2 and 99.2 %). QWEN38_FN_MIXER_MMA=0 gives the earlier kernels.

Every family's arithmetic fingerprint moves once in 0.15.0 (tests/test_adapter_guards.py), so the disk tier's files and the spilled conversations 0.14.2 wrote are not read, and each conversation is read again once.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
A sampled request (temperature above 0) is exact in distribution. At each verified node the engine draws the target's own token, and a drafted token survives exactly while the draw lands on it. When the draw lands elsewhere, that draw is the token. For a drafter that proposes one fixed token this is the standard rejection sampler, accept with min(1, p/q), with no second draw. The output therefore follows the target's own sampled distribution. A drafter that samples its own proposal carries its proposal distribution, and the accept uses it.

All sampling filters (temperature, top_p, top_k, min_p) run after the penalties, through one function in engine/sample.py. Drafted rows and plain rows see the same distribution.

A sampled request that names none of top_p, top_k and min_p takes the model card's filters (SPD-245, server/sampling_defaults.py): the first of these that says is the request's own fields, then --top-p / --top-k given at start (TOP_P, TOP_K), then the checkpoint's generation_config.json (Qwen3.8-27B and its fine-tunes: top_k 20, top_p 0.95, min_p 0), then the whole vocabulary. Before 0.15.0 a request that sent temperature alone sampled the whole vocabulary. Only the filters move: the temperature is the request's, a greedy request is untouched and the logits are not touched. /health sampling.unnamed_filters shows what an unnamed request runs with.

A request with a seed draws with noise keyed by its position in the sequence: the token at index t is the argmax of log p_t + G_t, where G_t is Gumbel noise from a generator seeded by (seed, t). That is an exact sample from p_t, and it does not depend on how many draws the drafters made before. The same seed therefore gives the same text whatever the drafters proposed.

A sampled request without a seed draws its own at admission (SPD-245, 63 bits of OS entropy) and takes the same keyed walk. The distribution is the same: Gumbel-max over _filter's kept set is a draw from the filtered p_t, the draw the unseeded multinomial took. Only the noise differs, and two requests get two seeds, so a regenerate of the same prompt still differs. Under an active plan the seed is in the decision row (extra.seed_drawn). The response has no seed field, as for a client's seed. QWEN38_FRESH_SEED: auto (default) draws where the sampled verify carries no q (--sampled-tree det), on draws everywhere (the q-aware min(1, p/q) accept of a sampling drafter gives way to the keyed walk), off never draws. /health sampling.unseeded says which applies.

tests/test_sample.py checks the samplers statistically on the CPU, and tools/sampled_dist.py checks the served engine's sampled answers against the target sampled alone.

docs.title: Caches
docs.text:
A cache restore gives back bytes, not an approximation. The prefix cache, the resident prefix and the disk tier take their snapshots on the prefill chunk grid, and a resumed request forwards the rest of its prompt on the same grid. It therefore computes the same arithmetic as a cold prefill on that grid. tests/test_cache.py, tests/test_resident.py and tests/test_disk_cache.py check, on a small random model, that a resumed request's logits and state equal a cold prefill's bit for bit. The disk tier's files carry a fingerprint of the weights, the engine's code and the arithmetic flags; a file of another fingerprint is never read. Whether Triton's autotuning after a restart can pick another prefill configuration, so that rows written before it differ from a cold prefill after it, the tests cannot say; tools/disk_restore_check.py checks it on the served engine in a hold, in two processes. On 2026-10-02 (0.3.14-test's code, a 10,701-token opencode-shaped prompt) the second process's cold prefill was the first's bit for bit (logits, recurrent states, convolution tails, every row, the state at each 1,024 line), and the first process's disk files restored to it: the state at the line, then the resumed prefill's logits, states and all six position-indexed buffers, and 48 greedy tokens.

The paper's long-context check sent a long prose prompt twice, cold and then resumed from the anchors. The two 256-token outputs were identical at 32k and 128k tokens and different at 64k, and that difference is not explained.

Session resumes are one step weaker. A session resume continues a conversation from the state its last turn ended in, which verify rounds wrote rather than prefill chunks. That state produced the previous answer, but it is not the state a cold re-read would compute. It is held to the engine's greedy gate (same tokens) and not to bit equality. caches.md has the details.

The resident prefix's end anchor (0.3.14-test, --end-anchor, on) is a session resume of the same kind: the recurrent state at the end of the last generation, which verify rounds wrote, with the rows in place, and the next turn forwards only its new messages from there. It is held to the greedy gate, as the session cache is, and so is every anchor a prefill that resumed there takes (the rows from the resident prefix's taint up). Two things keep the rest of the caches exact: the disk tier writes nothing of such a prompt and reads over those rows, and the state store takes no prefix snapshot of it; a grid anchor at or below taint, or a cold prefill, resumes bit for bit as before. The tokens the session monitor hid are put back into the client's copy where the rows hold them, so the prompt the engine continues is the context it really had, the hidden phrase included, as a router note is replayed; whitespace the re-rendered copy holds differently right next to a hidden span is the rows' own there too (0.3.15-test), and any other difference serves the copy as sent. tests/test_end_anchor.py checks, on the random model, that the turn after a generation resumed at its end writes the same greedy tokens as the same turn resumed at the prompt's last anchor (no drafter, wrong and right chains and trees), that a pending commit cut back is the shorter commit's state bit for bit, and that --end-anchor off leaves every prefill bit for bit as before. caches.md has the details.

An opt-in response cache (--response-cache) answers an identical greedy request from memory. It is off by default, so a benchmark can never be pointed at a dictionary.

docs.title: What changes output on purpose
docs.text:
Some features change the text because the client asked for it. They are not exceptions to the promise. Plain decoding with the same setting writes the same text.

  • Penalties (repetition_penalty, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty) and no_repeat_ngram_size.
  • Structured outputs and forced tool calls, which mask the tokens the constraint does not allow.

  • A reasoning budget or the stall close, which end the thinking block early (speculative-decoding.md).

  • A regenerate under TandemLLM (0.4.4-test, SRV-241; the project's rule of 2026-10-07). This was the first place where TandemLLM samples without the client asking for it; the loop escape below is the second. Open WebUI's Regenerate sends the same conversation again and no sampling parameter, so under greedy it got the same answer word for word. server/regenerate.py recognises a regenerate: a chat request under an active TandemLLM plan whose conversation (every non-system message, ending with a user message) equals an earlier request of the same session that produced an answer. X-Tandem-Regenerate: 1 also counts as a regenerate. That one request samples with temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, top-k 20 and a fresh seed (--regenerate-temperature, --regenerate-top-p, --regenerate-top-k). The seed is in the journal row (extra.regenerate), so sending it reproduces the answer. The sampled path is the exact one above: the answer follows the target's own sampled distribution, drafter and tree included. Every other request is untouched and greedy, byte for byte as before. That covers the first answer, a follow-up, Continue, an edited message and a tool round. Also untouched: a request that names any sampling parameter (it gets the client's own), a raw or bench request, a side request and a compaction. --regenerate off (QWEN38_REGENERATE=off) turns detection off, and X-Tandem-Regenerate: 0 turns it off for one request. The ledger column sampling is regenerate on these rows, and the dashboard's speed sample leaves them out.

  • The loop escape under TandemLLM (SRV-475, 2026-10-14). An agent turn that ends in a repeat or near-repeat of one tool call samples with the model card's settings (the checkpoint's generation_config.json) and a fresh seed, until the session makes progress; then it is greedy again (server.md). A profile with sampling.agentic_default: card samples every agent turn; the shipped profiles keep greedy. The seed is in the journal row (extra.loop_escape). The same requests as for a regenerate are untouched, the client's own sampling included. The ledger column sampling is loop_escape or card, and the dashboard's speed sample leaves those rows out.

Two relaxed accept rules also exist (--relax-tau, --relax-rank) that accept a drafted token when it is close to the target's choice. They break the promise, exist only for measurement, and are off in every profile. When either is set, the server prints a warning line.

docs.title: The checks
docs.text: check what it holds tools/verify_spec.py greedy output with no drafter, an adversarial drafter, a half-right drafter and the served drafters must match, up to the one-ulp near-tie rule tools/flagoff_identity.py the served configuration with new flags off is bit-identical to the build it replaces tools/api_text_check.py 13 plain requests byte-identical to the current release tools/cache_gate.py warm and cold runs agree (bit-identical on the chunk grid, same tokens for a session) tests/test_forward_tree.py, tests/test_tree.py tree verify equals chain verify on a tiny model, on the CPU tests/test_cache.py, tests/test_resident.py, tests/test_disk_cache.py restores are bit-exact, the disk tier's through a reopened tier and after a failed restore tests/test_end_anchor.py a resume at the end of the last generation writes the same greedy tokens as one at the prompt's line; off, every prefill as before tests/test_sample.py, tools/sampled_dist.py sampled output follows the target's distribution

docs.title: Questions and answers
docs.text:
Does speculation change the text? Under greedy decoding the engine writes what plain decoding on the same weights writes, up to the first near tie of at most one ulp between the two best tokens, where the batched verify can round the other way. The paper measured 17 of 30 outputs identical to the end of the answer and 13 that diverged at such a near tie. Exactness states it exactly.

Does the conductor change the text? It changes what the model reads (a hidden note, a thinking cap, a hidden close) and so what it writes, by design; the arithmetic is the same greedy decoding. X-Tandem: raw gives the release's raw path. Even there, two runs of one request can part at a near tie, because the length router sizes blocks from timings (Two runs of the same request).

Does it serve several requests at once? Yes. With --parallel N the engine decodes up to N requests in the same rounds: on 0.4.0 two at once gave 1.38× the total of one, four 1.42×, in single measured runs (Parallel requests). The shipped profile runs 8 lanes since 0.15.0 (SRV-707): on 0.15.0 the 27B ThinkingCap EXL3 4.0 pack decoded 1, 2, 4 and 8 requests of 512 tokens at 42.5, 73.5, 108.9 and 155.9 tok/s in total, greedy (0.15.0, eight lanes). The headline numbers in these docs are single-request numbers. With one sequence a short request still goes through the side lane, and the proxy serves other backends in parallel either way.

Will it run on another GPU? Best effort. The installer turns off the skinny kernel that is built for the GB10 only, and StairCut's prices were measured on the Spark, so the router starts from the wrong staircase and corrects its level online. Nothing about another GPU's speed is measured.

Why NVFP4 weights but 16-bit arithmetic? On this board the FP4 tensor-core path still has to move operands through shared memory, and a 4-bit activation path would need its own quantiser and gate to save at most the 8 % of traffic the activations are. NVFP4 saves bytes, and bytes are time on a memory-bound decode (Kernels).

Why are my speeds below the paper's? Check four things: the raw path (X-Tandem: raw), the lookup corpus (the paper's is not published), the store view (a store with the benchmark's text inflates it, a clean one does not), and the board's lock (another engine on the board halves the bandwidth).

Can I use the engine without the dashboard? Yes. A new install serves the engine alone, under its own model name, with no page and no chat (Engine only, or the chat (beta)). The dashboard is TandemApp, which runs on any machine with Python 3.11, with or without this engine (TandemApp's docs).

Does the proxy add latency? 0.33 ms to the time to first token at the median against a fake backend on one machine, and a decode rate within 0.8 % of the engine's own over the local network (measured, the 0.4.0 series).

Are my prompts stored anywhere? No log line, ledger row or metric holds a prompt or an answer. The suffix store holds token ids, never text. The conductor's transcripts keep a session's tool turns under the engine's home, mode 0600, secrets redacted, 30 days; memory notes are files you can read, edit and delete. Probe snapshots, off by default, hold activations, never text.

Is the engine's port safe to expose? No. The engine has no sign-in of its own: its OpenAI routes are always open, and everything else is open until an admin password is set. Sign-in, accounts and API tokens are TandemApp's (TandemApp's sign-in). If other people can reach the machine, keep the engine's port on loopback and let them in through TandemApp, a reverse proxy with its own sign-in, or a VPN (Access and sign-in).

docs.title: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
docs.text: A plain decode token of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on its 3.05 pack reads about 4.23 GB (arithmetic, from the pack's headers), and the engine decodes it at 45.8 tok/s at 1k tokens of context with no drafter (measured, 2026-10-11). Flash-Next is the second model TandemLLM serves. It runs on the same board as the 27B, one model at a time, through the same server, the same caches and the same speculation methods. This page collects what is different, from the model and its packs to the parts that are not measured yet. Adding a model describes the adapter path it came in through.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Flash-Next keeps the 27B's hybrid of Gated DeltaNet layers with an attention layer every fourth, and changes most of what sits around it (the table below). engine/models/flashnext/config.py reads its configuration and refuses any field it does not know, naming it, so a later release that adds an arithmetic switch is not served as if it were this one.

part Flash-Next the 27B layers 48: 36 Gated DeltaNet, 12 attention 64: 48 Gated DeltaNet, 16 attention MLP 512 experts a layer; 10 routed and 1 shared run a token dense, width 17,408 residual stream 4 streams of 2,560, joined by hyper-connection mixers one stream of 5,120 attention sparse past 2,051 tokens: an indexer scores blocks of keys and each row reads the 512 best full extra input a hashed n-gram embedding: 16 table rows a token, in front of layer 1 none draft layer one multi-token-prediction (MTP) layer in the checkpoint none; DFlash2 drafters beside it state of a sequence 110.3 MiB of sections plus 29,952 bytes a token about 147 MiB plus 64 KB a token weights served turboderp's EXL3 packs, 2.05 to 6.05 bits a weight NVFP4 with an e4m3 head, or EXL3

Flash-Next beside the 27B.

The tokenizer is the 27B's (248,320 ids), so the lookup drafter's corpus and the persistent suffix store serve both models unchanged; both carry the tokenizer's fingerprint and are checked against it at load.

docs.title: The packs and the window each one fits
docs.text:
turboderp publishes Flash-Next in five sizes, one branch each of turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3, and each size is a weight profile (ops/profiles/flashnext-<bpw>.env). The engine reads the packs as they are; Quantisation says what is inside one. The largest window of each pack is in its registry entry (models/qwen3.8-flash-next/model.yaml), and a start with a longer --max-len stops before the load and names both numbers.

profile disk weights n-gram table largest window flashnext-2.05 61.5 GB 32.85 GiB 24.44 GiB, warm 262,144 flashnext-3.05 85.1 GB 47.87 GiB 30.4 GiB, cold 262,144 (recommended profile) flashnext-4.05 106.1 GB 62.47 GiB 36.36 GiB, cold 208,896 flashnext-5.05 121.9 GB 77.16 GiB 36.36 GiB, cold load/generation unverified flashnext-6.05 137.7 GB 91.87 GiB 36.36 GiB, cold none: it does not fit

The Flash-Next packs on one DGX Spark. Weights: the GiB on the device, the draft layer and the int8 mixers included; (measured) for 3.05, estimated from the file sizes for the others.

One request of 260,800 tokens through the server, on each of the three packs that load, decided those windows (the figure below). The Setup Guide's estimate is calibrated on these three runs and predicts their lowest MemAvailable within 0.7 GiB. On the box the other programs took 4.6 GiB; the estimate's frame keeps 10 GiB for them, which is why 4.05 comes out at 208,896 tokens with the vision tower on (212,992 without) although its run at 260,800 kept MemAvailable above the floor. For 5.05 the estimate is 53,248 with the tower and 65,536 without; full-pack load and generation remain unverified.

pack lowest counted MemAvailable 2.05, table warm 25.5 GiB 3.05, table cold 31.9 GiB 4.05, table cold 17.8 GiB

The lowest MemAvailable, less a warm table's resident bytes, during one 260,800-token request at a 262,144-token window, sampled at 10 Hz. (measured), 2026-10-12, one run a pack, conductor on, with 4.6 GiB of other programs on the box.

The run also measured what a long prefill takes: 571 tok/s for the 260,800-token request on 3.05, 261,549 rows with the conductor's notes (585 on 2.05 and 581 on 4.05), and a prefill workspace of 10.47 GiB above the engine, which stops growing at about 140k tokens. Decoding at that length, with the prompt from the caches, 3.05 made 22.5 tok/s with the drafter at 2.0 tokens a block; 2.05 made 27.0 and 4.05 20.5 (measured, one run each). A server without a drafter decoded 36.6 tok/s at that length (one request), and Never slower than the plain step says what changed.

Full-pack load and generation of 5.05 remain unverified. Its earlier blocker was 7-bit dense projections, not routed experts: the MoE kernels already supported 7-bit experts, and dense dispatch now covers 2 through 8 bits. Its window is an estimate, not a measured run. 6.05 needs about 92 GiB for its weights, which leaves too little under the 15 GiB floor at any window. 3.05 reads its n-gram table cold. Warm, with the whole table resident, MemAvailable less the table fell to 8.4 GiB during a 146,400-token request at a 147,456-token window, under the floor.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
engine/models/flashnext/pack.py audits a pack before anything loads: every tensor the configuration expects, every shard's size against its header, and the hub's sha256 of every file. A missing tensor or a wrong size stops the load with its name. The loader reads each layer's experts as one file range into a 16-byte-aligned image and copies it to the device in one go, then drops the shards' page cache (52.3 GB on 3.05) and keeps the n-gram table's. On 3.05 a cold load took 56.2 s and a warm one 24.0 s (measured); through the server, 53.8 s.

The self-check runs at every load. It decodes 32 tokens one at a time, replays the recorded steps as chains of 2, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 32 rows and as an 8-row tree, and compares every row bit for bit: 3,936 rows on 3.05. A single differing bit turns speculation off for the process, and the log names the layer and the row. An injected one-bit difference failed it at row 5 of an 8-row chain.

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text:
Every Flash-Next kernel is row-invariant: a row's instruction sequence does not depend on how many rows the call has or where its neighbours sit (Kernels). The MoE expert kernel (tools/fn_kernels.py) gives each (row, expert) pair its own work, rotates the pair's input with that expert's scales, and sums each row's slices in a fixed order; unselected experts are never read. At one row it moves 186 GB/s, 21.7 MB a layer in 0.117 ms (measured). One decode token is one replay of a CUDA graph, about 21.8 ms at 1k of context (measured).

A prompt runs through other kernels (tools/fn_prefill_kernels.py): a chunk of 4,096 rows sorts its (row, expert) pairs by expert and runs one matrix product over each expert's rows. On 3.05 the prefill made 1,185, 1,243 and 1,161 tok/s at 2k, 8k and 32k tokens (measured). The prefill and the decode path differ by BF16 rounding. Teacher-forced on prose and code at 3k and 8k tokens, their top tokens agreed at 96.2 to 98.1 % of positions (measured). The gate the prefill passed asks that it agree with the decode path at least as well as the decode path agrees with the reference forward, less one point. Knobs that give the same bits on and off (SPD-249, docs/kernels.md): QWEN38_FN_PF_WINDOW runs a prompt's chunks layer-major in windows of up to that many rows (8,192 by default), each layer's experts once over the window and the rest a chunk at a time; a window asks the memory policy for its bytes first and runs its chunks one at a time when they are not there, and 0 restores the previous path; QWEN38_FN_PF_HC_FUSED, QWEN38_FN_PF_INJ_FUSED and QWEN38_FN_PF_NOCOPY (on by default) and QWEN38_FN_PF_ROT_ROWS (off) take fewer passes and copies; QWEN38_FN_PF_ATTN_STAGES sets the attention launch's pipeline stages (1; 2 is the decode path's).

docs.title: Speculation
docs.text:
The MTP layer is the drafter. Each round it drafts a chain of 4 tokens with its top two tokens a depth, from one captured graph, through a draft head cut to the 32,768 most frequent ids (QWEN38_FN_DRAFT_HOT). The shared StairCut (engine/methods/staircut.py) keeps the part of that draft with the most expected tokens a millisecond, and with QWEN38_FN_LOOKUP=1 (on in every Flash-Next profile) the lookup's best continuation joins the same tree. One verify a round checks it. A verified row is the decode step's row bit for bit, so greedy speculation writes the plain greedy text token for token, and a seeded sampled request draws what plain sampled decoding draws (Exactness).

class MTP, tok/s with lookup tokens a block with lookup edit 106.2 131.7 4.56 10.43 copy 102.3 132.9 4.37 11.88 prose 49.4 51.1 2.16 2.15 chat 62.1 64.0 2.47 2.49 code 84.9 82.7 3.43 3.48

One greedy request of up to 512 tokens a class (prose stopped at 421) through the server on 3.05, MTP alone and with the lookup. Every text equalled plain decoding, which made 41.5 to 45.7 tok/s. (measured), 2026-10-12, one request each.

Copies gain less in speed than in tokens a block because a verify costs more with every row on this model. Each row routes to its own experts, and a block reads the union: about 19 experts a layer at 2 rows, 26 to 33 at 4 and 72 to 82 at 16, across prose, code and chat at 1k and 8k (measured). The learned prices were 27.8 ms for 2 rows, 38.6 for 5, 52.2 for 10 and 68.8 for 16 at about 1k of context.

Sampled requests take the same tree (--sampled-tree det): at each node the target draws its own token with the 27B's sampler, keyed by seed and position. At temperature 0.7, top_p 0.9, top_k 20 and min_p 0.05 on 3.05, every seeded answer was the same with and without speculation, each seed repeated, and two unseeded draws differed (measured, one run each). Speculation made 43.1 and 40.2 tok/s on prose after 1k and 8k tokens of held-out text, 76.2 and 73.6 on code and 59.0 and 60.8 on chat, against 38.4 to 41.7 plain.

docs.title: Never slower than the plain step
docs.text:
A drafted round at long context can cost more a token than the plain step: on the first runs at 260,800 tokens the drafter decoded 22.5 tok/s and a server without one 36.6. StairCut on Flash-Next therefore prices every round by its wall time per context class. The class is 0 while the sparse attention is still dense, and above that the next of 4,096 · 2^k and 6,144 · 2^k at or above the context, up to 262,144. Per class it keeps the plain step's cost and a drafted round's cost a token, both starting from the price file (ops/prices/qwen3.8-flash-next/flashnext-3.05.dgx-spark.json, provisional).

  • A class whose drafted rounds cost more a token than its plain steps takes the plain step, and drafts one probe round at an interval that doubles while drafting keeps losing (16 rounds, up to 256).
  • A turn drafts only when what speculation saves over the expected answer pays for the draft head's backlog, the prompt rows it has not read (0.28 ms a row at 260,800 tokens).
  • What a class learned of its drafted rounds ages back to the prior while its turns take the plain step.
  • One second after the last request, the server captures the graphs the current class lacks, 25 to 30 in about 4.3 s. Before that, the first drafted request in a new class paid 3.4 to 5.1 s of captures inside its answer.
context speculation, tok/s plain, tok/s 1k 56.6 and 57.3 41.0 and 45.4 32k 34.9 and 55.6 33.0 and 42.5 140k 42.1 and 52.4 33.9 and 41.4 260,800 41.0 and 41.0, plain turns 39.6 and 40.5

One greedy request a length and the same request again (its prompt from the caches), the second round on one fresh 3.05 server, and the same pair on a server with no drafter. (measured), 2026-10-12. All 16 texts equalled plain decoding.

With the idle captures in place, the first request at a new length took the plain step and the next one drafted: 48.2 against 42.5 tok/s at 32k and 46.0 against 41.4 at 140k, every answer equal to plain decoding (measured, one fresh server a length).

docs.title: Exactness
docs.text:
On the 27B a batched verify can round a near tie the other way (Exactness). On Flash-Next it cannot: its verify kernels give every row the decode step's bits, and the load-time self-check proves it on the device before speculation turns on. tools/fn_server_check.py --compare sends 20 requests to a --drafter none server and a --drafter mtp server (greedy, thinking, streaming, every tool_choice mode, JSON, penalties with logit_bias, logprobs, seeds, a stop string): 19 gave the same answers and tool calls, and the largest logprob difference was 0.0. The 20th is a think budget at low effort, which closes at the first block boundary past the cap, so the two runs close the reasoning block a few tokens apart (1,049 and 1,052 reasoning tokens) and differ after it.

Two places hold the 27B's rule instead. The prefill and the decode path differ by BF16 rounding, so a conversation resumed from an end anchor, a state the decode kernels wrote, is held to the greedy gate and not to bit equality (Caches). And the weights themselves differ from the BF16 release by design; how much is not measured.

docs.title: Caches
docs.text:
Every cache tier keeps Flash-Next's state through its adapter (eng.cache_state()). Its sections are the 36 GDN states and convolution tails, the n-gram convolution and its token context, and mtp.h_last, the last committed row's streams that the MTP layer reads next: 115,662,864 bytes. Its views are K, V and the indexer keys of the 12 attention layers, and the MTP layer's own: 29,952 bytes a token. The pooled indexer keys are not stored; a restore rebuilds them. The grid is 4,096 tokens, the prefill's chunk, so a resumed prefill runs the same chunks as a cold one: a 4,096-token chunk file is 122.7 MB and an anchor file 115.7 MB.

tools/fn_cache_check.py sent a request sequence to a server with its caches on and the same requests to a cold server. Restores from grid anchors, the state store, the session spill after a restart and the disk tier after a restart answered bit for bit (logprobs equal). Two restores from end anchors answered the same first token: one the same text, logprobs within 0.044, and one a longer list from its 13th token at a near tie. A reset keeps the KV rows in place; before that fix, a short request run between the turns of a long conversation zeroed rows the conversation resumed over.

docs.title: The e4m3 KV cache
docs.text: FN_KV_FP8=1 keeps the 12 attention layers' keys and values as e4m3 codes with one fp32 scale a (head, token): 18,944 bytes a token of window instead of 31,040, with the indexer keys and the MTP layer's cache in bf16 (SPD-150). The output is no longer the exact model's, so the knob is off by default and the exactness checks hold only with it off. A decode token reads at most 2,051 keys a layer, so the gain is memory rather than speed. Its speed and its cost against the exact cache are not measured. To turn it on, switch on Long-context cache (FP8) under Features in the Setup Guide's Tools step, or add QWEN38_FN_KV_FP8=1 at the end of ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/serve.env and run ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem restart; /health then shows "kv_cache": "e4m3" under weights. docs/caches.md covers every model's switch.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
MemAvailable counts page cache as free. Under the warm policy the n-gram table is page cache the engine keeps on purpose, so every floor check (the residency planner, the roles' governor, the side slots' admission, the KV pool) takes the table's resident bytes off first. After a load of 3.05, MemAvailable read 68.0 GiB with 46.9 GiB allocated (measured).

Each profile sets its engine's ceiling and peak with the arithmetic in the file: the weights, 4.15 GiB of runtime measured on 3.05, slot 0's KV at 262,144 tokens (7.58 GiB) and 6 GiB of caches, and on top the prefill workspace (10.75 GiB, where it stops growing). 3.05 sets 66 and 77 GiB, 4.05 81 and 92. The adapter states the workspace: a floor of 2.75 GiB, 76,309 bytes a context token, and that cap.

docs.title: Serving and operations
docs.text:
ops/use-profile.sh flashnext-3.05 switches the box to Flash-Next as it switches between the 27B's profiles: it fetches the pack's branch when it is missing (pinned to its commit, checked against the hub's sha256, the shared n-gram table hard-linked), stops the engine under the box lock, starts the new profile and rolls back to the previous one, 27B or Flash-Next, when the smoke check fails. ops/start.sh passes the profile's QSE_ENGINE_FLAGS (--model <pack> --drafter mtp) and the server picks the engine from the checkpoint's own configuration. The watchdog and the reboot line start the active profile, whichever model it is. Operations has the rest.

Behind the server everything is the 27B's code: every route, reasoning formats and budgets, tool calls and grammar masks, penalties, logprobs, seeds, stops, the live view and the usage rows. The conductor and its roles run in front of it; the shadow reader does not, because its outputs were validated on the 27B's reasoning only, and the status says so. The dashboard's system view names the pack and its branch, shows max_len against the pack's largest window, and reports the table under its policy. Flash-Next reads images through the pack's own vision tower on the EXL3 kernels, with the image rows' three-axis rotary positions (VIS-97, VISION=on in its profiles). On 3.05 the image chats answered the same with the MTP drafter and without (5 of 5: two single-image chats, a two-image chat of 2,089 prompt tokens and a second turn from the caches), and a text-only answer is the same with the tower loaded and without. Against transformers' Qwen4ExpVisionModel on the dequantised weights the tower's outputs sit within the official model's own BF16 noise (0.048 to 0.090 from the fp32 model, against 0.046 to 0.104). In the language model the text rows after an image keep the text's own agreement (KL 0.019 after 140 image rows and 0.0025 after 2,184 with the sparse attention on, top-1 97.9 %; the text floor 0.022), and every verify pick equals the decode (tools/fn_vision_check.py, VIS-97).

Parallel requests work on Flash-Next without changing any answer, and its profiles turn them on: three slots over one engine with the KV pool (QSE_PARALLEL=3, QSE_KV_POOL=on). On fresh servers three requests arriving together took 27.18 s against 27.03 s one after the other, the same total throughput, and the first tokens came at 2.2 to 6.1 s instead of up to about 20 s for the last of three. One request alone decodes at 45.78 tok/s with three slots, 45.79 with one (measured). At a 262,144-token window with two 65,536-token side slots, a 260,800-token prompt kept MemAvailable at 31.6 GiB or more. The table below lists the limits.

Requests that arrive together on an idle engine prefill in one forward (QWEN38_FN_JOINT_PREFILL, on in the profiles, off in the family's defaults, SPD-249): each layer's experts run once over every prompt's rows, the rest of the layer a prompt at a time, and every prompt ends bit for bit as its own prefill leaves it. The burst gets more tokens per second in total, and its long prompts get their first token later, since every first token waits for the one forward.

setting value sequence slots (QSE_PARALLEL) 3 side window (QSE_SIDE_MAX_LEN) 0: MAX_LEN, every lane the same window (65,536 before SRV-707) admission floor (QSE_PARALLEL_FLOOR_GB) 15 GiB joint verify up to 32 rows turn quantum, batch timeout 50 ms, 2 ms KV pool hard floor 10 GiB, margin 256 rows, page 2 MiB memory ceiling, peak, reserve slack 66, 77, 2 GiB

Flash-Next's parallel limits in its profiles (ENG-241). A side slot took 0.20 to 0.22 GiB allocated at load.

docs.title: What is not measured
docs.text:
• Quality against the BF16 model, per pack. The BF16 release is 360 GB and does not fit the board; the registry's quality fields are empty.
  • Any task benchmark, and the benchmark row of Measurement. The rates in this page are single requests, mostly one run each.
  • A sweep of StairCut's prices. The price file is provisional: class 0 holds online-learned prices, and the other classes single requests.
  • Full-pack load and generation of the 5.05 pack after the 7-bit dense-dispatch fix, and the 6.05 pack, which needs more than one board.
  • Whether parallel requests pay on Flash-Next: one run of three, and no timing of the joint pass on its own.
  • The e4m3 KV cache (The e4m3 KV cache): its speed and its cost against the exact cache.

docs.title: Flint
docs.text:
Recursive's Flint is a mixture-of-experts model for coding agents: 39.8B parameters, of which about 2.5B run for each token. Support ships in release 0.14.0. TandemLLM serves it from our EXL3 packs at 4.0 and 6.0 bits a weight or from Recursive's BF16 checkpoint, and drafts with the lookup, since the checkpoint has no draft layer.

Code: engine/models/flint/ (registry name flint, selected by FlintForCausalLM in config.json). Setup Guide entry: models/flint/model.yaml. Measurements: models/flint/measurements/2026-10-22-summary.json.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
part value layers 49: 2 dense, 47 mixture-of-experts attention 32 query heads, 4 KV heads of 128; q and k RMS-normed per head; a learned sink logit per query head (softmax_offset) sliding layers 35 layers see the last 513 positions, the row included, with rotary (theta 10,000); the engine keeps each in a ring of 640 rows full layers 14 layers see every position and use no positional encoding; KV 28,672 bytes a token, 7.0 GiB at 262,144 tokens MLP layers 0 and 1: dense SwiGLU, 6,144 wide. Layers 2 to 48: 256 SwiGLU experts, 512 wide, 6 a token by sigmoid score with a per-expert bias, plus one shared expert 1,024 wide vocabulary 150,144 tokens; four end tokens context 262,144 tokens

A decode token reads 1.34 GB of the 4.0 pack and 2.00 GB of the 6.0 pack (PackIndex.decode_bytes).

Flint's router is sensitive to rounding. Its sigmoid scores sit close together, so one BF16 rounding of the residual stream changes the chosen experts for 2 % of tokens at layer 2 and for 46 % at layer 46. Two BF16 forwards of the same weights differ by KL 0.034 and agree on 92.9 % of top-1 on 8 rows of 1,024 tokens, and an fp32 forward against a BF16 one differs by KL 0.18. Read every KL on this page against that floor.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
DGX Spark, 2026-10-22. Decode step: tools/flint_check.py bench, one request, 512 greedy tokens, from its graph. Server: one request, 512 greedy tokens of code, thinking off, plain / lookup. Quality: the converter's model_diff against BF16 on 50 rows of 2,048 tokens of held-out docs (written after the model's training cutoff), and this engine against the converter's BF16 forward on 8 rows of 1,024 tokens of the same docs.

profile on disk weights at load decode step, tok/s server code, tok/s docs KL docs top-1 engine KL / top-1 flint-exl3-4.0 (default) 20.6 GB 19.25 GiB 133.5 to 134.2 133.2 / 139.8 0.194 79.7 % 0.160 / 80.5 % flint-exl3-6.0 30.5 GB 28.49 GiB 97.4 to 97.7 97.2 / 103.2 0.070 90.8 % 0.052 / 91.6 % flint-bf16 80.4 GB 75.53 GiB 42.3 to 42.5 42.4 / 50.9 0 100 % 0.034 / 92.9 %

4.0 is the fast size and 6.0 the one to take when quality matters more than speed: 6.0 loses KL 0.070 on the docs and 4.0 loses 0.194, and 4.0 decodes 38 % faster. The BF16 row's engine column is the rounding floor: two BF16 forwards against each other. The packs are public, 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Flint-EXL3-4.0 and 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Flint-EXL3-6.0; each card has its code and wikitext-2 rows. The BF16 profile reads RecursiveSI/flint at revision 2a247be0 and keeps its window at 131,072 tokens so the Chat tab's sandbox keeps room beside it.

The EXL3 packs store every routed expert's up projection divided by 128, and quantization_config.expert_interm_div says so: the experts' |silu(gate) x up| reaches 260,000 in the top layers, past fp16. The engine multiplies the routing weights back.

docs.title: Reasoning, effort and tools
docs.text:
Flint decides on each turn whether to reason, and opens its own <think> block as its first token; its template has no thinking switch. Thinking off puts an empty block after the generation prompt, so the answer starts at once (SRV-685); on a hard ask the model may still work through it in the visible answer. An effort level or a token budget closes the block at its cap with the closing phrase; on the server, effort low closed a hard ask's block at 1,045 tokens and a 64-token budget at 89, both counted from the model's own <think>.

Tool calls come in Flint's own form, <tool_call>NAME<arg_key>K</arg_key><arg_value>V</arg_value></tool_call> (tool_format argkey, SRV-683). The server types each value by the tool's schema and writes the calls back the same way, so a turn after a tool call resumes from the end anchor.

docs.title: How the engine runs it
docs.text:
• The row kernels compute each row on its own, so a verify block's rows equal the decode step's bit for bit; the load-time self-check compares 24 rows.
  • A sliding layer's keys live in a ring of 640 rows: the window's 512 earlier rows and the rows a verify block writes past the length, rounded up to 64. Its attention reads two 512-key chunks. A full layer reads its cache by position. The sink adds one term to the softmax's denominator.
  • The decode step runs the shared expert on a second CUDA stream beside the router and the routed experts, and its Triton kernels launch as programmatic dependents (FLINT_SIDE_STREAM, FLINT_PDL, both on). Same kernels, same bits: 4.0 went from 122.4 to 134.2 tok/s.
  • A prompt chunk runs on the flash kernel with the 4 KV heads as they are; the sink scales its output by sigmoid(lse - sink) in one pass. The routed experts run as one grouped GEMM over the chunk, 64 pairs an item.
  • The server captures the verify graphs of widths 2 to 17 of the first context class at start, so the first requests do not pay for them.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
One request through the server, 512 greedy tokens (the game file 2,048), thinking off, one fresh server a row, one run a cell, tok/s. Every drafted text is the plain one.
