profile prose code chat edit copy game file flint-exl3-4.0 plain 136.6 133.2 133.3 128.2 128.2 129.3 lookup 135.4 139.8 134.0 142.3 480.0 149.5 flint-exl3-6.0 plain 98.4 97.2 97.1 94.3 94.3 95.0 lookup 97.1 103.2 98.5 107.3 353.4 114.1 flint-bf16 plain 42.6 42.4 42.4 41.9 41.9 41.9 lookup 42.2 50.9 42.9 48.4 144.1 42.5

Prose with the lookup is 0.5 to 0.9 % under plain on 4.0 over three alternated pairs: it drafts 7 of 340 rounds, which together cost about what they save, and each plain round carries 21 µs of host work for the drafter.

Long prompts, 4.0, in the engine, 64 greedy tokens at each point:

context 4k 16k 64k 128k 256k plain decode, tok/s 123.0 101.7 61.0 39.5 23.0 prompt reading, tok/s, from the start 3,925 3,561 2,767 1,865

At 128k a decode step spends 17.8 of its 25.3 ms in the 14 full layers' attention: it reads 3.76 GB of keys and values at about 211 GB/s. A 4,096-token chunk at 128k spends 1,424 of its 2,180 ms there, on the flash kernel at about 87 TFLOPS. A 4,096-token prompt reads at 5,375 tok/s on 4.0, 5,045 on 6.0 and 4,319 on BF16.

docs.title: The e4m3 KV cache (FLINT_KV_FP8, off)
docs.text:
With FLINT_KV_FP8=1 the 14 full layers keep each key and value as e4m3 codes with one fp32 scale a (head, token): 14,784 bytes a token instead of 28,672. The output is no longer the exact model's. The knob is off by default, and the exactness checks hold only with it off. The manifest names it flint-kvfp8, so its cache entries are never read by the exact cache.

To turn it on in the Setup Guide (the dashboard's #/setup), pick Flint, go to the Tools step and switch on "Long-context cache (FP8)" under Features. Then finish Review and Install, which restarts the engine. To turn it off, switch it off there and install again.

To turn it on from the command line, add this line at the end of ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/serve.env:

QWEN38_FLINT_KV_FP8=1

Then run ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem restart. Check that it took: curl -s localhost:8000/health shows "kv_cache": "e4m3" under weights, and the engine log's load line says KV cache e4m3. To turn it off, delete the line and run tandem restart again; /health then shows "kv_cache": "bf16". Use one way or the other: a line in serve.env wins over the Setup Guide's switch.

Cost, 4.0, against the exact cache (tools/flint_check.py kvfp8). Each prompt is teacher-forced through 16-row verify blocks:

prompt KL mean KL median top-1 agree perplexity, exact / e4m3 converter bundle, from token 128 0.050 0.009 92.4 % 26.99 / 26.94 32,768 tokens of one source file, last 1,024 0.070 0.005 93.8 % 7.165 / 7.465 122,880 tokens of the same file, last 1,024 0.050 0.002 95.7 % 4.053 / 4.132

Speed, 4.0, in the engine, 64 greedy tokens at each point:

context 64k 128k 256k plain decode, exact cache, tok/s 60.6 39.3 23.05 plain decode, e4m3 cache, tok/s 79.4 57.1 36.6 prompt reading from the start, exact / e4m3, tok/s 3,532 / 3,368 2,741 / 2,554 1,848 / 1,634

On 6.0 the 122,880-token row reads KL 0.047, 95.2 % top-1 agreement and perplexity 4.062 / 4.097, and plain decode goes from 52.0 to 66.1 tok/s at 64k and from 35.4 to 50.1 at 128k.

On 4.0, decode reads about half the bytes and runs 31 to 59 % faster. Prompt reading is 5 to 12 % slower, since every chunk decodes the cached rows to BF16. The state for a 263,168-token window drops from 26.5 to 23.0 GiB. We ran each row once. We also tried per-channel key factors (powers of two, exact on the scores) on the same prompts. They helped some rows and hurt others, and the medians did not move, so we do not ship them.

docs.title: Tool calls
docs.text:
tool-eval-bench 2.8.1.dev13 (commit f2e368b), seed 42, temperature 0, one request at a time, one run a row (n=1), 2026-10-22, TandemLLM 0.14.1. Each pack ran the Setup Guide's defaults for Flint: one slot, effort medium by default (the shipped default, setup.md), conductor on, FP8 cache off, a restart before each row. The raw rows send their effort: thinking off or xhigh. The tools rows think at the server's medium, and the bench-pk rows at the level of each turn's class. BF16's window is 131,072 tokens. Score, then the time the row took:

row EXL3 4.0 EXL3 6.0 BF16 full suite, 69 scenarios raw, thinking off 75 (2 min) 76 (3.1 min) 76 (4.7 min) raw, thinking xhigh 85 (4.7 min) 86 (11 min) 86 (21.5 min) conductor, bench-pk (effort by turn class) 81 (5.1 min) 86 (8.9 min) 83 (16.8 min) conductor, tools (effort medium) 83 (4.1 min) 86 (6.3 min) 84 (15.3 min) hard mode, 28 scenarios raw, thinking off 36 (1.8 min) 41 (2 min) 41 (4.3 min) raw, thinking xhigh 71 (5.5 min) 61 (8.6 min) 62 (19.9 min) conductor, bench-pk (effort by turn class) 73 (3.5 min) 61 (5.8 min) 57 (12.8 min) conductor, tools (effort medium) 80 (2.2 min) 54 (4.4 min) 70 (12.8 min) Raw rows send X-Tandem: raw, so the model answers alone; thinking off is reasoning_effort: none. The conductor rows pin a profile with X-Tandem-Profile: tools is what the conductor picks for a client that offers tools, and bench-pk is a test profile we do not ship. Hard mode at n=1 varies a lot between runs, so we claim no ranking between the sizes. models/flint/measurements/2026-10-22-tool-eval-bench.json has every row with its misses.

The conductor puts no note into Flint's prompts. Its notes go before the last message's <|im_end|>, and Flint's template ends no message with a token, so there is no place for them: no class package, effort sentence, rule or memory note went into the conductor rows above. What acted there is what needs no note: the effort level's thinking switch and budget, the loop guards and the tool-call checks. Since 0.14.2 Flint's adapter says so (conductor fit notes: false, server.md), and the decision rows read memory {mode: off, why: model_notes} instead of on with the error no_insertion_point (SRV-703).

docs.title: Drafting
docs.text:
Flint has no draft layer, so the drafter is the lookup alone: a continuation of the request's own text, the corpus and the suffix store, cut by StairCut from the profile's price file (ops/prices/flint/). The price file holds the measured cost of a verify block by size for each context class, and the plain step's cost for each class. After a round with no draft, the next 1, 2, 4, then 8 rounds take the plain step without looking (FLINT_ANCHOR_BACKOFF, FLINT_LOOK_BACKOFF). A verify block reads the KV once, so the lookup pays more at long context: behind a 124,000-token prompt of code, 4.0 ran a copy ask at 79.5 tok/s against 41.3 plain and an edit ask at 129.7 against 42.4, with the same text.

Verify blocks of 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 rows on 4.0, ms: 7.84 / 9.71 / 13.13 / 17.93 / 25.64 at 2k, 16.27 / 19.24 / 23.59 / 33.39 / 52.93 at 64k, 25.12 / 28.55 / 34.56 / 48.37 / 83.43 at 128k.

docs.title: Not supported yet
docs.text:
• A draft head. A head we trained on the model's own outputs reached 21 % depth-1 acceptance on held-out text; StairCut's prices say it needs about 80 % for 1.4 times plain at 2k and 55 % at 128k.
  • NVFP4. Our round-to-nearest NVFP4 pack lost KL 0.63 against BF16, too much to ship.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• tests/test_flint.py: the config, the reference forward against a plain transcription of the model, the row kernels against their references, the prompt attention with sinks and the window, and a tiny random Flint through the engine against the reference and against itself (decode, verify blocks, commit).
  • tools/flint_check.py: engine and cmp against a converter bundle, bench, staircase and prices for the price files.
  • The converter's forward was checked against a plain fp32 implementation of the published model before the conversion: per layer within fp16 noise on a tiny random Flint, and all 49 real layers at cosine 0.99998 or better.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: [style=unboxed, leftmargin=0pt, itemsep=.5ex, font=] - adapter A model family's code behind the shared methods: its loader, forward and caches, declared once in engine/models/adapter.py's terms (Adding a model). TandemApp's proxy has adapters of its own, one per backend kind (TandemApp's docs). - anchor A copy of the 48 recurrent states and their convolution tails at one position, 147 MiB. The resident prefix keeps one at every 1,024-token line of a prefill; the disk tier keeps them as files. A request resumes at the largest anchor its prompt shares. - benchmark row serve-single-i256-o256-v1: one request at a time, 256 prompt tokens, 256 generated, thinking off, greedy, 50 requests after 3 warm-ups. Every speed in this book that says “the benchmark row” is this. - block drafter The drafter that proposes a whole block of tokens in one pass: DFlash2, five decoder layers reading five of the target's hidden states, fine-tuned at block 8 and block 16. - board The DGX Spark the engine runs on: one GB10 GPU and 128 GB of memory shared by the CPU and the GPU. “One engine per board” is the first rule of operations. - cache source Where a request's prompt resumed: resident, end, prefix, session, disk, spill, continuation, prepared or none. In the ledger and on the dashboard. - claim A role's declared memory peak, which the residency planner checks before a load. - class The kind of task the router decides a turn is (code_edit, chat and eight more). It sets the effort, the packages and the rules. - commit The step that keeps the accepted path's KV rows and recurrent state after a verify. For the recurrent layers it is one low-rank update per layer, folded into the next verify. - compaction A client's request to summarise a long conversation. The engine serves it as a continuation of the conversation it holds, or from a summary written ahead. - conductor The harness in front of the model: profiles, the router, packages, the session monitor, status lines, memory notes. It makes the model TandemLLM. - decider A decision model that answers a typed question in one forward pass, such as Laya; the router's decider stage, off in the shipped router, asks one. - draft tree The guesses of one round, merged so that a shared prefix is a shared node, stored in depth-first pre-order, at most 32 nodes. - drafter A cheap model or procedure that guesses the next tokens for the target to verify: the block drafter and the lookup drafter. - effort A turn's thinking level: off, low, medium, high or xhigh, with a reasoning cap of 0, 1,024, 8,192, 16,384 or none below the backstop. - end anchor An anchor at the end of the last generation, so the next turn that sends the answer back resumes there instead of re-reading it. - grid The 1,024-token lines of a prefill. Anchors, chunk files and prefix snapshots are taken on the grid, and a resumed request forwards the rest of its prompt on the same grid, so its state equals a cold prefill's bit for bit. - guest A short request between two turns of a longer resident conversation; the rows it can reach are stashed and put back. Also the short request the side lane serves inside a running turn, which gets its engine state back bit for bit. - harness The layer around the model that plans each turn and watches it run; in TandemLLM it is the conductor. - hold Taking the board for a measurement or a second model: ops/hold.sh stops the service, runs the command, and restores the service. - journal The conductor's record of every decision, acted on or not, in the usage ledger's file, kept 30 days. - lookup drafter The drafter that copies text: the longest match of the last tokens in the request, a corpus and the suffix store. - memory gate The check before every prefill that gives caches back, cheapest first, until the prompt's workspace fits under the declared peak, else a 503. - memory note One fact the model keeps as a file, written from a block in its answer or by the background writer, read back in later turns. - memory priority A chat's place in the line for memory, tandem.priority in the request: "high", "normal" or "low". TandemApp's Chat tab sets it per chat. - memory wait A request that does not fit above the floor waits before its prefill and starts by itself once memory frees; waiting_memory on the dashboard, X-Tandem-Wait: memory on the response (Waiting for memory). - narrator The small model that writes status lines: rewritten templates, thought summaries, or the voice. - near tie A position where the two best tokens score within one unit in the last place, where a batched verify and a one-token step may choose differently. - NVMe The box's SSD. The disk tier and the session spill keep their files on it. - note The router's hidden text at the end of a turn's last message: the effort sentence, rules, packages. Replayed at the same position on later turns. - outcome The structural reading of a tool-result turn: progress, no visible change, regression, error, stuck and others. - package A text the router may put into a note: a task skill, a test skill, a card, a coding guide, or a library skill. - park Copying another session's rows aside when a request of a new session replaces the resident prompt, so that session's next turn swaps them back. - pin Copying the head of the resident prompt aside before a long unrelated request cuts it. - profile Two things. A conductor profile is a document that sets what the harness does for a client (coding, chat and others). A serving profile is a serve.env file that sets the weights. - raw The engine without the conductor: the release's raw path. X-Tandem: raw or the raw and bench profiles. - residency planner The code that admits a role's load only when the board keeps its floor after the engine's growth to its peak. - resident prefix The last prompt's rows, left in the engine's own buffers, with anchors, an end anchor, a stash, a pin and a park. - role Anything beside the big model the conductor asks, with a contract: its kind, claim, window, latency budget, fallback and what it may write. - round One draft, verify, accept and commit: about 93 ms and 4.58 tokens on the benchmark row. - router Two things. The conductor's router decides a turn's class and plan. The speculation router (StairCut, the length router) decides each round's draft tree. - safe point One of the four moments the session monitor may act: before the prefill, after a block, at the end token, at the held tool calls. - session resume Continuing a conversation from state that verify rounds wrote (the end anchor, the session spill) rather than prefill chunks. It is held to the greedy gate (the same tokens), not to bit equality; the taint row marks where it begins. - session monitor The conductor's watch over a running turn: loop guards, the empty-turn continue, tool-call checks, the claim check, session tasks. - session spill Whole live conversations written to the NVMe at a planned stop, while idle or before an eviction, and read back: the swap of long chats to the SSD (Live conversations on the NVMe). - shadow A mode in which a part decides and journals what it would do and changes nothing. - shadow reader A small model that keeps its own exact state of each session, read in idle time, and answers typed questions over the whole session. - side lane Serving a short request at a safe point inside the running generation, which then gets its engine state back bit for bit. Its text equals an uninterrupted run's only while the tree shapes are the same (Two runs of the same request). - side request A client's title or summary call, known by its shape and served small. - spill See session spill. - SSD Two things. The box's NVMe drive, where the session spill swaps long chats out (Live conversations on the NVMe). In NemotronH, Mamba2's chunked state-space form of the prefill (Nemotron 3.5 Bolt and Super VL). - StairCut The router that cuts each round's draft tree to the node count with the most expected tokens per millisecond on the measured verify-cost staircase. - state store Whole state snapshots, for the session cache and the prefix cache. - status line One short line in the client for a step the conductor takes, stripped from whatever the client sends back. - suffix store An append-only log of the token ids the engine read and wrote, with a suffix array, for the lookup drafter. - swap Two things. The swap of long chats to the SSD is the session spill (Live conversations on the NVMe). The park swaps two sessions' rows in the engine's memory (The resident prefix). - taint The lowest row that a session resume wrote. Below it the caches are a cold prefill's bit for bit. - TandemApp The dashboard, the proxy, the Chat tab, the conductor and TandemNode: a separate project with its own docs, tandem-app its command. It talks to the engine over HTTP, and its conductor runs inside the engine in chat mode as the extension. - time to first token The time from a request's arrival to its first streamed token: the prefill, plus any wait in the queue. TTFT in the tables. - ulp A unit in the last place: one rounding step of BF16 at a value. - verify One forward pass of the target model over the whole draft tree, reading the model's own token at every node. - voice The narrator's live lines: facts from the engine and a short checked phrase from the small model. - writer The background turn that writes a session's facts as memory notes at its end or after a compaction.

docs.title: Installing TandemEngine
docs.text: This page installs the engine. It runs the models and needs a CUDA GPU; its test board is the DGX Spark (The test environment). The dashboard, the Chat tab and the proxy are TandemApp, a separate project with its own docs: it needs only Python, runs on any machine, and talks to the engine over HTTP. Find your setup in the table below, then follow the sections it names.

docs.title: Setups, and which ones work
docs.text:
The engine runs alone, or behind TandemApp together with other engines and cloud APIs. The table below says which combinations work today, and how far each one is tested.

setup how state the engine alone install.sh on the board (this page) live the engine and cloud APIs, one address tandem-app on the board or another machine, with the engine and the cloud API as backends (TandemApp's docs) live, with DeepSeek the engine and other engines on other machines tandem-app as above, the other engines as vllm, sglang or generic backends (TandemApp's docs) built; vLLM and SGLang live behind the proxy on their own the engine and a second GPU engine on one larger machine each engine on its own GPU, tandem-app launch for the second built the engine and a second GPU engine on one DGX Spark the engine plans its memory as if it owns the board (up to 77 GiB during a prefill, plus its small models); a board out of memory stops answering until it is power cycled not supported

Setups and their state in this release. Live: run on the test board in the 0.4.0 series. Built: the code supports it and its tests pass, but no live run is recorded.

flowchart TD
    q1{"a machine with a CUDA GPU?<br/>(tested: DGX Spark)"} -- yes --> q2{"other engines or<br/>cloud APIs too?"}
    q1 -- no --> q3{"Python 3.11 or newer,<br/>or docker?"}
    q2 -- no --> A["Path A: the engine"]
    q3 -- yes --> B["Path B: TandemApp, the dashboard and proxy"]
    q2 -- yes --> C["Path C: several engines and cloud APIs behind one address"]
    A -. add backends .-> C
    B -. add backends .-> C

Which install path. A machine with the GPU gets the engine (path A); any other machine gets TandemApp, the dashboard and proxy (path B, TandemApp's docs); either grows into path C by adding backends behind TandemApp, which lists the engine as one backend among others (Other engines and cloud APIs beside the engine).

docs.title: What the engine needs
docs.text:
The engine is tested on one NVIDIA DGX Spark, a GB10 GPU (sm_121) with 128 GB of memory that the CPU and the GPU share, running Linux on aarch64. On another CUDA GPU the installer turns off the one kernel built for the GB10, and the engine runs best effort. The installer checks four things before it changes anything: an NVIDIA GPU and driver, the CUDA compiler (one kernel builds on its first use), about 70 GB of free disk, and 64 GiB of free memory at the start. With --setup it downloads only Wren's model, so it asks for about 5 GiB of disk beside the Python environment and 8 GiB of free memory; use-profile.sh checks the disk and the memory a profile needs before it downloads or starts it.

The software is pinned. The engine imports PyTorch 2.13 built for CUDA 13.0, torchvision 0.28 (the CUDA 13.0 build that matches that torch), Triton 3.7, transformers 5.12, Pillow 11.3, safetensors and numpy, and nothing else. Python 3.11 is the tested version; under 3.12 one grammar test fails. The installer's lock lists every package with its version, for aarch64 and x86_64.

Two of those packages are there for images. Pillow decodes a request's images, and torchvision is the backend of the image processor that the checkpoint ships. The engine pins that backend (--image-backend torchvision) and refuses to start without it, because transformers would otherwise fall back to its Pillow backend, whose patches differ by up to two 8-bit levels after a resize (measured, 0.4 % of the values of one resized image). Every cache keys on those patches, so the backend has to be fixed. --image-backend pil is the explicit choice without torchvision, and --vision off serves text only.

Run one engine per board. Two engines loading side by side run the board out of memory, and a DGX Spark in that state stops answering until it is power cycled. One engine per board explains how the scripts enforce it.

docs.title: A new box: setup mode, then the Setup Guide
docs.text:
Since 0.8.1 a new DGX Spark needs two commands and no Hugging Face token. Every file a profile reads is public on Hugging Face: our own packs, the vendors' releases, and turboderp's Flash-Next packs (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next).

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TandemLLM/TandemEngine/v0.16.0/install.sh
bash install.sh --setup --yes

The first line fetches the installer from the release tag. With --setup the installer puts the code and the Python environment in place and downloads only Wren's model (Qwen3.5-2B, 4.3 GB), the setup guide's assistant, and the two Wikipedia shards of the lookup corpus (1.2 GB). The corpus itself needs the model's tokenizer, so ops/use-profile.sh builds it once the model is on the disk. It writes the configuration with no weights and starts setup mode on 127.0.0.1:8000: the Setup Guide's API (/v1/setup/*), Wren, and no model loaded. The engine serves no page.

Then pick a model with the Setup Guide. The guide shows each model with its weight packs, checks that the choice fits in memory, downloads it and starts the engine; a new browser opens its simple form, three pages: the model, its weights, and one page of folded settings. The switch at the top brings back all eight steps, through the model, the weights, the tools and the parallel slots. docs/setup.md describes the page.

  • In a terminal on the box, run ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem setup: the same guide, step by step.
  • In a browser, use TandemApp's Setup page and point it at the engine, http://127.0.0.1:8000 on the box itself.
  • From another computer, open an SSH tunnel to the box first, ssh -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 <user>@<box>, and use the same address on that computer.
  • On your network, install with --host 0.0.0.0 and use http://<box>:8000 from any computer that reaches the box. Until an admin password is set, anyone who reaches the port can run the setup.

The installer prints the addresses when it finishes, and while the engine is in setup mode TandemApp's page opens on the Setup Guide by itself.

docs.title: Advanced: from the command line
docs.text:
The Setup Guide runs ops/use-profile.sh for you. To pick the weights from a shell instead, run the copy in ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/, next to the serve.env the installer wrote:

bash ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/use-profile.sh --list
bash ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/use-profile.sh <profile> --dry-run
bash ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/use-profile.sh <profile>

--list prints every profile and marks the active one. With --dry-run the script prints every file's URL and size and changes nothing. Without it, the script downloads what the profile needs and checks every weight file against the sha256 the hub lists. It then leaves setup mode, starts the engine on port 8000 and sends one smoke request. Since 0.8.2, community/<id> runs a pack someone else published (Community weights).

profile downloads size free disk flashnext-3.05 the pack's branch of turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3; the drafts' corrector (0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-EXL3-3.05-corrector, into ~/TandemLLM/src/ops/correctors/qwen3.8-flash-next) 85.1 + 0.035 GB 145 GB exl3-4.5 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-4.5; the K3 drafters and the K4 head (...-EXL3-drafters); the BF16 drafters (...-DFlash2-b8, -b16, into ~/TandemLLM/src/train); the base checkpoint Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8, without mtp.safetensors 18.4 + 1.9 + 7.7 + 30.4 GB 118 GB

What two of the profiles download on a new box. Free disk: the download plus the 60 GB the script keeps free after it.

A folder appears only when all its files are there. If a download stops, run the same command again: it keeps the files that finished and continues. The corrector file of flashnext-3.05 is checked against the sha256 the profile pins. If it does not download, the script prints a warning and goes on, and Flash-Next drafts without it: the same text, fewer drafts accepted. The engine then needs about 80 GiB of free memory for a 27B profile and 70 GiB for flashnext-3.05. If the profile does not come up, the script brings setup mode back.

The installer checks out the tag v0.16.0 from the repository --repo names, the public one by default. Where the tag is missing, curl fails with a 404, and the installer stops at its clone step with “no tag, branch or commit 'v0.16.0'”. --ref picks another release, and --repo another repository.

docs.title: Updating a box in setup mode
docs.text:
A box with a running profile counts as configured, and --setup alone refuses to touch it. To update, add --force-setup: the installer stops the engine, checks out the new tag and comes back in setup mode. Then switch to the profile again; its files are on disk already, so nothing downloads twice.

bash ~/TandemLLM/src/install.sh --setup --force-setup --yes --ref <new tag>
bash ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/use-profile.sh flashnext-3.05

docs.title: The installer
docs.text:
Without --setup, one command sets up the NVFP4 profile, StairCut included:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TandemLLM/TandemEngine/v0.16.0/install.sh | bash

The installer works in seven steps, and each step is skipped when it is already done, so running it again updates an install and resumes a download that stopped.

  1. Checks. The GPU needs its driver and the CUDA compiler, the disk and the memory need room, and Hugging Face must answer.
  2. The engine: a clone of the repository --repo names into ~/TandemLLM/src at the pinned release, v0.16.0.
  3. A Python venv in ~/TandemLLM/venv with the pinned packages; torch and torchvision come from the CUDA 13.0 index. If neither uv nor Python 3.11 is on the machine, the installer fetches uv first.
  4. The weights, into the normal Hugging Face cache: the vendor's FP8 checkpoint (it supplies the tensors the NVFP4 overlays do not replace, and the tokenizer), the four NVFP4 files and both fine-tuned drafters. With --setup, only Wren's model; use-profile.sh fetches the rest later.
  5. A lookup corpus built from public text (one English and one German Wikipedia shard, plus Python sources from the venv's own packages, about 31 million tokens). --no-corpus skips it. With --setup, only the two shards: use-profile.sh builds the corpus for the model it installs, under corpus/tokenizers/, with no network.
  6. The configuration: ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/serve.env, the release's ops/serve.env with this machine's paths, and a control script, ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem.
  7. The start: the engine starts, the script waits for /health, and a smoke test prints tokens a second. --no-start stops after step 6.

The weights are public. --hf-token (or HF_TOKEN) is needed only for a repository that is private or gated, and a stored hf auth login works too. The table in commands lists every option; the most used ones are --setup (A new box: setup mode, then the Setup Guide), --repo (another repository, such as a fork), --dir (default ~/TandemLLM), --port and --host (default 127.0.0.1:8000), --ref (any git ref; v0.2.0-staircut is the paper's release), --hf-token, --systemd for a systemd user unit, --dry-run to print every step and change nothing, and --uninstall.

reference/commands.md lists every option.

The installer's corpus is not the corpus the paper's numbers come from; that one is not published. With the installer's corpus, or with --no-corpus, the lookup drafter proposes different continuations, so speeds can differ from the paper's. How much is not measured. On a CUDA GPU other than the GB10 the installer turns off the skinny NVFP4 kernel, which is built for sm_121a only, and StairCut's cost tables still come from the Spark, so such GPUs are best effort.

docs.title: After the install
docs.text:
The install directory holds everything the installer wrote:

path what ~/TandemLLM/src the repository at the installed release ~/TandemLLM/venv the Python environment, about 8 GiB with the CUDA wheels ~/TandemLLM/corpus the lookup corpus ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/serve.env the served profile with this machine's paths, rewritten on every run of the installer ~/TandemLLM/run/local.env your own settings; serve.env reads it last and the installer never touches it ~/TandemLLM/state the tokens file (the metrics token, and the admin password if you set one), once you create it ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem the control script ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/ the engine's state: the usage ledger, the conductor's documents and journal, memory notes, the disk tier, small models

The layout of an installed engine.

The control script takes one command:

~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem start      # ops/start.sh with run/ops/serve.env; waits for /health
~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem stop 120   # SIGTERM, wait for the drain, kill only after it
~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem restart
~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem status
~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem smoke      # /v1/models and one short completion, with tok/s
~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem logs       # follow the engine's log

docs.title: Engine only, or the chat (beta)
docs.text:
A new install serves the engine alone: the OpenAI API under the served model's own name, the dashboard reads under /v1/dashboard/* and the caches. Nothing runs beside it: no extension (no TandemLLM model, router, user memory, packages, library or session monitor), no decision models, narrator, shadow reader or roles. One setting decides it, QSE_MODE in serve.env: engine or chat.

In chat mode (beta) the engine loads TandemApp's conductor as its extension (QSE_EXT), with the small models the weight profile names; TandemApp's TandemNode runs chatd, the Chat tab's service, and the engine runs none. Turn it on with install.sh --with-chat --app-wheel FILE, TandemApp's wheel (a re-run works too), with the Setup Guide's Chat (beta) switch, which writes QSE_MODE=chat to run/setup.env and turns on Laya's decision models with it, or with QSE_MODE=chat in run/local.env and tandem restart. --engine-only turns it off again, and TandemNode stops a running chatd once the engine comes up in engine mode. On a box set up in the Setup Guide its switch decides: run/setup.env is read after the installer's QSE_MODE, so the two flags there only warn. The last block of ops/serve.env applies the mode after the weight profile, run/setup.env and run/local.env; ops/use-profile.sh keeps it.

An upgrade keeps each box's mode. Left empty, QSE_MODE is chat on a box whose conductor directory (QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG, by default ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/conductor) exists, so a box that ran the conductor stays a chat box with its documents, memory and sessions; QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG=off set by hand stays engine only. /health and /v1/models say "mode": "engine" or "chat" and what is loaded: the conductor and its monitor's mode, the decision models, the narrator, the loaded roles, and whether chatd answers; extensions names the extension that runs.

docs.title: The first request
docs.text:
The server speaks the OpenAI API on port 8000. In engine-only mode it serves the engine under its own model name (/v1/models lists it). With the chat on, it serves one model called TandemLLM, and any model name a client sends is served as TandemLLM:

curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model": "TandemLLM", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello."}]}'

Point other clients at the same address:

client setting an OpenAI SDK OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://<host>:8000/v1 and any key opencode an OpenAI-compatible provider with that base URL and the model TandemLLM; with the chat (beta) on it gets the coding profile by itself Open WebUI an OpenAI connection to that base URL, with the connection header X-OpenWebUI-Chat-Id: {{CHAT_ID}} so each chat is its own conductor session with the chat (beta) on (TandemApp's docs on profiles and the router); it gets the chat profile curl, a script as above; with the chat (beta) on it gets the general profile

Pointing a client at the engine.

An engine-only box (Engine only, or the chat (beta)) has no profiles: every client gets the raw path under the served model's own name, so opencode and Open WebUI name that model instead of TandemLLM. With the chat (beta) on, the header X-Tandem: raw gives the engine without the conductor for one request. That is the release's raw path, the one the benchmarks and the paper measure. TandemApp's docs explains the profiles (“Profiles and the router”).

Open WebUI with TandemLLM as its model: a demo request on the test board in October 2026, served under the chat profile, with the reasoning folded into “Thought for 1 seconds”. Only the message pane is shown.

opencode with TandemLLM as its provider: the end of a demo task on the test board in October 2026, under the coding profile. The model added a function, tested it, asked Laya for a verdict on the test log, removed its scratch files and reported what it did. The screenshot is from a build that sent the reasoning to opencode as text between <think> tags; every client but the Hermes agent now gets reasoning_content by default (QWEN38_CLIENT_REASONING), which opencode shows as folded reasoning parts.

The engine asks for no password; read Access and sign-in before anyone else can reach the port.

docs.title: Access and sign-in
docs.text:
TandemLLM has no sign-in turned on by default. The engine's OpenAI routes are always open, and so is everything else until you set an admin password: the dashboard, the conductor's settings, the memory notes, the transcripts, the decision models, the configuration and the cache routes. Anyone who reaches the port can read and change them. The installer binds the engine to 127.0.0.1, so only the machine itself reaches it. With --host 0.0.0.0, or when you start ops/serve.env from a checkout (its HOST is 0.0.0.0), the whole local network does.

The table below has the switches. Only /metrics has a token of its own, for a Prometheus scraper, and ops/make-secrets.sh writes that one alone unless --admin asks for the password too.

what by default with the switch the engine's OpenAI routes anyone who reaches the port no switch on the engine's own port; behind TandemApp, an account's session or an API token the dashboard's reads anyone --dashboard-login on and a password: the token or a session admin routes: conductor writes, memory, decision models, configuration, caches, the full /health anyone QSE_ADMIN_TOKEN (ops/make-secrets.sh --admin): the token or a session, or a tool on the machine itself /metrics anyone QSE_METRICS_TOKEN: that token

Who can reach what, by default and with the switches set.

The page, accounts, sessions and API tokens are TandemApp's (TandemApp's sign-in); the engine has no sign-in screen. A request from the machine itself (loopback, without proxy headers) needs no token, because the watchdog and the measurement tools rely on that.

TandemLLM serves one user. Every client that reaches the engine is that user, so a “remember that” from any client lands in the same memory notes. A request that must not touch them sends X-Tandem-Memory: off. Until sign-in and several users arrive, keep the port on loopback or a trusted network. To reach it from elsewhere, put a reverse proxy with its own sign-in, or a VPN, in front of it.

docs.title: The small models
docs.text:
Three small models can run beside the main model. They are off in the shipped profile, because each needs its weights on the disk. Each is one line in local.env and a restart.

part set in local.env the model Laya, the decision models QWEN38_DECIDER_MODELS=laya-english,laya-multilingual,laya-typed-decisions convaiinnovations/laya under ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/deciders/laya the narrator's voice QWEN38_NARRATOR_MODEL=qwen3.5-2b Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B under ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/models/qwen3.5-2b the shadow reader QWEN38_SHADOW_MODEL=qwen3.5-0.8b Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B under ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/models/qwen3.5-0.8b

The small models and the line that turns each on.

Download a model with hf download <repo> --local-dir <dir>. The small models load after the engine, one at a time, through the residency planner, which refuses a load that would leave the board short of memory (Roles beside the engine). The dashboard's System view shows what is loaded.

docs.title: Other engines and cloud APIs beside the engine
docs.text: The engine serves its own model only. Other engines and cloud APIs sit behind TandemApp's controller, tandem-app, on the board or another machine, with the engine as a backend of kind tandemllm (TandemApp's docs). Since engine API 1.8 the engine takes --backends (QSE_BACKENDS in serve.env) only as off: any other value stops the start with one line that says what to do, before anything loads. A box that relayed before moves its config database with tandem-app import-backends --from <file>, then turns the line off with tandem doctor --retire-backends, which keeps it as a dated comment; the installer's re-run and the Setup Guide stop before they change anything until then (docs/operations.md, “Other backends moved to TandemApp”). On a DGX Spark the other backends are cloud APIs or engines on other machines; a second GPU engine on the same Spark is not supported (the table below).

docs.title: Running from a checkout
docs.text:
The installer does nothing you cannot do by hand. In an environment with the packages above, download the published weights and drafters with hf, the Hugging Face CLI (pip install -U huggingface_hub):

hf download Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8
hf download 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --local-dir ~/tandem/nvfp4
hf download 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-b8 --local-dir ~/tandem/ft-b8
hf download 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-b16 --local-dir ~/tandem/ft-b16

Then edit the path lines at the top of ops/serve.env: REPO (the checkout), PY (a Python with the packages), NV (the three NVFP4 files, mlp, gdn and attn, comma-separated), HEAD (head-fp8.safetensors), CKPT8, CKPT16 and CORPUS. Start it with bash ops/start.sh. That is the served profile.

In a PyTorch container that already has torch 2.13.0+cu130, add the two image packages:

pip install pillow==11.3.0 torchvision==0.28.0+cu130 \
    --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130

A server started directly with python server/app.py and no further flags is the raw engine. The conductor, the disk tier and the usage ledger come only with --conductor-config, --disk-cache and --usage-ledger, which ops/start.sh passes from QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG, QSE_DISK_CACHE and QSE_USAGE_LEDGER. To try the engine with the vendor's base drafter instead of the fine-tuned ones:

hf download z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2
python server/app.py --port 8000 --max-len 32768 --drafter dflash2 --dflash2-path greedy \
    --nvfp4 ~/tandem/nvfp4/mlp.safetensors,~/tandem/nvfp4/gdn.safetensors,~/tandem/nvfp4/attn.safetensors \
    --fp8-head ~/tandem/nvfp4/head-fp8.safetensors

docs.title: Building the weights yourself
docs.text:
The published NVFP4 set was quantised once from Qwen's BF16 release with GPTQ on the NVFP4 grid. Rebuilding it needs the BF16 checkpoint and a GPU with about 80 GB of memory at the default --h-budget-gb 22; it took 25 minutes on an RTX PRO 6000 (measured):

hf download Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B
python tools/calib_corpus.py --out ~/calib
python tools/quant_nvfp4.py build --model <the BF16 snapshot> --methods gptq --out-dir ~/nvfp4-bf16 \
    --corpus ~/calib/calib-code.txt:80000,~/calib/calib-en.txt:60000,~/calib/calib-de.txt:16000
python tools/quant_head.py build --out ~/nvfp4-bf16/head-fp8.safetensors --ratios 1.0,0.95,0.90

The build writes gptq/mlp.safetensors, gdn.safetensors and attn.safetensors; tools/quality_gate.py --plan scores them against the BF16 model. The engine loads them over the FP8 checkpoint, as it does the published files. Quantisation explains the method and the gate.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
A serving profile is a serve.env file: which weights, which drafters, which settings. Three ship with the NVFP4 set. They differ only in their weights; drafters, StairCut, caches and the exactness gate are the same in all three. The weight profiles under ops/profiles/ are the other kind: nvfp4, six exl3-<bpw> sizes of the 27B and five flashnext-<bpw> packs, which ops/use-profile.sh switches between one engine at a time (One model at a time).

profile file weights bytes a step NVFP4 (served) ops/serve.env the published set: every projection NVFP4, FP8 head 15.0 GB balanced ops/serve-balanced.env the published NVFP4 MLPs and FP8 head; the checkpoint's FP8 recurrent and attention layers about 18.2 GB FP8 ops/serve-fp8.env the checkpoint's own FP8 projections and BF16 head 26.9 GB

The three serving profiles. Only the NVFP4 profile's speed is measured on this release; the bytes a step are (arithmetic) from the tensor sizes.

The balanced and FP8 profiles source ops/serve.env and change two lines, NV and HEAD. They inherit StairCut's verify prices, which were measured on the NVFP4 profile. The router corrects their level online, but the staircase's shape for those two profiles is not measured, and neither is their speed. Do not confuse these files with the conductor's profiles (coding, chat and the others), which are documents the dashboard edits.

docs.title: Upgrading and uninstalling
docs.text:
To upgrade, run the installer again with the same --dir. It checks out the new release, installs the new lock and rewrites serve.env from the release's template; local.env stays, and so does the box's mode (Engine only, or the chat (beta)). The usage ledger migrates in place at the first start: columns are added and every row is kept. A box installed with --setup and switched to a profile since then upgrades with --setup --force-setup and the profile switch after it, as Updating a box in setup mode shows.

Coming from 0.3.0, a client sees these changes:

  • The conductor is on in the shipped profile. /v1/models lists TandemLLM alone, every response carries the headers X-Tandem and X-Tandem-Profile, and every request runs through the router, with a real cap on the thinking per effort level. X-Tandem: raw gives the release path of 0.3.0. A benchmark client that cannot send a header should run against a server with CONDUCTOR=raw and an empty QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG in local.env.
  • The disk tier and the session spill are on: up to 50 GB under ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/cache/disk, never below 50 GB free on the disk. QSE_DISK_CACHE=off turns both off.
  • A streamed request that finds the engine busy waits as long as a request may run, with an SSE comment every 10 s, instead of a 429 after 240 s. A short request is served between two blocks of the running turn.
  • The image processor's backend is pinned to torchvision.
  • A malformed tools field is a 400 that names the item.
  • The memory limits are enforced: 70 GiB between requests, 77 GiB during a prefill.

To run 0.4.0 as 0.3.0 was served, put CONDUCTOR=raw, an empty QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG= and QSE_DISK_CACHE=off in local.env.

To roll back, run the installer with --ref set to the earlier tag; the ledger keeps its added columns and the older release ignores them. To uninstall:

bash ~/TandemLLM/src/install.sh --uninstall --yes

This stops the engine, removes the systemd unit if one was installed, and deletes the install directory. It keeps the weights in the Hugging Face cache, which other tools may share, and ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/ with the conductor's documents, the journal, memory notes, transcripts, the disk tier and the small models. Delete that directory to remove them too.

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text:
Decode on this board is a memory-read problem. Every round must read the projection weights once (about 13.7 GB of the 15 GB at NVFP4), and the GB10 GPU reads memory at about 235 to 240 GB/s in practice. A kernel is good here when it streams those bytes near that rate at the row counts a verify uses, which is 1 to 32 rows.

This page covers the matrix-product kernels, the recurrent-layer kernels, the head, and the one property every kernel must keep: a row's result may not depend on the other rows in the batch.

docs.title: Row invariance
docs.text:
Take a row of a 1-row product and the same row as row 5 of a 16-row product. Its result must be the same bits in both cases. The exactness gate compares speculative output against one-token-at-a-time output, and that comparison can only hold if the arithmetic of a row ignores its neighbours.

TandemLLM gets this by fixing the reduction order. Every tile table is keyed by the weight's shape (N, K), never by the row count, so the sum over K runs in the same order at 1 row and at 32. No kernel uses atomics, whose order would depend on the scheduler. Where K is split across warps, the partial sums are added in warp order. tools/fp8_probe.py --sweep keeps only FP8 tile choices that are bit-identical to the default at 1 to 32 rows, and the NVFP4 tables follow the same rule.

Row invariance is what keeps a tree verify, and later parallel requests, close to the one-token decode. It does not make them identical: the output head uses a different kernel for one row than for several, and the verify path of the recurrent and attention layers orders the one-token arithmetic differently, so a near tie between the two best tokens can go the other way. exactness.md has the full contract and its measured exception.

docs.title: Verify twins
docs.text:
A verify twin is the multi-row form of a one-row decode kernel, and its rows must be the one-row call's bits. The convention for kernel authors (ENG-221, from the Kolibri kernels):

  • The twin of a kernel is the same entry point called with M rows when the kernel is row-invariant by construction (every Flash-Next kernel in tools/fn_kernels.py: gemv, mix_up, router, moe, the norms), and an entry point named <kernel>_rows beside the one-row kernel when the one-row kernel is specialised.
  • By construction means a row's instruction sequence does not depend on M: the row, or the (row, expert) pair of a mixture of experts, owns its program on a grid axis; a split of K over warps or cluster ranks depends on the weight's shape only; partials are added in a fixed order; no atomics.
  • The test for a twin compares an M-row call with M one-row calls bit for bit, for M = 2 to 32, with rows that share inputs (for experts: rows that pick the same experts). tests/gpu/test_fn_kernels_gpu.py is the pattern.
  • The launch order of the programs may change, the arithmetic may not: the MoE kernels launch the pairs in ascending expert id so rows that share an expert read its tiles back to back from L2.

docs.title: Prefill kernels (Flash-Next, ENG-225)
docs.text:
A prompt chunk is not verified against anything, so its kernels have no twin contract: they share work across rows and are checked by next-token agreement (tools/fn_prefill_check.py): the kernel path against the decode path at least as close as the decode path is to the reference forward (within one point), no disagreement where both paths are sure (margins above 5), greedy continuations equal or first differing at a near tie. It is reported as agreement and margins, never as lossless. tools/fn_prefill_kernels.py:

  • moe_grouped: a chunk's (row, expert) pairs sorted by expert, each pair's input rotated with its expert's factors into the mma A-fragment order (an expert's rows padded to 16, one 16-byte load a lane and row tile), one GEMM over the experts' row groups that decodes each expert's trellis tiles once for up to 32 rows. The CTAs of one item (its matrix and column blocks) are adjacent on the grid, so its rows stream from memory once.
  • mm_rows: the mixers, the router, PLE and GDN a/b on the library GEMM with the weights exact in fp32 (QWEN38_FN_PREFILL_MM=fp32; fp16 weights failed the agreement gate at 3k). tc and tcn put the int8 weights on the tensor cores with nothing rounded (bf16 inputs, fp32 sums a scale group, the group's sum times its scale): tc a Triton kernel, tcn the native mix_gemm_kernel, which also applies the mixer's tail to its up products and writes x in bf16. Both are off by default, and neither gives fp32's bits.
  • qsa_scores_rows: a chunk's QSA block scores as one GEMM, the reference's arithmetic.
  • Attention, the GDN conv and gates, the PLE gate and conv reuse the decode path's sequence kernels with M rows (attn_rows, gdn_pre, ple_gate, ple_conv); the delta rule is tools/gdn_prefill_kernels.py with the key heads as they are.

QWEN38_FN_PREFILL=ref keeps the reference's batched forward; QWEN38_FN_PREFILL_CHUNK is the chunk length (4,096). QWEN38_FN_GROUP_ROWS is the rows an item of the MoE group GEMM takes (64; 32 is the earlier tile, any other value refuses at import).

Layer-major windows (SPD-249, engine/models/flashnext/layer_major.py): a prompt's chunks can run layer by layer in windows, each layer's experts once over the window's rows and the rest a chunk at a time at its own rows, so every chunk keeps the bits of its chunk-major forward. Each of these knobs gives the same bits on and off:

  • QWEN38_FN_PF_WINDOW: the most rows a layer-major window takes (a multiple of the chunk); 8,192 by default. A window sizes itself to free memory: before it runs it asks the server's memory policy for its bytes above the chunks' own workspace (the engine's peak and the admission's floor, layer_major.window_bytes), and holds them until the prefill has run; when they are not there the chunks run one at a time. QWEN38_FN_PF_WINDOW=0 restores the previous path (chunk-major).
  • QWEN38_FN_PF_ROT_ROWS: 1 rotates a chunk's (row, expert) pairs in row order, a row read once, each pair's arithmetic the same; 0 (the default) keeps the grouped order.
  • QWEN38_FN_PF_HC_FUSED: 1 feeds a chunk's mixer GEMMs from fewer launches (tools/fn_pf_hc.py), in every QWEN38_FN_PREFILL_MM mode (the default); 0 keeps the separate launches.
  • QWEN38_FN_PF_INJ_FUSED: 1 runs a chunk's hyper-connection inject and the next norm in one CTA a row (the default); 0 keeps fn_kernels.inject_norm.
  • QWEN38_FN_PF_ATTN_STAGES: the pipeline stages (1 to 4) of a chunk's attention split launch, a launch setting only; 1 by default, 2 is the decode path's launch.
  • QWEN38_FN_PF_NOCOPY: 1 (the default) leaves out a chunk's copies that a view or the reading kernel's stride serves; 0 keeps the copies.

Decode (SPD-249), both on by default and bit-equal to the path they replace:

  • QWEN38_FN_PACK_GRAPH: a packed MTP draft's steps after the feed (each lane's draft head, top-2 and coupled pick, the one-row MTP steps) replay from one CUDA graph a lane count; 0 runs them eager. tools/fn_pack_graph_check.py compares the two.
  • QWEN38_FN_ROUTE_FUSED: an MoE call of up to 32 rows takes its router, pad ids and expert order or groups from one launch (fn_kernels.route); 0 keeps the router, mask, sort and groups launches. tools/fn_route_check.py compares the two.

tools/fn_window_check.py and tools/fn_pf_hc_check.py compare a prefill with the knobs off and on, bit for bit; tools/fn_prefill_mm_ref.py checks the QWEN38_FN_PREFILL_MM modes against a prefill with fp64 mixers.

docs.title: NVFP4 matrix products
docs.text:
The weights are 4-bit and the activations 16-bit (W4A16). The engine never uses the FP4 tensor-core path. On this chip an FP4 operand still has to travel through shared memory and a decode step before a tensor core sees it, and the chip has 99 KB of shared memory per SM. A 4-bit activation path would also need its own quantiser and quality gate, to save at most the 8 % of traffic the activations are.

Three kernels share one stored format and pick by row count:

rows kernel file 1 to 32 (decode and verify) the skinny kernel, CUDA tools/nvfp4_skinny.py 33 to about 1,024 (prefill chunks) Triton, v2 tools/nvfp4_linear_v2.py above that expand to BF16 once, then the library GEMM tools/nvfp4_linear.py

The skinny kernel rests on one fact about the hardware. The instruction cvt.rn.f16x2.e2m1x2 turns one packed byte into one register holding two 16-bit values, and that register is exactly the operand layout of an mma.m16n8k16 tensor-core instruction. A thread loads 16 bytes of a weight row with one vector load and decodes each byte straight into an operand register, so nothing goes through shared memory. The group scale is decoded by cvt.rn.f16x2.e4m3x2 and multiplied onto the weight in fp16. That product is exact: e2m1 times e4m3 needs six significant bits, and fp16 has eleven. The weights are the B operand (8 rows an instruction) and the activations the A operand (16 rows an instruction). A 16-row verify therefore costs one instruction per weight tile, and 17 to 32 rows cost two.

It builds on first use from tools/csrc/nvfp4_skinny/ with torch.utils.cpp_extension for sm_121a, because the e2m1 converter is specific to that chip. A tile table per shape (ops/skinny-tiles.json up to 16 rows, ops/skinny-tiles-wide.json for 17 to 32) holds the launch settings the sweep picked.

docs.title: FP8 matrix products
docs.text: tools/fp8_linear.py reads the checkpoint's block-scaled FP8 as stored: e4m3 codes with one BF16 scale per 128 by 128 block. The tile is 128 wide along K so that each step covers one scale block. For the plain-FP8 profile, ops/fp8-tiles.json holds one launch setting per shape for every row count up to 32. The profile then walks and verifies with a single program shape per weight.

docs.title: The recurrent layers
docs.text:
A Gated DeltaNet layer updates a 128 by 128 state per head at every token:

S <- S * exp(g)
delta <- (v - S^T k) * beta
S <- S + k (x) delta
out <- S^T q

Each shape of this work has its own kernel:

work kernel what it does one token tools/gdn_kernels.py loads a state tile once, applies the whole step in registers, stores once a verify chain tools/gdn_verify_kernels.py walks up to 16 tokens over one loaded tile and returns the factors a rollback needs a verify tree tools/gdn_tree_kernels.py, tools/gdn_verify_kernels.py walks the tree in depth-first order, rebuilding each node's parent state from a stack of factors along its path a commit tools/gdn_commit_kernels.py writes the accepted path's state as one low-rank update a prefill tools/gdn_prefill_kernels.py the chunked form, with the chunk-local work kept in registers

Trees rely on depth-first order. When the walk reaches a node at depth d, the last node it visited at each shallower depth is that node's ancestor. A stack of one set of factors per depth therefore holds exactly the node's own path, and the kernel rebuilds the parent's state from the round's entry state. speculative-decoding.md explains the identity behind this.

In the served build the commit happens inside the next verify. The accepted rows are recorded, and the next verify applies them to each state tile as it loads it. That halves the state traffic of a round, from 604 MB to 302 MB.

A Gated DeltaNet layer updates a 128 by 128 state per head at every token:

S ← S · e^g
δ ← (v − Sᵀk) · β
S ← S + k ⊗ δ
o ← Sᵀq

Each shape of this work has its own kernel:

docs.title: Head, norms, attention
docs.text:
Two kernels serve the output head. tools/head_gemv.py handles one row, and a tensor-core GEMM handles more than one. At one row a GEMV reads fastest. At eight rows the same GEMV does eight times the scalar work without a tensor core, and a verify once ran 2.5 times slower because of that. Both kernels return fp32 logits.

Each RMS norm is one kernel instead of eight small ones, written with the reference's own rounding points (tools/norm_kernels.py). The gated norm of the recurrent layers rounds to BF16 between the weight multiply and the gate, and doing that multiply in fp32 changes the answer.

Attention uses the library's fused attention with a causal flag, a lower-right causal mask for chunks that start past position 0, and a decode kernel for short query counts.

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text: Every verify runs from CUDA graphs (engine/verify_graph.py), one per shape of round: chain or tree, row count, context class, flags. Positions and lengths live in device buffers, so one captured graph serves every round of that shape. Graphs took the launch gaps inside a verify from about 4.5 ms to about 1.5 ms. The drafter's forward runs from graphs too (engine/drafters/draft_graph.py). Graphed and eager runs agree bit for bit, and the tests check that.

docs.title: Where the source lives
docs.text:
The CUDA and C++ kernels are source files, compiled on first use with torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline and cached under ~/.cache/torch_extensions. A module <dir>/<name>.py that builds one keeps its sources in <dir>/csrc/<name>/:

file holds <unit>.cu a CUDA body (cuda_sources) <unit>.cpp the bindings' declarations, or host C++ (cpp_sources) <unit>.h declarations the build name hashes patches/<what>.old.cuh, patches/<what>.new.cuh a text a shared kernel's source holds once, and what a variant puts in its place

The module reads each file at import (engine/native_build.py source, the bytes as written) and assembles what it compiles in Python: the #define lines its knobs set, the slices it takes of a shared source (Flash-Next's kernels take the EXL3 decode helpers from tools/csrc/exl3_linear/exl3.cu), a variant's rewrites. It builds with native_build.load, under a name that ends in native_build.tag of the compiled text, so an edited kernel is a new build directory and two trees on one board never rebuild over each other.

folder built by kernels tools/csrc/exl3_linear/ tools/exl3_linear.py the EXL3 skinny GEMM, its rotations, the prefill reconstruct tools/csrc/exl3_tall/ tools/exl3_tall.py the EXL3 64-row tiles and the shared kernel's variants tools/csrc/exl3_relu2/ tools/exl3_relu2.py the EXL3 squared-ReLU expert bank tools/csrc/nvfp4_skinny/ tools/nvfp4_skinny.py the NVFP4 skinny kernel tools/csrc/fn_kernels/, tools/csrc/fn_seq_kernels/, tools/csrc/fn_prefill_kernels/ tools/fn_kernels.py, tools/fn_seq_kernels.py, tools/fn_prefill_kernels.py Flash-Next's decode, sequence and prefill kernels engine/csrc/native_tree/ engine/native_tree.py the block drafter's host walk and lattice tree (C++) engine/models/qwen3_5/csrc/frag/, engine/models/qwen3_5/round/csrc/lattice/ the 27B's frag.py, round/lattice.py its fragment-major EXL3 path, its round's lattice tree (C++) tools/csrc/l2_prefetch_bench/ tools/l2_prefetch_bench.py the L2 prefetch probe

A family's own kernels stay in its package (engine/models/<family>/csrc/); shared code never names a family (adding-a-model.md).

The fingerprint reads these files. engine/methods/manifest.py files lists, after each module of a model's manifest and each tools/ module those import, the files of the module's csrc/ folder, then engine/native_build.py. An edit to a kernel file moves the fingerprint of every model whose manifest reaches its module, and of no other (tests/test_native_sources.py).

docs.title: How a kernel gets in
docs.text:
Every kernel has a check() against the PyTorch function it replaces, and it answers to that before anyone times it. Only the engine's own round time decides whether it ships, measured with the flag flipped inside one process (measurement.md). A standalone timing is a ranking at best. The same NVFP4 configuration once read 0.254 ms in one process and 0.627 ms in another, and the two processes differed only in what they had allocated before.

Time a kernel over a working set larger than the chip's caches. tools/cold_bw.py does. A warm probe once reported 97.6 % of peak memory bandwidth on a GEMM, which is not possible.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text:
Each kernel path has a QWEN38_* switch, and ops/serve.env sets the served combination. engine/settings.py lists every switch with its default, and python -c "from engine.settings import SETTINGS; print(SETTINGS.describe())" prints the values in effect.

knob what QWEN38_NVFP4_SKINNY, QWEN38_SKINNY_TILES, QWEN38_SKINNY_TILES_WIDE the skinny kernel and its tile tables QWEN38_FP8_TILES the FP8 per-shape launch table QWEN38_FUSED_GDNVERIFY, QWEN38_GDNV_WY* the fused verify recurrence and its variants QWEN38_COMMIT_IN_VERIFY fold the commit into the next verify QWEN38_VERIFY_GRAPH, QWEN38_DRAFT_GRAPH CUDA graphs for the verify and the drafter QWEN38_FUSED_GDNPREFILL, QWEN38_NVFP4_PREFILL_V2 the prefill paths

docs.title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B
docs.text:
LiquidAI's LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the third model TandemLLM runs, beside Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Support ships in release 0.9.0. The model has 24B parameters; 4 of its 64 experts run for each token. It is a chat model and the fastest model on this engine.

Code: engine/models/lfm2_moe/ (registry name lfm2_moe, selected by Lfm2MoeForCausalLM in config.json). Setup Guide entry: models/lfm2.5-24b-a2b/model.yaml. Measurements: models/lfm2.5-24b-a2b/measurements/0.8.3-summary.json.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
part value layers 40: 30 short-convolution layers, 10 attention layers (indices 2, 6, 10, ..., 38) short convolution in_proj 2,048 to 3 x 2,048 (B, C, x); y = C * conv(B * x), 3 taps, one filter a channel; out_proj. State: the last 2 inputs B * x a layer, 240 KiB a sequence attention 32 query heads, 8 KV heads of 64; q and k RMS-normed per head; rotary over the whole head (theta 1e7). KV: 20,480 bytes a token, 2.5 GiB at 131,072 tokens MLP layers 0 and 1: dense SwiGLU, 11,776 wide. Layers 2 to 39: 64 SwiGLU experts, 1,536 wide, 4 a token, no shared expert router sigmoid of each expert's logit; a per-expert bias selects the 4; the 4 sigmoids are renormalised head tied to the 128,000-token embedding context 131,072 tokens

A decode token reads 4.9 GB of the BF16 weights: experts 2.87 GB, convolution projections 1.01, head 0.52, dense MLPs 0.29, attention 0.21 (PackIndex.decode_bytes). The decode step runs about 400 kernels, so it is one CUDA graph.

A decode token of LiquidAI's LFM2.5-24B-A2B reads 4.91 GB of its BF16 weights and 1.31 GB of our 4.0-bit EXL3 pack (arithmetic, from the headers), because only 4 of its 64 experts run in each of 38 layers. On one DGX Spark the engine decodes it at 188.2 tok/s from the 2.5 pack, 153.5 tok/s from the default 3.5 pack and 44.8 tok/s in BF16 (measured, 2026-10-14). It is the third model the engine serves and the first that is not a Qwen; its support ships in release 0.9.0. Adding a model describes the adapter path it came in through.

A short-convolution layer projects the normed input to three vectors B, C and x of 2,048, takes B times x, runs a depthwise convolution of 3 taps over that product along the sequence, multiplies by C and projects back. Its state is the last two products, so a sequence keeps 30 layers times 2 times 2,048 values. The router takes the sigmoid of each expert's logit, adds a per-expert bias to choose the 4, and renormalises the 4 chosen sigmoids. engine/models/lfm2_moe/config.py reads the configuration and stops on a field it does not know.

docs.text:
DGX Spark, 2026-10-14. Decode step: tools/lfm_check.py bench, one request, 256 tokens, from its graph. Chat: one greedy request through the server, 512 tokens, thinking off, plain / lookup. Quality: exllamav3 model_diff against BF16, 20 rows of 2,048 tokens of oasst1 chat and of wikitext-2. Engine KL: tools/lfm_quality.py, 100 rows of oasst1 chat.
