  • Packs: exllamav3 1.6.0, mul1 codebook, head 6 bits (8 for 6.0), default calibration. One Hugging Face repository a size, 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-LFM2.5-24B-A2B-EXL3-<bpw>, pinned by commit (QSE_WEIGHTS_REVISION). The repositories are public; a download needs no token. Every file is checked against the hub's sha256.
  • Default: lfm25-exl3-3.5. Rule: the fastest profile in chat as served (lookup on) with chat top-1 against BF16 of at least 85 %. 3.5: 143.7 tok/s at 86.7 %. 3.0: 168.5 tok/s at 83.6 %, below the floor.
  • Setup Guide tile: the fastest cell of the default profile's served row, 147.5 tok/s (3.5, prose).
  • -hq 4.0 (attention and convolution projections +2 bits, dense MLPs +1, 4.06 bpw, 12.81 GB): chat KL 0.082, top-1 89.7 %; served chat 131.2 tok/s against 144.0 for 4.0 and 127.6 for 4.5 in one window. Not offered.
  • The KL values are high for these rates. The same recipe on the 8B sibling at 4.10 bpw gives KL 0.0955 against 0.0862 for a reference conversion. The cause on the 24B is not known.
  • Half-integer rates: below 4 bpw exllamav3 1.6.0 gives some tensors 1.5, 2.5 or 3.5 bits a weight (a tile is 16 K + 8 int16 wide; an odd weight takes one bit more than an even one). The 2.5 and 3.5 packs use them. The EXL3 kernels decode them as the format defines (tools/exl3_linear.py, dq8_frac; bit codes 15, 25, 35) in the decode step, a verify block and the prefill. The pack reader refuses an unsupported rate or codebook by tensor name.

Switch: ops/use-profile.sh lfm25-exl3-3.5, or the Setup Guide (#/setup).

docs.title: Chat, reasoning and tools
docs.text:
• Template: the checkpoint's chat_template.jinja. It opens <think> at the end of every prompt; the server splits reasoning from the answer as for Qwen (server.md).
  • Thinking off (chat_template_kwargs: {"enable_thinking": false}, or the conductor's): the server closes the block right after the generation prompt.
  • Tool calls: a Python list between <|tool_call_start|> and <|tool_call_end|>, for example <|tool_call_start|>[get_weather(city='Berlin', days=3)]<|tool_call_end|>. server/api/toolcall.py (PythonicCalls) rewrites each block into the JSON tool tier as the text arrives; the client gets OpenAI tool_calls. Values are Python literals (and true, false, null), read with ast.literal_eval, never run. A block that is not a list of keyword calls stays text.
  • Sampling default when a request names none: temperature 0.1, top_k 50, repetition penalty 1.05 (TEMPERATURE, TOP_K, REP_PENALTY).
  • Conductor: on by default, with the model fit below (Conductor).

docs.title: Conductor
docs.text:
The conductor (Laya's three decision models, the narrator, the session monitor) is on by default. The router's documents target Qwen3.8; LFM2.5's adapter declares how the router fits it (Capabilities.conductor in engine/models/lfm2_moe/serving.py, read by TandemApp's tandemapp/conductor/modelfit.py; server.md):

key LFM2.5 effect served_classifier false Laya alone answers the class question, also where the router document leaves its stage off fallback lean a turn no stage classified at its bar thinks at the profile's default level, with no effort sentence, and its tool turns too; since 0.11.3 its class's core still goes in (SRV-534) packages core a class's core skill and the client's pins; no general package, no package question no_package_classes chat no package on the chat class effort_notes, rules, memory false the level sets the switch and the budget alone; no rules, no memory card or index

Why, measured on lfm25-exl3-2.5, 2026-10-14 (models/lfm2.5-24b-a2b/measurements/conductor-0.9.0.json):

  • With thinking off the model answers the router's class prompt as a chat request. Its one-id answers were right on 0 to 2 of 8 labelled requests at confidence 0.08 to 0.44 or wrong at up to 0.99. Laya stays under its 0.8 bar on short chats, so a short chat fell back to the profile's default class: chat through curl (everyday packages and memory notes, 2,036 to 2,347 hidden tokens), code_edit at xhigh in the Chat tab (coding packages, 5,825 to 6,022).
  • The router puts its notes at the tail of the user's message. The same note texts on the raw path, 4 short asks, greedy: 5,817 reasoning tokens at the tail, 2,969 as the system message, 2,155 without them. The package note alone at the tail: 7,363; the memory notes alone: 2,614. The reasoning follows the package's checklist line by line; with thinking off it moves into the answer.
  • Chat-tab tasks (5 tasks, 2 runs each, reasoning tokens): the fit with the class rules as its only note (75 to 84 tokens) 3,083 and 6,416 in two windows; with the effort sentences added 8,343; with the general packages added 12,934 (5,788 to 7,654 hidden tokens a turn); the router as written 13,426. The raw path in the same windows: 2,748 to 3,670. Runs at temperature 0.1 vary.

The model fit against the raw path and the router as written (QWEN38_CONDUCTOR_FIT=off). Same server, one request at a time; short asks greedy at 8,192 tokens at most; tasks at the sampling defaults (temperature 0.1), each run twice:

set raw router as written model fit 4 short asks, thinking on: reasoning tokens (right) 2,155 (4/4) 9,098 (4/4) 2,234 (4/4) 4 short asks, thinking off: answer tokens (right) 541 (3/4) 679 (3/4) 553 (3/4) 4 short asks in the Chat tab, 10 tools: reasoning tokens (right) 525 (3/4) 2,665 (3/4) 553 (3/4) 7 Chat-tab tasks x 2: success, reasoning tokens, tool errors 14/14, 7,535, 1 12/14, 68,170, 9 14/14, 9,850, 0 3 Chat-tab tasks with an "open it" follow-up x 2: success, present in the follow-up, tool calls, reasoning tokens 6/6, 6/6, 19, 8,627 4/6, 5/6, 145, 113,211 6/6, 6/6, 20, 7,228

The follow-up rows ran on the :8000 server after the deploy (raw and fit) and on the side server (router as written); there the router's testing packages had the model check the page through the shell: 15 shell calls in the follow-ups and 13 tool errors over the 6 runs. The raw column is the model fit's window; in the router's window the raw tasks gave 14/14, 7,352, 0. Rates in the model fit's window (no other request on the box): 171.6 tok/s on the short asks against 166.7 raw, 161.1 on the tasks against 165.7. The tasks: files, a Python script, a search, an HTML canvas animation, an analog clock, a landing page, a JSON edit; the check reads the files each run wrote.

Not yet: the packages, the memory notes and the effort sentences at a place this model does not read as part of the request (the system message cost 1.38 times the raw thinking where the tail cost 2.7 times); Laya's class question on short chats (below its bar, so they fall back).

docs.title: How the engine runs it
docs.text:
• One row path: the decode step and every row of a verify block run the same kernels a row at a time (engine/models/lfm2_moe/kernels.py). EXL3 projections use tools/fn_kernels.dense, experts its MoE bank kernels, BF16 projections a 16-row GEMM. A verify row has the decode step's bits, so greedy speculation writes the plain greedy text.
  • Self-check at load: a recorded 24-token decode verified as one block, every row compared bit for bit. A difference turns speculation off.
  • Rollback: a verify block writes nothing into the convolution state. The commit rebuilds the state from the accepted path's last two inputs and moves the path's KV rows. Rollback is exact.
  • Prefill: chunks of 4,096 tokens on batched kernels (cuBLAS or the EXL3 GEMM, experts grouped, SDPA with a lower-right causal mask). The next token agrees with the row path; the bits do not. 8,192 tokens prefill at 7,360 tok/s on 4.0.
  • Dense splits: ops/lfm25-dense-splits.json, from tools/fn_tiles.py --dense at each pack's shapes. Decode step with / without, tok/s: 2.5 188.2 / 171.2, 3.0 175.0 / 159.1, 3.5 153.5 / 143.4, 4.0 145.9 / 136.1, 4.5 128.8 / 121.6, 6.0 106.9 / 106.9. The graph saves 5 % against eager launches.

The decode step from its CUDA graph, one greedy request: 188.2 tok/s on 2.5, 145.9 on 4.0 (191 GB/s of the bytes a token reads), 44.8 in BF16 (220 GB/s) (measured). Each pack has its own dense splits (ops/lfm25-dense-splits.json; 4.0: 136.1 tok/s without them). Eager launches cost 5 %. An 8,192-token prompt prefills at 7,360 tok/s on 4.0.

docs.title: Speed by kind of text
docs.text:
One greedy request a cell through the server, 512 tokens, thinking off, suffix store off, plain / lookup, tok/s. Edit: a file back with one name renamed. Copy: a text back unchanged. Every lookup text equals the plain one.

profile prose chat code edit copy lfm25-exl3-2.5 185.6 / 177.0 185.4 / 175.6 185.1 / 179.3 181.1 / 350.5 181.9 / 271.3 lfm25-exl3-3.0 171.7 / 165.7 171.3 / 168.5 171.3 / 169.2 168.2 / 327.8 168.8 / 413.8 lfm25-exl3-3.5 151.3 / 147.5 150.9 / 143.7 150.9 / 147.2 146.9 / 268.7 148.8 / 286.6 lfm25-exl3-4.0 143.6 / 140.1 143.7 / 139.4 143.8 / 139.2 141.3 / 291.1 141.8 / 326.4 lfm25-exl3-4.5 128.4 / 123.3 128.2 / 124.7 128.0 / 124.5 126.5 / 281.2 126.9 / 339.4 lfm25-exl3-6.0 105.4 / 104.2 105.2 / 103.5 105.0 / 105.5 104.1 / 210.0 102.8 / 280.1 lfm25-bf16 44.6 / 43.4 44.5 / 43.3 44.5 / 44.5 44.3 / 153.7 44.2 / 157.8

The lookup costs up to 5 % in prose and chat and takes edit and copy asks to 1.8 to 3.6 times the plain rate.

Verify staircase, 4.0, chain blocks from their graphs, median of 20, 1,024 tokens of context, before the dense splits (tools/lfm_check.py staircase):

rows 1 2 3 4 6 8 12 16 ms 7.42 10.62 13.79 16.86 21.40 27.47 36.17 45.88 experts read, 38 layers 152 259 333 391 491 563 664 735

Each row adds about 3 ms because a block reads the union of its rows' experts. At 8,192 tokens of context the blocks cost 0.5 to 3.5 ms more. A block pays when it is accepted for about 1.4 tokens a row.

docs.title: Speculation
docs.text:
• Drafter: the lookup alone (the request's text and the suffix store) through the shared tree drafter with no head (engine/methods/mtp_drafter.py NoHead), cut by StairCut.
  • Prices: one file a profile, ops/prices/lfm2.5-24b-a2b/<profile>.dgx-spark.json, from its staircase and bench (tools/lfm_check.py prices).
  • No-head rules: a round with no lookup match is the plain step and is priced as one; each round's own match decides through the cut's calibrated acceptance; the class-wide skip is not consulted. The lookup's confidence carries its match length, so a long copy match scores above a short phrase match.
  • Identity: tools/fn_server_check.py --compare on 4.0, lookup against plain, 20 requests (greedy, thinking, streaming, every tool_choice, JSON, penalties with logit_bias, logprobs, seeds, a stop string): every answer equal, largest logprob difference 0.0.
  • A draft head plugs in through the adapter's draft_heads() in place of NoHead.

docs.title: Parallel requests and caches
docs.text:
• Three sequence slots over one copy of the weights (QSE_PARALLEL=3). A slot taking a plain step joins the round as one row (joint_plain); when every decoding slot does, the round is one joint decode step from a graph (JointDecodeGraph).
  • 4.0, lookup on, store off, 256 tokens each (tools/lfm_parallel.py): 1, 2 and 3 requests at once decode 139.9, 169.1 and 177.8 tok/s in total; every text equals its request alone.
  • Resident prefix and state store: 30 convolution states (240 KiB) as sections, K and V of the 10 attention layers as views, 4,096-token grid. A warm answer equals the cold one with equal logprobs at 4,096 and 12,288 tokens (tools/fn_cache_check.py).
  • Disk tier: 12,288 tokens restored in 0.96 s against 2.6 s cold, answer and logprobs equal. Session spill: 13,650 tokens drained in 309 ms (0.19 GB), read back in 163 ms. One tier folder a pack.

docs.title: The e4m3 KV cache (LFM2_KV_FP8, off)
docs.text:
With LFM2_KV_FP8=1 the 10 attention layers keep each key and value as e4m3 codes with one fp32 scale a (head, token): 10,880 bytes a token instead of 20,480, so 1.33 GiB instead of 2.5 GiB at 131,072 tokens. The output is no longer the exact model's. The knob is off by default, and the exactness checks hold only with it off. The manifest names it lfm2_moe-kvfp8, so its cache entries are never read by the exact cache.

A decode step or verify block writes each row's K and V in BF16 to a staging buffer, then one launch codes them into the cache (tools/kv_fp8.py). Attention turns the codes back into BF16 as it loads them. A verify row is still the decode step's row bit for bit, so speculation and the load-time self-check work as before. A prompt chunk attends to its own rows in BF16 and to the cached rows decoded, then codes its rows.

To turn it on in the Setup Guide (the dashboard's #/setup), pick LFM2.5-24B-A2B, go to the Tools step and switch on "Long-context cache (FP8)" under Features. Then finish Review and Install, which restarts the engine. To turn it off, switch it off there and install again.

To turn it on from the command line, add this line at the end of ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/serve.env:

QWEN38_LFM2_KV_FP8=1

Then run ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem restart. Check that it took: curl -s localhost:8000/health shows "kv_cache": "e4m3" under weights, and the engine log's load line says KV cache e4m3. To turn it off, delete the line and run tandem restart again; /health then shows "kv_cache": "bf16". Use one way or the other: a line in serve.env wins over the Setup Guide's switch.

Quality and speed against the exact cache: not measured.

docs.title: Not supported yet
docs.text:
• A draft head (none published for this model).
  • Vision: the model reads text only.
  • The shadow reader: it reads Qwen's token ids and was validated on Qwen text; off on this model.
  • The KV pool: off in the profiles (QSE_KV_POOL=off), not verified on this model. Each slot reserves its window at load.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
check where result reference forward against transformers' Lfm2MoeForCausalLM, tiny random model, fp32 tests/test_lfm2_moe_ref.py prefill and 3 decode steps within 2.1e-5 verify tree against sequential decode; commit and rollback tests/test_lfm2_moe_ref.py, tests/test_lfm2_moe_engine.py equal (engine: bit for bit) BF16 engine against transformers in BF16, 8 chat prompts x 128 tokens, teacher-forced tools/lfm_check.py hf, tests/gpu/test_lfm2_moe_box_gpu.py rung_b top token 98.05 % (1,004 of 1,024); 19 of 20 differences near ties; KL 0.0064 4.0 pack against the converter's own forward, same tokens tools/lfm_check.py exl3, rung_c top token 97.85 %; all 22 differences near ties trellis decode against the converter's own decode tools/lfm_check.py xcheck bit for bit verify rows against decode steps at every start load-time self-check 24 rows bit for bit pack reader, synthetic and real packs tests/test_lfm2_moe_pack.py, tests/test_lfm2_moe_packs_on_disk.py pass row kernels against torch twins; row invariance; one graph a decode step tests/test_lfm2_moe_kernels.py, tests/gpu/test_lfm2_moe_gpu.py pass Pythonic tool calls, parser and chat handler TandemApp's tests/test_toolcall_pythonic.py, tests/test_lfm25_api.py pass half-integer rates against LinearEXL3; kernels against the reference tests/gpu/test_lfm2_moe_gpu.py bit for bit at 1.5 to 8 bits; kernels within 3e-3, rows invariant up to 32 shared kernels at whole rates against the previous tree same random blocks through both trees 51 of 51 outputs bit for bit a served profile over HTTP tools/lfm_live.py health, answer, reasoning, tool calls

A near tie: the reference's two best tokens are within 8 bf16 steps of its largest logit (exactness.md).

docs.title: Measurement
docs.text: Speed claims for inference engines are easy to inflate by accident. Our lookup store once held the benchmark's own prompts and answers, and it added about 21 % to the benchmark row without the engine getting any faster. This page describes how TandemLLM measures itself, from the benchmark row and the teacher-forced bench to the release gate.

docs.title: The row
docs.text:
The benchmark row is serve-single-i256-o256-v1: one request at a time, 256 prompt tokens, 256 generated tokens, thinking off, temperature 0, seed 42, 50 requests after 3 warm-ups. Every configuration runs with the same runner and the same prompt set.

Each request's speed is computed from its own record:

tok/s = (completion_tokens - 1) / (end-to-end seconds - time to first token)

The first token belongs to the prefill, so it is subtracted, and the decode time is the request's wall clock after its first token. A row reports the mean, p50, p90 and max over the 50 requests, with the median time to first token.

The client measures the row's speed and time to first token itself. The server's own numbers come with every response, in timings and metrics (server.md lists them), and its [req] log line holds the same record. The Setup Guide's card cells take two of them from that line: tok_round is tokens_per_block, the mean accepted length, and ms_round is the decode time over blocks (tools/exl3_fastrun.py). No row reports draft_acceptance_rate. It depends on how many tokens a round drafts, and StairCut sets that number again every round.

Two readings of a row are easy to get wrong.

  • The gaps between tokens. A verified round writes several tokens into the socket at once, so half the gaps are microseconds and the other half a whole round. The median inter-token latency therefore says nothing about round time.
  • Mean against median. Some prompts ask the model to repeat text that is already in the context, and the drafters commit 15 tokens a round on them. That lifts the mean. The median reflects fresh text.

docs.title: Two views of every row
docs.text:
A row runs twice, in two views of the lookup store:

  • Store off. The engine's persistent suffix store is off, so nothing the engine has seen before can help it.
  • Clean store. The store is on but holds no text of the benchmark.

A row with the benchmark's own text in the store measures the store, not the engine. Benchmarks also run with --suffix-store-readonly when they read a store of real traffic, so they cannot write themselves into it.

docs.title: Noise, and what a row can decide
docs.text:
Two server processes of the same configuration can differ by several per cent. StairCut learns its costs and copy rates online, and the earlier length router decided each request's block width from timing taken inside that request, so two runs can make different decisions on the same prompts. Under the length router, rows taken from three separate server processes spread 10.4 % on the mean and 6.7 % on the median, and three rows through one process spread 5.9 % and 3.1 %.

tools/row3.py runs N rows per configuration through one server, recomputes each from its own records, and reports the median with the spread of the runs. --compare calls a difference resolved only when it is larger than the noise and the run ranges of the two sides do not overlap. A change worth less than about 3 % of the median cannot be settled by the row at any number of repeats.

Speed is a quotient: tokens a round over time a round. A change can trade one factor for the other and leave the quotient flat. The served loop therefore counts its own rounds, and every row reports tokens per round and milliseconds per round next to tok/s. Both are gated. A kernel change must not move tokens per round, and a drafter change must move it up.

A server run can hold the costs still: --no-learn-cost (0.3.24-test) keeps the length router's served price table, so the same text gets the same choices whatever the blocks before it took. In 0.3.23's narrator A/B, with learning on, one prompt took 366, 468 and 504 blocks for the same 2,000 greedy tokens at 93.5 to 94.1 ms a block, and the off runs spread 37 %. With the flag the first two requests of a process still wrote other texts (398 and 505 blocks); the next six wrote one text in 514 blocks each, and the off runs spread 0.19 % (41.64 to 41.72 tok/s). So a server A/B gets the flag, two warm-ups an arm, and compares only runs that wrote the same text. A row pair with the flag on both sides (f0e4931 with only the flag added, and 0.3.24-test) read 50.21 and 49.37 tok/s, 2,288 and 2,297 blocks: the rows still differ a little between two processes.

Every report names the code it measured with code_sha256, a hash over every file of the four code folders. The same commit hashes the same everywhere, so a report can be matched to a commit.

docs.title: Same hour, both sides
docs.text:
Nobody compares a candidate with a number from another day. It runs against the current release in the same session on the same box, alternated: base, candidate, base, candidate. A board drifts over hours (its temperature, its memory, whatever else runs), and alternation spreads that drift over both sides.

The adoption rule is "never worse". A candidate ships only if nothing resolves worse against the same-hour base, in both store views: not the mean, p50, p90 or max, not time to first token, and not tokens or milliseconds per round.

docs.title: The block A/B, for changes that keep the bits
docs.text: Most kernel changes are worth 0.5 to 3 ms of a round of about 93 ms, below what the row can resolve. For a change whose output is bit-identical, only time can differ. tools/block_ab.py loads the served engine once, switches each state's flags inside the process, warms each state, freezes the router's learned costs, and alternates base and candidate over three workloads for N pairs. Every run's tokens must equal the base's first run, and the rule is applied to milliseconds per round. Two states of the same code read "not resolved" with a spread of 0.35 to 0.87 %. Turning the verify graphs off resolved 3.15 ms worse on every workload.

docs.title: The release gate
docs.text:
ops/gate.sh is the whole protocol in one command, run on the box inside a hold (operations.md). It stops at the first failing step:

  1. The engine's CPU tests (tools/engine_tests.py), in a clean environment; TandemApp's run in its own repository.
  2. Every GPU test, tests/gpu/test_*.py.
  3. Identity: the served configuration with the new flags off must be bit-identical to the build it replaces (tools/flagoff_identity.py).
  4. Agreement: tools/verify_spec.py with the served flags and the candidate's, under the near-tie rule (exactness.md).
  5. Optionally, the block A/B above.
  6. Rows: two store-off rows and one clean-store row with the candidate's flags.
  7. Compare: tools/gatecheck.py against the base reports, with the never-worse rule.

It writes a dated report with every command and its output to results/gate/<label>/report.md. results/ is not under version control.

Rows are not enough on their own. A release candidate once passed every row and broke a real client's request shape. Before a deploy the gate is followed by:

  • tools/client_smoke.py: the request shapes real clients send, through the official openai client. It covers an agent client's tools with arguments validated against their JSON schemas, a 12k-token prompt with penalties and tools, every tool_choice mode, streamed tool-call deltas, n=2, and prompts from 8k to over 100k tokens. It passes with zero failures.
  • tools/api_text_check.py: 13 plain requests byte-identical to the current release.
  • A real agent session with its own tool calls, all of which must go through.

docs.title: The teacher-forced bench
docs.text:
A change of the verified tree's shape moves near ties (exactness.md), so two configurations rarely write the same text on the same prompt, and their rows measure different texts. tools/forced_bench.py removes that. Each workload has one fixed reference text (the greedy output of the earlier length-router configuration; any fixed text would do), and every configuration drafts and verifies with the real kernels at the real context but accepts along the reference, so all of them commit the same tokens and differ only in rounds and time per round.

The paper's run covers 25 workloads: prose, chat, code, a 48-token answer and a prose-then-code prompt; twelve prompts of the benchmark row; three edit tasks; a 256-token quotation and a 1,024-token copy; and, at 32k tokens of context, fresh text, a copy and a code edit. A workload's rate is the mean of three measured repeats after a warm-up. StairCut averages 90.45 tok/s against 81.95 for the fixed block 16 and 59.31 for the fixed block 8. It is above block 16 on 23 of the 25 workloads and above block 8 on 22. One router served every workload and repeat in that run; in a second run with a new router before every request, StairCut averages 89.88 tok/s against 91.16 for the kept router in that run.

docs.title: The weight cards' speed rows
docs.text:
Each weight card in the setup guide carries one speed row of the current build (SPD-245): the parallel rows of models/<id>/model.yaml. tools/parallel_card.py measures a row against the server running the profile and writes its raw file to models/<id>/measurements/. The file holds every request's record, the /health samples of every round, the server's limit knobs and the row itself. The registry refuses a row that differs from its raw file's row.

A row measures the engine (SPD-249). Every request goes to /v1/completions with its prompt as text and X-Tandem: raw, so no conductor or chat-layer step runs. The prompt is the model's chat template over the card's messages with thinking off: the tool asks /v1/tokenize for the template's ids ("ids": true), turns them into text with the model's tokenizer (--tokenizer, the weights' directory), and checks that /v1/tokenize reads that text as the same ids, which are the ids /v1/completions reads. A prompt whose ids differ stops the run, and the raw file counts the prompts checked (prompts_checked). /v1/chat/completions works and is in beta; no published speed number comes from it.

  • Prompts: bench/card-prompts-v1.json, a code and a prose workload of about 190 to 250 tokens. The prefill filler is bench/heldout_prose.txt, repeated to the length. Every request starts with a nonce line and sends cache_prompt: false, with thinking off and a seed of its own. The row records the prompt set's version and hash, and the prompt tokens of each workload.
  • Decode: each workload alone, three runs after one warm-up each. A run's rate is (completion tokens - 1) / (last token - first token), and the row gives the median per workload.
  • Prefill: cold prompts of 2,048, 8,192 and 32,768 tokens, counted with /v1/tokenize and checked against the request's own prompt_tokens, three runs each, one token out. The row gives the median time to first token and prompt tokens over that time.
  • At once: 1, 2, 4 and 8 prose requests released together, one discarded warm-up round and three measured rounds a level, 512 tokens a request. The wall rate is all completion tokens over the time from the send to the last end, so it includes the first tokens. The decode rate counts the tokens after each request's first one, over the time from the first first token to the last token. The row gives the median of each over the rounds, and the median time to first token.
  • Proof: /health every 0.2 s during every round. A round counts only when the most slots decoding at once equal N and no more than N requests ran (none came from elsewhere). An invalid round is run again. A level's at_once is the smallest maximum over its rounds, and the registry refuses a level whose at_once is not N or whose valid rounds are fewer than the row's. Before the levels the tool reads the server's live slot limit (parallel.max_running) and refuses to start when it is below the largest N.
  • Setup: the row names the setup file, the lanes, the window, the tokens a request, the sampling, the suffix store and the response cache (both off for a card row), the build and the commit.

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text: The paper compares StairCut with the same engine in two other configurations, on the same weights and the same box: plain greedy decoding (speculation off), and one drafter at a fixed block width (8 or 16) with its released tree budgets (speculative-decoding.md). On the benchmark row with the store off that is 49.89 tok/s for StairCut, 47.13 for block 8, 44.80 for block 16 and 13.69 for plain greedy decoding.

docs.title: One measuring method
docs.text:
Release pages, weight cards and the quality gate measure the same things: decode at one request, prefill, requests at once, long prompts. tools/measure measures each of them once and keeps the result, so a number measured for one of them is never measured again for another.

  • One row list, tools/measure/rows.yaml. A row has a stable id (length.32k, conc.card.c8, prefill.64k, ...), what it measures, its request shape (prompt and its length, tokens out, requests at once, runs or rounds), the views that use it, and the server it runs on. Two rows of a different shape are two rows: the card's 1/2/4/8 at once use 169-246-token prompts, the report's requests at once use ~2k-token prompts with their prefill in the wall time; prefill.32k is one token out, length.32k is 512.
  • One runner. python -m tools.measure run --url URL --rows ... | --view report --out DIR measures only the rows the record store at DIR does not hold for this server's key: the row, the build, the pack, the box and a hash of the server's limit knobs. --force measures a row again. Every request goes to /v1/completions with X-Tandem: raw and every answer's mode is checked; a row of N requests at once is invalid without the server's own count of N decoding together.
  • A record store. One JSON per run under DIR/runs/, and DIR/index.json from the key to the run file. python -m tools.measure merge imports records that exist already (a gate report and its raw results, a report's data.json and the card tool's raw files). An imported record keeps its source, the tool, the date and the file, and the page shows it beside its rows.
  • Three views, none of which measures anything. render report writes the HTML page (benchmark-report.md), for one pack or several packs of one model on one page. render card writes a weight card's numbers in the shape tools/parallel_card.py writes them. render gate --base DIR --head DIR gives the gate's verdict table from two stores, with the gate's own rules; every gate run writes its arms' records to OUT/records/base and OUT/records/head (quality-gate.md). compare --old A --new B sets two builds' rows side by side with a noise band.
  • A plan before the GPU. python -m tools.measure plan --view report --pack P --build B --out DIR lists every row with its record and source, or the hold that will measure it. Rows that need their own fresh server are grouped by server, and the groups are packed into holds of at most 62 minutes. It refuses when a row would be measured twice: a row asked by id that has a record, a warm row whose earlier rows already have records, or code that measures a recorded row beside the one asked.

tools/parallel_card.py, python -m tools.release_report and python -m tools.gate run keep working; their help says where the one method is.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
Each of these cost a wrong number once.

  • A standalone kernel timing is a ranking, never a budget. The same configuration read 0.254 ms in one process and 0.627 ms in another.
  • The first configuration in a fresh process pays for autotuning. It once read a verify of 260.2 ms against 115.5 ms for every later one, and the policy under test "won" by 35 %.
  • A bandwidth-bound engine measured beside another engine measures the other engine. Two engines halve the bandwidth each one gets. Take the board lock.
  • A speculative decoder judged on a short generation hides bugs. One drafter bug read 81 % acceptance at 48 tokens and 24 % at 128.
  • Acceptance with the reasoning block open differs from acceptance with it closed, by up to 72 % on one prompt. Measure in the serving regime.
  • A kernel probe whose working set fits in cache measures the cache. 266 GB/s on a 273 GB/s board is not a real reading.
  • Two runs that agree to six decimals have not agreed. They are the same run: once, a test server had bound its port beside another.
  • A quiet log is not a hung process. Python block-buffers into a pipe, so use python -u.
  • A lane count past the pool's guarantee reads as a slow model. Requests that wait for a lane and for the turn look the same as slow decoding, and a Prometheus row of the decode rate alone cannot tell the two apart. Compare the /health parallel.turn waits with the lane count.
  • A fresh engine can measure better than a used one. The resident conversation and the side slots keep their KV, and a long-lived session has more of it. Restart before comparing configurations.
  • The engine's own turns look like a client's. The preparer and the memory writer run generations over the client's context; count them with qse_prepare_runs_total and qse_memory_writer_runs_total (server/METRICS.md), or measure raw with the conductor off.
  • A first request after a restart is not a baseline. The pack's page cache is dropped at the start, so the first measurement runs on a busy disk.

docs.title: Measuring Flash-Next
docs.text:
Flash-Next's numbers in these docs come from tools of their own (tools/fn_*.py), each answering one question, and every one ran under the board's lock with one model loaded. Most are single runs of one request, labelled so where they appear; none is a benchmark row yet.

tool the question it answers fn_server_check.py --compare do 20 request shapes give the same text, tool calls and logprobs with and without speculation; --sampled: do seeded sampled answers fn_spec_check.py does speculative greedy equal plain greedy in the engine, with the state bit-equal after every run fn_fit_run.py does a pack hold its largest window: one long request, MemAvailable at 10 Hz, every limit knob the server reports fn_cache_check.py does a request restored from each cache tier answer as on a cold server fn_resume_check.py, fn_guest_check.py does a resumed prefill equal a cold one; does a short guest request leave the resident conversation's rows intact fn_lookup_ab.py one greedy request a class through a server, for an A/B of the drafters fn_memory_check.py memory after the load, the prefill workspace, the table's resident bytes under each policy fn_exl3_xcheck.py, fn_refcheck.py our reading of a pack against the converter's; our forward against transformers'

The Flash-Next tools behind the numbers in Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Every speculative rate in Qwen3.8-Flash-Next comes with the statement that its texts equalled plain decoding, because a rate whose text changed measures another answer. The runs by context length started a fresh server and report its second round, so the first round's one-time graph captures do not count in them. What Flash-Next has not had yet is the release gate: no row of serve-single-i256-o256-v1, no block A/B and no task suite.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The published numbers come from one board, one model and one request at a time. Long prompts are measured separately (caches.md). Parallel requests are measured on the weight cards only (above). The quality gates are held-out loss, confident argmax agreement and free generation. No task benchmark suite has been run, so this repository makes no claim about task accuracy.

docs.title: NemotronH (Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Bolt, Super VL)
docs.text:
NVIDIA's NemotronH hybrid is the fourth model family TandemLLM runs: Mamba2, NoPE attention and mixture-of-experts blocks, with an MTP head on some checkpoints. The engine serves Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B from NVIDIA's own 24 GB GGUF (IQ2_XXS experts, NVFP4 Mamba2 projections, Q8_0 head and attention), read as stored, and from EXL3 packs converted from NVIDIA's BF16 checkpoint (2.0 to 6.0 bpw; the 2.0 pack has 4-bit dense projections), all with NVIDIA's LiLiCorr drafter; Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B from NVIDIA's ModelOpt checkpoint (NVFP4 experts, FP8 Mamba2 and attention projections and head) and from EXL3 packs of its BF16 checkpoint, with its own LiLiCorr drafter; and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B in BF16, the test model it was built on. Super VL reads images through its checkpoint's RADIO tower (Super VL: images); Bolt and Lightning are served text only.

Code: engine/models/nemotron_h/ (registry name nemotron_h; the image path vision.py, selected by NemotronHForCausalLM, NemotronHPuzzleForCausalLM and the Omni architectures NemotronH_*Omni_Reasoning_V3). Ladder tool: tools/nh_check.py; quality against BF16 logits: tools/nh_quality.py. GGUF weights (IQ2_XXS, NVFP4, Q8_0): tools/iq2_linear.py. EXL3 packs: tools/fn_kernels.py (dense_rows) and tools/exl3_relu2.py. ModelOpt NVFP4 / FP8 checkpoints: tools/nvfp4_relu2.py. Draft head: engine/drafters/lilicorr.py.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
part Lightning 30B-A3B Bolt 74B-A9B Puzzle 75B-A9B (Bolt's trunk design) Super VL 120B-A12B layers 52: 23 Mamba2, 23 MoE, 6 attention 88: 40 Mamba2, 40 MoE, 8 attention the same as Bolt the same as Bolt (layers_block_type) hidden 2,688 4,096 4,096 4,096 Mamba2 64 heads of 64, state 128, 8 groups, conv 4 taps with bias 128 heads of 64, state 128, 8 groups 128 heads of 64, state 96, 8 groups 128 heads of 64, state 128, 8 groups attention 32 query heads, 2 KV heads of 128, no positional encoding the same the same the same MoE 128 experts, top 6, relu^2 experts 1,856 wide, shared expert 3,712 240, 304, 368, 432 or 496 experts a layer, top 9, width 1,536..2,560, latent 1,024, shared 5,376 512 experts, top 4..18 and width 1,280..2,688 a layer, latent 1,024, shared 5,376 512 experts in every layer, top 22, width 2,688, latent 1,024, shared 5,376 router sigmoid, correction bias for the choice, top k / (sum + 1e-20) x 2.5 the same, x 5.0 the same, x 5.0 the same, x 5.0 MTP one block pair, attention + MoE none the same as Lightning, top 22, width 2,688 one block pair, attention + MoE (mtp_layers_block_type), top 22, width 2,688 vocabulary, context 131,072, 262,144 the same the same 131,072, 1,048,576

Bolt's checkpoint is an Omni wrapper (NemotronH_Omni_Reasoning_V3) with a RADIO image tower; its GGUF holds the text trunk only (the tower is the separate mmproj file), and TandemLLM serves text.

The config reader (config.py) builds one layer table from hybrid_override_pattern, layers_block_type or block_configs (per-block num_experts_per_tok, moe_intermediate_size and n_routed_experts), and from an Omni checkpoint's llm_config. An unknown field stops the load with its name.

A decode token reads 5.16 GB on Bolt: the NVFP4 Mamba2 projections 2.47 GB, the Q8_0 head 0.57, shared experts 0.45 and routed experts 0.44 (IQ2_XXS, 9 a layer), latent projections 0.36 and attention 0.30 (Q8_0), the SSM states 0.34 (read and written), the F32 routers 0.23 (GGUFIndex.decode_bytes); 52.9 tok/s at 273 GB/s is the bytes ceiling. A decode token reads 6.55 GB of Lightning's BF16 weights: experts 2.75 GB, Mamba2 projections 1.78, shared experts 0.92, head 0.70, attention 0.28 (PackIndex.decode_bytes); 41.7 tok/s at 273 GB/s is the bytes ceiling.

docs.title: Bolt: nemotron-bolt-iq2
docs.text:
nemotron-bolt-iq2 (ops/profiles/nemotron-bolt-iq2.env): NVIDIA's GGUF of revision 724e3fee of nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-GGUF (22.0 GB, the registry entry's asset, fetched from NVIDIA's repository and never re-hosted; QSE_NH_GGUF names it), with the config, tokenizer and chat template of the BF16 repository (revision 153d4551) in the profile's weights directory; 22.19 GiB at load; 262,144 tokens; 3 slots; the lookup cut by StairCut (Bolt has no MTP head). With NVIDIA's LiLiCorr drafter beside the lookup (QSE_NH_HEAD=lilicorr) StairCut kept plain steps on this build, every ask at 1.0 token a block; cause not isolated. Lookup alone, 2026-10-16, one run: prose / code / chat 27.6 / 31.7 / 27.7 tok/s, edit / copy 97.9 / 131.2 (10.43 / 14.19 tokens a block), plain 27.4-27.5, every text the plain run's; price file re-measured on this build. Setup Guide entry: models/nemotron-3.5-bolt-74b-a9b/model.yaml.

DGX Spark, 2026-10-15, one fresh server a run, the GPU to itself, max_len 32,768, conductor raw, suffix store off.

measurement plain lookup decode step from its graph (nh_check.py bench, 256 tokens) 27.94 tok/s (35.79 ms) prose / chat / code, 512 greedy tokens, thinking off (fn_lookup_ab.py) 27.47 / 27.45 / 27.44 27.53 / 27.31 / 29.34 edit / copy asks 27.39 / 27.39 57.70 / 58.90 (4.52 / 9.46 tokens a block) 1 / 2 / 3 requests at once, 256 tokens each, total (lfm_parallel.py) 26.94 / 32.57 / 38.30 tok/s, 2 and 3 slots decoding together (254 joint rounds), each text its request's alone verify chain of 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 rows at 1,024 tokens (nh_check.py staircase, the profile's price file) 34.8 / 41.5 / 47.2 / 73.2 / 114.3 ms
  • Every lookup answer is the plain run's text. Through fn_server_check.py, 19 of 20 answers are identical; the thinking-on one is identical up to the reasoning budget's forced close, which lands one token later at the end of the verified block (docs/exactness.md, output changes).
  • A verify row costs 2.7 to 14.6 ms more than the one before it (about 4 ms, a step at 5 and 9 rows): the IQ2_XXS shared expert decodes its weights once for up to 16 rows (5,376 x 4,096: 0.10 ms for one row, 0.36 for 8, 0.47 for 16) and the routed experts run one (row, expert) pair a program, so the lookup pays off on edit and copy asks and not on prose.
  • A CUDA GEMV for the IQ2_XXS shared experts took the decode step to 32.7 tok/s and 8 / 16-row chains to 57.9 / 93.2 ms; it is not in this tree, so this profile decodes at the rates above, and the LiLiCorr rows of the IQ2 table under LiLiCorr, measured with it, are higher than this tree gives.
  • Prefill (random tokens, one engine): 246 tok/s at 1,024 tokens, 799 at 8,192, 752 at 32,768, 698 at 131,072, 680 at 262,000 (385 s; 28.9 GiB reserved at the peak, the box never under 82 GiB available). Decode at 32,768 and 131,072 tokens of context: 26.06 and 23.27 tok/s.

docs.title: Bolt: nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.0
docs.text:
nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.0 (ops/profiles/nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.0.env): an EXL3 pack converted from NVIDIA's BF16 checkpoint (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-BF16, revision bca0a8cb) by exllamav3 1.6.2 with a patch for the Puzzle/Bolt layer table: routed experts at 2 bits, the Mamba2, attention, latent and shared-expert projections at 4, head 6 (23.48 GB, the RADIO tower in the pack in BF16 and not loaded); 20.22 GiB at load; 262,144 tokens; 3 slots; NVIDIA's LiLiCorr drafter and the lookup cut by StairCut (prices ops/prices/nemotron-3.5-bolt-74b-a9b/nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.0.dgx-spark.json, measured on the rows path). The pack is in a public Hugging Face repository (0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-EXL3-2.0, pinned by commit).

Quality against BF16 (tools/nh_quality.py, the BF16 checkpoint's logits on 8 wikitext-2 rows of 1,024 tokens; BF16 perplexity 5.97):

weights KL top-1 perplexity nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.0 0.170 84.1 % 6.81 nemotron-bolt-iq2 (NVIDIA's GGUF) 0.259 79.6 % 7.48

exllamav3's model_diff on 100 wikitext-2 rows of 2,048 tokens: the 2.0 pack KL 0.088, top-1 87.6 %. A pack with the dense projections at 2 bits as well measured KL 0.379, top-1 73.9 % in this engine and is not published as a profile.

DGX Spark, 2026-10-15: decode step 44.2 tok/s from its graph on the rows path (41.0 with a CTA a row); with LiLiCorr and the lookup, prose / code / chat / edit / copy 65.8 / 99.0 / 69.3 / 152.8 / 256.0 tok/s, every text the plain run's (table and conditions under LiLiCorr).

docs.text:
nemotron-bolt-exl3-<bpw> (ops/profiles/nemotron-bolt-exl3-<bpw>.env): EXL3 packs of the same BF16 checkpoint: below 4.0 the routed experts at the level and every other projection at 4 bits, from 4.0 up every projection at the level; head 6 (8 at 6.0); each in its public repository 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-EXL3-, pinned by commit; 262,144 tokens; 3 slots; LiLiCorr and the lookup cut by StairCut on the pack's price file (ops/prices/nemotron-3.5-bolt-74b-a9b/, SPD-127).

Quality as above (tools/nh_quality.py, 8 wikitext-2 rows of 1,024 tokens against the BF16 logits); decode step from its graph with one CTA a row (dense, measured before the rows path; the 2.0 pack: 41.3 there, 44.2 on the rows path); DGX Spark, 2026-10-15:

profile download at load KL top-1 perplexity decode step plain, server nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.0 23.48 GB 20.22 GiB 0.170 84.1 % 6.81 41.3 tok/s 43.3 tok/s nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.5 27.61 GB 24.07 GiB 0.094 87.3 % 6.34 39.9 tok/s 42.1 tok/s nemotron-bolt-exl3-3.0 31.75 GB 27.92 GiB 0.061 89.7 % 6.21 39.6 tok/s 41.7 tok/s nemotron-bolt-exl3-3.5 35.88 GB 32.01 GiB 0.044 91.1 % 6.12 38.7 tok/s 40.6 tok/s nemotron-bolt-exl3-4.0 40.01 GB 36.18 GiB 0.034 92.7 % 6.10 38.4 tok/s 40.5 tok/s nemotron-bolt-exl3-5.0 49.13 GB 44.42 GiB 0.016 94.8 % 6.00 32.0 tok/s 34.1 tok/s nemotron-bolt-exl3-6.0 58.37 GB 53.00 GiB 0.0087 96.2 % 5.98 27.8 tok/s 29.2 tok/s nemotron-bolt-iq2 (NVIDIA's GGUF) 22.04 GB 22.19 GiB 0.259 79.6 % 7.48 27.9 tok/s 27.8 tok/s

Each pack passed the load-time self-check and a chat on the Spark. The plain column is 0.10.0's (ENG-345, below); the drafted rows of every pack follow.

Plain, server (ENG-345, 0.10.0, 2026-10-16): one fresh server a run on the Spark with the GPU to itself, tools/fn_lookup_ab.py (prose, chat, code, edit and copy asks, 512 greedy tokens, thinking off, max_len 32,768, conductor raw, the suffix store off), --drafter none, one slot; the mean over the five asks, then the mean of 3 runs (spread 0.1 to 0.5 tok/s).

Drafted against plain (SPD-127, 0.11.1, 2026-10-16): the same asks, one fresh server a run, 3 slots, the session and prefix caches off; plain --drafter none, drafted the profile's own drafting (EXL3: LiLiCorr and the lookup, --draft-head lilicorr --depth 3; IQ2: the lookup alone) with the release's price files; 3 runs of each, alternating; means in tok/s:

profile plain prose chat code edit copy tokens a block, prose / chat / code nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.0 43.2 65.6 71.1 102.1 163.5 247.2 3.0 / 3.09 / 4.88 nemotron-bolt-exl3-2.5 41.9 65.8 68.9 114.7 161.9 208.7 3.23 / 3.37 / 5.68 nemotron-bolt-exl3-3.0 41.6 58.1 69.3 100.8 149.6 203.7 2.83 / 3.27 / 5.06 nemotron-bolt-exl3-3.5 40.6 59.5 65.9 101.0 129.7 217.4 2.97 / 3.25 / 5.4 nemotron-bolt-exl3-4.0 40.4 52.0 62.0 97.9 137.4 210.2 2.49 / 3.01 / 5.43 nemotron-bolt-exl3-5.0 33.9 51.7 55.5 81.7 121.3 184.4 2.98 / 3.14 / 4.91 nemotron-bolt-exl3-6.0 29.1 40.1 50.1 76.3 110.8 157.3 2.57 / 3.05 / 5.32 nemotron-bolt-iq2 27.7 27.7 27.8 31.9 97.8 131.6 1.02 / 1.03 / 1.22

Every drafted text is the plain run's. Each EXL3 price file comes from one load on the Spark: nh_check.py bench (256 tokens), staircase (1,024 and 8,192 tokens, 20 replays a count) and lilicorr (8 prompts of 256 tokens, thinking on), then nh_check.py prices --lilicorr: the chain of 1 to 16 rows and the plain step per context class, and the spec prior, (8-row chain + draft) / (0.75 x accepted length), 13.9 ms a token on 2.5 to 20.2 on 6.0.

Without a price file (0.11.0, 2.5 to 6.0) the one-row block kept a price of 1 ms: a round the cut cuts to the anchor alone prices spec, never the chain. Once the 2- to 8-row blocks were priced at 33 to 44 ms, the cut took the anchor alone wherever the draft was unsure, after the draft (about 10 ms) had run. On 4.0, 247 of 277 prose rounds were such rounds, 35.6 ms a token against the 24.6 ms plain step, and 3.0 to 4.0 wrote prose at 31 to 33 tok/s and chat at 39 to 40. A price file without the spec prior (0.10.0, 4.0) kept every ask on plain steps, at 40.3 to 40.5 tok/s. The IQ2 profile drafts with the lookup alone: prose and chat run at its plain rate (27.7 and 27.8 tok/s against 27.7), code at 31.9; LiLiCorr beside it with a spec prior is not measured yet.

docs.title: Super VL: nemotron-super-vl-exl3-4.0, nemotron-super-vl-exl3-2.0, nemotron-super-vl-nvfp4
docs.text:
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B with its RADIO image tower (VISION=on, Super VL: images), each profile with NVIDIA's LiLiCorr drafter for Super VL (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4-LiLiCorr: five taps, layers 1, 22, 43, 64 and 85, a window of 8,192, its own NVFP4 head) and the lookup, cut by StairCut (price files ops/prices/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b/, each with a spec prior: the 8-row chain plus the draft over 0.75 of LiLiCorr's offline accepted length).

  • nemotron-super-vl-exl3-4.0: an EXL3 pack of the BF16 checkpoint (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-BF16, revision 97e00975) by exllamav3 1.6.2 with the Puzzle/Bolt and Super VL patches: every projection at 4 bits, head 6, the MTP head at 4 (65.0 GB); 58.35 GiB at load (59.75 with the MTP head). Public repository 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-EXL3-4.0, pinned by commit.
  • nemotron-super-vl-exl3-2.0: the same converter at 2 bits with -hq: routed experts at 2, every other projection at 4, head 6, the MTP head at 4 to 6 (36.84 GB); 31.24 GiB at load. Public repository 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-EXL3-2.0, pinned by commit.
  • nemotron-super-vl-nvfp4: NVIDIA's ModelOpt checkpoint (revision 8a115b9d, 75.1 GB) read as stored (Weights); 66.63 GiB at load without the MTP head; 131,072 tokens.

Quality against BF16 (tools/nh_quality.py, the BF16 checkpoint's logits on 8 wikitext-2 rows of 1,024 tokens from an HF job; BF16 perplexity 3.840) and speed, DGX Spark, 2026-10-16, one fresh server a run, the GPU to itself, conductor raw, suffix store off, 512 greedy tokens, thinking off (client-side streaming rate, mean of 3 alternating runs):

profile at load KL top-1 perplexity plain LiLiCorr + lookup: prose / chat / code / edit / copy nemotron-super-vl-exl3-4.0 58.35 GiB 0.049 92.9 % 3.94 31.1 33.1 / 43.9 / 53.6 / 101.0 / 108.3 nemotron-super-vl-exl3-2.0 31.24 GiB 0.325 82.1 % 4.93 36.5 35.6 / 46.2 / 46.3 / 125.1 / 139.2 nemotron-super-vl-nvfp4 66.63 GiB 0.041 93.4 % 3.83 19.6 23.9 / 28.7 / 39.9 / 73.5 / 81.7
  • exllamav3's model_diff on 100 wikitext-2 rows of 2,048 tokens, the 4.0 pack: KL 0.0224, top-1 94.3 %; on the 8 rows above KL 0.049, top-1 93.0 %, perplexity 3.948 (the engine 0.0486, 92.9 %, 3.941).
  • A decode token reads 10.11 GB of the NVFP4 checkpoint: the FP8 Mamba2 projections 4.38 GB, routed experts 2.73 (22 a layer), shared experts 0.99, the BF16 latent pair 0.67, the FP8 head 0.54, the SSM states 0.34; 19.6 tok/s is 198 GB/s.
  • Verify chains of 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 rows at 1k context: EXL3 4.0 31.3 / 39.8 / 53.3 / 74.5 / 105.8 ms, NVFP4 51.7 / 60.0 / 78.4 / 109.0 / 156.7 ms. A row reads 22 experts in each of the 40 MoE layers (880); 8 rows read about 4,170, so a verify block costs more a row than on Bolt (9 experts a row).
  • LiLiCorr offline (nh_check.py lilicorr, 4 prompts x 192 tokens, thinking on): accepted length 4.82 on NVFP4 (2.86 .. 6.16), 4.65 on EXL3 4.0; the draft takes 21.3 ms (its NVFP4 head over 131,072 tokens and the 8,192-key window).
  • The checkpoint's MTP head (nh_check.py mtp, depth 3, the 4.0 pack's 4-bit head): the draft equals the trunk's greedy token at depth 1, 2 and 3 in 90.6, 82.2 and 69.4 % of positions, mean accepted run 2.38 of 3. Not served: it runs eagerly and LiLiCorr drafts 7 tokens at a higher accepted length.
  • Every LiLiCorr text of the five asks is the plain run's. fn_server_check.py, 20 requests: 16 the same on NVFP4 and on EXL3 4.0, 17 on EXL3 2.0; the others (thinking on with a low cap, JSON with a reasoning budget) the same up to the reasoning budget's forced close, which lands at the end of the verified block (docs/exactness.md, output changes).
  • 1 / 2 / 3 requests at once with LiLiCorr + lookup (256 tokens, the server's parallel.running sampled every 50 ms: 1, 2 and 3): EXL3 4.0 20.8 / 18.5 / 19.6 tok/s in total, EXL3 2.0 22.5 / 19.4 / 20.7, NVFP4 16.7 / 15.9 / 17.6. Speculating slots take turns; with 22 experts a row the turns gain nothing over one slot.
  • Prefill (one cold prompt): EXL3 4.0 564 / 577 / 572 tok/s at 7k / 30k / 115k tokens, NVFP4 476 / 490 / 502 (the engine runs one GEMM pair an expert, 512 a layer).
  • The 2.0 pack: KL 0.325 is twice the loss of Bolt's 2.0 with the same recipe (0.170); decode 36.8 tok/s.
  • Window (ENG-363): up to 1,048,576 tokens, the checkpoint's own (llm_config.max_position_embeddings, the tokenizer's model_max_length), for slot 0 and the side slots; the default stays 262,144. Attention has no positional encoding, and nothing in the engine is sized below that: K and V are [2, window, 128] a layer (8 GiB at 1,048,576), attention runs 4 to 2,048 programs of 512 keys, prompts run in 4,096-row chunks. Checked on EXL3 4.0 with slot 0 at 1,048,576, three side slots at 262,144, LiLiCorr and the lookup, the caches and conductor as served, the response cache off, a request raw (2026-10-16): five facts at 5 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 95 % of synthetic filler, greedy, thinking off, all five answered at 131,054 prompt tokens (first token after 228 s, 574 tok/s of prefill) and at 249,983 (475 s, 526 tok/s). A 1,000,000-token prompt was not measured.
  • The prefill's workspace does not grow with the prompt: 3.34 GiB above the engine at 131,054 tokens, 3.18 at 249,983 (the memory policy's observed). The adapter says so (cost(): a floor of 3.5 GiB, capped at 4.0); before, the 27B's line (30 kB a token) refused a 1,000,000-token prefill as 29 GiB of workspace. A slot 0 window above 262,144 adds its KV above it to the memory policy's ceiling and peak (+6 GiB at 1,048,576), as the side slots' bytes are added, so the caches are not refused for it during a long prefill.
  • Each side slot at 262,144 takes 2.82 GiB allocated and 3.10 GiB of MemAvailable at load (its KV 2.00 GiB), built in 9.2 s; measured with 3 and with 4 slots. With slot 0 at 1,048,576 and 4 slots the residency planner refused Laya (its 3 GiB claim under the 15 GiB floor against the engine's peak); with 3 slots it fits.

Three profiles run it. Two are our EXL3 packs, converted from NVIDIA's BF16 checkpoint (revision 97e00975) by exllamav3 1.6.2 with a patch for Super VL's layout; each is a public repository 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-EXL3-<bpw>, pinned by commit. The third reads NVIDIA's NVFP4 release as stored: ModelOpt NVFP4 for the routed and shared experts, FP8 with a tensor scale for the Mamba2 and attention projections and the head (tools/nvfp4_relu2.py). A decode token reads 10.1 GB of that release.

docs.title: Super VL: community EXL3 packs
docs.text:
ENG-377. A community pack on Super VL (community-weights.md) is served as community/<id>: the nearest own EXL3 profile (nemotron-super-vl-exl3-4.0 for 3.5 bpw) with the pack in place of its weights, so the same limits, sampler, LiLiCorr drafter and lookup; price file ops/prices/nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b/community/<id>.dgx-spark.json.

The first one, aitamedia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-EXL3-3.5bpw at 358667cf (57.8 GB), differs from our packs in layout:

community 3.5 pack our 4.0 pack config flat NemotronHForCausalLM (remapped from the Omni wrapper, which is kept as config.json.orig-omni) the Omni wrapper, the trunk in llm_config keys backbone.*, lm_head.*, mtp.* language_model. before each tower none (text only) RADIO tower and projector in BF16 head fp16 lm_head.weight, with tie_word_embeddings: true in the config EXL3 at 6 bits, untied bits routed experts 3.5, every other projection 5; MTP experts 4, MTP projections 6, eh_proj 5 4 everywhere, MTP 4 converter exllamav3 1.6.0, mul1 codebook, out_scales auto exllamav3 1.6.2, mul1 codebook

The reader takes it as stored: the prefixes map to the same canonical names, every trellis rate is one the kernels decode (3.5 / 4 / 5 / 6), the channel factors are suh / svh. The original Super VL head is untied, and the flat config's tie flag is the remap's: a stored head is read and the tie dropped (PackIndex.stored_head, an audit note); without a stored head the embedding stays the head. Anything else the layer table does not expect stops the load by name.

Checked on the DGX Spark, 2026-10-20, on the 0.12.1 code before its version bump (measurements/0.12.1-summary.json has the runs):

  • Against the converter's own forward (1.6.0, on the same pack, flash_attn_nc, teacher-forced on the engine's greedy tokens; nh_check.py engine, 8 prompts x 64 tokens, thinking on): top-1 510 of 512 (99.6 %); both differences are near ties (the reference's margin 0.22 and 0.00 logits); mean |diff| 0.23 logits (0.0047 of the row's largest), mean |diff| over the reference's top 10 0.27, KL 0.0019 nats; max |diff| 6.1 on a token of rank 21,810. Every position with a margin of 0.25 logits or more agrees (494 of 494).
  • The MTP head (nh_check.py mtp, depth 3, 4 prompts x 128 tokens): equal to the trunk's greedy token at depth 1 / 2 / 3 in 92.6 / 84.4 / 73.6 % of positions, mean accepted run 2.45 of 3.
  • Greedy answers in English and German, code, a two-turn chat and one tool call (get_weather with its arguments) through /v1/chat/completions are correct.
  • One fresh server a run, the GPU to itself, conductor raw, suffix store off, --max-len 32768, 512 greedy tokens, thinking off, one request at a time (n = 1): plain (--drafter none, 1 slot) 25.9 tok/s; LiLiCorr + lookup (--drafter mtp --draft-head lilicorr --parallel 3) prose 33.2, code 53.9, chat 37.4, edit 99.0, copy 112.3 tok/s (2.97 / 5.38 / 3.41 / 15.5 / 16.0 tokens a block), every text the plain run's. Prefill of one cold 7,507-token prompt 529 tok/s.
  • Load: weights 53.58 GiB allocated (55.3 GiB of MemAvailable), 47 to 58 s; the served profile (ops/use-profile.sh community/nemotron-super-vl-exl3-3.5bpw: 262,144 tokens, 3 slots, LiLiCorr) up and smoked in 110 s, the process 61.7 GiB on the GPU, MemAvailable 118 -> 52 GiB.
  • Plain decode 25.9 tok/s against the 4.0 pack's 31.1. What a decode token reads, from the headers: 7.95 GB here, 6.74 GB for the 4.0 pack (here the 5-bit dense projections 4.23 GB, the fp16 head 1.07 GB, the 3.5-bit experts 2.13 GB). The decode step's profile here: 5-bit dense rows 20.7 ms, the head and the routers 5.8 ms, the experts 10.2 ms, about 205 GB/s each; the 4.0 pack's profile was not measured in this run. Verify chains of 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 rows at 1k context: 38.2 / 45.6 / 58.7 / 77.1 / 106.2 ms (4.0: 31.3 / 39.8 / 53.3 / 74.5 / 105.8). LiLiCorr offline (nh_check.py lilicorr, 8 prompts x 256 tokens, thinking on): accepted length 4.79, the draft 21.9 ms.

docs.title: Super VL: images
docs.text:
ENG-365. Every Super VL checkpoint carries the Omni model's image tower in BF16: the EXL3 packs copy it unquantised (shard 9 of the 4.0 pack, shard 5 of the 2.0), NVIDIA's ModelOpt checkpoint keeps it BF16 (shard 1; its 392 tensors are byte for byte the 4.0 pack's). engine/models/nemotron_h/vision.py loads it beside the trunk (ctx.vision, the server's image path of the Qwen towers) and runs the checkpoint's own arithmetic: transformers' RadioModel and NemotronH_Omni_Reasoning_V3VisionProjector, bf16, the reference's ops in its order.

part Super VL tower C-RADIO ViT-H/16: 32 blocks, hidden 1,280, 16 heads of 80, MLP 5,120 (exact gelu), qkv with bias, no layer scale; 10 prefix tokens (3 class, 7 registers) dropped after the last block positions a learned 128 x 128 table (2,048-pixel images), bilinear in fp32 to the grid's longer side squared, then cropped (RADIO's cropped position embedding); past a 247-patch side the same without the square, to fp32 rounding projector vision_final_layernorm (the trunk has an MTP head), the v2 pixel shuffle of 2 x 2 patches into one 5,120-wide row, mlp1: RMSNorm (fp32, eps 1e-5), 5,120 -> 20,480, relu^2, 20,480 -> 4,096 processor one tile an image: the 16-pixel grid of image_processing_nemotron_h_omni.py (_compute_target_patches: rounded up, scaled into 1,024..13,312 patches, each side even), torch's antialiased bicubic in fp32, CLIP mean and std; no remote code prompt the template writes <image> (18) for an image part, in a user or a tool message; the engine writes <img> (19), one <image> a row, </img> (20): 256 to 3,328 rows, 1,000 for 1,280 x 800 rows written over the placeholders' embeddings in the prompt chunk that holds them; no positional encoding, so no position moves and every text row is computed as without the image memory 1.57 GB of tensors, 1.60 GiB allocated beside the EXL3 4.0 trunk; the image cache 512 MB (--image-cache-mb); the admission bound for the largest image 1.6 GiB of activations

The caches key an image's rows on its content (key_ids from the digest of the patches), as on the Qwen models: the same image resumes, another one under the same placeholder does not. A request with images runs on slot 0: the tower builds its own context, which the side slots do not read yet (the 27B's images take a side slot since SRV-629). Video, the sound tower and RADIO's summary output are not served. Bolt's EXL3 packs hold the same kind of tower and stay text only (not checked).

Checked against the checkpoint's own processor and modeling code (tools/nh_vision_check.py, DGX Spark, 2026-10-17, three synthetic pictures: shapes 640 x 480, a scene 1,024 x 768, a dark app screen with text 1,280 x 800):

picture rows pixels ours vs reference bf16 ours vs reference fp32: cosine (lowest row), relative reference bf16 vs its fp32 shapes 300 identical max abs 0 0.99990 (0.99668), 0.0138 0.0138 scene 768 identical max abs 0 0.99973 (0.98957), 0.0234 0.0234 app 1,000 identical max abs 0 0.99985 (0.99628), 0.0171 0.0171

The prompt ids equal the checkpoint processor's input_ids for each. On the engine (EXL3 4.0 trunk, "Describe this image.", thinking off, 96 greedy tokens), the answers with our rows and with the reference's rows are identical; they name the three shapes with their colours and places, the sky, sun, grass and red-roofed house, and the app's "Garden settings" header and orange START button. The trunk's own distance to BF16 is the pack's (KL 0.049 above); a BF16 reference of the whole model does not fit the board. tests/test_nh_vision.py: the processor's grids, the position table, the shuffle, the splice across prompt chunks, and the checkpoint's modeling code built small.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
The reference forward (ref.py) follows transformers' NemotronH and the CUDA path the checkpoints were run with (mamba_ssm's selective_state_update, causal_conv1d_update, rmsnorm_fn):

  • RMS norm in fp32 times the plain weight; the gated norm norm_before_gate=False: y silu(z) in fp32, RMS over groups of 512 (inner / 8), times the weight, one rounding.
  • dt = softplus(dt + dt_bias), no clamp (time_step_limit [0, inf]; transformers' torch path clamps at time_step_min, its CUDA path does not).
  • The SSM state is fp32 (mamba_ssm_cache_dtype), y = S C + D x rounded to bf16.
  • Router: fp32 logits, sigmoid, the bias for the choice only, ties to the lower id.
  • Experts: bf16(relu(bf16(up x))^2), down; the weighted sum in fp32 in ascending expert id, one rounding.

tests/test_nemotron_h_ref.py holds it to transformers in fp32 within 2e-5 on three tiny models (Lightning-like, latent, Puzzle per-layer). transformers' multi-chunk torch SSD disagrees with its own one-chunk result by 3e-2 on these weights; the references run one chunk a sequence.

docs.title: How the engine runs it
docs.text:
• Row path: every projection on 16-row tiles, the Mamba2 conv over the row's window, the SSM update walked from the committed state along the row's path in fp32, the gated norm, attention over fixed key chunks, the router, relu^2 experts and the ordered combine: a row of a verify block is the decode step's row bit for bit. A verify block walks the SSM once a head (_ssm_walk): a row whose parent is the row before it goes on from that row's state, a branch walks its path from the committed state again, so the 4 MB state of a Bolt layer is read once a block, not once a row.
  • Verify writes nothing but its KV rows. A commit walks each SSM state along the kept path with the decode step's own kernel (the same products in the same order) and takes the conv state from the path's last three inputs: the committed state is the decode steps' state bit for bit.
  • Prefill: 4,096-token chunks, the chunked SSD form in fp32 matmuls (chunk 128), SDPA, one GEMM pair an expert. The next token agrees with the row path; the bits do not.
  • CUDA graphs: the decode step per attention class, verify blocks, commits, joint decode steps of the side slots.
  • Parallel rounds (SPD-233): the round runner's lanes verify in one joint pass (each lane's rows its lone verify's, bit for bit), 32 rows at most and 16 at 8 lanes (joint_policy, QSE_NH_JOINT_ROWS8): the routed experts are read once for the union the rows pick, so the pass grows with its rows (Bolt EXL3 4.0, 8 lanes x 2 / 3 / 4 rows: 79.4 / 93.3 / 103.4 ms). The lanes' LiLiCorr drafts run as one packed pass (QSE_NH_LILICORR_PACK, on): one context product and one graph a set of heads, the drafter's weights and the head read once a round (8 lanes: 80.9 -> 17.3 ms). The runner weighs, at each lane count, its drafted rounds' tokens a GPU ms against its joint plain steps' and takes the better, probing the other mode every 16th round (lane_plain, QSE_RUNNER_LANE_PLAIN auto; 8 lanes of T1 prose: the joint plain step 64.3 ms for 8 tokens against a drafted round of 114.6 ms for 11). Bolt EXL3 4.0, the card's 8-at-once row (T1 top-k 20 top-p 0.95, 512 tokens), 2026-10-27: 55.6 to 56.5 tok/s before, 96.5 / 97.6 with the three (steady at 8 lanes 64.1 ms a round, 125 tok/s); TTFT 4.7 to 4.9 s both (the eight prompts prefill one after another). Tool: tools/nh_round_profile.py (a round's phases and kernels in process, the packed and joint checks).
  • Taps (set_taps, a block drafter's context): the residual stream entering the tapped layers of every row, copied inside the graphs; a committed row's taps go to the state's ring by position (window + 64 rows): a decode step's in the step, a verify block's kept path's in the commit, a prompt chunk's last rows in the chunk. A restore or a restart moves tap_gen, so a drafter drops what it read of the rows below the length.
  • EXL3 projections (a pack's Mamba2, attention, latent, shared-expert and head blocks): tools/fn_kernels.dense_rows for the decode step and verify blocks up to 33 rows (a call takes 32, so a 33-row block runs as 32 rows and 1). Each row's input is rotated once (dense_rot_kernel, the arithmetic dense fuses), then one CTA a 128-column block, group of 16 rows and cluster rank decodes the trellis tiles once for the group: rows 0..7 in the m16n8k16 tile's a0/a2 lane groups, rows 8..15 in a1/a3. A row's K slices, warp and rank order, output rotation and svh are the one-row dense call's, so every output byte is its byte; the ranks' partials are added by every warp of the cluster, a row a warp. QSE_NH_DENSE_ROWS=off runs dense, a CTA a row.
  • EXL3 experts (tools/exl3_relu2.Relu2Bank): a verify block's (row, slot) pairs in ascending expert id, cut into groups of up to 8 pairs of one expert; a group's CTA decodes the expert's tiles once (row r in lane group r) with each pair's lone-call arithmetic. QSE_NH_BANK_GROUP=off: a CTA a pair.
  • Load-time self-check: a 24-token decode replayed as one verify block, every row and the committed states compared bit for bit (with taps, each row's taps and the committed ring too); a difference turns speculation off.
  • Caches: sections mamba.conv.<L> (bf16 [3, conv_dim]) and mamba.S.<L> (fp32 [heads, 64, state]), views K and V. Lightning: 46.8 MiB of sections a sequence, 6,144 bytes of KV a token.

docs.title: The e4m3 KV cache (NH_KV_FP8, off)
docs.text:
With NH_KV_FP8=1 the attention layers keep each key and value as e4m3 codes with one fp32 scale a (head, token): 528 bytes a layer and token instead of 1,024.

model attention layers bytes a token, BF16 / e4m3 at the full window, BF16 / e4m3 Lightning 30B-A3B 6 6,144 / 3,168 1.5 / 0.77 GiB at 262,144 Bolt 74B-A9B 8 8,192 / 4,224 2.0 / 1.03 GiB at 262,144 Super VL 120B-A12B 8 8,192 / 4,224 8.0 / 4.13 GiB at 1,048,576

The output is no longer the exact model's. The knob is off by default, and the exactness checks hold only with it off. The manifest names it nemotron_h-kvfp8, so its cache entries are never read by the exact cache.

One launch codes a decode or verify row's K and V into the cache straight from the projection (tools/kv_fp8.py). Attention turns the codes back into BF16 as it loads them. A verify row is still the decode step's row bit for bit, so speculation and the load-time self-check work as before. A prompt chunk attends to its own rows in BF16 and to the cached rows decoded, then codes its rows. That decoded copy is one layer's K and V in BF16, 1,024 bytes a token (1 GiB at 1,048,576 tokens), and the adapter adds it to the cap of the prefill workspace (not measured). The MTP head keeps its own cache in BF16.

To turn it on in the Setup Guide (the dashboard's #/setup), pick the model, go to the Tools step and switch on "Long-context cache (FP8)" under Features. Then finish Review and Install, which restarts the engine. To turn it off, switch it off there and install again.

To turn it on from the command line, add this line at the end of ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/serve.env:

QWEN38_NH_KV_FP8=1

Then run ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem restart. Check that it took: curl -s localhost:8000/health shows "kv_cache": "e4m3" under weights, and the engine log's load line says KV cache e4m3. To turn it off, delete the line and run tandem restart again; /health then shows "kv_cache": "bf16". Use one way or the other: a line in serve.env wins over the Setup Guide's switch.

Quality and speed against the exact cache: not measured.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text:
source reader notes BF16 safetensors pack.py, load.py backbone. and an Omni wrapper's language_model. stripped, tower tensors skipped; experts stacked; page cache dropped while loading ModelOpt NVFP4 / FP8 (Super VL's NVFP4 release, hf_quant_config.json MIXED_PRECISION) pack.py, load.py, tools/nvfp4_relu2.py NVFP4 (weight uint8 [N, K / 2], e4m3 weight_scale [N, K / 16], fp32 weight_scale_2): the routed experts an NVFP4Bank (one program a (row, expert) pair and 32 outputs, fp32 products, the tensor scale on the sum, the BF16 experts' roundings; row-invariant), the shared experts on tools/nvfp4_skinny (a down projection's input scaled by a power of two into fp16's range first, NVFP4Wide); FP8 (weight e4m3 [N, K], fp32 weight_scale): FP8Linear, the codes widened to bf16 in a 16-row tensor-core product, the scale on the fp32 sum (fp32 logits for the head). input_scale, k_scale and v_scale are read past: activations and the KV cache stay bf16 GGUF (nemotron_h_moe) gguf.py, gguf_load.py config from the metadata (per-layer expert counts from the router's rows), checked against the checkpoint's config.json when there is one; IQ2_XXS, NVFP4 and Q8_0 matrices and the expert banks kept packed (the embedding dequantised to bf16 for its row gather); other types refused by name

The GGUF types Bolt holds, each with a twin equal to gguf-py's dequant bit for bit (tests/test_iq2_kernels.py; NVFP4 needs a gguf-py that has GGUF type 40):

type where in Bolt format kernel (rows 1..32 row-invariant) prompt chunk IQ2_XXS (16) routed and shared experts 256 weights in 66 bytes, w = d (0.5 + s) / 4 x grid x sign dense: 8 outputs and 4 groups a step, decoded once for up to 16 rows of a program (IQ2Linear); bank: one (row, expert) pair a program (IQ2Bank) decoded to bf16 on _iq2_dequant, cuBLAS NVFP4 (40) every Mamba2 in_proj and out_proj 64 weights in 36 bytes: 4 UE4M3 scales (one a 16) and E2M1 nibbles, w = kvalue x ue4m3; a per-tensor fp32 scale (blk.N.ssm_in.scale, ssm_out.scale) multiplies the matmul's output repacked at load into the checkpoints' NVFP4 layout without changing a value (kvalues = 2 E2M1, ue4m3 = E4M3 / 2) and run on tools/nvfp4_skinny.py, the tensor scale on the fp32 sum (tiles in ops/skinny-tiles.json) nvfp4_matmul Q8_0 (8) head, attention, latent projections, embedding 32 int8 and an fp16 scale 16-row tiles, one bf16 tensor-core product a block of 32 (int8 is exact in bf16) times its scale: the same time for 1..32 rows (Q8Linear) the twin in bf16, cuBLAS

IQ2_XXS needs K a multiple of 256: Lightning's 2,688 and 1,856 are not, so its community IQ2 GGUFs hold IQ4_NL / Q5_0 experts. Bolt's widths 1,536..2,560, latent 1,024 and shared 5,376 are multiples.

docs.title: Speculation
docs.text:
• The lookup (the request's text, the corpus, the suffix store) cut by StairCut through the shared tree drafter, from the staircase's prices (ops/prices/nemotron-3.5-bolt-74b-a9b/, ops/prices/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b/).

  • The checkpoint's MTP head (mtp.py, --draft-head mtp): one native depth, deeper drafts iterate the head on its own final normed row and the drafted token; its attention KV is a cache view. On Lightning BF16 (nh_check.py mtp, 8 chat prompts, 1,000 positions, depth 3): the head's draft equals the trunk's greedy token at depth 1, 2 and 3 in 91.9, 80.6 and 69.5 % of positions; mean accepted run 2.38 of 3.

docs.title: LiLiCorr
docs.text:
NVIDIA's drafter for Bolt (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-LiLiCorr, revision 4c6a5613, 0.96 GB, ModelOpt NVFP4 W4A16, arXiv 2608.20530), engine/drafters/lilicorr.py, written from the drafter's paper, its config and its tensors:

  • context: for every committed token Bolt's residual rows entering layers 1, 18, 35, 51, 68 and 85 (the engine's taps), concatenated, fc (NVFP4) and hidden_norm = g; each of the five layers' K (k_norm, RoPE) and V of g at the token's position, kept in a window ring of 1,024 positions; computed for the rows a draft has not read yet, from the engine's tap ring
  • block: [anchor, mask 990 x 7] at positions n .. n + 7 on Bolt's embedding; per layer RMSNorm, the grouped dynamic convolution's input side (kernel 2, group 16), q/k/v with q_norm and k_norm, RoPE (theta 10,000), attention of each block row over the context keys within its window (query - key < 1,024) and the whole block with a sink logit a head in the softmax, o_proj, the convolution's output side; the same around the SiLU MLP (12,288, NVFP4); the final norm; Bolt's head on rows 1 .. 7
  • lattice: the top 8 candidates a slot with their features (log p, p, log p - log p_top, rank / 7, rank 0) through a LayerNorm and an MLP, token, pass, slot and rank states, two transformer layers over the 56 nodes with a learned bias by slot distance, then factor vectors: score(slot 1) = 8 cos(anchor, in), score(slot s | slot s - 1) = 8 cos(out, in)
  • walk: greedy, left to right, on the GPU: 7 tokens, each with its row's softmax as its confidence (the decile calibration of StairCut: AUC 0.89 against acceptance, 0.86 for the drafter's own token probability)
  • the draft is one CUDA graph (11.2 ms on Bolt IQ2: Bolt's Q8_0 head 4.3, the NVFP4 MLPs 2.6, the bf16 attention and convolution projections 2.3); the context's rows run eagerly
  • the NVFP4 kernels multiply in fp16, and the draft's MLP inputs pass 65,504 (the convolution reaches +-800 before the gate and up products): a row past 2^15 is scaled by a power of two around the product (_lin_wide, exact)
  • a draft head of the shared tree drafter beside the lookup, cut by StairCut; the lookup beside it matches 6 tokens at least (LOOK_MIN_ORDER_HEAD; at 3 its short matches cost chat 7 % and code 4 %); QSE_NH_LOOKUP=off drafts with the head alone
  • load-time gate: drafts against the trunk's greedy decode of the self-check's prompt; a mean run under 1.0, missing files or a load error leave the lookup drafting alone, with the reason in the log and in /health (weights.lilicorr)

Offline, a draft at every position of the trunk's greedy text (nh_check.py lilicorr, 8 chat prompts x 256 tokens, thinking on): accepted length 4.55 (3.43 .. 6.49), against NVIDIA's 4.68 (greedy, SPEED-Bench); the draft agrees with the trunk at depth 1 .. 7 in 89.3, 80.0, 70.3, 60.4, 53.0, 45.5, 39.5 % of positions.

logprobs within 0.07 where the end anchor restored (the tail's prefill chunks differ from the cold prompt's) taps (tests/test_lilicorr.py): verify rows' taps and the committed ring against the decode steps', graphs, joint steps, prompt chunks bit for bit; chunk rows near the row path SSM walk of a verify block (tests/test_nemotron_h_kernels.py): a chain and a branching tree every row the decode steps along its path, bit for bit LiLiCorr against an fp32 reference written from the drafter's definition (tiny weights) block within 2e-5, lattice scores within 1e-4, the same walk Bolt server: plain vs LiLiCorr + lookup, 20 requests and 5 asks 22 the same, 3 the same up to the reasoning budget's close EXL3 rows path (tools/fn_dense_rows_check.py): dense_rows against the one-row dense at Bolt's, the 27B's and Flash-Next's shapes, M 1..32, clusters, 8 warps, groups, the fp32 head, every rate; all 281 projections of the 2.0 pack; dense against 0.9.x's every byte the same EXL3 bank grouped (tests/gpu/test_nemotron_h_exl3_gpu.py, fn_dense_rows_check.py bank): M 2..32, every row on the same 9 experts up to few shared every pair its lone call's bytes Bolt EXL3 2.0 engine on the rows path (fn_dense_rows_check.py engine, 3 prompts): self-check at 24 and 8 rows, a 16-row tree against each branch's sequential decode, graph replay, 32 decode steps with QSE_NH_DENSE_ROWS on and off bit for bit Bolt EXL3 2.0 server: plain vs LiLiCorr + lookup, 20 requests and 5 asks 21 the same, 4 the same up to the reasoning budget's close

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: A DGX Spark has 128 GB of memory that the CPU and the GPU share, and a board that runs out of it does not recover by itself: the GPU driver locks, the box stops answering, and only a power cycle brings it back. Most rules on this page exist to keep that from happening on a box nobody can reach.

docs.title: One engine per board
docs.text: Two engines loading side by side will wedge the board. The served engine reserves about 69 GB, and a second one of the same size does not fit. Every script here checks for a running engine first, and a loading engine counts even though it answers nothing yet. The server binds its port only after the weights are in, so for the minutes of a load neither /health nor the port shows it. ops/engines.sh finds engines by their process instead.

docs.title: Memory rules
docs.text:
Keep at least 15 GiB of MemAvailable at the worst case of anything you run. Before any change that can raise memory (a cache budget, the context length, more parallel sequences, a new resident copy), write down its worst-case bytes first. During a trial, run a guard that kills your test process when MemAvailable drops under 10 GiB.

What the served stack costs:
