item size NVFP4 weights and the FP8 head, on the device about 16.4 GiB KV buffer, allocated for the whole context at load 104.25 KiB a token (106,752 bytes): 64 KiB for the target, 20 KiB for each of the two block drafters, which the served profile loads although StairCut drafts with one, and 256 B of rotary table (28.0 GB, 26.1 GiB, at 262,144 tokens) the whole stack at load, 262,144-token context 53.45 GB (measured with tools/mem_audit.py) the served engine at load, 262,144-token context (2026-10-01, memory.split) 57.0 GiB allocated (weights 16.35, KV pool 16.00, the drafters' context caches 10.00, GDN state 0.14, vision 0.86, the rest 13.7: drafter weights and buffers about 5.9, verify graphs 5.4, warm-up workspace 2.2), 58.2 GiB for the process, 62.7 GiB of MemAvailable the same at 131,072 tokens 44.0 GiB allocated, 45.2 GiB for the process: halving the window frees 13.0 GiB (KV pool 8, drafter caches 5) the caches as they fill (2026-10-01, with that day's budgets: an 8 GiB state store, 4 GiB of anchors, a 2 GiB stash) state store up to 4 GiB (its budget less the 4 GiB pin), resident prefix up to 10 GiB (anchors, stash and the 4 GiB pin); 75.0 GiB for the process after a short session state store 2 GiB budget (CACHE_GB), at most 1 GiB a snapshot (STORE_ENTRY_GB, about 7,000 tokens) resident prefix 2.5 GiB of anchors (RESIDENT_GB), a 1 GiB guest stash (RESIDENT_STASH_GB), a 4 GiB pin (RESIDENT_PIN_GB), 4 GiB for a parked session (RESIDENT_PARK_GB)

The last two rows are the shipped ops/serve.env, which the box these figures come from also runs; its serve.env differs only in running two parallel sequences (parallel-requests.md). tests/test_docs_defaults.py checks both rows against the server's flag defaults and ops/serve.env.

Page cache counts as available memory but is not always given back in time. After a load, the engine never reads the weight files again, and ops/start.sh drops their page cache (tools/drop_page_cache.py, posix_fadvise with DONTNEED, no root needed). Without that drop, an 8,192-row prefill took free memory to 1 GB and the driver logged NV_ERR_NO_MEMORY. With it, the same request left 53 GB free.

The FP8 profile needs about 27.5 GiB of weights on the device instead of 16.4. The BF16 checkpoint needs about 54 GB: keep --max-len at 65,536 or less with it unless the byte math says otherwise.

part GiB weights 16.35 KV pool 16.00 drafter caches 10.00 the rest 14.70 caches at their caps 13.5 left for the rest of the board 48.65

Where the served engine's memory goes at the 262,144-token context. The first four parts are the engine at load, 57.0 GiB allocated (measured, the engine's memory split, 2026-10-01; “the rest” is the recurrent state, the vision tower, drafter weights and buffers, verify graphs and warm-up workspace). The caches at their caps add about 13.5 GiB under the 70 GiB ceiling (arithmetic, from the served budgets).

docs.title: Running the service
docs.text:
ops/serve.env is the served configuration. It holds about 60 settings, from paths and the port to every QWEN38_* switch, each with the reason for its value in a comment. The scripts read it.

script what it does ops/make-secrets.sh creates secrets.env with the metrics token (mode 600), once; --admin adds the admin password (QSE_ADMIN_TOKEN), which turns the admin rule on; --rotate replaces what is there ops/start.sh [--setup [--host ADDR]] starts the engine on the port from serve.env and waits for /health; refuses if an engine is alive or the port is held. --setup, or the marker run/setup-pending, starts setup mode instead (setup.md) ops/stop.sh [seconds] sends SIGTERM, waits for the drain (60 s by default), and kills only after that ops/watchdog.sh one health check, for cron every minute; restarts after 3 failures in a row ops/hold.sh <minutes> <command> runs a command with the board to itself, then restores the service ops/gate.sh <label> the release gate (measurement.md) ops/roles.sh load ROLE \| up \| down \| settle loads the roles beside the engine one at a time through the residency planner; up is what start.sh runs after /health

ops/start.sh is safe to run at any time. If the engine is healthy it says so and exits. It refuses, with a non-zero exit, while any engine is alive or while something else holds the port without answering /health.

The watchdog restarts only what it is sure about. A healthy server is left alone, and so is a draining one, because killing a graceful stop halfway is worse than a slow stop. A loading engine is left alone for up to 900 s. Only a server that fails three checks in a row is restarted, so one slow check during a long verify does not bounce a working server. A server whose /health answers 500 with status: failed (SRV-671: its CUDA context failed, after a device-side assert every CUDA call of the process fails) is restarted after two checks, with no loading grace, and the status page's reason says why while it stops and loads again.

The engine runs no chatd (engine API 1.7): ops/start.sh, ops/watchdog.sh and bin/tandem never start or stop it, and bin/tandem chat runs TandemApp's tandem-node chat (TandemApp's chat.md).

At boot, two cron lines bring the service up:

@reboot sleep 90 && bash $HOME/<checkout>/ops/start.sh >> $HOME/<checkout>/logs/boot.log 2>&1
* * * * * bash $HOME/<checkout>/ops/watchdog.sh

On a box that install.sh set up, the scripts run from run/ops, beside the serve.env the installer rendered with this box's paths; the checkout's src/ops/serve.env is the release's template. The installer copies start.sh, stop.sh, engines.sh, roles.sh, watchdog.sh, hold.sh, use-profile.sh, make-secrets.sh, engine_status.py and fetch_weights.py there on every run; chatd is TandemApp's. The lines are:

@reboot sleep 90 && bash $HOME/TandemLLM/bin/tandem start >> $HOME/TandemLLM/src/logs/boot.log 2>&1
* * * * * bash $HOME/TandemLLM/run/ops/watchdog.sh

Every line runs its script through bash, as the scripts call each other: a copy that lost its execute bit (a deploy that did not keep file modes) still runs. tests/test_no_exec_bit.py fails on a new direct call (OPS-167).

bin/tandem reads run/ops/serve.env under set -e. A missing ops/active-profile is the normal state of a plain install and loads the template's values; a command in the config that fails stops it with the file and the line. Boxes installed before 0.11.2 need one run of the installer to get both, and the scripts above (OPS-159, OPS-161).

docs.title: tandem doctor
docs.text:
bash ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem doctor checks an install and repairs what is safe to repair; --check only reports, --json prints the report (OPS-171). It runs by itself before every tandem start and in the check step of every Setup Guide install, which keeps its report on the job. On a checkout it is python -m server.setup.doctor. It repairs file modes (against ops/executables.txt, the release's executable files), a missing copy in run/ops, bin/tandem's mode, stale pid files of the engine and chatd, a hold's pause left behind, a setup marker with an address start.sh refuses, and a secrets file readable by others (600). It reports, and never changes: a run/ops copy that differs from src/ops (run the installer again), a serve.env that does not load (the failing line), an interpreter that does not run, a secrets file where the engine does not read it, a fresh hold, and too little disk for a download (--profile P or --need-gb N). A QSE_BACKENDS other than empty or off is reported with the file that sets it; only --retire-backends changes that (Other backends moved to TandemApp). Each run appends to logs/doctor.log; the exit status is 0 when nothing is left to look at.

ops/qwen38-engine.service is a systemd user unit for the same job. A user unit only survives logout with loginctl enable-linger, which needs root. Install one mechanism, never both: two supervisors for one port start the service twice.

docs.title: Setup mode and the setup guide
docs.text:
The Setup Guide installs a configuration through the engine's Setup API, /v1/setup/* (setup.md), from TandemApp's Setup page (#/setup) or from bin/tandem setup in a terminal. On a new box, install.sh --setup or ops/start.sh --setup starts setup mode: server/app.py --setup with the Setup API and Wren, the guide's small assistant, and no served model. It binds 127.0.0.1 unless --host says otherwise, and /health answers "mode": "setup", which the watchdog takes as healthy. While run/setup-pending exists, every start, the reboot's included, comes back in setup mode.

The guide's install writes run/setup.env, which ops/serve.env reads last (after the weight profile), and switches through ops/use-profile.sh. It never edits ops/serve.env. A box whose serve.env was copied before the setup guide needs the overlay's last lines from the repository's ops/serve.env, or the guide refuses to install (no_overlay_hook). Reset level 2 removes the overlay; the other reset levels remove caches, weights or history (setup.md, "Reset").

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a serve.env file. ops/serve-fp8.env and ops/serve-balanced.env source ops/serve.env and change two lines: NV (the NVFP4 files) and HEAD (the FP8 head). The balanced profile takes its MLP overlay and head from the published NVFP4 set, the same files ops/serve.env loads. Everything else comes from ops/serve.env, StairCut included.

That includes StairCut's verify prices, ops/stair-tables-nvfp4.json, which were measured on the full-NVFP4 profile. The router corrects their level online, with its per-class block factor (engine/lenrouter.py), but the staircase's shape is not measured for either profile, and neither profile's speed is measured on this release.

  • To gate a profile: ops/gate.sh <label> --profile ops/serve-fp8.env.
  • To serve a profile on the service port: copy its two lines into ops/serve.env and restart the service through ops/hold.sh.
  • For the engine tools, export the same values: QWEN38_NVFP4= and QWEN38_FP8_HEAD= (empty) for plain FP8.
  • The FP8 profile also reads its own launch table (QWEN38_FP8_TILES=ops/fp8-tiles.json) and its router prices (--price-table ops/prices.json:fp8-plain).
  • --fp8-head build builds the FP8 head at load, without the file.

docs.title: One model at a time: the 27B and Flash-Next
docs.text:
The box serves one model at a time; ops/active-profile says which. The 27B's profiles are nvfp4 and exl3-<bpw>; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's are flashnext-2.05 to flashnext-6.05, one per turboderp EXL3 pack (ops/profiles/_flashnext.env and one small file each). The same scripts serve both:

  • ops/use-profile.sh flashnext-3.05 switches as for the 27B: it checks or fetches the pack, stops the engine under the box lock, starts the new profile and runs the smoke; a failed smoke starts the previous profile again, 27B or Flash-Next. The two never run at the same time. A Flash-Next profile names no 27B drafter, draft head or base snapshot (QSE_ASSETS is empty), and the MemAvailable a start waits for is the profile's own (QSE_MEM_NEED_GIB: 55 to 114 GiB by pack; 80 for the 27B).
  • The pack comes from one branch of turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3 (QSE_WEIGHTS_REVISION), pinned to its commit when the download starts. The branch has no checksum list, so ops/fetch_weights.py writes the hub's sha256 of every LFS file to _hub_manifest.json and checks against it. The 4.05, 5.05 and 6.05 packs share one n-gram table file (same sha256); a pack fetched next to one that has it hard-links the file instead of downloading 39 GB again.
  • ops/start.sh passes the profile's QSE_ENGINE_FLAGS (--model <pack> --drafter mtp) and --corpus in place of the 27B's model and drafter flags; with no such key the 27B's command line is the one it was. The server chooses the engine from the checkpoint's config.
  • The page-cache drop after a start (DROP_PAGE_CACHE=1) adds the pack (QSE_PAGE_CACHE_DROP) and leaves a warm n-gram table in the cache (QSE_PAGE_CACHE_KEEP): the engine keeps reading it.
  • The watchdog and the @reboot line run ops/start.sh of the tree that serves, so a crash or a reboot brings back the active profile, whichever model it is.
  • The status file and page name the profile that is loading (profile).
  • A start refuses a --max-len above the profile's largest window in its registry entry (max_window), naming both numbers, before the minutes of loading.

Each profile sets its engine's ceiling and peak (MEM_CEILING_GIB, MEM_PEAK_GIB), with the arithmetic in the file: the weights, the runtime, slot 0's KV at 262,144 tokens and the caches, then the prefill workspace on top. The n-gram table is not in them. Warm, it is page cache, which every MemAvailable floor check counts as used (the warm table's resident bytes, read with cachestat); cold, it is read past the page cache through a row cache of QWEN38_FN_TABLE_CACHE_GB (2) in host memory.

docs.title: Holding the board
docs.text:
Measurements need the board to themselves, and so does anything that loads a second copy of the model. ops/hold.sh makes the safe sequence the easy one:

flock ~/.qwen38-box.flock bash ops/hold.sh 30 python tools/verify_spec.py ...

It arms a pause file so the watchdog stands back, and keeps it fresh for the whole hold. Then it stops the service and runs the command. Afterwards it restarts the service and waits for /health. On every exit path, including a killed command, it removes the pause. The lock file makes two holds wait for each other. A pause file older than 2,400 s is ignored, so a crashed hold cannot leave the service unsupervised for long.

Taking the service down stops everyone who uses it. Hold the board when nobody needs the service, and keep holds short.

docs.title: A second engine on one box
docs.text:
A peer is a second engine run from a checkout of its own (same commit, its own logs/ and run/), for tests that need two engines on one box. Its tree's ops/start.sh starts it with QSE_PEER set:

QSE_PEER=p1 QSE_PEER_PORT=8100 QSE_PEER_NEED_GB=20 bash ops/start.sh
  • QSE_PEER_PORT and QSE_PEER_NEED_GB (the GiB its load takes) are required. QSE_PEER_HOST is an address, 127.0.0.1 by default. QSE_PEER_ENGINE_FLAGS replaces QSE_ENGINE_FLAGS; QSE_PEER_DISK_CACHE gives it a disk tier of its own (off by default).
  • The start refuses in setup mode, when any engine holds its port, when a peer of the same name is alive, and when MemAvailable is under QSE_PEER_NEED_GB plus QSE_PEER_FLOOR_GB (15 by default), read by tools/memgate.py.
  • A peer runs the engine alone: no conductor, roles, decision models or chatd, and no status file, responder, usage ledger or backends. Its pid file and log are logs/peer-<name>.pid and logs/peer-<name>.log. Its first start writes run/peer, which marks the tree as the peer's.
  • In a peer's tree, ops/stop.sh stops that peer and nothing else, the watchdog does nothing, and a plain ops/start.sh refuses. ops/stop.sh --list prints the pids a stop would signal, without signalling.
  • The box's own scripts do not count a peer: its start.sh starts beside one, and its stop.sh and watchdog never act on one. ops/hold.sh refuses to begin while a peer is alive and names it, since a hold needs the whole box.

tools/memgate.py also watches MemAvailable during a run (--floor-gib, every 0.2 s) and stops a load driver on a breach. tools/linkrelay.py puts a link between two processes on loopback: a TCP relay with a set delay and rate per direction, and a control socket that cuts, stalls (blackhole) and heals it. Its stats report its own added latency (own_us); measured at delay 0, that is the relay's floor on loopback, not a link cost. Nothing on one box measures speed: both engines share one GPU and one memory bus.

docs.title: A split model's two stages
docs.text:
One model can run as two stage processes on two boxes (docs/server.md "One model as two stage processes"). Each box's install serves one stage; the keys go in that install's run/local.env (never in the template, so a box without them serves the whole model):

key what TANDEM_STAGE=LO:HI 0:k the front stage, k:layers the tail TANDEM_LINK_LISTEN=IP:PORT or TANDEM_LINK_PEER=IP:PORT wait for the other stage here, or dial it there; one of the two on each side, an IP literal, never a wildcard TANDEM_LINK_KEY=PATH the path of the key file both stages share (mode 0600, at least 32 bytes); never the key itself TANDEM_STAGE_CACHES=on\|off both stages alike, with the same QSE_PARALLEL (off: one slot, nothing kept) TANDEM_STAGE_SNAPSHOTS_GB, TANDEM_STAGE_CACHE_DIR, TANDEM_STAGE_CACHE_GB the front with caches on: memory for its kept states a slot, its half of the disk tier, that folder's size

ops/start.sh (ops/engines.sh stage_layer) turns them into the server's flags, runs the engine alone (no conductor, roles, decision models or chatd) with the KV pool off, and refuses a bad combination in one line before anything starts: a link key without a stage, a range that is not LO:HI, no link address or both, a wildcard or a name for an address, a key in place of its path, a key file that is not there, a front with a disk tier (QSE_DISK_CACHE is the tail's: set it off on the front), the front's keys on a tail or without caches, more than one slot without caches, setup mode. A stage that exits before it answers /health ends the start at once with its log's tail. bin/tandem status names the stage, its layers and its link.

Start the front first and wait for its /health (its weights load in about 12 s for Flash-Next 2.05 at cut 12; its first kernel launches took 0.9 s twice and 198 s once on one box), then the tail, which waits up to 120 s for the link at its start and answers /health once linked and warm (about 240 to 270 s for the same pack). Stop the tail first, then the front.

docs.title: While the engine is away (status page)
docs.text:
A stop, a hold or a start takes the engine away for minutes, and whatever sits in front of it used to answer every URL, the dashboard included, with its own fallback text. ops/engine_status.py (stdlib, 0.3.41-test, OPS-65) lets the service say what is going on:

  • ops/start.sh, ops/stop.sh and ops/hold.sh write logs/engine-status.json (QSE_STATUS_FILE): the state (stopping, held, starting, up, failed, down), since when, the reason (a hold's: HOLD_REASON, or the first line of the file HOLD_NOTE names, else its command) and a hold's budget. A start records how long it took; the median of the last five is the next estimate (300 s before any).
  • With QSE_STATUS_PORT in serve.env (8009 on the reference box), start.sh and hold.sh keep a small responder on 127.0.0.1 at that port (engine_status.py ensure). It answers only what the reverse proxy sends it when the engine does not answer: a page for /dashboard/ (and any request that accepts HTML), 503 with Retry-After, that names the state, the reason, the time and about how long is left, checks /health every 5 s and opens the dashboard when the engine is back; and for everything else the OpenAI error shape (503, Retry-After, type: provider_unavailable, code: engine_<state>) with the same facts under engine. A file that says up while the engine does not answer reads "not answering". An open dashboard shows the same facts in its offline banner. GET /v1/models and /v1/models/{id} are the exception (0.3.43-test, OPS-67): they answer 200 with the engine's last model list, which set up keeps in the status file (a fixed TandemLLM entry when none was recorded), and the state under tandem_engine. Open WebUI refreshes its model list from /v1/models and dropped TandemLLM from it on a 503, so a chat during a restart said only "Model not found"; now the model stays and the chat gets the 503 with the engine's own sentence. A front proxy that merges several model lists should ask the responder when the engine's list is empty (the reference box's ai-models-merge on the Pi does).
  • A responder belongs to one tree (serve.env's REPO) and one status file, and says which at GET /_tandem/status (OPS-173). ensure, which start.sh and hold.sh run, keeps a responder of the same tree, status file, release and address, and replaces any other responder: one of another tree, or of a release without the route, found by its listening socket and its command line. A program that is not a responder is reported and left alone. A responder of an old tree once answered an install's restart with that tree's status from two days before. A reason older than 6 h is not shown, and a start or stop older than twice the typical start plus 10 minutes reads "not answering".
  • While a Setup Guide install restarts the engine, the responder carries the page (OPS-175): GET /v1/setup/jobs/{id} as the server sends it (SSE: the log, the job, each new event, done; or JSON) from the tree's run/setup-jobs, and GET /v1/setup/status: the engine's facts, the running or newest setup job with its step n of N, and the load's progress from logs/engine.log (weights, drafters, warm-up, verify graphs, the port). The server answers /v1/setup/status in the same shape while it runs, and /health names the responder's port (status_port). Its read-only routes answer any origin, so a page on the engine's port reaches it directly when no reverse proxy sends it there; it listens on QSE_STATUS_HOST, else the engine's HOST. install.sh sets QSE_STATUS_PORT to the API port + 9 on every install; install.sh --uninstall stops it.
  • python3 ops/engine_status.py show prints what the responder would say; stop --port N stops this tree's responder.

The reverse proxy sends a failed upstream there and keeps a fixed answer for the case where the responder is down too (nginx):

# in the server block that proxies the engine
recursive_error_pages on;
error_page 502 503 504 = @engine_away;
location @engine_away {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8009;          # QSE_STATUS_PORT (through the same tunnel as :8000)
    proxy_set_header Accept $http_accept;
    error_page 502 503 504 = @engine_away_fixed;
}
location @engine_away_fixed {
    default_type application/json;
    add_header Retry-After 30 always;
    return 503 '{"error":{"message":"TandemLLM is not answering right now (restarting or stopped for maintenance); retry shortly","type":"provider_unavailable","code":"engine_unreachable"}}';
}

The engine's own 503s (a drain, a full queue) pass through unchanged: nginx only replaces an answer it did not get (proxy_intercept_errors stays off).

A browser that has TandemApp's page open keeps working through a restart, through the page's own service worker (TandemApp's dashboard.md).

docs.title: Roles beside the engine (residency)
docs.text:
The engine loads first and holds most of the board. Anything else that should run beside it (a decision model, a librarian, a reader) loads after it, one at a time, through the residency planner (server/conductor/residency.py). A role may load when MemAvailable, less what the engine may still take up to its declared peak (MEM_PEAK_GIB, 77, less what it holds now, from its /health; the whole peak when it does not answer), minus its claim stays at or above the floor plus a margin (15 + 6 GiB by default), never during a hold, and never while another load runs (another role, or the engine itself before /health answers). A refusal names its reason (refused_hold, refused_load_in_progress, refused_memory, refused_unknown_role) and is journaled in <conductor root>/residency.jsonl.

A claim is the role's peak, not its idle size, and it is what the role takes from MemAvailable, not what nvidia-smi shows: arbiter shows 5.1 GB there and took 8.2 GiB of MemAvailable (2026-10-01); Laya inside the engine claims 3.0 GiB (OPS-69, the shipped claim since 0.11.3). A role the roles document switches off (the narrator by default since 0.11.3, the reader) is left out of the plan. The floor, the margin, the settle time, the load order and the claims are the conductor's residency document, versioned like the others and edited in the dashboard (Conductor, Profiles, Residency). The System view shows the plan: the engine's own split (memory.split of /v1/dashboard/system, every part read off the object that holds it, and the load stages), MemAvailable, every role with its claim and whether it fits now, and the last refusal.

ops/roles.sh does the loading. ROLES_AUTOLOAD in serve.env names the roles start.sh brings up after the engine (none today); each role has ROLE_<NAME>_START, ROLE_<NAME>_HEALTH, ROLE_<NAME>_RUNTIME and ROLE_<NAME>_WAIT. A role served by vLLM runs BF16 weights with the KV cache unquantised, and its --gpu-memory-utilization is the planner's byte math (claim over the board's total, rounded down), never vLLM's default 0.9, which on this board would be the engine's memory too. The script refuses a command that sets another --dtype, --quantization, a quantised KV cache or its own memory fraction. Roles never load on the Mac. A hold stops the roles before the engine; after a stop, hold.sh and the watchdog wait the settle time (5 s by default) before the next 80 GiB load. Nothing unloads on its own when MemAvailable falls after a role loaded: the plan shows it.

docs.title: Open WebUI
docs.text:
Open WebUI sends no conversation id unless told to. Without one the conductor tells chats apart by their head and their first turn (docs/server.md, the router's session), which cannot separate a regenerated first message from a new chat that opens the same way. Give TandemLLM's connection the chat id as a header: Admin Settings, Connections, the TandemLLM connection's settings, Headers:

{"X-OpenWebUI-Chat-Id": "{{CHAT_ID}}"}

The placeholder is filled per request (Open WebUI 0.11 or later, parse_custom_headers); the model list and the task requests get it too, which costs nothing (an empty value is ignored, a title request is a side request with no session). Prefer this to ENABLE_FORWARD_USER_INFO_HEADERS=true, which sends the same header but also four fields about the user (name, id, email, role) on every connection, external providers included. The engine reads X-OpenWebUI-Chat-Id either way; a decision row with extra.session = id shows it arrived.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
engine/settings.py is the one registry of every QWEN38_* switch the engine reads (110 of them), with its default and the module that reads it. tests/test_settings.py fails if any module reads a switch another way. To see what is in effect:

python -c "from engine.settings import SETTINGS; import json; print(json.dumps(SETTINGS.describe(), indent=1))"

Server behaviour (ports, limits, caches, reasoning) is set by command-line flags. python server/app.py --help lists them, and ops/start.sh builds them from serve.env.

docs.title: Release checklist
docs.text:
Every release runs these on the box before its tag, and ships only when all pass:

  1. ops/gate.sh <label>: the CPU and GPU tests, identity, agreement, the rows (measurement.md).
  2. tools/client_smoke.py and tools/api_text_check.py against the candidate.
  3. bash tools/release_gate_setup.sh (OPS-177), mandatory: a fresh scratch install of the candidate runs the whole Setup Guide flow beside the live engine without touching it. Run A installs with install.sh --setup, applies a profile through the Setup Guide's API, checks the job, /health and a chat, and removes a second profile's weights through the API. The browser half (TandemApp's Setup page at 390 px) is TandemApp's gate: the engine serves no page. Run B strips the execute bit from start.sh, stop.sh and use-profile.sh first and must still install. The scratch installs use spare ports (never 8000, 8009 or 8016), no chatd, the CPU fake engine and a few KB of stand-in weights, a HOME of their own, and an interpreter copy the live box's ops/engines.sh does not count; every process they start is stopped at the end. The report is in results/gate-setup/<utc>/.
  4. A real agent session with its own tool calls.

tools/release.sh X.Y.Z runs the rest as one command (OPS-223). --only bump writes the version into VERSION, install.sh's default tag and the lines that point at the previous tag (the install commands of README.md and the docs, the generated install flags); the changelogs and the README's release paragraph stay the author's. Then, from the release commit on main:

bash tools/release.sh X.Y.Z --notes notes.md --box <ssh host> --box-py <python on the box> --dry-run
bash tools/release.sh X.Y.Z --notes notes.md --box <ssh host> --box-py <python on the box>

preflight checks the tree (clean, on main, a fast-forward of origin's), every version line, the changelog sections, the commits since the previous tag (no co-author or session trailers) and the weight packs a profile added or changed (an anonymous download at the pinned revision). gate copies a git archive of HEAD to the box and runs tools/release_box_gate.sh there: the engine's CPU suite (tools/engine_tests.py) through tests/script_suite.py, tools/release_gate_setup.sh, tools/client_smoke.py on the conductor and the raw path, then tools/loose_ends_live.py (a streamed call cut by the token limit, a turn behind a running one), both against --smoke-base, whose /health must already name the version (deploy the candidate first; --skip suite,setup,smoke,loose leaves parts out; RELEASE_SMOKE_KEY is the API key both use). tag, push and release make the annotated tag, push main and the tag, and publish the GitHub release with the notes. milestone closes the GitHub milestone vX.Y.Z and creates the next patch's, vX.Y.(Z+1), when it is missing. verify reads what was published: the tag, main, the release, README.md, install.sh and VERSION at the tag, and anonymous downloads. --dry-run runs all but tag, push, release and the milestone changes, whose commands it prints; --only verify checks a published release at any time.

After the tag, the release gets its benchmark report (benchmark-report.md). GitHub has no GPU, so it is made on the reference DGX Spark: a fresh server of the tag, the full suite in parts, then the page.

python -m tools.release_report run --ref vX.Y.Z --pack flashnext-3.05 --out <dir> --prose wikitext2
python -m tools.release_report render <dir>/data.json

Check the page by eye: the verdict, every invalid row and its reason, any number far from the last release's. Then publish uploads it to the release as tandemllm-X.Y.Z-report-<model>.html (gh release upload --clobber). It measures nothing, and it refuses a page of another version or one that still names the box:

python -m tools.release_report publish <dir> --tag vX.Y.Z

docs.title: Deploying a new version
docs.text:
1. Copy the current serving directory to a dated backup (<checkout>.bak-YYYYMMDD-HHMM).
  2. Copy the new files in, keeping the local serve.env values that are site-specific (paths, port).
  3. Restart through ops/hold.sh, so the watchdog does not race the restart.
  4. Check that /health says ok and that VERSION is the new one, then send a short request.

Run the gate and the client smoke set before step 1 (measurement.md). A deploy that fails step 4 goes back to the backup.

On a box that install.sh set up, the installer is the deploy: bash ~/TandemLLM/src/install.sh --yes --ref <new tag> checks out the tag, installs the new lock and rewrites run/ops/serve.env from the release's template; run/local.env stays. A box installed with --setup and then switched to a profile counts as configured, and --setup alone refuses it. Run install.sh --setup --force-setup --yes --ref <new tag>, then ops/use-profile.sh <profile> again; the profile's files are on disk already.

docs.title: Other backends moved to TandemApp
docs.text:
Since engine API 1.8 the engine relays to no other backend (ENG-413). Up to 1.7, QSE_BACKENDS named a config database, for example ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/backends/config.sqlite3, and the engine's port also served the vLLM, SGLang or cloud models in it, checked the users' keys and listed those models in /v1/models. TandemApp's controller, tandem-app, does all of that now, in front of the engine.

A box that still sets QSE_BACKENDS would lose those models without a word, so every path stops instead and says what to do:

where what happens ops/start.sh refuses with one line before anything starts, exit 2; setup mode still starts server/app.py --backends PATH stops before the load with the same line tandem doctor reports it with the file that sets it; --retire-backends repairs it the Setup Guide the plan fails with backends_moved before anything changes, so no install rolls back install.sh on a re-run stops before it changes any code; --retire-backends goes on

None of them opens, moves or deletes the config database. The move takes three steps:

  1. Copy the backends into the controller: tandem-app import-backends --from ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/backends/config.sqlite3 shows what it would copy, and --write copies it (TandemApp's proxy.md). It copies the backends, their keys, models, prices and routing rules. The users' keys stay in the old file: TANDEM_API_USERS_FROM=<that file> in the controller's settings checks them there, read only.
  2. Send the clients' OpenAI routes through the controller (the data plane in TandemApp's proxy.md). The engine no longer checks those users' keys on its own port.
  3. Turn the setting off: bash ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem doctor --retire-backends, or python -m server.setup.doctor --retire-backends in a checkout. Each line that sets QSE_BACKENDS in serve.env, run/setup.env or run/local.env becomes a comment under a dated note, so the old value is still there to read. Then start the engine. An install can do this step in its re-run instead: install.sh --retire-backends.

To go back, run the release from before 1.8 and remove the # in front of the old line.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
/health returns the status, the queue counters (running, waiting, served, refused, errors, timeouts, abandoned), the cache report and the allocator's memory figures. On this board nvidia-smi reports no used memory, so torch.cuda.memory_allocated and memory_reserved are the numbers to watch. Allocated memory that climbs across requests is a leak. Reserved memory that climbs while allocated memory stays flat is fragmentation.

/metrics serves Prometheus metrics, listed in metrics.md. ops/monitoring/ has a scrape config, alert rules with their tests, and a Grafana dashboard generated by tools/grafana_dashboard.py.

/metrics serves Prometheus metrics (Metrics and the ledger). ops/monitoring/ has a scrape configuration, alert rules with their tests, and a Grafana dashboard that tools/grafana_dashboard.py generates. The conductor's stall watchdog can send a push notification when an unattended session's client has gone; the URL comes from TANDEM_NOTIFY_URL or the policy, and is empty in the shipped policy.

docs.title: When something is wrong
docs.text:
• An answer stops in the middle. Find the request's log line. finish=length hit the token limit, timeout the wall clock, error an exception (its traceback is in the log), and abandoned means the client hung up.
  • An agent turn waits minutes before the first token. Check cached_tokens for that request in the usage ledger. On a growing conversation it should be close to the previous turn's prompt. If it is not, read the resident block of /v1/cache/stats.
  • The server answers 503 or 429 while it looks idle. Read inflight in /health. A 503 means a full queue, and a 429 a request without a stream that waited longer than the queue timeout (a streamed chat request waits up to the request timeout and gets : waiting comments; docs/server.md). A high waiting count with nothing running is a bug.
  • The port answers but nothing generates. The watchdog handles three failed checks. By hand: bash ops/stop.sh 30 && bash ops/start.sh.

docs.title: Ornith-1.5-122B
docs.text: Ornith AI's Ornith-1.5-122B is an agentic and coding model on the Qwen3.5 mixture-of-experts layout. About 10B of its 122B parameters run for each token, and a decode token reads about 4.76 GB of our 4.0-bit EXL3 pack (arithmetic, from the headers). On one DGX Spark the engine decodes it at 37.2 to 38.4 tok/s plain and at 85.3 to 124.8 tok/s with its MTP layer and the lookup (measured, 2026-10-20). Its support ships in release 0.13.0. This page says what is different about it and what is measured; Adding a model describes the adapter path it came in through.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
part Ornith-1.5-122B Flash-Next layers 48: 36 Gated DeltaNet, 12 gated attention 48: 36 Gated DeltaNet, 12 attention MLP 256 experts a layer, 8 routed and 1 shared (sigmoid-gated) 512 experts, 10 routed and 1 shared residual stream one 4 streams of 2,560 attention dense, 2 KV heads of 256 sparse past 2,051 tokens KV a token 24,576 bytes, 2,048 more for the MTP layer 29,952 bytes context 262,144 tokens 262,144 draft layer one MTP layer one MTP layer images a Qwen3.5 vision tower, 27 blocks a vision tower weights served our EXL3 pack at 4.0 bits a weight turboderp's EXL3 packs

Ornith-1.5-122B beside Flash-Next.

engine/models/qwen3_5_moe holds the trunk. It reads the configuration strictly and the EXL3 pack with its per-expert projections and mixed rates. The row step and the prefill run on Flash-Next's EXL3 kernels with one residual stream, and the router kernel takes up to 512 experts. The reference forward (ref.py) matches transformers on tiny random configs of both Qwen3.5 MoE shapes. The tokenizer has 248,320 ids, so the lookup keeps a suffix store of its own.

docs.title: The pack
docs.text:
Our pack has every projection at 4 bits: the routed and shared experts, the Gated DeltaNet and the attention layers. The head is at 6 bits, the MTP layer at 4, and the vision tower at 6. exllamav3 1.6.2 converted it from the BF16 checkpoint at revision e09bc0dfbe. In layers 3 to 13, 13 routed experts have weights that are all zero once cast to fp16, and stock exllamav3 stops on them; the conversion used a patch that keeps their input scales, published in the pack's repository. The repository 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Ornith-1.5-122B-EXL3-4.0 is public, 64.6 GB, pinned by commit (92f7483c).

check result this engine against BF16 KL 0.139, top-1 86.2 %, perplexity 7.27 against 7.09 the converter's forward against BF16 KL 0.136, perplexity 7.32 this engine against the converter's forward top token at 498 of 512 positions (97.3 %), KL 0.027 prefill against the engine's reference the same top token a verify block's rows against the decode step equal, chains of 2 to 32 rows and a tree

The pack against the BF16 checkpoint's logits, 8 wikitext rows of 1,024 tokens (tools/q35m_quality.py), and this engine against the converter's own forward (1.6.0) on the same pack, fed the engine's greedy tokens (512 positions). (measured), 2026-10-20.

The engine and the converter's forward do not agree on every token. Of the 14 positions where the top token differs, 9 have a margin under 0.5 logits, 2 a margin between 0.5 and 1, 2 between 1 and 2, and one over 4. The cause is not tested.

docs.title: Drafting
docs.text:
The profile drafts with the pack's MTP layer as a chain of 3 and the lookup, in one tree that StairCut cuts with the pack's price file (ops/prices/ornith-1.5-122b/). After a round that StairCut cut to the anchor alone, the next 1, 2, 4, then 8 rounds take the plain step before the next draft (QWEN38_Q35M_ANCHOR_BACKOFF=8); a round that drafts starts the count over. QSE_ORN_HEAD=dflash2 drafts with incoai's DFlash2 drafter for Ornith instead (1.86 GB, Apache-2.0), with its projections in NVFP4 and its head over the 32,768 most used tokens; it takes 2.86 GiB.

prose code chat edit copy 2,048 code plain 37.6 38.4 37.8 38.0 38.1 37.2 MTP layer + lookup (the profile) 85.3 114.2 110.0 115.9 124.8 103.3 DFlash2 + lookup 67.3 91.7 92.2 106.9 122.8 96.8

Decode through the server, tok/s: one fresh server a row, greedy, thinking off, 512 new tokens on prompts of 3,146 to 4,165 tokens, one run a cell; the last column a 2,048-token code answer through the raw path. Every drafted text equals the plain one. (measured), 2026-10-20.

docs.title: Serving
docs.text: One slot, a window up to 262,144 tokens, the pack's own vision tower on the EXL3 kernels (0.35 GB at load). The model thinks in a <think> block and calls tools in the XML form. The checkpoint's generation config sets the defaults: temperature 0.6, top_k 20, top_p 0.95. The conductor and Laya are on and the narrator is off; the conductor runs its default fit, which is not measured on this model yet. A start loads the pack in 65 s: the weights take 59.95 GiB, 61.16 with the MTP layer, and a start needs 93 GiB of free memory. models/ornith-1.5-122b/measurements/0.13.0-summary.json has the runs.

docs.title: The e4m3 KV cache
docs.text: Q35M_KV_FP8=1 keeps the 12 attention layers' keys and values as e4m3 codes with one fp32 scale a (head, token): 12,480 bytes a token of window instead of 24,576, the MTP layer's cache in bf16 (SPD-150). The output is no longer the exact model's, so the knob is off by default. Turn it on with Long-context cache (FP8) under Features in the Setup Guide's Tools step, or with QWEN38_Q35M_KV_FP8=1 at the end of ~/TandemLLM/run/ops/serve.env and ~/TandemLLM/bin/tandem restart. Its speed and cost are not measured.

docs.title: What is not measured
docs.text:
• Requests at once: the joint verify of several slots is not built for this trunk yet (SRV-653), so the profile has one slot.
  • Prompt reading speed, first-token times, images, sampled decoding and repeat runs.
  • Any task benchmark beyond tool-eval-bench. On the 0.13.0 code, one run a row, it scored 93 and 94 on the raw path at every thinking setting, 96 with the conductor's tools profile, and 80 raw against 84 with the conductor in hard mode (docs/tool-eval-bench.md).
  • The cause of the 14 differences from the converter's forward.
  • The e4m3 KV cache's speed and its cost against the exact cache.

docs.title: Overview: what TandemEngine is
docs.text:
TandemLLM runs the models your agents need on your own hardware, behind one OpenAI-compatible address. A coding agent such as opencode or a chat client such as Open WebUI sends its request to that address. TandemLLM picks the model that answers, plans the turn, and watches the turn while it runs.

Several models work on one request. Qwen3.8-27B writes the answer. Two small drafters guess its next tokens and a lookup drafter offers text it has seen before, so one step of the big model commits 4.58 tokens on average on the benchmark row (measured, the paper). More models can run beside them in the same process. Laya's decision models answer typed questions such as “is this turn code or prose”. A Qwen3.5-2B narrator writes one short line about what the big model is doing, and a Qwen3.5-0.8B shadow reader keeps its own copy of each coding session. A residency planner refuses any model that would not fit in memory (Roles beside the engine).

You get on your own machine what a cloud provider gives you. Clients use the OpenAI API with streaming and tool calls. Every request leaves one row in a usage ledger with its tokens and its timings. TandemApp, a separate project with its own docs, puts this engine and other backends (vLLM, SGLang, cloud APIs) behind one address.

An agent's next turn does not read its whole prompt again. The resident prefix keeps the last prompt's rows with a snapshot of the recurrent state every 1,024 tokens, and the end anchor keeps the end of the last answer. A parked session holds a second conversation while another one runs, and the state store keeps whole snapshots. Two caches live on the NVMe and survive a shutdown. The disk tier keeps prefixes that come back. The session spill writes live conversations at a stop and reads them back at the next start: a 41,587-token conversation came back in 0.94 s (measured, the 0.4.0 series). Last, the persistent suffix store keeps the n-gram tables the lookup drafter copies from. Caches describes every cache.

With memory notes on, the model keeps notes as files, one fact per file and at most 400 words. Notes about the user and about each project last across sessions. Session notes hold what is true for one conversation only (TandemApp's docs on memory notes).

The engine says what each request is doing right now under /v1/dashboard/* and counts it in /metrics (Metrics and the ledger). TandemApp's dashboard shows it, beside the other engines it watches.

Requests run in parallel. The shipped profile's 8 lanes decode up to eight requests in the same rounds (Parallel requests), and the proxy relays any number of requests to other backends at once.

TandemLLM is not tied to one model. Its main model is Qwen3.8-27B, and a second, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, runs on the same board in its place (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). The small models are Qwen3.5 and Laya checkpoints, the proxy serves any model behind an OpenAI-compatible API, and Adding a model lists the seams where a main model plugs in.

docs.title: The test environment
docs.text:
Every number in this book comes from one machine with one main model: an NVIDIA DGX Spark running Qwen3.8-27B. The Spark has a GB10 GPU and 128 GB of memory that the CPU and the GPU share. That is the project's test hardware and its test model, and the project has tested nothing else so far. Its kernels' tile tables and StairCut's price tables come from that board. Much of the engine follows that model's mix of 48 Gated DeltaNet layers and 16 attention layers (Architecture).

The project is growing past both. Other CUDA GPUs run the engine with the one Spark-only kernel turned off; their speed has no measurement yet. The proxy and the dashboard run on any machine with Python 3.11. The roadmap (Roadmap) names the next models and boards. When these docs say “the board” or “the model” without a name, it means the DGX Spark and Qwen3.8-27B.

docs.title: Two levers
docs.text:
A decode step of Qwen3.8-27B reads about 27 GB of weights in the vendor's FP8 format. The DGX Spark reads its memory at 273 GB/s on paper and about 240 GB/s in practice, so every step costs at least 100 ms before any code runs (arithmetic). That is a ceiling of 10 tokens a second for one request. The engine is built to get under that floor while writing the model's own greedy text.

With the published NVFP4 weights and StairCut on, it writes 49.89 tokens a second for one request on the benchmark row, against 13.69 for plain greedy decoding on the same box (measured, the StairCut paper, 50 requests each). The rest of this section says how.

The engine pulls two levers on the same cost.

The first lever cuts the bytes a step reads. The served weights store every projection in NVFP4, four bits a weight with a scale per 16 weights, and the output head in FP8. A step then reads 15.01 GB instead of 26.93 GB (arithmetic, from the checkpoint's tensor sizes). Quantisation shows how the 4-bit copies were made and what they cost in quality.

The second lever makes each step produce several tokens. Small drafters guess the next tokens, and the big model checks all the guesses in one forward pass. A guess the model agrees with is a free token. At the first wrong guess the model puts in its own token, so nothing a drafter proposes reaches the output unless the model would have written it. On the benchmark row a round takes 93.4 ms and commits 4.58 tokens (measured, the paper). That is where the name comes from: two models working in tandem, one guessing and one checking.

The verify is cheap because of the memory floor. A forward pass over 16 tree rows reads the same weights as a pass over one row, so on the published weights at 1k tokens of context it takes 74.4 ms against 75.5 ms for 8 rows (measured, ops/stair-tables-nvfp4.json). Extra guesses in the same pass are nearly free until the row count crosses a kernel's tile boundary. StairCut, the router that sizes each round's draft tree, is built on that staircase (Drafters, StairCut and tree verify).

docs.title: What is in the repository
docs.text:
This repository is the engine and what it needs to run. The dashboard, Chat, the gateway in front of other engines and cloud APIs, and the fleet of machines are TandemApp, a separate project with its own releases.

  • The engine engine/, tools/ (kernels) and server/app.py: the model, its kernels, the drafters and routers, the caches, and an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server built on Python's standard library. It needs a CUDA GPU (measured on the DGX Spark only), PyTorch, Triton and the weights. The small models run on its own code: the Qwen3.5 narrator and shadow reader on its Qwen forward, Laya's decision models in the same process.
  • The conductor server/conductor/: a layer in front of the model. It classifies each turn, sets the thinking effort, adds hidden notes and skills, watches the generation for loops and broken tool calls, keeps memory notes and shows the client what it does. It is off unless a configuration directory is given.
  • The contracts contracts/: the engine's HTTP API, the interface of the extension it loads in chat mode, the control verbs of tandem remote and pairing by code. TandemApp copies them at one engine commit and pins them.
  • The installer install.sh: one command that sets up the served profile on the test board, and best effort on another CUDA GPU. With --setup it starts setup mode instead: the Setup Guide in the browser, or ops/use-profile.sh from a shell, then downloads and starts any weight profile (A new box: setup mode, then the Setup Guide).

docs.title: What runs today
docs.text:
The roadmap (Roadmap) widens each of these, one step at a time.

  • Models: Qwen3.8-27B is the main model the engine serves, a hybrid of 48 Gated DeltaNet layers and 16 attention layers; Architecture explains why much of the engine follows that mix. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a mixture of experts on the same hybrid, is the second, served from turboderp's EXL3 packs one model at a time (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). Beside it run the two fine-tuned DFlash2 drafters, the lookup drafter and, when you turn them on, Laya, the narrator and the shadow reader. Behind the proxy, any model a backend serves.
  • Hardware: the DGX Spark is the only board with measured kernels and prices (The test environment). Other CUDA GPUs are best effort.
  • Requests: --parallel N gives the engine N sequences, and requests that decode at the same time share one draft pass and one verify pass a round (Parallel requests). The shipped profile runs 8 lanes since 0.15.0 (SRV-707, QSE_PARALLEL=8 in ops/serve.env), and every weight card has a speed row with 1, 2, 4 and 8 requests at once. With one sequence a request that finds the engine busy waits in a bounded queue, and a short request is served at a safe point inside the running one (the side lane, The side lane). The proxy relays any number of requests to other backends at once (TandemApp's docs on the conductor in front of any backend).

docs.title: Two rules
docs.text:
Every change to the engine keeps two rules, and the release gate checks both before anything ships.

The first rule is agreement with greedy decoding. For every greedy request the engine's output tokens equal what plain decoding on the same weights writes, one token at a time, up to the first near tie where the two best tokens are within one unit in the last place. There the batched verify can round the other way. The paper measured how often: of 30 prompts, 17 outputs equal plain greedy decoding to the end of the answer, and 13 diverge at a near tie with a gap of 0.04 to 0.76 ulp (measured). Exactness has the full statement and the checks.

The second rule is that no measured number gets worse. A candidate runs against the current release in the same hour on the same box, alternated, and ships only if no figure resolves worse: not the mean, the median, the 90th percentile or the maximum, not the time to first token, and not tokens or milliseconds per round. Measurement describes the method and the traps it avoids.

docs.title: The headline numbers
docs.text:
the table below collects the numbers that describe the served engine on the test board. Each comes from the StairCut paper's measurements on the published NVFP4 weights, with the lookup drafter's persistent store off.

what value single request, StairCut, benchmark row (mean of 50) 49.89 tok/s the same drafter at a fixed block of 8 47.13 tok/s the same drafter at a fixed block of 16 44.80 tok/s plain greedy decoding, speculation off 13.69 tok/s teacher-forced bench, 25 workloads, StairCut 90.45 tok/s one round on the benchmark row 93.4 ms, 4.58 tokens time to first token, cold, at 32k / 64k / 128k tokens 44.4 / 93.7 / 208.3 s the same prompt sent again, resumed from the cache 0.3 / 0.6 / 1.1 s held-out loss against Qwen's BF16 release, prose / code +0.0221 / +0.0426 nats

The served engine's headline numbers. Source: the StairCut paper, published NVFP4 weights, (measured).

decoding tokens a second, one request (mean of 50) plain greedy decoding 13.69 fixed block 16 44.80 fixed block 8 47.13 StairCut 49.89

Single-request speed on the benchmark row serve-single-i256-o256-v1: StairCut against the same drafter at fixed block widths and against plain greedy decoding. Measured: the StairCut paper, published NVFP4 weights, persistent store off.

These are single-request numbers. Parallel requests on the engine are measured in Parallel requests. Long prompts are measured separately in Caches. No task benchmark suite has been run, so these docs makes no claim about task accuracy.

docs.title: The paper
docs.text:
Khaled Bakeer's paper describes the engine's decoding method:

Khaled Bakeer. StairCut: sizing speculative draft trees on a measured verification-cost staircase. Zenodo, 29 September 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.23045275.

The paper measured the release tagged v0.2.0-staircut (commit c111fa7) with the published NVFP4 weights on the test board. It backs these parts of this book:

  • the draft tree merged from the block drafter and the lookup drafter, and StairCut, which cuts it each round on the measured verify-cost staircase (Drafters, StairCut and tree verify);
  • the commit of an accepted path through the Gated DeltaNet layers in closed form, and the NVFP4 kernels with a fixed reduction order (Kernels);
  • the NVFP4 quantisation from Qwen's BF16 release and its held-out loss (Quantisation);
  • the speeds of the table below: 49.89 tok/s for StairCut, 47.13 and 44.80 at fixed blocks of 8 and 16, 13.69 for plain greedy decoding, 50 requests each on the benchmark row, and the teacher-forced bench of 25 workloads;
  • the agreement with plain greedy decoding: of 30 outputs, 17 identical to the end of the answer and 13 that part at a near tie (Exactness);
  • the time to first token of a 32k to 128k-token prompt from cold, and again when it resumes from the anchors (Caches).

What came after that release is not in the paper: image input, the conductor, the caches on the NVMe, memory notes, parallel requests, the proxy and the plugins. Their numbers come from the release series, and the text labels them that way. The release gate holds every later release to the paper's single-request numbers and to the agreement rule. CITATION.cff in the repository carries the citation; in BibTeX:

@misc{bakeer2026staircut,
  author    = {Bakeer, Khaled},
  title     = {StairCut: sizing speculative draft trees on a measured
               verification-cost staircase},
  year      = {2026},
  publisher = {Zenodo},
  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.23045275},
  url       = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23045275}
}

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: Qwen made the model weights and their reference implementation. The base block drafter is DFlash2 for Qwen3.8-27B, released by its vendor under Apache-2.0. The engine runs on PyTorch and Triton over CUDA, and its own kernels are written in Triton and CUDA. The lookup corpus that the installer builds comes from public, permissively licensed text. The decision models the conductor can ask are Laya's published checkpoints (Apache-2.0).

docs.title: One request, end to end
docs.text:
This page follows one chat completion from a coding agent through every part of TandemLLM. Each step names the page that explains it. The figure below is the map.

flowchart LR
    c["Client<br/>opencode, SDK, curl"] --> p["Proxy<br/>route by model id"]
    p -. relayed .-> o["Other backends<br/>vLLM, SGLang, cloud"]
    p --> r["Conductor: router<br/>class, effort, notes"]
    subgraph engine["the engine"]
        r --> a["Admission<br/>queue, side lane, memory gate"]
        a --> k["Caches<br/>resume or prefill"]
        k --> d["Drafters<br/>block + lookup"]
        d -- tree --> t["Target model<br/>verify the tree"]
        t -- accepted --> d
        t --> m["Conductor: monitor<br/>safe points"]
        m -- "committed tokens stream back" --> r
    end

The request path. A client sends an OpenAI request; the proxy routes it by model id; the conductor's router plans the turn; admission decides when it runs; the caches decide where the prefill starts; then drafters and the target model take turns, round after round, while the conductor's monitor watches the output at fixed safe points. Requests for other backends leave at the proxy.

docs.title: The client sends a request
docs.text: The client is any program that speaks the OpenAI chat completions API: the OpenAI SDK, opencode, the Hermes agent, Open WebUI or curl. It sends POST /v1/chat/completions with its messages, its tools and its options, usually streamed. The engine's server reads every OpenAI field it can honour, accepts the ones that have no effect here, and refuses the rest with a 400 that names the field (What the API supports).

docs.title: The proxy routes it
docs.text: When TandemApp's controller (tandem-app) is in front, the request is routed by its model field. A model of another backend (vLLM, SGLang, a cloud API) is relayed there: the answer's bytes go back to the client unchanged, and the proxy writes one ledger row with the tokens, the time to first token, the decode rate and the cost. A request for TandemLLM goes to the engine. TandemApp's backends page sets this up, and its proxy page puts the conductor in front of other backends.

docs.title: The conductor plans the turn
docs.text:
With a conductor configuration the server serves one model name, TandemLLM: the weights with a conductor in front. Before the request queues, the conductor resolves a profile (by header, by client, or the default), and its router decides what kind of task the turn is. A tool-result turn keeps the session's class; only a new user message asks a classifier, and the default classifier is Qwen itself under a choice grammar. The class sets the thinking budget and adds a hidden note at the end of the last message: the effort sentence, rules and packages (skill texts). Later turns replay that note at the same token position, so the cached prefix keeps matching. TandemApp's docs on profiles and the router explains the router and TandemApp's docs on packages, the library and the deciders the packages.

A client's side request, such as opencode's title call, is recognised by its shape and served small: no classifier, no note, at most 64 output tokens for a title.

docs.title: Admission decides when it runs
docs.text: The engine holds one sequence unless --parallel N gives it more (Parallel requests). A request that finds it busy waits in a bounded queue (8 by default). A streamed request that waits more than 10 s gets its stream opened and an SSE comment every 10 s, with an estimate of the wait. A short request (at most 2,048 prompt tokens and 64 output tokens, thinking off) does not wait at all: the running generation serves it at its next safe point, between two decode blocks or two prefill chunks, and gets its state back byte for byte. Before every prefill a memory gate checks that the prompt's workspace fits under the declared peak, giving caches back cheapest first. Serving covers the queue, the side lane and the memory gate.

docs.title: The caches decide where the prefill starts
docs.text: A prefill is the most expensive thing the engine does: 208.3 s for a 128k-token prompt from cold (measured, the paper). Before it prefills, the engine looks for state it already has. In an agent session each turn's prompt is the previous prompt plus the answer plus a tool result, and the resident prefix still holds the previous turn's rows in the engine's own buffers, with recurrent-state anchors every 1,024 tokens and an end anchor at the end of the last generation. The next turn resumes there and forwards only what is new. Further down are a state store of snapshots, a disk tier on the NVMe for prefixes that come back, and a session spill that keeps whole conversations through a restart. Caches describes them all.

docs.title: The decode loop
docs.text: Then rounds run until the answer ends. In each round the block drafter proposes up to 15 tokens and the lookup drafter proposes continuations it has seen before; StairCut merges them into one tree and cuts it to the size that maximises expected tokens per millisecond on the measured verify cost. One forward pass of the target model verifies the whole tree through all 64 layers. The engine walks the tree with the model's own tokens, keeps the longest agreeing path plus one token of the model's own, and commits that path's KV rows and recurrent state. Drafters, StairCut and tree verify explains the round and Kernels the kernels that make the verify cheap.

docs.title: The monitor watches the output
docs.text: While the model writes, the conductor's session monitor reads the output at four safe points: before the prefill, after every committed block, at the end token, and when the answer's tool calls are complete. It can close a reasoning block that loops, continue a turn that ended empty, repair or regenerate a malformed tool call, and stop a tool call whose arguments repeat. Everything it adds is hidden from the client and never counted in usage. TandemApp's docs on the session monitor lists its tasks.

docs.title: The stream goes back
docs.text: Committed tokens stream to the client as they are verified, several at a time. A tool call streams as argument deltas while the model writes it, with values typed by the request's JSON schema. With a profile's status lines on, the client also sees one short line for each step the conductor takes (“› reading 20,745 tokens, about 18 s left”), which the engine strips again from the next prompt (TandemApp's docs on status lines, the voice and the shadow reader).

docs.title: After the request
docs.text: The request leaves one log line (counts, finish reason, rate, never text) and one row in the usage ledger. The conductor writes its decisions to a journal, a transcript block for a request with tools, and, when memory notes are on, any <tandem_memory> block the model wrote. When the session goes quiet, a background writer may write the session's facts as notes (TandemApp's docs on memory notes). /v1/dashboard/* serves all of it live, and TandemApp's dashboard shows it.

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text: TandemApp controls an engine host over SSH, with a key that runs only tandem remote (remote-control.md). Pairing puts that key on the engine host without a password: you type a 6-digit code the engine host shows, and TandemApp gets back the SSH host key, the SSH user and port, and an HTTP token of its own. The code also proves the host key, so TandemApp does not have to trust it on first sight. The contract is contracts/engine-pair-v1; the code is server/pairing/.

docs.title: The install ends in pairing
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TandemLLM/TandemEngine/main/install.sh | bash

No sudo is needed. The install starts the engine, or setup mode with --setup, then opens a pairing window. Its last lines are:

  Code:          482913
  Fingerprint:   SHA256:jvC1...   (ED25519 SSH host key)
  Address:       192.0.2.10:8000

In TandemApp, choose Add engine, pick this host (or type the address), and type the code.

  • A new install without --host binds 0.0.0.0, so TandemApp on another machine can reach it.
  • Before anything is paired, it writes the HTTP token's lock line to src/run/http-token, the hash of a token nobody holds. Callers on other machines get 401 until pairing gives TandemApp its own token. Callers on the engine host need no token.
  • A re-run keeps the address the install has.
  • --host chooses the address yourself. On 127.0.0.1 only this machine can pair, and tandem pair says so.
  • --no-pair skips all of it: no window, no address chosen, no lock.
  • --no-start opens no window either; run tandem pair after the first start.

docs.title: tandem pair
docs.text:
bin/tandem pair            a new window: 5 minutes, 5 tries, single use
bin/tandem pair --status   the window's state
bin/tandem pair --close    close it

Run it on the engine host itself; it needs no SSH. The window lives in the engine process, in setup mode or while serving, so start the engine first (bin/tandem start). A new window closes an open one. tandem pair reaches the engine over loopback with the window key, src/run/remote/pair-local.key, which only the installing user can read and which changes at every start. A paired key cannot open a window: tandem remote has no pair verb.

docs.title: What the exchange does
docs.text:
TandemApp makes a new ed25519 key and runs SPAKE2 with the code against POST /v1/engine/pair/1 and /2. These routes take a caller without the token only while a window is open, at most 20 requests a minute from one address. The allow-from list (QSE_ALLOW_FROM) still applies.

Once TandemApp's confirmation checks, the engine host: 1. appends one line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys of the user that installed the engine:

   command="/bin/bash DIR/bin/tandem remote --key-id ID",no-pty,no-port-forwarding,no-agent-forwarding,no-X11-forwarding ssh-ed25519 AAAA... ID
  1. issues an HTTP token for that key id; src/run/http-token keeps only its sha256, on the key id's own line;
  2. answers, sealed with the run's key: the SSH user and port, the host keys, the HTTP port and the token;
  3. closes the window.

Limits and safety: - A wrong code installs nothing. Each run spends one of 5 tries; after 5 the code is spent. After 5 minutes it expires. - A host key or a TandemApp key swapped on the way makes the confirmation fail, so nothing is installed and nothing is trusted. - ~/.ssh is created 0700 and the file 0600 if missing. No other line is touched. - A ~/.ssh or authorized_keys that is a symbolic link, belongs to another user, or is writable by group or others is refused. tandem pair says so before it opens a window. - A key that already has a line of its own is refused.

tandem remote unpair removes the key's line and its token line. tandem remote token rotate over a key's channel replaces only that key's token, so several TandemApps can each be paired with their own. Removing the last paired key's token leaves the lock, never an open network.

Every step is a line of src/run/remote/journal.jsonl (pair open, pair try, pair abandoned, pair confirm, pair paired, pair expired, pair closed). Each line has the address, the key id and the key's fingerprint, never the code, the token or a key.

docs.title: Finding the engine on the LAN
docs.text:
While it listens beyond loopback, in setup mode or serving, the engine process answers mDNS for _tandem._tcp. The answer carries the host name, the release, the HTTP port and fp, the SSH host key's fingerprint that tandem pair prints. No secret is ever in it.

  • QSE_ADVERTISE=off, in run/local.env or through tandem remote settings, switches the advertisement off. TandemApp then takes the address by hand, a tailnet one included.
  • The responder shares UDP 5353 with avahi or systemd-resolved (SO_REUSEADDR, SO_REUSEPORT) and uses its own target name, <host>-tandem.local.
  • If another program holds the port without sharing it, the engine registers through avahi-publish-service when that is installed. Otherwise it advertises nothing and says so in one line at the start.
  • IPv4 only.

QSE_SSH_PORT names the SSH port pairing reports; unset, it is sshd_config's Port, else 22.

docs.title: Parallel requests
docs.text:
With --parallel N the engine holds N sequences (lanes) over the one copy of the weights and decodes up to N requests at once. Two or more decoding requests share each verify pass, so the weights are read once for all of them. The flag's own default is 1; the shipped ops/serve.env, the profiles of every family with side slots and the Setup Guide run 8 lanes (SRV-707), every lane with the same window, except ops/profiles/_ornith.env and _flint.env, which keep QSE_PARALLEL=1 (a setup through the guide writes the card's count over it, setup.md).

How it works inside (slots, the GPU turn, lockstep rounds, admission) is in server.md, section Parallel requests. This page is about using it.

docs.title: Switching it on
docs.text:
In ops/serve.env (or local.env):

QSE_PARALLEL=8            # lanes: slot 0 and N - 1 side slots; 1 is one sequence
QSE_SIDE_MAX_LEN=0        # 0: every side slot has MAX_LEN, slot 0's window (a shorter value is kept)
QSE_KV_POOL=on            # windows are addresses, pages are committed as conversations grow
QSE_PARALLEL_FLOOR_GB=15  # admission keeps MemAvailable at or above this

then restart the service. The same settings as flags: --parallel N, --side-max-len, --parallel-floor-gb.

flag default what it does --parallel N 1 (serve.env: 8) sequence slots; N - 1 side slots beside the engine --side-max-len 0 a side slot's window; 0 is --max-len, every lane the same window (SRV-707). A shorter one is kept for old setups; a request whose prompt plus max_tokens does not fit it waits for slot 0 --parallel-floor-gb 15 a request waits while what the caches may still grow into (at most the engine's room to --mem-peak-gib), the workspaces of the prefills in flight, its own and the KV pages still to commit would push MemAvailable under this, a request alone too (0.15.1, SRV-775); a side slot is built only if it fits above it. The wait is queue time (wait_mem_ms in the ledger) and the client sees a waiting line QSE_GUARD_MARGIN_GB 5 the floor a check holds is the live guard (SRV-785): one prefill chunk's workspace at the class of the longest prefill in flight, one KV commit, a chat sandbox's ask from the last minute and this margin, never above --parallel-floor-gb (for the KV pool's commits, never above QSE_KV_HARD_FLOOR_GB). The wait line names its inputs QSE_MEM_WAIT_S 10800 the longest a streamed request, or one that sends wait_for_memory: true, waits for memory (3 h); any other request without a stream waits at most --queue-timeout. Then it is refused with the reason: a 503 with Retry-After, or an error event (memory_wait_timeout) on a stream opened while it waited (SRV-787, SRV-797; Waiting for memory) QSE_PEAK_STRICT 0 1: a lone request the memory gate refuses waits too instead of running over the peak, and the gate counts the workspaces of the prefills in flight on the reserve (SRV-775; in no profile) QSE_REQ_PEAK 0 1: the [req] line adds peak_gib=, the allocator's peak over a request that ran alone less what was allocated at its prefill's start (a measurement, SRV-773) --parallel-batch on decoding slots verify their trees in one joint pass (off: they take turns) --parallel-draft on the decoding slots' draft calls in one packed pass over the drafter --parallel-cut the family's share: each slot's tree cut to a fixed share (16 rows at two slots, 10 at three, 8 at four); joint: the round cuts all trees together, best nodes first; auto (SPD-155): joint from QSE_PARALLEL_AUTO_N (3) decoding slots, share below. Unset, the model family's joint_policy decides (the 27B: auto), else share --parallel-draft-rows 128 rows of a packed draft pass (SPD-157): eight slots' 16-row draft blocks in one pass; drafting decides speed only --parallel-max-rows the family's rows of a joint pass at most (QSE_PARALLEL_MAX_ROWS; 0 or unset: the model family's joint_policy, else 32). SPD-159: the 27B on EXL3 weights takes 64, each engine's rows in an 8 x 8-row joint pass bit for bit its own eager verify; on NVFP4 and FP8 it keeps 32, since NVFP4 sends 33-64 rows to another tile; past max_rows // 2 decoding lanes (2 rows each) a round runs more passes --side-precapture off capture a side slot's verify graphs at start (about a minute a slot) instead of at first use --side-graphs on off: a side slot holds no verify graphs and verifies eager when it decodes alone (about 1.5 GiB instead of 7.5 beyond its window) --side-slot-const-gb 7.5, or 1.5 with side graphs off a side slot's bytes beyond its window in the build's estimate (QSE_SIDE_SLOT_CONST_GB)

8 lanes are measured on the 27B, Flash-Next, Ornith and Flint (SRV-711, 2026-10-24, 1/2/4/8 requests at once, total tok/s, 3-round medians, N decoding at once: the 27B ThinkingCap EXL3 4.0 38.3 / 67.6 / 100.1 / 154.5, Flash-Next 3.05 36.5 / 45.6 / 57.5 / 71.3, Ornith EXL3 4.0 37.7 / 47.0 / 58.4 / 69.8, Flint EXL3 4.0 111.7 / 154.9 / 193.3 / 232.3). Every weight card has a speed row with 1, 2, 4 and 8 requests at once on the current build (measurement.md); a card's lanes default is never above the lanes its row measured.

The shipped ops/serve.env runs 8 lanes on the pool with QSE_SIDE_GRAPHS=off and QSE_SIDE_SLOT_CONST_GB=1.5, the values the Setup Guide writes for the 27B. Until SRV-707 it kept one sequence, and the box the older measurements come from ran two with a 65,536-token side window.

docs.title: One window for every lane (SRV-707)
docs.text:
Every lane has the window the setup names (MAX_LEN); the Setup Guide has no side window of its own any more, and writes QSE_SIDE_MAX_LEN equal to the window. With the KV pool on a lane's window is addresses: a side slot built at 262,144 tokens takes its constant part and nothing of its window at load (engine/models/*/serving.py side_slot_bytes: no bytes a token when paged), and its pages come from the one pool as its conversation grows. With the pool off (the families whose pool is not verified yet: NemotronH, LFM2.5, Flint, Ornith) every lane's window is memory at load, and a lane is built only while the floor holds.

The guide counts how many lanes can all hold the full window at once, the guarantee (lanes_full in the estimate): min(lanes, floor(room / (window x KV bytes a token))), where room is what the budget leaves after the weights, the tools and every lane's constant part. With the pool off it is every lane whenever the selection fits. Past the guarantee the lanes share what is left, in this order:

  1. A new request waits for memory before its prefill (the admission reserves its prompt and up to QSE_KV_ADMIT_ROWS of its max_tokens in pages): its stream says "waiting: memory is almost full", the Lanes view and the live view show it as waiting_memory with what it needs, what is free, what is being freed or which prefill is in the way, and when the wait ends. A streamed chat request gets its stream's headers at once and an SSE comment every 15 s while it waits, so no client's read timeout cuts the wait; it waits up to QSE_MEM_WAIT_S (SRV-787). With the KV pool the admission checks two things, each as the pool's gate will see it, in the order the pages commit (SRV-797): the prompt's pages (and the router's notes' room) against the pool's hard floor while the prefill runs, without the request's own workspace (the 27B maps the prompt's rows before its prefill; Flash-Next maps each chunk's rows before that chunk and gives the allocator's blocks back after every chunk once the state holds more than 4,096 rows, and the pool's floor already holds one chunk's workspace); the whole request (workspace, every page) against the admission's floor, as before. So the pool never refuses a page the admission counted, and nothing is counted twice: a 142k turn with a 10.8 GiB workspace resumed in place is admitted at 19.9 GiB.
  2. A turn short only by the caches' room (what the state store and the resident prefix may still take under the memory policy's ceiling, which nothing holds) does not wait: it is let in on that room, which the policy keeps from the caches until its prefill has run, or until it ends when its answer's pages needed it too ([parallel] ... let in on N GiB of the caches' room). Only the shortfall is held: the caches still grow by the rest of their room, and a cache that would grow into the held part (a stash, another chat's guest rows, a state-store snapshot) is refused meanwhile, so that conversation may read more again on its next turn. The response cache's budget (host memory) stays counted.
  3. Before anyone waits for memory something holds, idle conversations give their pages back, as much as the admission is short and in this order, each level in the log with its bytes and ms: the caches' levels and the allocator's free blocks, the small models, idle side slots' conversations already current on the NVMe (the idle backfill wrote them: trimmed only), the others (oldest first, a turn that ended within 30 s last, each to the NVMe first with the spill on), slot 0's idle conversation (to the NVMe first unless current), then the side conversations no save could write (SRV-779), then the kept park; after it the host heap is trimmed (malloc_trim, at most every 30 s).
  4. A running lane whose next pages would take the box under QSE_KV_HARD_FLOOR_GB gives way (SRV-709, QSE_KV_RECOMPUTE=on), a streamed one in its prefill as in its answer and alone too (SRV-797): it gives every page back (its conversation to the NVMe first), waits at the head of the line for memory (before any request that has not started; among such lanes, the one that gave way first) and goes on in the same stream by reading its prompt and the text it wrote again. A streamed client sees an SSE comment (: paused: waiting for memory) meanwhile, no token. Each give-way with fewer than 256 tokens written since the one before backs off twice as long before it is admitted again (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, up to 60 s; : paused: backing off after giving way when memory is there), so a lane the pool keeps refusing does not read its rows back every few seconds; while it backs off, requests that fit go. Its re-admission is priced as its first (image rows, cache_prompt, its home slot, its priority), the request's --request-timeout does not count its waits (nor its first admission's), its waits for memory add up toward QSE_MEM_WAIT_S from its first admission on, and a planned stop during the wait ends it with the restart's retryable error (engine_restarting). /health parallel.recompute counts the lanes that gave way, resumed and gave up. Reading again costs a prefill; the text goes on where it stopped, and a sampled or near-tie token after the resume may differ from the one an uninterrupted run would write. The thinking budget goes on from where it was once the lane wrote a token; refused before that, it starts as it would have.
  5. A streamed lane stops only once its waits for memory add up to QSE_MEM_WAIT_S, with the wait's refusal (memory_wait_timeout). One not streamed (its client reads nothing until the answer is whole) keeps SRV-709's count: alone it stops at the pool's refusal with memory_full, beside other lanes it gives way at most KV_RECOMPUTE_MAX (16) times. What changed for it (SRV-797): each of those waits is now a non-streamed request's wait, at most --queue-timeout after a 1 s backoff, ending with memory_wait_timeout (a 503 to send again); before, each could last up to QSE_MEM_WAIT_S with nothing sent. The Chat tab keeps the text and continues it once memory is free.
  6.
