The published NVFP4 set against Qwen's BF16 release: the change in held-out loss on the two gate files and on three wider texts that neither the calibration nor anything else reads. Measured: the StairCut paper's quality section.

docs.title: The FP8 head
docs.text:
As shipped, the output head is 248,320 by 5,120 in BF16, 2.54 GB, and every verify reads all of it. tools/quant_head.py build writes it as e4m3 with one fp32 scale per vocabulary row (1.27 GB), searching the multipliers 1.0, 0.95 and 0.90 of each row's largest weight. One scale per row, because rows are tokens and their sizes differ more than a block scale shared by 128 neighbouring ids can follow.

This head decides what the engine writes, so it took the full gate: prose +0.0015 nats, code -0.0009, and agreement 1.0000 on all 2,618 confident positions. Its kernel returns fp32 logits at every row count. --fp8-head build builds the same head at load, without the file.

docs.title: What stays at full precision
docs.text: The 48 recurrent states stay fp32. They are 151 MB, read and written once a step, about 1.5 ms of traffic. A recurrent state is a sum over the whole sequence carried across every step, so its rounding error grows with every step, and a weight's does not. The convolution weights, A_log, dt_bias, every norm and the drafters' own layers also keep their shipped precision.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a serve.env file. The three that ship differ only in their weights. Drafters, StairCut, caches and the exactness gate are the same in all of them. StairCut's verify prices (ops/stair-tables-nvfp4.json) were measured on the full-NVFP4 profile. The router corrects their level online, with its per-class block factor (engine/lenrouter.py), but the staircase's shape for the balanced and FP8 profiles is not measured, and neither is their speed on this release.

profile file MLP GDN and attention head bytes a step single request NVFP4 (served) ops/serve.env NVFP4 NVFP4 e4m3 15.0 GB 49.89 tok/s with StairCut (paper) balanced ops/serve-balanced.env NVFP4 (the published set's) checkpoint FP8 e4m3 (the published set's) about 18.2 GB not measured on this release FP8 ops/serve-fp8.env checkpoint FP8 checkpoint FP8 checkpoint BF16 26.9 GB not measured on this release

An FP8 profile reads nothing but the vendor's files, so its quality is the checkpoint's. Balanced keeps the recurrent and attention layers on the vendor's weights and quantises only the MLPs, which carry 70 % of a verify's projection bytes.

Profiles and bytes interact with speculation. At one token a step, the full NVFP4 set is worth 14 % over NVFP4 MLPs alone. On a 16-node tree it is worth 0.2 %, because a round that commits 13 tokens has already spread its weight read over 13 tokens. Bytes and accepted tokens substitute for each other.

The 27B also has weight profiles in EXL3 (ops/profiles/exl3-<bpw>.env, switched with ops/use-profile.sh, operations.md). The six sizes are public on Hugging Face, 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-{2.5,3.0,3.5,4.0,4.5,6.0}, with the K3 drafters and the K4 draft head in 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-drafters; the collection is TandemLLM Qwen3.8-27B EXL3. We quantised them with exllamav3 from Qwen's BF16 release. Each card lists every size's KL against BF16 on wikitext-2, from 0.1112 at 2.5 bits to 0.0018 at 6.0, and its speed on one DGX Spark. Running them needs nothing beyond those repositories, the BF16 drafters (...-DFlash2-b8 and -b16) and the base checkpoint; ops/use-profile.sh exl3-<bpw> fetches all of it. This page does not cover how the EXL3 files were made.

docs.title: Standalone 27B EXL3 checkpoints
docs.text:
A complete BF16-origin, mul1 EXL3 checkpoint of the supported 27B family can be passed directly as --model. 0xWhiteMage wrote this path in pull request #1 (0.8.2), and the first community pack runs on it (community-weights.md). The loader recognises quantization_config.quant_method: exl3 in its config; a separate BF16/FP8 base download is not needed when the pack includes the embedding, norms and GDN auxiliary tensors. For example, for a text-only run without speculation:

python server/app.py --model /path/to/exl3-pack --drafter none --vision off

The projected weights and output head retain their original EXL3 codes, channel scales and mixed bit widths, including indexed packs whose projection components span multiple shards. When a standalone pack declares a BF16 source through dtype or torch_dtype, the loader re-encodes its finite FP16 plain tensors as BF16 only when every stored value survives an exact round trip. Comparisons use bounded chunks, including for a plain output head. Missing or non-BF16 source metadata, non-finite values and lossy conversions fail with a named error rather than silently changing precision. This preserves the pack's stored numerical values, not necessarily its pre-conversion BF16 source: precision already lost while creating the pack cannot be recovered. Source-equivalence needs the original checkpoint, and the original BF16 base plus an EXL3 overlay remains an alternative. The existing separate-base overlay precision path is unchanged, and explicit EXL3 paths take precedence over detection (an empty exl3 setting disables detection).

This does not add another codebook, model architecture or MTP format. The existing mul1 reader and its validation still apply. A stock DFlash2 checkpoint can be supplied with --drafter dflash2 --dflash2-ckpt /path/to/drafter for one sequence; speculative parallel serving still requires the engine's lenrouter configuration and a suitable block-16 drafter. Vision and quantised MTP loading are not qualified by this text-only path.

docs.title: The 27B in EXL3: sizes and quality
docs.text:
Since 0.5.0 the 27B also runs from EXL3 weights at six sizes, one weight profile each (ops/profiles/exl3-<bpw>.env, switched with ops/use-profile.sh, One model at a time). We quantised them with exllamav3 from Qwen's BF16 release, and all six are public on Hugging Face as 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-<bpw>. The drafters for these profiles are in 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-drafters: both DFlash2 drafters with their projections in EXL3 at 3 bits a weight (the K3 files) and a draft head at 4 bits (K4). The six sizes and the drafters form one collection, TandemLLM Qwen3.8-27B EXL3.

profile disk KL vs BF16 top-1 agreement note exl3-2.5 12.0 GB 0.1112 86.3 % the fastest exl3-3.0 13.5 GB 0.0621 89.8 % exl3-3.5 15.2 GB 0.0298 93.1 % exl3-4.0 16.9 GB 0.0171 94.8 % exl3-4.5 18.4 GB 0.0096 96.1 % the default of a new box exl3-6.0 23.3 GB 0.0018 98.5 % the closest to BF16

The 27B's EXL3 sizes against the BF16 model on wikitext-2, where BF16's perplexity is 6.849. Measured: copied from the model cards on Hugging Face.

Each card also has a speed table for every size on one DGX Spark (TandemLLM 0.6.2, one greedy request of 512 tokens, speculation on). An EXL3 profile needs four more downloads beside its weights: the K3 drafters and the K4 head (1.9 GB), the BF16 drafters 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-b8 and -b16 (7.7 GB, into the repository's train/), and the base checkpoint Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (30.4 GB, without mtp.safetensors). Since 0.8.1 ops/use-profile.sh fetches all of them, checks each weight file against the hub's sha256, and needs no token. Each card's calibration/ folder has the recipe; the calibration repository itself stays private, and no profile reads it.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text: knob what --nvfp4 a,b,c or QWEN38_NVFP4 the NVFP4 files to load, one per target; empty means the checkpoint's FP8 --fp8-head FILE, --fp8-head build or QWEN38_FP8_HEAD the e4m3 head; empty means the checkpoint's BF16 head tools/quant_nvfp4.py quant --mode rtn\|clip --targets --stats the quantiser tools/quant_head.py build --ratios the per-row scale search for the head tools/quant_nvfp4.py build --model <BF16> --corpus --methods clip,gptq --h-budget-gb the statistics and both quantisers (clip and GPTQ) from one load tools/calib_corpus.py --out DIR --eval-chars the calibration, sensitivity and wide-gate texts tools/quant_sensitivity.py measure and mix --keep-gb the per-piece costs and the FP8/NVFP4 mix file tools/quality_gate.py --plan plan.json --corpus name=path weight sets against a reference checkpoint, on extra texts

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The gate files are one held-out file per domain, 2,048 tokens each; the wider texts add 8k to 12k tokens per domain. No task benchmark ran against the quantised engine, so this page makes no claim about task accuracy. The clip search assumes that input channels are uncorrelated, which is a first-order model.

docs.title: Flash-Next on turboderp's EXL3 packs
docs.text: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next comes in five sizes on Hugging Face, turboderp/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3, one branch each. The engine reads those packs as they are. It runs no quantiser of its own on them and adds no format. A pack is lossy against Qwen's BF16 release by design; speculation is still lossless against the pack that is served (exactness.md).

docs.title: The five packs
docs.text:
The branch name says what is inside: 3.05bpw_h5_ng5 is 3.05 bits a weight on average, the output head at 5 bits, and the n-gram table at 5 bits a value. The figures below are the registry's (models/qwen3.8-flash-next/model.yaml). The weights are the GiB the engine holds on the device, the draft layer and the int8 mixers included: measured for 3.05 at load, and estimated from the file sizes for the other four.

profile branch disk, with the table weights on the device n-gram table largest window on one DGX Spark flashnext-2.05 2.05bpw_h4_ng4 61.5 GB 32.85 GiB (estimate) 24.44 GiB, warm 262,144 flashnext-3.05 (recommended) 3.05bpw_h5_ng5 85.1 GB 47.87 GiB (measured) 30.4 GiB, cold 262,144 flashnext-4.05 4.05bpw_h6_ng6 106.1 GB 62.47 GiB (estimate) 36.36 GiB, cold 208,896 flashnext-5.05 5.05bpw_h6_ng6 121.9 GB 77.16 GiB (estimate) 36.36 GiB, cold load/generation unverified flashnext-6.05 6.05bpw_h6_ng6 137.7 GB 91.87 GiB (estimate) 36.36 GiB, cold none: it does not fit

The windows come from the Setup Guide's estimate (setup.md), calibrated on one 260,800-token request each on 2.05, 3.05 and 4.05 (2026-10-12). It predicts the lowest MemAvailable of those three runs within 0.7 GiB. 2.05 and 3.05 hold the model's full 262,144 tokens. 4.05 ran a 260,800-token request with MemAvailable never under 17.8 GiB on a box whose other programs took 4.6 GiB; under the Setup Guide's frame of 10 GiB for the rest of the system, its window comes out at 208,896 with the vision tower on (0.31 GiB, up to 0.81 with the 512 MB image cache; VIS-97) and 212,992 without it.

The 5.05 pack's earlier blocker was its 7-bit dense projections. The dense dispatch now covers K 2..8; the MoE kernels already supported 7-bit experts. Full-pack load and generation are still unverified. By the estimate its window would be 53,248 with the vision tower and 65,536 without. 6.05 needs about 92 GiB for its weights, which leaves too little under the 15 GiB floor at any window.

The 4.05, 5.05 and 6.05 branches carry the same n-gram table file (the same sha256), so ops/fetch_weights.py hard-links it between packs instead of downloading 39 GB again (operations.md).

docs.title: What a pack holds, and how the engine reads it
docs.text:
engine/models/flashnext/pack.py (PackIndex) reads every shard header and puts each tensor in one kind:

kind what how the engine holds it expert the routed experts' gate, up and down projections, 98 % of the bytes EXL3, one image a layer, through the MoE kernels exl3 every other coded projection: GDN, attention, the sparse-attention indexer, the shared expert, the MTP layer's projections, the head EXL3 mixer the hyper-connection mixers' projections fp16 in the pack; on the device int8 with one fp32 scale for each group of 128 weights plain norms, the router, in_proj_a and in_proj_b, the n-gram projections, conv weights, the embedding as stored table the n-gram table, its own file never on the device; read a row at a time vision the vision tower not loaded

An EXL3 projection is four tensors. X.trellis (int16) holds the codes at K bits a weight, and K is read from each tensor's own shape, so a pack that mixes K inside a layer is described as it is. X.suh and X.svh (fp16) scale and sign the input and output sides, which are rotated, and X.mul1 is the codebook's multiplier. On the 3.05 pack the header audit counted 303,121 tensors: every routed expert at K 3, the dense projections and the head at K 5, except the sparse-attention indexer's projection at K 3 and the MTP layer's projections at K 3 to 5. By those headers a plain decode token reads about 4.23 GB in all at 1k of context, with the mixers as int8 (PackIndex.decode_bytes).

tools/fn_exl3_xcheck.py holds our reading against the converter's own on the 3.05 pack. The trellis decode is equal bit for bit on 16 tensors (experts in layers 0, 11 and 47, GDN, attention, the indexer, a shared expert, a slice of the head). The dequantised weight agrees within 0.36 % of the largest weight, which is our BF16 rounding of the fp32 rotations. 4,096 n-gram rows are equal bit for bit.

docs.title: The mixers as int8
docs.text:
The pack stores the mixers in fp16, and every token reads them. The engine keeps them as int8 with one fp32 scale for each group of 128 weights of a row (gcd(128, K): 128 for the down and inject weights, 64 for the up weights). A weight is then off by at most its group's largest weight over 254, plus fp32 rounding. The kernels sum each 16-weight chunk's products and add them times the chunk's group scale, and the prefill dequantises with the same scales. QWEN38_FN_MIX=int8rows keeps one scale a row, the form before ENG-221, for an A/B; fp16 keeps the pack's values.

tools/fn_mix_quality.py measures what that costs against the pack's fp16 mixers, on the same kernels. On 3.05 with 8,192 tokens, the groups gave a KL of 0.0031 on code and 0.0188 on prose. The arithmetic noise between the reference forward and the kernels is 0.0038 and 0.0255 on the same prompts, so both are inside it. One scale a row gave 0.267 on code and 0.047 on prose: a row whose largest weight is 10 to 420 times its median left its small weights coarse. Int4 gave 0.38 on prose (0.35 in groups of 128) and changed the continuation at its first token, so the mixers stay int8. The groups cost no decode speed (one run each at 1k, rows against groups: prose 41.91 and 41.76, code 42.64 and 43.24, chat 42.24 and 42.21 tok/s) and 0.02 GiB of device memory. Speculation stays lossless with them, and the load-time self-check passes.

docs.title: The n-gram table
docs.text:
For every position the model hashes the token and the one or two before it into 16 row indices (8 hash heads for the bigram, 8 for the trigram), reads those 16 rows of 160 values from one table of about 320 million rows, and joins them into a 2,560-wide feature. The table is coded too: each row is a ring of trellis codes at K bits a value (ng4 to ng6), with one fp16 scale a row and one bias vector a hash head (engine/models/flashnext/ple.py).

The table is 32.6 GB in the 3.05 pack, and it never sits in device memory. The engine reads the packed rows a step needs and decodes them on the device. Where the rows come from is the profile's table policy (QWEN38_FN_TABLE):

  • warm: the file mapped and kept in the page cache. MemAvailable counts that page cache as free, so every floor check takes the table's resident bytes off first (caches.md).
  • cold: the rows read with O_DIRECT through a set-associative row cache of QWEN38_FN_TABLE_CACHE_GB (2) in host memory; nothing stays in the page cache.

On 3.05, cold wrote the same greedy text as warm at 1k and 8k and decoded 40.9 tok/s against 42.0 (one run each). 2.05 keeps its table warm. 3.05 reads it cold: with the whole table resident, MemAvailable less the table fell to 8.4 GiB during a 146,400-token request at a 147,456-token window, under the 15 GiB floor. 4.05 and up read it cold because their weights and a warm table do not fit together.

docs.title: Exact weights where the prefill needs them
docs.text: The prompt runs through other kernels than a decode step (kernels.md). There the mixers, the router and the small projections take exact fp32 copies of their weights (QWEN38_FN_PREFILL_MM=fp32). With fp16 copies the prefill failed its agreement gate on a 3k-token code prompt (95.6 % against the 96.2 % the gate asked), so fp32 is the default.

docs.title: What is not measured
docs.text: Nobody has measured a pack's quality against the BF16 model yet. The BF16 release is 360 GB and does not fit the box, and the reference run that would give KL a pack is not done, so the registry's quality fields are empty. What is measured is our arithmetic against the reference on the same pack: all 48 layers equal the official transformers decoder layer on the served weights within BF16 noise (relative error 0.19 to 1.49 %). Teacher-forced, the decode path picks the reference's top token at 64 of 64 positions at 3k of context and 63 of 64 at 8k, where the one miss is a near tie (a margin of 0.0095). No task benchmark has run on any pack.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text: knob what ops/use-profile.sh flashnext-<bpw> switch to a pack; fetches the branch when it is missing QWEN38_FN_MIX int8 (the default): int8 with an fp32 scale a group of 128 weights; int8rows: one scale a row; fp16: the pack's values QWEN38_FN_TABLE, QWEN38_FN_TABLE_CACHE_GB the n-gram table's policy (warm or cold) and the cold row cache in GiB QWEN38_FN_PREFILL_MM the prefill's weights for the mixers, router and small projections: fp32 (the default); tc, tcn: the int8 weights unrounded on the tensor cores, opt-in and not bit-identical to fp32 tools/fn_exl3_xcheck.py our reading of a pack against the converter's tools/fn_mix_quality.py a mixer weight form against the pack's fp16 mixers

docs.title: Remote control
docs.text: tandem remote is the engine's control CLI for a controller on another machine. The controller reaches the engine box over SSH with a key whose line in authorized_keys runs only tandem remote: the key can start, stop and restart the engine, switch its mode, change its settings, install extensions, upgrade the engine, set the HTTP token, read its logs and run its checks, and nothing else. No shell, no terminal, no port forward. No sudo is needed. The contract is contracts/engine-ctl-v1; the code is server/remote/. Pairing by code puts the key's line in place (pairing.md).

docs.title: The key's line
docs.text:
One line in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys of the user that installed the engine:

command="/bin/bash /home/u/TandemLLM/bin/tandem remote --key-id ctl-1",no-pty,no-port-forwarding,no-agent-forwarding,no-X11-forwarding ssh-ed25519 AAAA... ctl-1
  • command= is the forced command: sshd runs it whatever the client asks, and hands the client's command over in SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND. It goes through bash, as every call of the engine's scripts does.
  • --key-id names the key. unpair removes the line that carries it. Without it, unpair needs sshd's ExposeAuthInfo yes.
  • from="192.0.2.0/24" before command= narrows the addresses the key works from.

A call:

ssh -i ctl-1 u@engine-box status
ssh -i ctl-1 u@engine-box 'settings plan MAX_QUEUE=4'

By hand on the box, the same verbs: bin/tandem remote status.

docs.title: The verbs
docs.text:
verb what status the engine's state (healthy, loading, draining, failed, down), its pid, port, release (engine_version), engine_api, the configured and the running mode, the overlay version, the last job; answers with the engine down start, stop a job that starts the engine (an install's bin/tandem start, else ops/start.sh) or stops it (ops/stop.sh); a stop stays a stop: ops/watchdog.sh leaves the engine down until the next start restart [--when now\|idle\|at=TIME] [--deadline S] stop, then start. idle waits until no request runs or waits (the Setup Guide's rule), at most --deadline seconds (600); past it the job fails with nothing changed. at=2026-11-16T03:00:00Z waits until then, then as idle. The default is now mode get the mode serve.env resolves, its source, and whether it was inferred from an empty QSE_MODE mode set engine\|chat [--ext NAME] [--when ...] writes QSE_MODE and QSE_EXT into the overlay, never an empty mode, and restarts (default idle) settings get [KEY ...] every key with its value, its source (default, install, profile, setup, local, managed, mode), its type, its restart class and whether it feeds the disk cache's fingerprint settings plan KEY=VALUE ... [--unset KEY] checks the values, shows what the engine would see after the restart, and gives a confirm token; nothing is written settings apply KEY=VALUE ... --confirm T [--confirm-fingerprint T] [--when ...] the same changes as a new overlay version, made current by a restart job (default idle) settings versions, settings restore N --confirm T the versions; a restore is a new version with version N's keys logs [--follow] [--lines N] [--which engine\|launcher] the engine's log, or what the jobs' start and stop printed (logs/launcher.log); --follow streams one JSON line a log line doctor tandem doctor --check: each finding with a code and a fix unpair removes the authorized_keys line of the key this call came with, and no other ext list the extensions in the engine's venv, each read as the engine reads it at load: its name, version and EXT_API, whether this engine takes it, and whether chat mode runs it (1.1) ext install --sha256 HEX --name FILE.whl [--module M] [--when ...] an extension's wheel, on stdin, into the venv (below) (1.1) ext remove DIST [--and-mode engine] [--when ...] the distribution out of the venv; the one chat mode runs only with --and-mode engine (1.1) upgrade plan --ref REF or upgrade plan --sha256 HEX the engine's tree at another release, from the origin or from an archive on stdin: what changes and a confirm token (1.1) upgrade apply ... --confirm T [--when ...] the upgrade as a job (default idle), rolled back when it fails (1.1) token rotate a new HTTP token, answered on this channel only (1.1)

Every answer is one JSON document with ok, and the exit status says the same: 0 ok, 1 not ok (doctor found something, or the venv's installer failed), 2 usage, 3 refused, 4 busy (a job acts), 5 internal. Lifecycle verbs answer at once with their job; status follows it. One job acts at a time; a new one replaces a job that still waits.

docs.title: The settings overlay
docs.text:
The settings a controller changes live in their own file, run/managed.env of the engine's tree, read by ops/serve.env after an install's run/local.env and before the mode is applied. ops/serve.env and the profiles are never edited. Each apply writes a new version, run/managed.d/<n>.env; manifest.json names the current one and the good one, the last the engine reached /health with. A start with a new version that does not reach /health puts the good version back, starts the engine again, and the job reports both.

The keys are the ones ops/serve.env sets or documents. The install's (paths, the address), the weight profile's (weights, drafters, corpus, the model's flags) and QSE_BACKENDS are not the overlay's. A value is letters, digits and . _ , : = @ % + / -, with ${HOME} and ${REPO} the only expansions; a path lies under the install or ~/.qwen38-spark-engine.

A key that feeds the disk cache's fingerprint (the QWEN38_* arithmetic switches, the weight and drafter arguments, NARROW_ARM, FUSE_PROJ) changes which saved prefixes and parked chats the engine can read: after the restart they all miss. Its plan says so and gives a second token, and the apply needs both. With an empty overlay, ops/start.sh starts the engine with the command line and environment it had before the overlay existed.

An install whose run/ops/serve.env was written by an older release does not read the overlay; settings plan says so (hook_missing) until the installer runs again.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
An extension is an engine-ext-v1 module the engine loads in chat mode (QSE_EXT). ext install takes its wheel on stdin:

ssh -i ctl-1 u@engine-box "ext install --sha256 $(sha256sum x-1.0-py3-none-any.whl | cut -d' ' -f1) --name x-1.0-py3-none-any.whl" < x-1.0-py3-none-any.whl
  • The bytes are refused, with nothing written, when their sha256 is not --sha256, when they are more than 256 MiB, or when they are not a wheel whose METADATA names the file's distribution and version.
  • The extension module is the one --module names, else the one the wheel's entry point group tandemllm.engine_ext names, else its one <package>/engine_ext module.
  • ops/venv-wheel.sh installs it into the install's venv, with the engine's pins (run/requirements.lock) as constraints, the same way install.sh --with-chat --app-wheel installs the chat's wheel. Only an install has a venv: a checkout is refused.
  • The answer reads the module back as the engine's extension host does. run/remote/extensions.json keeps its distribution, module, wheel and sha256.
  • The running engine keeps the code it loaded. The answer says a restart is needed; --when now|idle|at=TIME starts the restart job.

ext remove DIST uninstalls the distribution. If its module is the extension chat mode runs, the call is refused unless --and-mode engine is given; then the overlay gets QSE_MODE=engine and an empty QSE_EXT, as mode set engine writes them, and a restart job (default idle) makes them current.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
upgrade puts the install's tree at another release. Only an install has one: DIR/src is the git checkout install.sh made, and it must have no local changes.

ssh -i ctl-1 u@engine-box 'upgrade plan --ref v0.16.0'
git archive --format=tar.gz v0.16.0 | ssh -i ctl-1 u@engine-box "upgrade plan --sha256 $SHA"
ssh -i ctl-1 u@engine-box "upgrade apply --sha256 $SHA --confirm $TOKEN --when idle"
  • --ref fetches the install's origin and resolves REF as install.sh does (a tag, a branch, a commit). An archive comes on stdin, at most 512 MiB, the tree at its root (git archive without --prefix). Its sha256 must be --sha256. Absolute paths, .., links that leave the tree and macOS ._ files are refused. The plan keeps it as run/remote/upgrades/<sha256>.tar for the apply.
  • The target must have tandem remote and an install.sh that takes --update and --no-fetch, so the key still reaches the engine afterwards.
  • The plan names both trees (commit, version, engine API, this contract's version, the venv's pins), whether the venv is synced to new pins, what is kept and the steps, and gives a token bound to the current commit and the target.
  • The job, once it acts:
  • keeps the previous tree: its commit as refs/tandem/previous, and a copy of run/ops, bin/tandem and its install.sh;
  • stops the engine;
  • makes an archive a commit of src's repository;
  • runs the target's install.sh --update --no-fetch --ref COMMIT: the checkout, the venv synced to its pins, run/ops and bin/tandem written again with this install's keys, no weights, no start;
  • starts the engine.
  • A failed install or a start that does not reach /health rolls back: the previous commit checked out, the venv synced back with the previous install.sh --update when the pins changed, run/ops and bin/tandem put back byte for byte, the engine started again. The job fails and says rolled_back.
  • The overlay, run/local.env, the weights, the logs and the engine's data are not touched.

docs.title: The HTTP token
docs.text:
token rotate makes a random token and answers it on this SSH channel, and nowhere else: it is in no log and no journal. The engine box keeps only its sha256, in the tree's run/http-token (mode 600). The engine reads the file again within a second, so a rotation needs no restart and the old token stops working.

Each paired key has a token of its own: pairing writes its hash on a line that names the key id (sha256:<hex> ID), token rotate over a key's channel replaces only that key's line, and unpair removes it with the key's line. By hand on the box (no key id), token rotate replaces the whole file. A token of any line passes. The line sha256:<hex> * is an install's lock before pairing: a token nobody holds (pairing.md).

While the file exists, a caller that is not on the engine's host needs Authorization: Bearer <token> on every route, inference included, or it gets 401. A caller on this host (loopback, without X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP) needs none, so the watchdog, the status checks and a controller on the same box keep working. /health, /healthz, /v1/health, /readyz and /metrics/up answer without it: a probe or a controller can tell a down engine from one that refuses it. Without the token, /health gives only its status; with it, the full body follows the admin rule (docs/server.md).

QSE_ALLOW_FROM (addresses and CIDRs, comma-separated; empty: every address) answers 403 to any other address on every route, the status included. Loopback always passes. It is a managed setting that changes live: PATCH /v1/engine/settings from this host, or with the token, or settings apply over SSH, which restarts. Engine API 1.9 has the details (contracts/engine-api-v1, "Access").

The status responder (ops/engine_status.py), which answers while the engine restarts, takes no token. Set QSE_STATUS_HOST=127.0.0.1 when nothing outside the host may read it.

docs.title: The journal
docs.text: Every call, refused ones included, is one line of run/remote/journal.jsonl: the UTC time, the verb, its arguments (the value of a secret-looking key cut out), the exit status, the duration, the key id and the address it came from. ext install and upgrade add the sha256 of the bytes they checked (checked), and a PATCH /v1/engine/settings is a line too (via http). Past 4 MiB the file moves to journal.jsonl.1, up to three old files.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: TandemLLM runs several models (Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and, from 0.9.0, LFM2.5-24B-A2B, one at a time) on one board (DGX Spark). The 27B serves one request at a time by default; Flash-Next's and LFM2.5's profiles run three slots. Each step below widens one of those limits, and each keeps the two rules that hold today: the output stays the model's greedy text, up to the documented near-tie exception (exactness.md), and no measured number gets worse. We plan to take the steps in this order. Nothing here is a promise of dates.

docs.title: A mixture-of-experts model: served, with four parts open
docs.text:
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is served from turboderp's EXL3 packs through the same server, caches and ops scripts as the 27B (architecture.md, quantisation.md). The plan written here before it named the NVFP4 checkpoint; the published EXL3 packs replaced it. What is still open:

  • The 5.05 pack's earlier blocker was 7-bit dense projections. The dense dispatch now covers K 2..8, and the MoE kernels already supported 7-bit experts. A full 5.05 load and an answer still need validation.
  • Quality against the BF16 model, per pack. The BF16 release is 360 GB and does not fit the box, so the reference run that gives KL a pack is not done.
  • Parallel requests are on in its profiles (three slots). Three requests together take as long as one after the other and only the later first tokens come sooner; CUDA graphs for the joint pass are the next step (parallel-requests.md).

Later, other EXL3 models that fit one box, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B among them.

docs.title: Parallel requests
docs.text:
Several requests share one verify pass in lockstep rounds: each request brings its own tree, and one forward over all the trees costs little more than one over a single tree, because the weights are read once. Phase A is built behind --parallel N, off by default (server.md, section Parallel requests): side slots, the GPU turn, the joint verify, the packed draft, and admission by bytes (a request queues while its worst case would push the board under its floor). First single runs on the box: two requests at about 1.4 times the single-request total, four at about 1.4 times, the single-request row unchanged. Next: the host side of a round, one tree cut across the slots, graphs for the joint pass and one graph pool for every slot. A second request costs at least the step from 16 to 32 rows of the verify kernel, so two requests at about 1.6 times is the target at today's kernels; 2 times needs a 32-row verify priced like 16 rows.

Later, multi-user serving: an API key per user, with caches isolated per user, so no user can resume from another user's prefix.

docs.title: A cache tier on NVMe
docs.text: Built in 0.3.13-test (caches.md): recurrent-state anchors and KV chunks on the NVMe, a 50 GB budget, a time to live and a 50 GB free-space floor, set from the dashboard. What remains: the restore's rate measured on the board after the deploy (the 0.6 s for a 30,000-token head is arithmetic from CPU-side rates), whether rows written before a restart equal a cold prefill after it when Triton autotunes again (the fingerprint holds the code and the flags, not the chosen kernel configurations), and a background backfill of the resident prompt's chunks while the engine is idle.

docs.title: Profiles as data
docs.text:
Today a profile is a serve.env file. Part of this plan shipped: weight profiles in 0.5.0 (ops/use-profile.sh switches one engine at a time and rolls back when the new one fails its smoke), the model registry and the setup guide's memory estimate in 0.7.0 (setup.md), and in 0.8.1 a fetch of every file a profile reads, each checked against the hub's sha256. The plan is a small profile format that a validator checks. It names every weight file with its format and hash, and it holds all the settings. A facts block records what we measured: memory and disk, speed at prompt lengths from 256 to 64k tokens, and quality against the reference. Each number carries a label that says how we got it, such as "measured" or "estimate".

Still open: the format and its validator, and a signed catalog of tested profiles in the repository that the setup guide installs from.

docs.title: Other GPUs, then several GPUs
docs.text:
1. Other single GPUs (H100, H200, RTX Pro 6000, L40S). Most have no FP4 tensor cores, so they need to decode the 4-bit weights in software, or run an FP8 or BF16 profile. Each GPU needs its own tile tables, and the router needs new prices: an H100 reads memory more than ten times faster than the Spark, so the best tree width and drafter size change. Discrete GPUs also change the memory model, since admission must count the GPU's own memory and not the system's.
  2. Several GPUs: tensor parallel inside one server, two DGX Sparks over their 200 Gb/s link, and servers with 8 GPUs. A reduction across GPUs changes the order of a floating-point sum, so row invariance needs a fixed reduction order across devices.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text:
• Runtime names still carry the old project name, from the QWEN38_ and QSE_ variable prefixes to the metric names. They change together in one release, and the old variable names keep working for one release after that.
  • Engine settings move from import-time globals to a settings object handed to the engine, so two engines with different settings can share a process.
  • The engine moves into an installable package.

docs.title: Server and API
docs.text: server/app.py speaks the OpenAI HTTP API, so any OpenAI client can use the engine by changing its base URL. It is built on the Python standard library (ThreadingHTTPServer), with no web framework. This page covers the routes and the request fields, then tool calls and structured outputs, then how the service behaves under load.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text: route who may call it what POST /v1/chat/completions anyone chat, streamed or not POST /v1/completions anyone plain text completion GET /v1/models anyone the served model name, and TandemLLM when the conductor is on GET /v1/replica/identity as /v1/models what two engines compare before they serve one model as replicas: the code, the model's family and layers, the weights, drafters, rows and tokenizer by content, the decode settings and the window (server/identity.py); 503 identity_pending until it is computed, once after the start GET /health anyone gets the status; the full body follows the admin rule status, queue counters, cache report, memory; on a stage process the stage block (below) GET /metrics the metrics token when one is set, else the admin rule Prometheus metrics (metrics.md) GET /v1/cache/stats the admin rule the caches' counters POST /v1/cache/clear the admin rule; with a password set, only as a bearer header empty the caches in RAM; ?tier=disk the disk tier, ?tier=all both POST /v1/cache/peek, /v1/cache/prewarm the admin rule a chat body's warm tokens and their tier before it is sent; the conversation read back from the NVMe while the engine is idle (caches.md) /v1/dashboard/* anyone by default; with a password set and --dashboard-login on, the admin token or a dashboard session the engine's own reads: live activity, the system, the log, parallel requests, usage and the request rows (the contract) /v1/engine/* the admin rule the engine-only screens: the residency plan, the disk tier, the decision models, the narrator and the shadow reader (the contract) GET, PATCH /v1/engine/settings reads as /v1/dashboard/*; a change from this box, with the HTTP token or the admin token the settings a running engine changes without a restart, today QSE_ALLOW_FROM: a change is a new overlay version, applied at once (engine API 1.9) POST /v1/systemone, /v1/predict the admin rule typed decisions from the engine's own decision models (below); only with QWEN38_DECIDER_MODELS set GET /readyz anyone whether a decision model is loaded and warm; only with QWEN38_DECIDER_MODELS set /v1/conductor/*, /v1/library*, /v1/laya*, /v1/memory*, /dashboard/ reads as /v1/dashboard/*, writes and every memory route the admin rule, the library and Laya anyone the extension's routes in chat mode (below); a headless engine answers 404 not_on_engine, and /dashboard/ 404 no_ui

docs.title: The admin rule
docs.text:
The admin password is the admin token, QSE_ADMIN_TOKEN in secrets.env (mode 600, never in the repository). It is the one switch, and by default it is not set.

  • With no password set, the default, every route in the table answers anyone who reaches the port: the dashboard reads, the engine-only screens, the disk tier, the decision models, both cache routes and the full /health, and in chat mode the extension's writes and memory. Keep the server on a trusted network: anyone on it can read and change the configuration and the memory. Only /metrics keeps its own token when QSE_METRICS_TOKEN is set, for Prometheus.
  • With a password set, the admin routes need the admin token as a bearer header or a dashboard session. POST /v1/cache/clear takes only the bearer header. Requests from the box itself (loopback, no proxy headers) need no token; the watchdog and the measurement tools depend on that. A bad password stops the start: it must be at least 32 characters.

docs.title: The HTTP token and the allow-from list (engine API 1.9)
docs.text:
Before any route, the server checks two things that are off by default (server/api/access.py):

  • With the tree's run/http-token (made by tandem remote token rotate, which answers the token over SSH and keeps only its sha256 here), every caller that is not on this box needs Authorization: Bearer <token>, inference included. Calls from the box itself (loopback, no proxy headers) need none. /health gives its status without it; with it, the full body follows the admin rule as before; /healthz, /v1/health, /readyz and /metrics/up answer too. The admin token passes as well. A rotation counts within a second.
  • QSE_ALLOW_FROM (addresses and CIDRs): any other address gets 403 on every route; loopback always passes. It changes live through PATCH /v1/engine/settings.

With neither, the server answers as before. remote-control.md has the details.

The dashboard login (--dashboard-login, from QSE_DASHBOARD_LOGIN, off by default) matters only with a password set: then on makes /v1/dashboard/* need the token or a session too. With no password it changes nothing. Failed logins are throttled per client: a fronting proxy's X-Real-IP is believed only when the TCP peer is loopback (a proxy on this box) or names itself in TANDEM_TRUSTED_PROXY — the LAN shape, where every real client shares the one peer; any other peer is keyed as itself (server/api/auth.py). The proxy must set X-Real-IP itself (proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; in nginx): a proxy that passes the client's own header on lets the client pick its bucket. TandemApp's dashboard.md says what the page shows.

docs.title: What the API supports
docs.text:
server/compat.py gives every OpenAI request field one of three answers, and tests/test_compat.py pins the table.

  • Honoured: messages, model, stream, stream_options, max_tokens, max_completion_tokens, stop, temperature, top_p, seed, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, logit_bias, logprobs, top_logprobs (up to 20), n (up to 16, not streamed), tools, tool_choice, parallel_tool_calls, reasoning_effort, response_format, modalities (text output only). Messages may carry image_url parts (see Images below).
  • Accepted and without effect by their own definition: user, metadata, store, service_tier, prompt_cache_key, safety_identifier, prediction.
  • Refused with a 400 that names the field: audio, functions, function_call (use tools), web_search_options, verbosity, and for completions suffix and echo.

Fields that are not OpenAI's pass through without a 400, because clients send extensions meant for other servers. The engine reads its own: top_k, min_p, repetition_penalty, no_repeat_ngram_size, max_reasoning_tokens, reasoning_format, draft_temperature, chat_template_kwargs and cache_prompt, and the other servers' thinking-budget shapes (reasoning, thinking, thinking_budget, enable_thinking and more, see Thinking budgets from the client).

docs.title: cache_prompt
docs.text:
The prompt caches are on for every request (caches.md). A request that leaves out cache_prompt, or sends true, resumes from the longest prefix a cache holds, and timings.cache_n counts the tokens it reused. Any other value but false does the same.

cache_prompt: false reads the whole prompt: timings.cache_n is 0 and timings.prompt_n is the prompt's length. A benchmark that measures a cold prompt read sends it. The request also leaves every prompt cache as it was. It reads and writes no state-store entry, no disk-tier anchor and no end anchor, and the response cache neither answers it nor keeps its answer. A conversation already in place is set aside as for another client's. A prompt of up to RESIDENT_GUEST_MAX tokens (8,192 served) and under a quarter of that conversation runs as a guest, and the conversation's rows go back after it. A longer prompt parks the conversation, or writes it to the NVMe when the park cannot hold it. Its next request without the flag then finds it where it would have found it before. Nothing parks or keeps the rows a cold request wrote, since they belong to no conversation. One store stays on: the suffix store is the lookup's memory of text, not a prompt cache, and takes the request's tokens as it does for every request.

docs.title: Reasoning
docs.text:
The model thinks inside <think> tags. --reasoning-format (or reasoning_format in the request) picks how the thinking reaches the client:

value content reasoning_content tags (default) thinking inside <think>...</think>, then the answer empty reasoning_content the answer only the thinking, as OpenAI-style deltas both as tags as reasoning_content

A client kind can have its own format when it names none and the server's is tags, under a conductor plan (QWEN38_CLIENT_REASONING, kind=format,..., * for every kind not named; default *=reasoning_content,hermes=tags; empty: tags for every client). On the raw path the same rule holds for a plain API client, an SDK, curl or an unnamed one such as a benchmark: the reasoning goes to reasoning_content and its stop strings read the answer alone. Every other kind keeps the server's format there (SRV-617; up to 0.11.4 every raw request kept it). Since 0.3.50-test every client but the Hermes agent gets reasoning_content by default: an OpenAI SDK or curl client printed message.content and showed the model's thinking as its answer, and opencode with the installer's provider config showed it as literal <think> text (SRV-245, SRV-219). A client that wants the tags inline sends reasoning_format: tags. The answer starts with its first character; the blank lines the template writes after </think> are not sent. A small max_tokens counts the thinking: a response cut inside it has finish_reason: length, an empty content and the reasoning in reasoning_content.

Under a conductor plan a request's stop strings apply to the answer, never inside the reasoning, and the blank lines that start the answer are not matched (0.3.50-test, SRV-245: stop: ["\n\n"] ended a response at the first blank line of the thinking, 55 tokens and no answer). The raw path matches them on the whole text, as the release did. State lines never go into a plain API client's content (curl, an OpenAI SDK, an unnamed client): they go to reasoning_content, or are left out with tags; a memory line still goes into the answer. Open WebUI 0.11.3 folds <think> blocks out of the content after the fact and forwards the piece that carries </think> to its live view as the text of a new message, where it stays until the round's stream ends; in reasoning_content it has no tag to show, and every tool round's reasoning is its own block. For that client the template's blank lines go out as one content piece where the reasoning ends, so Open WebUI closes and times each round's block even when the round goes straight to a tool call (a blank message is not shown). A request's own reasoning_format always wins (0.3.45-test, SRV-193).

Open WebUI's terminal tools end run_command's description with the terminal's working directory (The current working directory is: <path>), which Open WebUI fetches again for every user message. The description sits in the system prompt's tool block, about 4,800 tokens into the prompt, so the first cd of an agent changed the prompt there and the next user message read the whole conversation again: 41,749 tokens, 56 s, live on 0.3.46-test, where the conversation's own rows matched only up to that line. Under a conductor plan that is on (0.3.47-test, SRV-209, QWEN38_CLIENT_CWD, default note), the sentence leaves the description and the same sentence goes into the turn as a router note, when the directory differs from the last one noted (the first turn, a cd, a cd back): the tool block stays the same for the whole session, and the note replays where it was put, like every router note. The model reads the same words, at the turn they became true. Shadow, off, raw and QWEN38_CLIENT_CWD=off: the tools as sent.

Recorded against the served engine (published NVFP4 weights, StairCut on); sped-up parts are marked in the clip.

The chat template opens the block in the prompt, so the model only ever writes </think>. Our server re-emits <think> as the first delta so that clients which fold on a matched pair see one. reasoning_effort (low, medium, xhigh) goes into the chat template, and the served default is medium. At xhigh, one request spent all 8,192 of its tokens thinking and never answered. --reasoning-effort none (or off, SRV-477) turns thinking off for every request that says nothing about thinking (no switch, effort word or budget in any shape): such a request gets chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking: false before anything reads it, and one that says anything keeps it. /health then reports reasoning_effort: off and sampling.thinking_default: off.

docs.title: Thinking budgets from the client
docs.text:
A client may cap the thinking in any of the shapes clients send, and server/api/thinking.py reads them all into one budget:

shape sent by read as max_reasoning_tokens, thinking_budget this engine, DashScope a cap in tokens chat_template_kwargs.thinking_budget, .max_thinking_tokens, .reasoning_budget, .thinking_token_budget template-argument clients a cap in tokens reasoning: {max_tokens, effort, enabled, exclude} OpenRouter-style clients max_tokens a cap, effort a word, enabled: true alone medium, enabled: false off thinking: {type, budget_tokens} Anthropic-style clients enabled with budget_tokens a cap, enabled or adaptive alone on without a cap, disabled off reasoning_budget, max_thinking_tokens, thinking_token_budget, thinking_budget_tokens (top level) other servers' clients a cap in tokens reasoning_effort, reasoning.effort, chat_template_kwargs.reasoning_effort OpenAI SDK, opencode, Hermes agent the effort level's cap: minimal and low 1,024, medium 8,192, high 16,384, xhigh and max none; none is thinking off enable_thinking: false (top level or in chat_template_kwargs) DashScope, template-argument clients thinking off

Precedence: whether the model thinks is decided first, by chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking when it is set, else by the top-level enable_thinking, else by any off form. The cap is then the first number in the table's order, else the first effort word's cap (chat_template_kwargs before reasoning_effort before reasoning.effort), else enabled: true or a thinking.type. A number beats a word. 0 is no cap. A word the template knows (low, medium, xhigh; minimal renders as low, max as xhigh) also goes into the template; high leaves the template at the server's default and is the cap alone. Before this, high, none, minimal and max reached the template, which raises on them, and the request got a 500. An unknown word or a negative number is a 400 that names the field. reasoning.exclude is read and not honoured: the reasoning goes out in the request's reasoning_format.

Under TandemLLM's router, a client's number always wins. An effort word is a ceiling (0.3.22-test, decided 2026-10-03): where the router decides the effort (decisions.effort: on), the turn gets the router's level, but never a cap above the word's (medium holds an xhigh turn to 8,192 reasoning tokens; a low class under medium keeps its 1,024). The answer reserve still applies after. The journal row's extra.client_word says when the word held the router down. A profile's thinking.client_word (ceiling, the default, or ignore) decides it per client: the shipped coding and overnight profiles say ignore, because opencode sends medium on every turn whatever the user picked, and there the router's level alone is the turn's, as before. enabled: true without a word yields to the router. Elsewhere (the raw engine, X-Tandem: raw, a profile with the effort decision off or in shadow) the word is the cap.

Thinking off is the client's (0.3.40-test). none and every other off form (enable_thinking: false, reasoning.enabled: false, thinking.type: disabled) close the thinking block in the template under every profile, the ceiling rule's lowest word. The router's journal row then says thinking: off_client with no budget, and extra.client_thinking names the field and the class's level that did not run ("client turned thinking off"); the dashboard reads "thinking off (client)". The class's effort sentence ("Reasoning effort is set to xhigh. Please think carefully …") is not added to such a turn (effort_note_skipped:client_off in the row's notes); the rest of the note (a package's rules, the class's rules) still is. Before, the row read thinking: on at the class's level and the prompt carried the xhigh sentence into a turn that could not think (Open WebUI's agent model sent reasoning_effort: "none", 2026-10-06).

The answer reserve: when a client asked for a budget in any shape and the reasoning would otherwise run into the output limit (max_tokens, max_completion_tokens, or the server's default), the reasoning closes early enough to leave the answer --answer-reserve tokens after the closing phrase (QSE_ANSWER_RESERVE; auto, the default, is min(2,048, a quarter of the limit); 0 turns it off). The phrase is counted in because it streams where no monitor hides it. An uncapped request gets the limit less the reserve and the phrase as its cap. The close is the session monitor's hidden one where a monitor acts (SP1: the vendor's phrase goes into the model's context, the client receives </think> and the answer; the journal's CLOSE_REASONING has task client, or reserve when the reserve lowered the cap), and ThinkBudget's streamed phrase otherwise (no monitor, shadow, X-Tandem: raw, n > 1). The server log has one [think] <id> client budget ... line per such request, and with the router its journal row has extra.client_budget (field, kind, asked, reserve, limit, cap). usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens counts the visible reasoning through </think>, the streamed phrase included and the hidden one not.

A request with none of these fields is served as before, token for token: the template gets the same arguments and the loop the same budget. enable_thinking alone asks for no budget. | thinking: {type, budget_tokens} | enabled with budget_tokens a cap, enabled or adaptive alone on without a cap, disabled off | | reasoning_budget, max_thinking_tokens, thinking_token_budget, thinking_budget_tokens | a cap in tokens | | reasoning_effort, reasoning.effort, chat_template_kwargs.reasoning_effort | the level's cap: minimal and low 1,024, medium 8,192, high 16,384, xhigh and max none; none is thinking off | | enable_thinking: false (top level or in chat_template_kwargs) | thinking off |

docs.title: Tool calls
docs.text:
The request's tools go into the chat template, and the model answers a call in its own XML form:

<tool_call>
<function=read>
<parameter=offset>
150
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>

Recorded against the served engine (published NVFP4 weights, StairCut on); sped-up parts are marked in the clip.

server/api/toolcall.py turns that into OpenAI tool_calls with finish_reason: "tool_calls", on both the streamed and the JSON path. Under a conductor plan a request that offered no tools never gets tool_calls: a call the model writes anyway is read out of the answer and dropped, the finish stays stop, and the journal row names it in extra.calls_refused (0.3.50-test, SRV-247: a curl client with memory on received the model's own memory search as a call to a tool named tool, with the session's share address in its arguments). It reads the strict form, a lenient form and a JSON call object, and it reads only the answer, never the thinking. On a stream, a call goes out as argument deltas while the model writes it: the id and the name first, then each string value in pieces. A whole-file write therefore shows progress instead of minutes of silence.

Argument values carry their schema's types. The model writes every value as text, so offset arrives as the characters 150. Our parser looks up the request's own schema, and a parameter whose schema does not allow a string is returned as JSON: 150, true, a list. A typed value is held back on the stream until it is complete, then sent whole. On an 8-task agent run, a strict client that validates arguments against the schema refused 58 of 80 calls before this change, and 0 of 26 after.

tool_choice works as OpenAI defines it. none renders the prompt without tools. required and a named function become a constraint on the answer, the same token masks structured outputs use, so the model cannot answer without the call. parallel_tool_calls: false keeps one call. Beside a response_format, auto is the calls or the document (Structured outputs below).

docs.title: Structured outputs
docs.text:
response_format with json_object or json_schema, and structured_outputs with a regex, a choice list or a JSON schema, constrain the answer to a regular language. engine/grammar.py compiles each form to a finite automaton over bytes, because the tokenizer is byte-level and a token can end halfway through a character. A token is allowed in a state when walking its bytes never reaches the dead state. The engine computes that for the whole vocabulary at once per state and caches it, so a state costs a few milliseconds once.

A </think> the model writes again in its answer, alone on a line, is not sent (0.3.43-test, SRV-187): Open WebUI's parser closes a reasoning block at the first </think> and showed the second one as the text </think> between two tool rows. The tag in a sentence, in inline code, in a fenced code block, inside a <tool_call> or a <tandem_memory> block, or closing a <think> line the answer opened itself, stays; the stream holds back at most the start of a line that can still become the tag. Only under a conductor profile: the raw path sends what the model wrote. The journal row counts the tags taken out (extra.stray_close).

The constraint applies to the answer, after the reasoning. A JSON answer (json_object, json_schema) is parsed whole by its client, so a request that names no reasoning_format gets reasoning_content for it: the thinking goes to reasoning_content and message.content (or the concatenated content deltas) is the JSON alone, which json.loads and the SDKs' structured-output helpers read as they are. A client that sends reasoning_format: tags (or both) keeps <think>...</think> in the content. Such a request also gets the answer reserve a client's own thinking budget gets (see Thinking budgets from the client): the reasoning is closed early enough to leave the JSON its share of max_tokens (the journal's extra.json_reserve), and it carries no state lines. Until 0.3.41-test the content opened with the think block and a small max_tokens could end inside the JSON (SRV-169: a 270-token think block, then finish_reason: length at 300).

With tools offered and tool_choice auto, a document (json_schema, json_object, a structured_outputs form) constrains the answer to the calls or the document alone (SRV-619): one automaton, the union of the tool-call language that required uses (any offered function, its required parameters in declared order, typed values; more than one call unless parallel_tool_calls: false) and the document's. The model thinks freely, then its own first answer token picks the branch: the automaton is the product of the two languages, and where both are still open the mask follows the row's argmax before the mask. A call's first token (the <tool_call> id, <) commits to the calls; any other token (the document's {, a code fence, prose, the end token) commits to the document; whitespace leaves the choice open. The plain union let the masked-out fence's next best token decide, and that was the call marker, not {: on a first live run the model said "I can just output the JSON directly" and then answered with a run_code call that built the JSON (TC-65). Prose and code fences are outside the language. The mask stays a function of the prefix and the target's row, so speculation changes no token. The log line [structured] <id> branch=calls|document and the journal's extra.structured_branch say which branch an answer took. The call markers keep the model's own ids under this constraint (<tool_call> is one token; spelled out byte by byte it is off the model's distribution). A call goes out as tool_calls, the document as the content, with the thinking in reasoning_content as above. tool_choice: none is the document alone; required and a named function are the calls alone, the document checked and left out. An agent loop that asks for its final answer as JSON with its tools still attached (the OpenAI SDKs' structured-output helpers, tool-eval-bench's structured scenarios) was a 400 through 0.11.4 (structured outputs with tools are not supported) and fell back to prompt-only JSON, fenced or with prose around it. A model whose calls are not the XML format (--tool-format pythonic) keeps the 400.

Each mask applies to every verified row of a draft tree, not only to one row per step. Constrained output under speculation is therefore the text plain constrained decoding writes, with the same near-tie exception as any greedy text (exactness.md). JSON schemas with recursion ($ref cycles) are refused, and json_object allows a fixed nesting depth.

An extension can ask for the same constraints (engine-ext-v1 3.2, SET_CONSTRAINT at the request's safe point): a regex, a choice list, a JSON schema or a logit bias, carried out by this grammar as the request field it is the same as (structured_outputs or logit_bias), so the act's answer is that field's answer token for token, under speculation too. The request's own constraint wins over the extension's. A constraint the engine cannot carry out leaves the request unconstrained, unless the extension marked it strict: then the client gets a 400 that names SET_CONSTRAINT. contracts/engine-ext-v1 has the rules.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
A streamed response sends one chunk per token, carries usage on the last chunk when the client asks for it (stream_options.include_usage, and by default with --usage-default on), then a chunk with finish_reason and data: [DONE]. A verify round accepts several tokens at once, so they reach the socket together. Half the gaps between tokens are therefore microseconds, and the other half a whole round.

By default, usage counts what the client sent and what it received. prompt_tokens is the client's messages (with its tools) as the chat template renders them; the conductor's notes (the router's note for the turn, the session's replayed notes, the closed think block of a turn it turned thinking off, the monitor's SP4 note, an earlier answer's hidden tokens put back) are not in it, and when there are any prompt_tokens_details.hidden_tokens says how many the model read besides (absent when none, so a raw request's usage has its old shape). cached_tokens is the client's tokens served from a cache: the cached span less the hidden tokens inside it, which the server tracks by position (the notes, the end anchor's replay, a reasoning the client left out, SP4's note); when the positions are not known it is at most prompt_tokens, as before. timings.cache_n and prompt_n stay the engine's own counts of the whole prompt, and the ledger keeps them as engine_cached and forwarded_tokens (schema 8). Until 0.3.50-test the hidden rows inside the cached span counted as client tokens: an opencode turn that re-read 3,827 of its 24,706 client tokens reported all 24,706 cached (SRV-233); it now reports 20,879. The ledger keeps the client's count in prompt_tokens and the conductor's in conductor_hidden_tokens. Until 0.3.41-test the router's notes were counted: a "hi" reported 238 prompt tokens under the chat profile (926 on 0.3.39-test), 11 raw (SRV-165).

--usage-context engine (or QSE_USAGE_CONTEXT=engine) makes usage.prompt_tokens count the occupied prompt after replay, alignment and image expansion, including retained reasoning and injected notes. Use it for clients that trigger context compaction from the API's prompt-token count: reasoning the client leaves out can otherwise fill the context while the reported count remains below the client's threshold. prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens then counts the engine's cached rows, bounded by the occupied prompt, and total_tokens is that prompt plus completion_tokens. When the count differs, prompt_tokens_details.client_tokens carries the default client count and client_cached_tokens its cached share, the client mode's cached_tokens; chatd reads that pair, so the Context panel's warm and cold add up to the client prompt. hidden_tokens keeps its existing meaning. The default is --usage-context client. Both modes keep the ledger, usage.tandem breakdown and timings on their existing accounting basis; generation and cache replay are unchanged.

docs.title: Speed and draft fields: timings and metrics
docs.text:
Every response carries two objects beside usage, with the engine's own counts of the request. A response without a stream has them in its body. A stream has them in one chunk only, the one that carries usage: the finish chunk when the client sends no stream_options, the separate choices: [] chunk with include_usage: true, and none with include_usage: false or --usage-default off. metrics.md has an example with consistent numbers.

field what it is timings.cache_n prompt tokens restored from a cache timings.prompt_n, prompt_ms, prompt_per_second prompt tokens forwarded, and the time from the engine lock to the first token timings.predicted_n tokens the engine committed, the end token included (completion_tokens) timings.predicted_ms, predicted_per_second the first token to the last, and (predicted_n - 1) / predicted_ms timings.blocks decode forwards: each verify round is one block, and so is a plain step without a draft timings.tokens_per_block (completion_tokens - 1) / blocks timings.draft_n, draft_n_accepted drafted tokens the verify checked, and those it kept timings.reasoning_n committed tokens of the reasoning block timings.ttft_ms, queue_ms, total_ms arrival to the first token, arrival to the engine lock, arrival to the end metrics.speculative_decoding.mean_acceptance_length the same number as tokens_per_block metrics.speculative_decoding.draft_acceptance_rate draft_n_accepted / draft_n, to four decimals

A block commits the drafted tokens the verify kept plus one token the verify decides itself. tokens_per_block counts that token too, so 1.0 means no drafted token was kept, and a round that kept 4 drafted tokens counts 5. The first token comes from the prefill, which is why both speeds subtract 1. As an example, a response with completion_tokens 412, blocks 90, draft_n 1,350 and draft_n_accepted 322 has a mean accepted length of 411 / 90 = 4.57 and an acceptance rate of 322 / 1350 = 0.2385.

finish_reason is one of stop (end of text or a stop string), length (max_tokens), tool_calls, timeout (the request's wall-clock cap), or error. On error the partial text has already been sent and an error object sits beside the finish reason. A client that hung up is logged as abandoned, not as an error.

server/stream.py turns tokens into characters. A character can span tokens, because the tokenizer works on bytes, and a stream that sent every decoded prefix would send a replacement character (U+FFFD) that never goes away. Our detokenizer holds back a trailing partial character until the next token completes it. Every character it sends is final.

docs.title: A long prefill, and a client that leaves
docs.text:
A long prompt prefills for minutes: 208.3 s at 128k tokens on the published NVFP4 set (caches.md). After every prefill chunk the handler checks its socket. If the client has gone, the prefill stops there, the request ends abandoned, and the engine is free at once. Rows already prefilled stay in the resident prefix (caches.md), so a retry continues from there. A request whose client left while it waited in the queue is dropped before it runs.

A streamed prefill that has run for 5 s (--prefill-heartbeat-s) also sends an SSE comment after each chunk, at most once a second:

: prefill 12288/95131

Clients ignore comment lines. Proxies see a live stream and do not time it out.

docs.title: Admission and limits
docs.text:
With one sequence (QSE_PARALLEL=1; the shipped profile runs 8 lanes, parallel-requests.md) requests wait for it in a bounded queue.

limit served value what happens --max-queue 8 the next request gets a 503 with Retry-After: 5 --queue-timeout 240 s a request without a stream that waited that long gets a 429 with Retry-After: 10; a streamed chat request and a client's side request wait as long as --request-timeout (see "A turn behind a running turn") --request-timeout 3,600 s a generation that runs that long ends with finish_reason: "timeout" --max-len 262,144 tokens a prompt that does not fit gets a 400; max_tokens is clamped to what fits --default-max-tokens 32,768; 131,072 on Ornith used when the request sends no max_tokens; a request's own max_tokens wins QSE_MAX_BODY_MB 512 MiB a body that promises more is a 413 before its first byte is read; a chunked body hits the same line as it passes it (server/api/http_body.py) QSE_HANDLER_TIMEOUT_S 60 s a client that stalls inside the request body gets a 408 and the connection closes; a stall in the request line or the headers closes the connection with no answer; an answer the client stops reading ends there, logged as abandoned, and the connection closes; the clock restarts at every socket op that makes progress, as nginx's *_read_timeout

At load the server allocates the KV buffer for the whole context, so the context length is a memory decision taken before the first request (operations.md).

The answer limit is DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS. ops/serve.env sets 32,768, and a weight profile sets its own where the model's card names another number: Ornith's card names 131,072 new tokens, so its profile sets 131,072. /v1/models shows the running value as tandem.max_output. setup.md says how to change it.

The memory gate (OPS-47) runs before every prefill: back under the ceiling, then the prompt's workspace under the declared peak, shedding caches cheapest first (store, anchors, end, stash, park, pin, and since 0.3.26-test roles), or a 503 with Retry-After. The store gives back only what the gate needs plus 256 MiB, in chunks, plain entries oldest first and the snapshots at a prompt head's mark last (SPD-249): a chunk whose bytes stay in the allocator's cache (the reserve falls by less than half of them) ends the store's shed and the gate goes on to the next level, and the heads go after a chunk that lowered the reserve, when nothing else is left in the store, or when the chunks before them were under 256 MiB (too small to show what the reserve does), and only when what the store still holds can cover what the gate still needs (else they stay and the next level goes). On 2026-10-04 it refused every request, 12-token ones included, at "needs 82.0 GiB, peak 77.0 GiB", until :8000 was restarted at 16:41. The cause was the shadow reader's model pool: it had read 123,000 rows of a 195,694-token conversation, and every KV growth and every chunk's attention temporaries (larger with each chunk, as the context grows) took a new segment of its own MemPool. A live MemPool never gives its free segments back (torch 2.13, measured: 556 MiB stayed reserved after every tensor in it was freed; empty_cache returned it only once the pool was deleted), so 17.6 GiB of free memory sat in it and counted as the engine's reserve. Now:

  • After each idle-window burst, a shadow pool with more than QWEN38_SHADOW_POOL_SLACK_GIB (2) free parks its sessions on the disk and unloads the model, which drops the pool; the next turn loads it again and reads on from the disk.
  • roles is the gate's last level: the same release, then empty_cache.
  • Before a refusal the gate runs gc.collect() and empty_cache once more. A prompt whose workspace fits in the free reserve of the engine's own allocator (free memory inside a role's pool does not count) is admitted (stale_admit in the memory events): the allocator serves it from blocks it already holds.
  • Every refusal is an error line in the Dev tab's log, with allocated, reserved and how many refusals in a row.

The abandoned 195,694-token prefill was not the cause: the log shows the shadow's ten reading bursts after it, and the first refusal right after them.

Since 0.15.1 (2026-11-02, SRV-773) the gate charges a prefill the workspace of the rows it forwards, not of its whole context. Where the prompt resumes in place (the end anchor, the last prompt's end, the anchors) gives the rows, and the model's adapter prices them (CostModel.workspace_rows); a family without that model keeps the line through workspace_per_token, and a cold prompt is never charged under the line. On Flash-Next a resumed turn of 21 rows took 0.10 GiB at every context from 8k to 146k tokens, where the line charged 2.75 to 10.39 GiB: on 2026-11-02 slot 0's gate refused a 21-token follow-up at 62,886 tokens ten times. The [req] line shows fwd= (the rows forwarded) beside ws_rows= and ws_gib= (what the gate charged); QSE_REQ_PEAK=1 adds peak_gib=, the allocator's peak over a request that ran alone.

With --parallel N the gate runs for every slot, side slots too, on the live reserve, before the admission reserves the request's bytes (SRV-775). On a side slot it runs the peak stage only; the ceiling stage, which walks the allocator's pools, stays slot 0's. A prefill no reserve could ever take (the engine's load plus its workspace over the peak) gets its 503 at once. One the gate still refuses after shedding waits while another prefill runs, and runs alone over the peak when none does, counted: /health memory.over_peak_admits, over_peak_slot and over_peak_gib (the reserve over the peak now), a [memory] over_peak_admit log line. QSE_PEAK_STRICT=1 makes a lone request wait too. The admission checks a lone request against its floor as well (parallel.admission.lone_checked); it caps the cache growth and the workspaces in flight at the engine's room to its peak, and a request admitted over the peak counts its workspace past that room, in full less the allocator's free default-pool blocks it takes before any new memory (Budget.workspace_spare), so the floor bounds it. Its line then names the part that is new memory, for example "this request over the peak 1.6 new (2.3 of its 3.9 in the allocator's free blocks)".

flowchart LR
    due["prefill due:<br/>workspace estimated"] --> l1["state store"] --> l2["body anchors"] --> l3["end anchor"] --> l4["guest stash"] --> l5["parked session"] --> l6["pinned head"] --> l7["roles' pools"]
    l7 -- still over --> r503["503 + Retry-After"]
    l1 -. "fits under the peak" .-> run["the prefill runs"]

Cheapest first; each level only while the prompt's workspace does not fit.

The memory gate before every prefill. Each level is given back only while the prompt's workspace does not fit under the declared peak (77 GiB); a cache given back costs a later cold read, never a different token.

docs.title: The side lane (0.3.27-test)
docs.text:
A short request no longer waits for a long turn to end. On 2026-10-04 between 16:43 and 16:48 one opencode turn thought for minutes. A second session's first turn queued behind it and got a 429 after 256 s, twice. Before queueing, the router asked Qwen its two questions for that turn (the package and the library choice, TandemApp's tandemapp/conductor/classify.py): both waited in the same queue and gave up at their 8 s timeout, so the ledger shows them as abandoned after 9.0 s, client anon, model qwen38-spark-engine.

A request goes to the side lane (server/preempt.py) when it finds the engine busy and is short: at most --side-lane-prompt-max (2,048) prompt tokens and --side-lane-new-max (64) output tokens, one choice, no images, thinking off, and either a raw request (the router's questions are raw) or a client's side request (opencode's or Hermes' title). It becomes a job, and the generation that holds the engine serves it at its next safe point: between two decode blocks, or between two prefill chunks (--side-lane decode leaves the prefill out, off turns the lane off). The guest is prefilled from position 0 on the prefill's grid and decoded one token a forward, with no drafter. Its answer is plain greedy decoding of its prompt (or the client's sampling), so it follows the exactness promise (exactness.md).

The generation gets the engine back as it was. engine/cache.py Borrow copies what the guest can write: the KV rows below the guest's prompt plus its output plus 64, the recurrent state, the convolution tails, a walked chain state in its scratch buffer, and the references the next block reads (a pending commit is copied unsettled, so the next verify folds the same record into the same bytes). The drafter is never touched: the guest runs without one and with the drafter's tap off. A copy costs about 0.3 GB for a 2,000-token guest and is freed after it. tests/test_side_lane.py checks on the random model that the next block's logits, the state and every KV row are bit for bit an uninterrupted run's, after a guest between blocks, after a partial accept and between prefill chunks; tools/lane_check.py checks a long request on the real engine against runs without guests: its tokens are the runs' tokens up to the first fork, and a fork must be a near tie, each run taking the other's runner-up with a top-2 gap within --tie-nats (0.125), as exactness.md judges one.

Three guards. A job waits for a later safe point when the engine's reserved memory plus the guest's copy and workspace would pass the declared peak (a long prefill near its peak). A disk-tier write that has not copied the rows below the guest yet stops where it is (DiskTier.guard_rows); the head's chunks are copied seconds after a prefill, so during a decode nothing stops. A job no holder takes (the turn ended, or the lock is held outside a generation) is run by its own request thread under the lock, at the side rank, with the resident rows lent and given back the same way.

The ledger row of such a request has lane (decode, prefill or self); its queue_ms is the wait for the safe point. The [req] line adds lane=, wait_ms= and lent_ms= (how long the turn waited). Side-lane rows are not speed samples: a short plain decode beside a turn says nothing about the engine's decode rate. A client's side request too long for the lane (opencode's summary) is never refused for its wait: it waits as long as a request may run.

sequenceDiagram
    participant G as guests
    participant L as long turn
    participant S as second turn
    Note over L: prefill chunks
    G->>L: title request, served between two chunks
    Note over L: decode blocks
    G->>L: router question, served between two blocks
    S-->>S: arrives and waits in the queue
    Note over S: the stream opens after 10 s, a waiting line every 10 s
    L-->>S: the turn ends, the second turn runs

The scheduler. A long turn holds the engine. Short guests (a title request, the router's own question) are served at the turn's next safe point and the turn gets its state back bit for bit. A second full turn waits in the queue; its stream opens after 10 s and carries a comment every 10 s.

docs.title: A turn behind a running turn (2026-10-05)
docs.text:
The side lane serves short requests only. A second session's full turn still waits for the running turn to end, and until 0.3.31 it got a 429 after --queue-timeout (240 s), as on 2026-10-04 at 16:47: minutes of waiting, then a refusal, then the same again.

A streamed chat request is no longer refused for its wait. It waits as long as one request may run (--request-timeout, 3600 s on :8000). After 10 s in the queue its stream opens (status 200, the headers) and an SSE comment goes out every 10 s: : waiting, position 1, about 40 s, 30 s so far. A comment is not an event, so no client reads it as a token, and a client or proxy with an idle-read timeout keeps the connection. When the profile shows progress lines, the waiting line carries the estimate: "waiting: another request is running, position 1, about 40 s" (kind queue_eta, switched with queue; the voice says "about 40 s left"). A new line goes out when the reason or the position changes, and once a minute otherwise. A request that has waited less than 2 s gets no line (queue_wait.QUIET_S). When TandemLLM's own work holds the engine the line says so in plain words ("TandemLLM finishes its background work first", "TandemLLM decides how to handle the request first"); the live view keeps the technical holder.
