The 2B sometimes mixes the numbers of two profiles in an answer, so the page's own numbers stay the reference.

0.7.1 on a phone (2026-10-11 10:13): after an answer on the Model step, the 2B called explain("overview"), the name of the step. The server took it as valid, the page refused it, and the page asked again four times. Each round brought two more refused calls. The question about coding tasks got eight notices and the 4-round stop instead of an answer, and the sheet dropped to a peek once per call. Measured again on the box with 0.7.2 (tests/gpu/setup_wren_gpu.py cases, the 2B at the narrator's 4,096 rows): 15 of 15 right on ten requests for a change and five questions, the two of the report among them. No call was invalid, Wren said what it changed after every change, and a turn took 0.7 to 1.6 s. The question about coding tasks now gets exl3-2.5 at 124.17 tokens a second, in one round.

docs.title: The install job
docs.text:
POST /v1/setup/plan returns the review step's facts: what is wrong, what changes against ops/serve.env (each key whose effective value differs, old and new; a key the current run/setup.env sets and the new one drops is removed), the commands that will run and the estimate. POST /v1/setup/apply checks the selection again and starts a job; GET /v1/setup/jobs/{id} streams it (SSE): the log lines on disk, the job as it is now, then each event as it comes; Last-Event-ID resumes, ?format=json gives the job.

The job runs a fixed list of steps from server/setup/apply.py, and nothing a client sends becomes a command:

step what it runs check tandem doctor first (file modes, the run/ops copies, stale pid files, the marker; its report on the job as doctor, OPS-171), then the selection, the memory, the disk, the files the profile needs, the HF token (only a private repository needs one; every published profile is public), the box lock unload_assistant Wren is unloaded before the job starts fetch bash ops/use-profile.sh <profile> --fetch-only: the profile's weights and the files it needs beside them (the assets_required with a fetch list in the registry), and the models of the tools the selection turns on (QSE_FETCH_ASSETS: the shadow reader's, the narrator's, Laya's; each once); skipped when all of them are on disk preflight before anything stops (OPS-169): the scripts the switch runs are there and parse (bash -n; the Python ones compile), serve.env with the profile and the overlay the job will write sources under set -u as start.sh sources it, the weights are complete (the folder's files and the hub manifest's sizes), memory (MemAvailable now and what the running engine gives back cover the profile's need), the new port is free, no box lock and no hold, the engine's and chatd's interpreters run; a failure ends the job here, in plain words, and the running setup keeps running write_config first waiting until no request runs or waits on the engine (10 minutes at most, else nothing changes); then run/setup.env, every value quoted, the old one kept as run/setup.env.bak-<time>; with a port change, bash ops/stop.sh 120 first, and a failure after that stop goes through the rollback; with "generate", bash ops/make-secrets.sh --admin switch bash ops/use-profile.sh <profile> with QSE_NO_ROLLBACK=1: the drafts' corrector the profile names, when it is not on the box yet (flashnext-3.05; a failed download is a warning), then stop, start, smoke; a failure is this job's rollback, not the script's (which would start the old profile under the new overlay); in setup mode run/setup-pending goes first, a copy kept in the job's folder smoke /health names the profile and one chat answers (512 tokens at most, as use-profile.sh asks); then the tools with a model of their own, from /health roles and the decision models, polled up to 90 s: one that failed to load is a warning on the job (warnings, with its error), one waiting for memory a note (notes); the job still ends done rollback on a failed switch or smoke: with a port change the engine on the new port is stopped first, then the old run/setup.env comes back and the previous profile starts with its own served name in the smoke (in setup mode, the marker comes back unchanged, its HOST too, and setup mode starts again; a runner that crashes puts the marker back as well)

ops/serve.env is never edited. It reads run/setup.env after the weight profile, so the overlay never sets the weights. The overlay leaves out a key that serve.env leaves unset when its value is what the engine runs with anyway, so the engine's environment does not change for nothing: the disk tier's fingerprint counts every QWEN38_* variable that is set, and a new one sweeps that profile's saved heads and parked chats at the next start. A box whose serve.env predates the setup guide must get those last lines first; the plan says so.

The Chat (beta) switch (the conductor component, OPS-260) is off by default: the guide sets up the engine alone (QSE_MODE=engine, CONDUCTOR=raw, QSE_CONDUCTOR_CONFIG=off). On, it writes QSE_MODE=chat with the conductor's directory and turns on the small models it ships with (with_parent in model.yaml: Laya's decision models on every model, the 27B's shadow reader too); the narrator stays a choice, and each of them can be switched off again. Off again, TandemNode stops a running chatd once the engine comes up in engine mode. A box that runs the chat starts the guide with the switch on, so an install from the guide keeps its mode. On a box set up in the guide this switch decides the mode: run/setup.env is read after the installer's QSE_MODE, so install.sh --with-chat or --engine-only there only warns.

The job runs as a process of its own, because the switch replaces the server that started it. Its state is in run/setup-jobs/<id>/, and the status responder (ops/engine_status.py) answers GET /v1/setup/jobs/{id} (the same stream) and GET /v1/setup/status while the engine restarts: the page shows one restart card with the job's step and the load's phase, and the job's true end when the engine is back (OPS-175, VIS-209, VIS-211). Apply is refused while requests run (409 busy), while another job runs (409 job_running), when the selection does not fit (409 over_budget), and when the box lacks something (412 missing_assets, missing_token, disk_full, no_overlay_hook).

A failed step says what broke in plain words, from the runner's reason and the command's last lines: a script that lost its execute bit (tandem doctor repairs the mode at once and the step says so), a hold, too little memory, an engine that did not answer in time with its log's last line, a download that stopped (VIS-213). The failed and rolled-back screens list what tandem doctor repaired, offer Retry and Copy diagnostics. POST /v1/setup/jobs/{id}/retry starts a new job from the failed one's selection (retry_of): the check and tandem doctor run again and a finished download is not repeated, because the plan finds the weights. GET /v1/setup/jobs/{id}/diagnostics is the job as text for a bug report: the versions, the steps, tandem doctor's reports, the selection and the last 200 log lines, passed through the secret filter; where the browser does not let a page copy (plain http on a phone), the page shows it to select.

On a new box the fetch step downloads the 27B's K3 drafters, K4 draft head, BF16 drafters and base with the weights, and the plan's download_gb counts them (OPS-95). The NVFP4 profile's base is the FP8 checkpoint (30.4 GB). An EXL3 profile's is base-plain (OPS-133): the checkpoint's files fetched by range requests without the F8_E4M3 projections, their scales and lm_head.weight, which the EXL3 pack replaces, 3.54 GB; a box with the full checkpoint uses that. The review lists each download with its size (downloads), the tools' models too. Only a file nothing downloads fails the check with missing_assets, before anything changes; for a tool's model the error names the tool, and the fix is to turn it off in the Tools step.

docs.title: Removing a model
docs.text: The weights step lists the weights on the box (GET /v1/setup/weights): each profile's folder with its size, the running one marked, a folder two profiles share as one row; the drafters, the draft head and the base checkpoint, which the models share, are listed apart and never removed here (SRV-560, VIS-215). Remove asks first, with the GB it frees and the line that downloads the weights again, then POST /v1/setup/remove {profiles, confirm: true} deletes the folder. It refuses the running profile (switch first, or tick "Remove ... after the switch" in the review step: remove_after of the apply, done once the new setup answers), a folder a kept profile shares, and any folder that is not a real folder under the home folder or the Hugging Face cache, holds the installation, or holds what something else reads; in the Hugging Face cache the repository's whole folder goes, only when nothing else reads from it. Each removal appends a line to run/weights-removed.txt: the time, the profile, its repository at its revision, the folder, the GB and bash ops/use-profile.sh <profile> --fetch-only. A download that does not fit is refused before it starts, with the GB too few and the weights that could be removed.

docs.title: The answer limit
docs.text:
A request that sends no max_tokens may write up to DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS tokens. A request's own max_tokens always wins, clamped to what fits in the window. ops/serve.env sets 32,768. A weight profile sets its own value when the model's card names another limit, and the registry field default_max_tokens (Default answer length, in the Methods and advanced step) has the same number as its default. Today only Ornith does: its card evaluates with up to 131,072 new tokens, and an answer at effort xhigh can run past 32,768. Qwen3.8's cards name 131,072 for the final answer alone, with the reasoning counted apart in a 1M window; here reasoning and answer share max_tokens, so the Qwen profiles keep 32,768. ops/use-profile.sh and the Setup Guide both start Ornith at 131,072, and /v1/models shows the running value as tandem.max_output.

To change it, set Default answer length in the Methods and advanced step and install. The guide writes the value into run/setup.env, which ops/serve.env reads after the profile. From a shell, put DEFAULT_MAX_TOKENS=<tokens> in run/local.env and restart. A box that the guide set up for Ornith before 0.14.2 keeps the 32,768 it wrote then, until you change the field and install again.

docs.title: Reasoning effort
docs.text:
A fresh install thinks at effort medium when a request says nothing about thinking: REASONING_EFFORT=medium in ops/serve.env, for every model. Each level caps the thinking: low at 1,024 tokens, medium at 8,192, xhigh not at all, and none turns thinking off. A client's own effort word, budget or thinking switch wins (server.md has every shape). Under the conductor, the tools profile that tool clients get uses the server's level, and a profile that decides the effort by turn class (chat) sets its own level each turn.

To change it, set Thinking effort in the Methods and advanced step and install, or put REASONING_EFFORT=xhigh in run/local.env and restart. none (thinking off) is the shell's value only.

The published numbers name their effort. Speed rows run greedy with thinking off, since thinking changes what the model writes and so what a row measures. Quality rows against BF16 (KL, top-1, perplexity) read fixed text and have no effort. Each tool-eval-bench row names its effort and the server's default in its section (tool-eval-bench.md, flint.md). The 27B and Ornith tool-eval-bench runs used xhigh as the server's default, and the Flint runs the shipped medium. To match a row on a fresh install, set the effort the row names.

docs.title: Benchmarks and the overlay
docs.text: tools/exl3_fastrun.py --env-file ops/serve.env reads serve.env without run/setup.env (it sources it with QSE_SETUP_ENV pointing nowhere): a benchmark row is the file's knobs, not what the box was last set up with. Its report says setup_overlay: <path> (ignored) when an overlay was there. Pass a knob with --env KEY=VALUE to measure an overlay's value.

docs.title: Where the wizard starts
docs.text: A model the browser has no progress for starts from what the box runs now (GET /v1/setup/models/{id}/current): the active profile and every registry knob as ops/serve.env resolves it, run/setup.env included, so host, port, served name and every hand-tuned value are the box's own, and Review lists only what the user changed. A key serve.env leaves unset counts as what the engine then runs with, when that is one of the tool's two values: the lookup store's default folder from engine/settings.py (on), or the ${KEY:-default} of ops/start.sh (VISION on, RESPONSE_CACHE off, SESSION_SPILL on). A box whose serve.env predates these keys starts with the tools it runs. A value the registry has no option for (a HOST that is neither address) stays at the recommended one and is listed in unmatched. Review warns when HOST, PORT or SERVED_MODEL change, since every client notices. A box that still sets QSE_BACKENDS gets the plan error backends_moved instead of an install: the engine relays to no other backend since engine API 1.8 and would not start (operations.md). The models' "Other backends" tool went with it; TandemApp's Backends page has the feature, and a selection that names proxy gets the 400 unknown_component that says so. On an install.sh box the profiles and active-profile are read under serve.env's REPO, as ops/use-profile.sh reads them.

docs.title: Reset
docs.text:
GET /v1/setup/reset lists the levels with what each removes and how big it is; POST /v1/setup/reset {level, confirm, dry_run} removes one.

level what goes confirm restart 1 the page's progress and Wren's chat (the browser's own storage) the page's no 2 run/setup.env and its backups; the recommended profile starts true yes (a job, as apply) 3 the disk caches of every profile, the parked chats, the RAM caches, the lookup store (a running one is emptied by the engine, its folder stays), the shadow reader's disk delete caches no 4 the weights of every profile but the active one, and their HF cache copies; never what an engine on any port reads (its --nvfp4, --fp8-head, QWEN38_EXL3, QWEN38_DRAFT_*), nor ~/nvfp4-bf16 while ~/tandem-staircut is there; nothing at all while the active profile is unknown (409 active_unknown) delete weights no 5 the usage ledger file and its -wal, -shm and -journal files (not its folder), the conductor's settings and journal, the memory notes delete history yes

Levels 2 to 4 never touch the active profile's weights, the K3 drafters, the K4 draft head, the base checkpoint, the small models, the HF token, the secrets file the engine reads (QSE_SECRETS, else $QSE_STATE_DIR/secrets.env, else ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/secrets.env; an install's DIR/state/secrets.env) and its folder, the history (QSE_USAGE_LEDGER) or the conductor's data. Level 5 never touches the secrets file either. A cache the running engine holds is cleared by the engine's own function; the shadow reader's disk is kept while it runs. A symbolic link goes as a link and its target stays. Every reset is refused while requests run or a job runs, and every call writes one line to run/setup-audit.log.

docs.title: The routes
docs.text:
All of them are admin routes: open while no admin password is set, and the admin token, a dashboard session or a tool on the box itself once one is. Every POST must also be same-origin JSON: Content-Type: application/json (else 415 json_only), no Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site, and an Origin, when sent, that names the server's Host or X-Forwarded-Host (else 403 cross_site / cross_origin). A page on another site cannot run apply or reset through a visitor's browser, even on an open box or through a tunnel's loopback. The shapes are TandemApp's dashboard/src/api/types.ts, contract 1.0.

GET  /v1/setup/models                  a tile per model
GET  /v1/setup/models/{id}             model.yaml as JSON, with wizard_fields
GET  /v1/setup/models/{id}/steps       the step schema and Wren's tools
GET  /v1/setup/models/{id}/current     what the box runs now as a selection: the wizard's start
GET  /v1/setup/device                  memory, GPU, disk, profiles on disk, Wren's state
GET  /v1/setup/community               every model's community packs and where the list came from
POST /v1/setup/community/sync          fetch the list from GitHub now (the page opened, Refresh)
POST /v1/setup/estimate                {selection} -> the estimate
POST /v1/setup/plan                    {selection} -> the review step's plan
POST /v1/setup/apply                   {selection, dry_run?} -> 202 {job}
GET  /v1/setup/jobs/{id}               SSE of the job (?format=json: the job)
GET  /v1/setup/reset                   the reset levels
POST /v1/setup/reset                   {level, confirm, dry_run?}
GET  /v1/setup/assistant/status        Wren's state; a poll keeps it loaded
POST /v1/setup/assistant/load          load Wren
POST /v1/setup/assistant/unload        unload Wren
POST /v1/setup/assistant/chat          {messages, page, tools?} -> SSE (/v1/setup/chat is the same)

docs.title: The shadow reader
docs.text:
A small Qwen3.5 model keeps its own state of each session: its KV rows and its Gated-DeltaNet state for every token the session holds, the served prompt and Qwen's output. It reads each turn's new tokens and nothing else, so a small model can answer a question about a 100,000-token session in one forward of the question.

Code: engine/shadow.py (one session's state, the grid, forks, the disk), server/conductor/shadow.py (the service: feeding, scheduling, the cap, the questions), the wiring in server/app.py. Tests: tests/test_shadow.py. Measurements: tools/shadow_measure.py, tools/shadow_fresh.py, tools/shadow_ab.py.

docs.title: Why a shadow and not a bridge
docs.text:
Two cheaper ways to give a small model Qwen's context failed on 2026-10-04. Sixteen soft tokens made from Qwen3.8-27B's hidden rows (B2) answered at chance, 0.13 against 0.13. A per-layer map from the 27B's KV and GDN state into Qwen3.5-4B's (B3) reached a held-out R² of about 0.5, and its own oracle needs about 0.95 for 90 % agreement. The oracle also showed what does work: the small model's own state of the same tokens, which is exact.

The Qwen3.5 small models (0.8B, 2B, 4B) use the same BPE vocabulary and merges as Qwen3.8-27B. Qwen's token ids pass to the small model as they are, with no detokenising. The engine's own Qwen3.5 forward runs them (engine/generative/qwen35.py); the reader is a second engine object over the same weights.

docs.title: One session's state
docs.text:
part 0.8B 2B 4B KV a token (6 or 8 attention layers) 12 KiB 12 KiB 32 KiB recurrent and convolution state 19.5 MB 19.5 MB about 50 MB a 41,472-token session (measured) 0.60 GiB 0.60 GiB a 57,856-token session (measured) 0.88 GiB

The KV buffer grows in steps of 8,192 rows. A session also keeps up to six checkpoints of its recurrent state (19.5 MB each on the 0.8B), one at the end of each turn's prompt.

docs.title: Exact on a grid
docs.text:
The state advances only in whole chunks of 512 rows at absolute positions k × 512. A fresh prefill of the same ids on the same grid runs the same chunks on the same inputs, so the two states are equal bit for bit, however many turns it took. The ids past the last grid line (fewer than 512) wait as the pending tail. A question prefills the tail and its own tokens above the committed rows and puts the recurrent state back afterwards (a fork); nothing below the committed length changes.

Measured on the GPU (2026-10-04, 0.8B, two real conversations of 41,802 and 58,278 tokens): the replayed state equals a fresh prefill on the same grid in every KV row, the recurrent state and the convolution state. Against a fresh prefill on a 2,048-row grid it is not bit-equal (largest difference 0.44 in a K row, 0.018 in the recurrent state, the rounding of another chunking), and 8 of 8 question probes give the same top token, KL at most 4.1e-5.

When a new prompt differs from what was read (the chat template drops an earlier turn's reasoning once a new user message comes), the reader goes back to the newest checkpoint at or below the first differing token and reads from there. Without one it starts over. KV rows need no checkpoint: rows below the cut stay valid.

docs.title: When it reads
docs.text:
The bandwidth rule: while Qwen decodes, only Qwen and its drafters use the GPU. The reader has two windows.

  • The idle window. shadow_once in server/app.py looks every 0.2 s. When no request runs or waits and no hold or box lock is on, it takes the engine lock behind every waiter (rank 4, after the summary written ahead) and the box lock without waiting, and reads for at most 2 s. Before every chunk it checks whether a request waits, so a request that arrives waits at most one chunk: 36 to 50 ms on the 0.8B at grid 512.
  • Inside a turn, rationed. Between two of Qwen's rounds, on the request's thread, the reader may use 2 % of the time since Qwen's first token, in slices of at most 150 ms (whole chunks, the next one's cost estimated from the last). The device is synchronised first, so nothing of the small model runs beside Qwen. It reads the prompt first, then Qwen's output so far. The share counts from the first token on purpose: the first build counted it from the turn's start, so a 17 s prefill earned about 340 ms that the reader then spent inside a 9.6 s decode, and the decode lost 5.3 %.

The idle window alone is not enough for an agent. On the usage ledger's 41 opencode sessions (1,624 turns, 2026-10-02 to 10-04) the median gap between the end of one request and the start of the next is 0.31 s: opencode runs the tool and sends the next request at once. Replaying those timelines with the measured read rate (87 ms per 1,000 tokens), the idle window alone leaves the shadow fresh (less than one grid chunk behind) at 41 % of turn starts, p90 49,000 tokens behind. With 2 % of each turn's decode time on top it is fresh at 84 % of turn starts, p50 307 and p90 4,347 tokens behind. A session's first long prompt is the exception: 40,000 tokens take about 3.5 s to read.

docs.title: What it costs Qwen
docs.text: tools/shadow_ab.py in a hold (2026-10-04, a candidate server on :8011, the served engine flags, one 16,350-token prompt, 346 tokens out, a new session each run so the shadow reads the whole prompt each time, 1.5 s between requests, the arms alternating). Qwen's decode rate, median of 6 runs an arm: shadow off 36.02 tok/s, shadow on 35.28 tok/s, -2.05 %; paired run by run the deltas are -2.2, -2.0, -1.9, -1.8, -2.2 and +0.5 %. That is the 2 % share, as designed. TTFT did not move (17.46 s off, 17.40 s on): the idle bursts stop before the next chunk once a request waits. The gate was 3 %.

docs.title: Read rate
docs.text:
tools/shadow_measure.py, the served process's arithmetic flags, cold weights excluded, ms per grid chunk (median of 3):

model grid depth 0 depth 16k depth 41k 0.8B 256 22.9 24.4 30.1 0.8B 512 36.4 41.1 49.9 0.8B 1,024 63.1 74.5 94.0 0.8B 2,048 126.8 149.5 186.9 2B 512 50.5 56.1 69.1 (33k)

At grid 512 that is 71 to 97 ms per 1,000 tokens on the 0.8B and 99 to 135 ms on the 2B. A whole 58k conversation read in one go took 5.1 s. A larger grid reads faster per token but makes a waiting request wait longer; 512 is the default (QWEN38_SHADOW_GRID).

docs.title: Who asks
docs.text:
• ask(session, question, choices), also POST /v1/conductor/shadow/ask: a typed decision of the small model over the whole session. Each choice is a letter; one forward of the question gives the letters' softmax, as the router's in-context stage asks Qwen (TandemApp's tandemapp/conductor/incontext.py). At the end of a 41k session the router's 9-class question (290 tokens plus a 330-token pending tail) took 68 ms on the 0.8B and 96 ms on the 2B.
  • The router's class question, in shadow mode (shadow.router: shadow). For a turn whose prompt has at least router_min_tokens tokens (8,192 by default), the question the router's in-context stage asks Qwen goes to the shadow at the turn's insertion point (the prompt's last <|im_end|>). It is answered when the reader reaches that point and journaled in <conductor root>/shadow.jsonl beside the router's own class: the label, its probability, agreement, how far behind the shadow was when the turn began, and the lag. Nothing of the turn changes.
  • The narrator's thought summary (shadow.narrator: on with ui.narrator: thoughts). The narrator's job reads what the shadow misses up to the end of the thought, then asks for the summary on top of the whole session instead of the last 1,500 ids of the thought. It runs in the narrator's slices (at most 3 % of Qwen's time). The fork decodes eagerly: 12 to 17 ms a token on the 0.8B (the narrator's own path has a CUDA graph at about 9.5 ms).

docs.title: Memory and the disk
docs.text:
Resident states are capped at QWEN38_SHADOW_GB (4 GiB). Past the cap, the least recently used session goes to the NVMe (QWEN38_SHADOW_DISK, one safetensors file a session, 48 h, at most QWEN38_SHADOW_DISK_GB) and comes back exact when the session is fed again; without a disk it is dropped and read again from the start. A planned stop writes every resident session after the work in flight. A file records the weights' hash and the grid; another model or grid does not read it.

The model loads through the residency planner (role shadow: the model's claim plus QWEN38_SHADOW_GB): its first load in an idle window soon after the start, when some profile has shadow.mode: on and no other model is loading (0.3.34-test; before, the first turn of such a profile started it, waited behind it and landed it on full caches), and again with the next turn after a release. Its own pool, up to the claim the planner admitted, is left out of the engine's memory ceiling, as the narrator's (server/memlimits.role_exclude). A load that failed (its weights not on the box yet, a load error) is tried again in an idle window once SHADOW_RETRY_S (300 s) has passed, and /health roles.shadow.error says why it failed. When QWEN38_SHADOW_MODEL names the narrator's model, both share one slot and one copy of the weights.

docs.title: Switches
docs.text:
• serve.env: QWEN38_SHADOW_MODEL (empty: off, nothing imported), QWEN38_SHADOW_DIR, QWEN38_SHADOW_GB, QWEN38_SHADOW_GRID, QWEN38_SHADOW_DISK (auto: ~/.qwen38-spark-engine/cache/shadow), QWEN38_SHADOW_DISK_GB.
  • A profile's shadow block (absent: off): mode (off, on), narrator (off, on), router (off, shadow), router_min_tokens.
  • GET /v1/conductor/shadow/status: the slot, every session's read position, backlog, bytes and checkpoints, the router's agreement, the last answers.

docs.title: Live
docs.text: 0.3.25-test runs it for the coding profile since 2026-10-04 16:05: shadow: {mode: on, router: shadow, router_min_tokens: 8192, narrator: off}, Qwen3.5-0.8B sharing the narrator's slot. A 5-turn test session of opencode's shape (prompts of 12,676 to 21,491 tokens): the shadow followed every turn, went back to a prompt-end checkpoint 3 times when an answer came back re-rendered (1,176 ids read again), and ended 83 ids behind. The router's question, asked of the 0.8B on all 5 turns, agreed with the router 0 times: it picked debug 4 times and design_ui once at 0.15 to 0.50, where the router said chat or code_edit at 0.72 to 0.997. As a router the 0.8B is not usable with this question; the journal will show whether that holds on real sessions, and a 2B or 4B shadow, or a narrower question, is the next thing to try.

docs.title: The router question with the 2B and the 4B (2026-10-05)
docs.text:
tools/shadow_router_eval.py asked the router's question again, offline, at the places the live shadow asked it: 58 journaled turns of 6 opencode sessions (2026-10-04 16:30 to 22:00), rebuilt from each session's parked file. The live model is the control: its offline answers gave the journal's probabilities again within 0.02 on 46 of the 58 turns and the same label on 57. Two questions: live (the classes with their descriptions, as the shadow asks) and labels (the classes' short labels only).

model live question labels question read, ms per 1,000 tokens (offline, no graph) qwen3.5-0.8b 8 of 58 (5 of 46 exact, 1 of 9 fresh) 2 of 58 146 qwen3.5-2b 25 of 58 (18 of 46, 3 of 9) 8 of 58 175 qwen3.5-4b 19 of 58 (16 of 46, 2 of 9) 44 of 58 (34 of 46, 4 of 9) 447

"Fresh" are the 9 turns whose class Qwen decided on that turn; the others carry the session's class forward. The router said code_edit on 42 of the 58 turns, so a constant code_edit scores 42 of 58 and 4 of 9 fresh. The 4B with the short labels is at that baseline: it says code_edit 47 times. None of the three reads the class better than the constant does, so the shadow keeps the 0.8B (shared slot, 1.5 GiB of weights, the fastest read) and the question stays in shadow. A 2B shadow would share the voice's weights, but it buys nothing here. A useful next step is a question the small models can answer: two or three classes (code, chat, other), asked only where the router decides fresh.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• The read rate. The 0.8B reads only 1.3 times faster than the 2B, so its chunks are bound by kernel launches and small GEMMs, not by its weights. A graph per chunk shape or a fused GDN prefill for the small sizes would help.
  • The fork decode has no CUDA graph: the session's KV buffer moves when it grows, and a graph holds its address.
  • The first long prompt of a session is read in about 3.5 s per 40,000 tokens; until then a question about that session waits or is late.

docs.title: Drafters and tree verify
docs.text:
A verify of 16 tree rows costs about the same as a verify of 8. On the published NVFP4 set at 1k tokens of context, a tree verify with its commit takes 75.5 ms at 8 rows, 74.4 ms at 16, 83.1 ms at 24 and 87.8 ms at 32 (ops/stair-tables-nvfp4.json, median of 8). That flat stretch is the reason this engine speculates at all: the model's forward pass is bound by reading weights, and extra rows in the same pass are nearly free. TandemLLM therefore lets cheap drafters guess many tokens and checks them all at once.

This page covers the drafters, how StairCut decides what to spend each round, how the guesses become one tree, and how the tree is verified through recurrent layers.

docs.title: The round
docs.text:
Each round has four steps.

  1. Draft. The block drafter proposes a block of tokens, and the lookup drafter proposes continuations it has seen before. The router merges them into one draft tree of at most 32 nodes.
  2. Verify. One forward pass of the target model runs over the whole tree, and reads the model's own next token at every node.
  3. Accept. Walk down from the root. At each node take the model's token, and move to the child that carries it. Stop where no child carries it. The model's token at the stopping point is kept too, so a round yields at least one token.
  4. Commit. Keep the KV rows and the recurrent state of the accepted path, and drop the rest.

On the benchmark row a StairCut round takes 93.4 ms and commits 4.58 tokens (both means over the row; the row's 49.89 tok/s is the mean of the requests' own rates, measurement.md).

flowchart LR
    A[anchor token] --> B[block drafter lattice]
    A --> L[lookup drafter tree]
    B --> M[merge and prune to the node budget]
    L --> M
    M --> V[one verify pass over the tree]
    V --> W[walk the tree with the model's tokens]
    W --> C[commit the accepted path]
    C --> A
flowchart LR
    last["last committed<br/>token and state"] --> bd["block drafter<br/>15 slots × 16 candidates<br/>(about 25 ms)"]
    last --> ld["lookup drafter<br/>context, corpus, store<br/>(about 0.2 ms)"]
    bd --> sc["StairCut<br/>merge and cut"]
    ld --> sc
    sc -- "8 to 32 rows" --> v["verify<br/>one forward, 64 layers"]
    v -- "the model's token at every node" --> acc["accept<br/>longest agreeing path"]
    acc -- "path + 1 token" --> c["commit<br/>KV rows and state"]
    c -- "next round" --> last
    acc -.-> out(["tokens stream to the client"])

One speculative round. Both drafters propose; StairCut merges their proposals and cuts the tree to the node count with the most expected tokens per millisecond; one verify pass checks every node; the longest agreeing path and one token of the model's own are committed.

docs.title: The block drafter
docs.text:
engine/drafters/dflash2.py runs DFlash2, a small drafter that proposes a whole block of tokens at once. It has five decoder layers of its own (hidden size 5120) and reads five hidden states of the target (the residual stream entering layers 5, 19, 33, 47 and 61), fused into one input. It has no embedding and no head: it borrows the target's embedding and output head. Inside a block every row attends to every other row, which is what lets it guess 15 tokens in one pass instead of 15 chained steps.

The engine holds two fine-tunes of the released drafter, trained on the target's own output. One proposes 7 tokens a block (trained at block 8), the other 15 (trained at block 16). Both are on Hugging Face: 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-b8 and 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-b16. StairCut, the served behaviour, drafts with the block 16 one only. The served profile loads the block 8 one too and releases it at the first round; it drafts only with StairCut off. A draft moves about 6 GB (3.6 GB of drafter layers plus one read of the head for all rows), about 25 ms. The EXL3 profiles run the same two drafters with their projections in EXL3 at 3 bits a weight (the K3 files) and a draft head at 4 bits (K4), from 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-27B-EXL3-drafters; ops/use-profile.sh downloads them, and the BF16 drafters into train/, before it switches.

The drafter's head gives the top 16 candidates per slot, and a small bigram selector scores how each candidate follows the one before. That is a lattice of 7 or 15 slots by 16 candidates. The greedy path through it becomes the spine of the tree, and the next-best candidates become branches.

docs.title: The lookup drafter
docs.text:
engine/drafters/ngram.py copies text instead of predicting it. It looks for the longest match of the last few tokens in three places:

  • the request itself, prompt and output so far (orders 2 to 8);
  • a corpus of public text, memory-mapped with a suffix array: 38 million tokens on my box, 31 million on an install (below);
  • the persistent suffix store, a log of what this engine has read and written before (caches.md).

A verbatim quotation in opencode: the lookup drafter copies whole lines and the decode rate rises. Recorded against the served engine (published NVFP4 weights, StairCut on); sped-up parts are marked in the clip.

Every continuation found is a vote, and the votes form a tree whose node scores are path probabilities. A lookup costs about 0.2 ms, against about 25 ms for the block drafter. On fresh prose it rarely fires. On an edit of a file already in the context, or a quotation, it can commit 15 tokens in a round.

It fires only when the tree it would propose is worth its verify cost. A drafter that proposes on every step and is usually wrong costs the round, because the alternative on a declined step is the block drafter.

After two wide rounds in a row that commit their whole width, the lookup drafter may propose one deep chain of up to 32 rows (QWEN38_DEEP). On an editing workload that raised the accepted tokens per round from 12.6 to 15.75.

docs.title: The corpus of each tokenizer
docs.text:
A corpus holds token ids, so it serves only the tokenizer that wrote it. Its meta.json records the sha256 of that tokenizer's tokenizer.json. A read skips a store that records another one, with one log line naming both fingerprints, and the lookup reads the conversation only; a write to such a store is refused. Qwen3.8 and Flash-Next share one tokenizer; Ornith, Flint, LFM2.5 and the Nemotron models use others.

The corpus I serve with has 38 million tokens and is not published. install.sh builds a public one with the same recipe: one English and one German Wikipedia shard (CC BY-SA 4.0) and the Python sources of transformers, torch, triton and this repository, about 31 million tokens. It builds it for the 27B, at ~/TandemLLM/corpus.

One CORPUS folder holds one store a tokenizer (server/setup/corpus.py):

path what it holds CORPUS/ the store install.sh builds for the 27B, or a store built by hand CORPUS/tokenizers/<16 hex>/ the store of one tokenizer, named by the first 16 hex digits of its fingerprint

ops/use-profile.sh builds the profile's store once its weights are complete, when neither folder serves its tokenizer. The Setup Guide's install runs it, so a box that install.sh --setup set up drafts from a corpus too. install.sh --setup downloads the two Wikipedia shards, and the build reads them from the Hugging Face cache, so it needs no network. A shard that is missing there is fetched, and without the network the store is built from the local sources alone. The build runs on the CPU and takes a few minutes. It changes speed only: if it fails, the switch goes on and the lookup reads the conversation and the suffix store. QSE_CORPUS_BUILD=off skips it.

ops/start.sh then passes the engine the store of the served model's tokenizer: CORPUS when it records that tokenizer, else that tokenizer's folder. A CORPUS that records no tokenizer, as one built before the fingerprint existed, is read as every model's, with a warning, as before. No folder is built beside it.

The card rows of Ornith and Flint do not record which corpus they ran with. I have not yet measured decode with no corpus, the public corpus and the served one on the same prompts, greedy and at the card's sampling. That measurement goes here, with its build and date.

docs.title: StairCut: the node count, calculated each round
docs.text:
StairCut is the served behaviour. QWEN38_LEN_SWITCH=1 QWEN38_LEN_MODE=wide turns it on; the flags are off in the code, and ops/serve.env sets them. Every round drafts with the wide drafter and builds four candidates at up to 31 nodes: its lattice tree, its chain, the lookup tree and their merge. Each candidate is then cut to the node count that maximises its expected committed tokens per millisecond:

(1 + sum of q over the kept nodes) / (verify(rows) + draft + commit)

Schematic animations; the numbers in them are the paper's measurements on the published weights.

A node's q is its path probability from the drafter's lattice (read at temperature 1.4), or the lookup's vote share, scaled by the calibration the router already learns online, and capped at 1. Nodes are admitted in the order of the drafter's own score, each with the ancestors it needs, and the expected gain counts at most one token per kept node (min(sum q, n)). The price of a tree is verify(rows) + draft + commit; a chain pays the rollback instead of the commit, weighted by the chance that it is rejected. The verify price is a staircase, not a line, so the router tries every count instead of a search that assumes a smooth cost. A cut ends at 7, 15, 23 or 31 nodes (8, 16, 24 or 32 rows) or at the whole candidate, so other sizes occur when a candidate is smaller. The draft cost is the drafter's own measured time at the current context length, because the drafter reads the whole context; it is learned online, per context class. learn_block=True (off) also learns a multiplicative correction per block shape from measured round times; it was noise-driven on the box and is not used.

QWEN38_STAIR_TABLES names a JSON file of verify prices by context length, chain and tree apart (tools/verify_curve.py at a few lengths). At 32k a 24-row tree costs about 16 ms more than a 16-row one against 9 ms at 1k, and a tree costs 2 to 4 ms more than a chain of the same rows. QWEN38_STAIR_RHO names a prior for the lookup's continuation rate on 8-token matches (ops/lookup-rho.json, counted on held-out traces; its provenance is in the file), in place of the fixed decay of 1/1.6 a level, which lets a long verbatim copy keep its whole line. The rate is a Beta-binomial per (source, match length, copy-run bin), and the router updates it online against every committed block, halving the counts past 4,000 trials. QWEN38_STAIR_SKIP=1 decides whether to draft the head at all on the same prices, but only once a copy run has started: on a copy round the lookup line alone often wins, and at 32k a draft costs more than at 1k.

What the router learns online (the draft cost per context class, the calibration, the copy counts) belongs to the router object. The server keeps one router for its whole life, so what one request teaches reaches the next; router.reset() clears the per-text evidence (the arms' acceptance, the calibration) and keeps the costs and the copy counts. tools/forced_bench.py also keeps one router per configuration for a whole run, while tools/verify_spec.py builds a new one for every prompt.

The router releases the narrow drafter at the first round. With the node count calculated, the wide drafter's lattice cut to 16 nodes is a bush near the root on fresh text and a long line on copies, and the narrow drafter has nothing left to add. tools/router_replay.py replays these policies exactly on recorded lattices of both drafters, and tools/forced_bench.py measures them on the box on one reference text, so that different verify shapes, which move BF16 ties, compare on the same text.

On the benchmark row with the published NVFP4 set, StairCut reaches 49.89 tok/s against 47.13 for the fixed block 8 and 44.80 for the fixed block 16. On the teacher-forced bench of 25 workloads it averages 90.45 tok/s against 59.31 and 81.95 (measurement.md).

docs.title: Longer contexts
docs.text:
Every token of context adds 64 KB of KV rows that each round reads, and the drafter reads the whole context too, so a round costs more as the conversation grows. The verify itself shows it: a 16-row tree with its commit takes 74.4 ms at 1k tokens of context and 81.5 ms at 16k, and 88.1 ms at 32k (measured, the price table). The figure below puts the two measured decode rates the public record holds beside that curve and beside the bandwidth bound of plain decoding.

prompt length StairCut, measured plain decoding bound, arithmetic 256 tokens 49.89 tok/s 16.0 tok/s 16,350 tokens 36.02 tok/s 14.9 tok/s

The bound is 240 / (15.01 + 0.0000655 · context) tokens a second: 15.01 GB of weights and 64 KiB (65.5 KB) of KV a token of context, the 64 KB above, read at 240 GB/s every step.

docs.title: StairCut on Flash-Next, and the shared price files
docs.text:
Flash-Next drafts with its own MTP layer and the shared StairCut (engine/methods/staircut.py, ENG-245): each round the MTP head drafts a chain of 4 with its top-2 tokens a depth (engine/models/flashnext/mtp.py, one captured graph), and the cut keeps the chain's prefix (and, with siblings, second-choice leaves) that maximises (1 + sum of q) / (V(rows) + draft). q comes from ProbDeciles: the head's probability mapped to the measured acceptance per tenth of probability, starting from the probability itself and learned from every verified round. The drafter that drives it in the server loop is written once for any model's MTP head (engine/methods/mtp_drafter.py).

With QWEN38_FN_LOOKUP=1 (the Flash-Next profiles set it, ENG-229) the lookup joins the same round. It reads the request's own text, --corpus and the server's suffix store, the same stores as the 27B's lookup, because the tokenizer is the same. Its best continuation enters the cut as one more branch. While its tokens match the head's chain the two share nodes, and a shared node's q is 1 minus the chance that both are wrong. Where they differ, the lookup's chain hangs under the last shared node; where the head's chain ends, it runs on. The cut admits nodes best-first by q, as long as (1 + sum of q) / (V(rows) + draft) rises, up to 32 rows. A round still runs one verify, and the text does not change.

class (one greedy request of up to 512 tokens) MTP alone, tok/s with the lookup, tok/s tokens a block, alone and with the lookup edit 106 132 4.6 and 10.4 copy 102 133 4.4 and 11.9 prose 49 51 2.2 and 2.2 chat 62 64 2.5 and 2.5 code 85 83 3.4 and 3.5

That A/B ran on 3.05 on 2026-10-12, and every text equalled plain decode. The gain on copies is smaller than the gain in tokens a block, because a verify of 16 rows costs about 69 ms against 28 ms for 2 rows on this MoE.

docs.title: Coupled drafts and the corrector
docs.text:
A seeded sampled request drafts coupled (QWEN38_FN_MTP_COUPLED, on in the Flash-Next profiles, SPD-249). At each depth the MTP head proposes argmax(log q + G). Here q is the head's distribution under the request's own top-k and top-p, and G is the target's keyed noise for that output position, the same noise the target samples with. A draft lands on the target's token whenever the head and the target put the same token on top of that noise, and every emitted token is still the target's draw. A sampled request without a seed draws its own at admission where /health sampling.unseeded.keyed is true, as in the default setup (exactness.md), and drafts coupled as well. Greedy requests draft the argmax. The cut reads a calibration of the coupled drafts measured on 15 held-out prompts (QWEN38_FN_MTP_COUPLED_CAL, ops/prices/qwen3.8-flash-next/flashnext-3.05.dgx-spark.coupled.json).

On the 3.05 pack a learned corrector re-ranks the head's top 8 tokens before that pick, so more drafts land on the token the target samples (QWEN38_FN_MTP_CORRECTOR, engine/models/flashnext/corrector.py). Its file is 34.9 MB on Hugging Face, in 0xBakeer/TandemLLM-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-EXL3-3.05-corrector. ops/use-profile.sh flashnext-3.05 downloads it at the commit the profile pins to ops/correctors/qwen3.8-flash-next/flashnext-3.05.corrector.safetensors and checks its sha256. It covers requests sampled at T 1.0, top-k 20 and top-p 0.95; other requests keep the plain coupled pick. With no file, or one that fails the engine's check, the drafts stay plain coupled and the log says why in one line. GET /health shows the state under weights.corrector: loaded, why, the file's name and its sha256. In the A/B on 3.05, 4 pairs of fresh servers with fixed prompts and seeds, every token was the same with the corrector on and off.

V(rows) comes from PriceModel. Its prior is a price file, ops/prices/<model>/<profile>.<device>.json (Flash-Next 3.05 on the DGX Spark: ops/prices/qwen3.8-flash-next/flashnext-3.05.dgx-spark.json), in the format of the 27B's stair tables:

{"<context class>": {"<kind>": {"<rows>": ms, ...}, ...}, ..., "step_ms": 3.7, "measured": "how and when"}

kind is chain or tree; the context class is the model's. The 27B's tables key it by context length. Flash-Next's price_class is 0 while its sparse attention is still dense (up to 2,051 tokens), and above that the next of 4,096 × 2^k and 6,144 × 2^k at or above the context, up to 262,144. Its file also holds, per class, the plain step's cost (plain), a drafted round's cost a token (spec) and the draft head's cost a backlog row (prime). A class not in the file takes the nearest lower one, rows between two measured counts interpolate, rows past the last add step_ms a row (else the last two counts' slope). The model follows the live prices online (EMA 0.1 a count, the unmeasured counts shifted by the learned offset), and a price never falls with more rows. A profile without a file for its device logs the missing path once and starts every count at the same 1 ms, so the cut drafts to the full depth until the first rounds price it; the text does not change either way. The device is dgx-spark for the GB10, else the GPU's name in lower case (engine/methods/device.py).

The flashnext-3.05 profile keeps the cut on its price file (QWEN38_FN_DRAFT_FREEZE=1, SPD-249): the cut learns no prices, no turn ages and the usual answer length stays at its start, so a request drafts the same rounds whatever ran before it; the text does not change. Without a price file for the device the knob does nothing and the cut learns, with one log line; the other Flash-Next packs have no price file and learn.

The 3.05 file is provisional (ENG-155). In class 0, rows 2 to 16 are the prices the cut learned online on the ENG-229 A/B server (about 1k of context, 600 rounds): 27.8 ms for 2 rows, 38.6 for 5, 52.2 for 10, 68.8 for 16; row 1 is the bench of 2026-10-11. Classes 32,768, 131,072 and 262,144 come from single requests at 32,000, 140,000 and 260,800 tokens. No sweep has run; the cut follows the live prices either way.

docs.title: Never slower than the plain step
docs.text:
At long context a drafted round can cost more a token than the plain step. On the first runs at 260,800 tokens the drafter decoded 22.5 tok/s (the second request of a 3.05 run, its prompt from the caches) and plain decoding 36.6 (one request on a server without a drafter). StairCut on Flash-Next therefore keeps, per context class, the plain step's cost and a drafted round's cost a token, both by wall time and both starting from the price file:

  • skip: a class whose drafted rounds cost more a token than its plain steps takes the plain step, and drafts one probe round at an interval that doubles while drafting keeps losing (16 rounds, up to 256).
  • turn: a turn drafts only when what speculation saves over the expected answer pays for the draft head's backlog, the prompt rows it has not read yet (0.28 ms a row at 260,800 tokens). A turn that does not draft takes the plain step throughout and never reads the backlog.
  • What a class learned of its drafted rounds ages back to the file's prior while its turns take the plain step, so one slow request does not keep a class plain for good.
  • While the server is idle (one second after the last request), it captures the verify, commit and draft graphs the current context class lacks, 25 to 30 graphs in about 4.3 s a class. A drafted turn is charged for graphs its class still lacks. Before this, the first drafted request in a new class paid 3.4 to 5.1 s of captures inside its answer.
  • The idle window also captures the classes ahead of the current length (the next one, and each further one that starts within 6,144 tokens of it; from an empty state the 1,024 class, from 2,051 tokens, and the 2,048 class, from 4,096) and every class a turn found without its graphs, whatever length the state was left at. The warm-up captures class 0 only. Every request through the conductor starts in the 2,048 class (its plan's prompt is 4.1k to 4.8k tokens), so before this such turns took the plain step until an idle window found the state in that class (SRV-713).
  • The idle window captures nothing while the engine's reserve plus the smallest prefill's workspace is over its declared peak (--mem-peak-gib; SPD-273, 2026-11-02). Each captured graph keeps a private pool that no cache shed and no empty_cache returns, about 20 MB a graph: in 80 minutes of mixed load the idle windows took 635 of 1,390 captures, and one window moved the reserve from 76.1 to 80.0 GiB over a 75.8 GiB peak. The log says [graphs] idle captures paused once; a request's own class still captures at its first use.

Measured on 3.05 on 2026-10-12: one fresh server, two rounds at each length of one greedy request and the same request again (its prompt then from the caches), and plain decode from a --drafter none server. Each cell is the first request and its repeat:

context speculation, round 2, tok/s plain, tok/s 1k 56.6 and 57.3 41.0 and 45.4 32k 34.9 and 55.6 33.0 and 42.5 140k 42.1 and 52.4 33.9 and 41.4 260,800 41.0 and 41.0 (plain turns) 39.6 and 40.5

All 16 texts equalled plain decode. With the idle captures, the first request at a new length took the plain step and the next one drafted: 48.2 against 42.5 tok/s at 32k and 46.0 against 41.4 at 140k, every answer equal to plain decode.

docs.title: The length router (StairCut off)
docs.text:
Before StairCut, the served profile picked the block width once per request. With the StairCut flags off, engine/lenrouter.py still does, so a serve.env without them behaves as before.

Which block width wins depends on the text rather than the model. On a quotation the wide drafter commits 14.9 tokens a round against 8.0 for the narrow one. On fresh prose the narrow one does as well, 2.7 against 2.6, for less work.

It decides once per request. It runs four wide rounds first. A wide round prices both widths at once, because a narrow block is a prefix of a wide one, and the target's token at row i does not depend on rows after i. Where that says the narrow width still has room, it runs up to four narrow probes, because the narrow drafter is a different checkpoint and drafts its own 7 slots better than a cut-down wide block. Then it decides and keeps the decision for the rest of the request.

It decides once because switching costs acceptance. A drafter keeps its own cache of the context, and a switched-in drafter starts behind. A schedule that alternated the two widths as often as a per-round router, while knowing nothing, lost 3 % on chat, 10 % on code and 18 % on a quotation against never switching. Once the decision is made, the losing drafter is released (DROP_IDLE=1) and stops syncing, which added a median 3.2 % on a five-workload bench.

docs.title: Building the tree
docs.text:
engine/router.py merges the block drafter's lattice and the lookup tree into one DraftTree (engine/tree.py), where a shared prefix becomes a shared node. With StairCut on, the merge is built at up to 31 nodes and the staircase cut above sets its size. With StairCut off, the router prunes it to a node budget: a node stays only while its expected gain in accepted tokens pays for its share of the verify cost, priced on a verify curve (QWEN38_TREE_MS, or a price table from ops/prices.json). That budget is 16 nodes for either drafter, and the wide drafter gets 24 once the request has committed 32 tokens, so a short answer never pays for branches it cannot use. A deep chain may use up to 32 rows. These budgets are also the configuration of the fixed-width baselines the paper measures StairCut against.

The router's cost estimates are learned in the loop. It scores the lookup tree against the tokens the target actually wrote on every round, chosen or not, so its calibration settles before the lookup drafter has had a turn.

docs.title: Tree verify through recurrent layers
docs.text:
Verifying a tree through attention layers is known work: give each node an attention mask of its ancestors and a position equal to its depth. The 48 Gated DeltaNet layers are harder. Their state after node t is the state after t's parent, updated by t, and a plain left-to-right walk overwrites the parent's state before t's sibling needs it.

engine/tree.py stores a tree in depth-first pre-order: every node's parent has a lower index, and every subtree is a contiguous range. In that order the ancestor relation is part of the strict lower triangle, and every prefix operation of a chain verify has an exact tree counterpart:

chain tree causal mask the committed prefix plus the node's ancestors position = index position = depth, so two siblings share a position the convolution slides over neighbours it gathers each node's 3 nearest ancestors cumulative gate along the sequence the sum of gates along the node's path the delta rule's lower-triangular solve the same solve on the ancestor relation accept a prefix, roll back to a length accept a path, commit it by a gather

The state after any accepted path can be written from quantities the verify already computed. Let S0 be the state before the round, and for each node on the path let k be its key, u its pseudo-value and gc its cumulative gate. Then

S_path = exp(gc_last) * S0 + sum over t on the path of exp(gc_last - gc_t) * k_t (x) u_t

u_t depends only on t's own path, because the inverse of an ancestor-masked matrix is ancestor-masked too. This formula holds for every root-to-node path, not only for prefixes. The commit is therefore one read of the state and one small matrix product per layer, and it reads no weights. For a chain the same identity is the rollback: keeping the first n tokens of a block is the path of length n.

The KV side is simpler. The cache holds every node at its depth-first slot, and a commit gathers the accepted rows down into place.

node:   0      1      2      3 ...  7      (depth-first pre-order)
token:  -      cat    sat    ...
the model's own token at node 0 is "cat" (node 1 carries it),
at node 1 "sat" (node 2 carries it), at node 2 "on" (no child carries it)
-> the round commits "cat sat" and the model's "on"

A draft tree of 8 nodes in depth-first pre-order. The model's own token at node 0 is “cat”, which node 1 carries; at node 1 it is “sat”, which node 2 carries; at node 2 it is “on”, which no child carries. The round commits “cat sat” and the model's “on”. Right: the ancestor mask the verify applies in the attention layers, and the relation the recurrent layers walk.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
Greedy requests (temperature 0) take the path above. A sampled request stays exact in distribution: the target draws its own token at each node, and a drafted token survives exactly while the draw lands on it. For a drafter that proposes one fixed token this is the standard rejection sampler, with no second draw. With --sampled-tree det a sampled request keeps the tree. When it was adopted (rc5, before StairCut), a five-workload bench at temperature 0.7 went from about 4.1 to about 5.3 tokens a round (19 to 21 % more tok/s).

A request with a seed draws with noise keyed by position (the Gumbel-max trick), so the same seed gives the same text whatever the drafters and the router did. exactness.md covers both.

docs.title: Reasoning
docs.text:
The model thinks inside <think> tags. A reasoning budget (--think-budget, max_reasoning_tokens or reasoning_effort) closes the block when it is spent. The server appends the vendor's closing sentence and </think>, runs those tokens through the engine at their real positions, and the model answers from there. This changes the answer, and the sentence is visible in the response.

Closing a block that loops is the conductor's job (server.md): its reasoning-loop task watches the block with three arms (a pattern repeated over 128 tokens or more, the share of the last 256 tokens' 16-grams already seen earlier in the block, and novelty collapse) and, with --conductor on, closes it with a hidden phrase, of which the client sees only </think>. With --conductor raw, the default, nothing closes a block but a budget.

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text: knob what --drafter lenrouter, --dflash2-ckpt, --dflash2-ckpt16 the block drafters (both loaded; StairCut drafts with the block 16 one) --len-fixed 8\|16, --len-latch with StairCut off: pin one width, or decide once per request --drop-idle release the drafter that is not drafting --tree, --budget, QWEN38_TREE_NODES, QWEN38_TREE_NODES_NARROW, QWEN38_TREE_WIDE_AFTER the tree and its node budgets QWEN38_TREE_MS, --price-table the verify price curve the node budget is pruned on (StairCut off) --corpus, --suffix-store the lookup drafter's corpus and persistent store QWEN38_DEEP, QWEN38_DEEP_AFTER the deep chain after long accepted paths QWEN38_LEN_SWITCH=1, QWEN38_LEN_MODE=wide StairCut: the node count calculated each round, wide drafter only (off in the code, on in ops/serve.env) QWEN38_STAIR_TABLES, QWEN38_STAIR_RHO, QWEN38_STAIR_SKIP verify prices by context length, the lookup's continuation rates, and the head-skip rule on the same prices, for that mode QWEN38_LATCH_PRICE=1 the per-request decision priced on the verify curve (off by default) --sampled-tree det\|mixed, QWEN38_DRAFT_TEMP sampled requests on the tree, and the drafter's temperature --think-budget, --reasoning-effort, --think-stall the reasoning controls (--think-stall lets the conductor's loop arms run)

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text: This page is for security researchers and for reviewers of a change. It says where untrusted input enters TandemLLM and which parts matter most. SECURITY.md says how to report.

docs.title: What runs and where input enters
docs.text:
The engine runs on one machine on a home or office LAN. This page covers what the engine's repository serves:

part what it does code engine server, port 8000 OpenAI-compatible API on the standard library's ThreadingHTTPServer, plus the engine's dashboard reads, the engine-only screens and the setup API; in chat mode also the routes of its extension server/, engine/ status responder, QSE_STATUS_PORT what the reverse proxy shows while the engine is stopped, starting or held ops/engine_status.py

TandemApp (the dashboard, the controller, chatd and its chat sandbox, TandemNode) is a separate project with its own threat model: TandemApp's threat-model.md.

The supported deployment, from server.md and server/api/auth.py (AU1): the server listens on the LAN, sometimes behind nginx or a tunnel. The admin password (QSE_ADMIN_TOKEN, at least 32 characters) is optional and off by default. With no password, every route answers anyone who reaches the port. With one, the admin routes need the bearer token or the qse_dash session cookie. One exemption, trusted-local, lets a request in without a token: its TCP peer is loopback and it carries neither X-Forwarded-For nor X-Real-IP. The chat API (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/models) is open in both modes.

In chat mode the engine imports the module QSE_EXT names into its own process (server.md). That module runs with the engine's rights, so whoever can write serve.env, the install's local.env or the venv runs code in the engine; treat those files as the engine's code.

One more listener exists only when one model is split across two engine processes (architecture.md): the stage link, one TCP connection between the two stage processes of one engine (engine/methods/link.py). Its handshake is a challenge keyed with a shared secret of at least 32 characters, which the server reads from a file of mode 0600 (--link-key-file, server/stage.py; serve.env names only the file's path, TANDEM_LINK_KEY) and never writes it to a log or an answer, and the identity frames that follow carry a MAC under the same key. Data frames are neither signed nor encrypted. A frame is capped at 64 KiB until the peer has proved the key and at 256 MiB after it, and its length is checked before any payload is allocated. The listener binds one explicit IP literal and refuses a wildcard address. Run the link only on a direct cable or a network segment you trust, and treat the key as a secret: anyone who can change bytes on that path can change the model's answers.

Treat each of these as attacker-controlled:

  • every HTTP request that reaches port 8000 or the status responder: method, path, headers, body, chunked framing;
  • chat messages and their images (decoded with Pillow in server/images.py), and image URLs the server fetches for a client;
  • the model's output: the tool calls it writes are parsed and typed by the engine (server/api/toolcall.py), and a client may run them;
  • every byte that reaches the stage link's port before the handshake has passed;
  • weight files and their headers downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub: safetensors, EXL3 packs, GGUF; and the community index of weight packs (server/setup/community.py);
  • config files the setup API writes: the profile it switches to, and the overlay setup.env that ops/serve.env reads last.

docs.title: Parts that matter most
docs.text:
In this order:

  1. Auth in server/api/auth.py (TandemApp keeps its own copy): any way past the admin rule with a password set, a forged trusted-local, a forged X-Tandem-* header, a session cookie that outlives its token, a CSRF on /v1/setup/* (the same_origin_json check in server/setup_api.py).
  2. The fetch of an image URL for a client (server/images.py): a way to reach loopback, the LAN or the box through it.
  3. Parsers for untrusted files: GGUF headers (engine/models/nemotron_h/gguf.py), safetensors and EXL3 headers (engine/loader.py, engine/models/*/load.py), images (server/images.py). Integer overflow in sizes and offsets, allocations of many GB and out-of-range reads count.
  4. The setup API: it downloads, applies and removes weights and runs install steps. A crafted request or community pack that deletes files outside the weight folders, or runs a command, is in scope.

These matter less and stay in scope: the dashboard reads, the engine-only screens, the metrics route.

Out of scope: bench/, the scripts under tools/ (measurement, quantising, training; nothing serves them), docs/, the GPU kernels in engine/, and tests/.

docs.title: Where to test
docs.text:
Every CPU test is a standalone script: python tests/test_<name>.py, exit 0 is a pass. They need the Python packages of install.sh's lock, with a CPU build of torch, and no GPU or Docker. tests/gpu/ needs a DGX Spark.

area run it tests server, auth, admin rule python server/app.py --fake-engine --port 8000 --served-model qwen38-spark-engine --usage-ledger /tmp/l.sqlite3; set QSE_ADMIN_TOKEN to turn the rule on test_auth.py, test_fake_engine.py, test_server_model_card_auth.py setup API the fake engine above test_setup_api.py, test_setup_remove.py, test_setup_apply.py stage link no server needed; tools/linkrelay.py cuts and stalls a link test_link.py, test_stages.py, test_stage_server.py loaders and images no server needed test_nemotron_h_gguf.py, test_exl3_standalone.py, test_images.py

TandemApp's tests (chatd, the sandbox, the controller, the dashboard) are in its own repository, and its threat model names them.

docs.title: Not in scope
docs.text:
• Numerical differences in the GPU kernels and quantised weights, and the quality or safety of model output.
  • Third-party weights and their contents, beyond how our loaders parse them.
  • Rate limits and resource use of the chat API for a client the deployment lets in.
  • The installer's need for network and sudo on a fresh machine.

docs.title: tool-eval-bench results
docs.text: We ran tool-eval-bench against TandemLLM on one DGX Spark on 2026-10-19: the raw path at five thinking settings, the conductor in four profiles, and the bench's hard mode on both paths. Thinking adds 3 to 5 points. Packages double the time a tool client waits and add no points, so the tools profile, which tool clients get by default, adds none. benchmarks.md says how to run the bench and which settings change a score.

docs.text:
• Model: Qwen3.8-27B in the EXL3 6.0 pack, on the 0.12.0 code. /health still said 0.11.4+exl3-6.0, because the runs came before the version bump.

The raw rows send their effort and the turn-class rows set their own, so the tools rows are the ones that depend on the server's level.
  • Bench: 2.8.1.dev13, commit f2e368b, on another machine on the LAN.
  • Every run: --seed 42 --temperature 0 --timeout 600, --parallel 1, one run at a time on the box, each row one run (n = 1).
  • The server restarted before the batch, which empties the response cache. No answer in a row below came from the cache. The first raw xhigh run did replay 190 answers of the high run, which sends the same prompt, so the server restarted and that row ran again.

docs.title: How each row ran
docs.text:
The base command, then each row's flags:

tool-eval-bench run --base-url http://<host>:8000/v1 --model TandemLLM --backend tandemllm \
  --seed 42 --temperature 0 --timeout 600
row flags raw, off --header X-Tandem=raw --no-think raw, an effort --header X-Tandem=raw --backend-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort": "low"}' (medium, high, xhigh) conductor, tools none: an unnamed client that offers tools gets tools conductor, another profile --header X-Tandem-Profile=<profile> hard mode add --hardmode-only

low caps thinking at 1,024 tokens and medium at 8,192. high and xhigh send the template's xhigh effort sentence, and high caps thinking at 16,384 tokens.

chat is the profile Open WebUI gets. It classes each turn, sets the effort and adds packages and memory notes. bench-pk and bench-nopk are test profiles that do not ship. Each is tools with the turn class and the effort on and the conductor's prompt, and bench-pk adds packages. Run this on the box to create them; a write from another machine needs the admin token:

for p in on off; do
  name=bench-pk; [ $p = off ] && name=bench-nopk
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/conductor/profiles/tools \
    | jq --arg p $p '{note: "bench, packages \($p)", doc: (.doc
        | .decisions += {classify: "on", effort: "on", packages: $p}
        | .prompt = "conductor")}' \
    | curl -s -X PUT -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data @- \
        http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/conductor/profiles/$name
done

docs.title: What the rows show
docs.text:
Run-to-run noise is about 2 points. The raw high and xhigh rows send the same prompt and scored 95 and 97. The tools profile scored 96 on the same build the night before, and 95 here. Read rows within 2 points of each other as the same.

  • Thinking on scores 95 to 97 against 92 with thinking off. With thinking off the suite runs in 8.0 min against about 12 to 13.
  • Packages cost time. bench-pk and bench-nopk differ in packages alone: 94 against 96, inside the noise, and 26.0 min against 13.5. TC-03, TC-31 and TC-63 fail only in the two rows with packages. On TC-03 the model drafts the message instead of sending it (SRV-615).
  • On the full suite the conductor without packages scores the same as raw.
  • In hard mode the conductor scored 91 against 84 for raw. It passed TC-88, TC-91 and TC-97, where raw failed TC-88 and got partial on the other two. That is one run a side, and we have not tested which part of the conductor makes the difference.
  • TC-68, schema violation resistance, fails in every row: the scenario wants a value that the prompt leaves out, and the model declines to invent it. The graders of TC-23 and TC-49 read "doesn't provide historical data" and "no email will be sent" as failures (OPS-193).
